article_content: Jacqueline Fernandez arrived at a recent outing dressed in a blush Constructed in lace, the sari is worked through with pearl embellishment, extending from the scalloped border across the body of the fabric. The detailing is most concentrated along the edges, where pearls of varying sizes trace the hemline and pallu, creating a denser outline against the more lightly scattered field. Fernandez shifts the drape slightly, pulling the pallu across her back and letting it fall from one arm, which keeps the border in view for longer. The true showstopper of her ensemble is the blouse. A  departure from conventional codes, it is a silk bralette layered with a matching lace cropped cape. The cape is high-necked, with pearls applied with meticulous density at the scalloped hem and the neckline that almost mimics the effect of wearing a statement neckpiece. Lace and pearls have a lineage that stretches back to the Edwardian era, when gauzy lace-trimmed gowns defined the period's feminine ideal and pearls sets were among the most prized adornments a woman could wear. The pairing was revived and democratised in the early 20th century when Coco Chanel famously reimagined pearls as symbols of female independence rather than mere aristocratic status. That spirit has been revisited on international runways repeatedly. Dior has leaned into pearl accents across clothing and accessories, and then Simone Rocha and Vivienne Westwood played with subversive pearl styling. With Fernandez’s sari, Manish Malhotra has given this long-standing Western obsession an Indian occasion-wear translation. Fernandez keeps the accessories minimal, with diamond studs and a cocktail ring. A pearl hair detail is worked into her half-up hairstyle, while her makeup stays within a tonal range, with sheen concentrated on the eyes and skin to mirror the finish of the fabric.

article_title: The 400-year-old Khada Dupatta remains the soul of Hyderabadi bridal dressing
sub_title: From royal origins to contemporary brides, the Khada Dupatta endures—balancing heritage with personal expression
article_content: Every bride anticipates her wedding day—not just for the ceremony, but for what it allows her to become. It is a rare moment of expansiveness: to be seen, celebrated and, if only for a day, become the centre of it all. A wedding dress, then, is never just an outfit. It marks a transition, carrying meaning beyond fabric. In Hyderabad, that presence is often shaped by the Khada Dupatta, a signature The Khada Dupatta is a three-piece outfit, typically consisting of a kurta, a churidar and a six-yard dupatta. Its true essence, however, lies in the dupatta itself—the element that gives the ensemble its name, structure and cultural presence. Unlike more common styles of draping, it is worn in a distinctive manner that covers both shoulders and falls down the back. The term Worn across generations, the Khada Dupatta reflects a legacy spanning nearly 400 years, shaped by craft passed from one woman to another. Its history is often traced back to the Mughal era. Nur Jahan—widely regarded as a tastemaker of her time—is credited with influencing textiles and courtly dress, with As Mughal influence extended into the Deccan, this aesthetic evolved. When Nizam-ul-Mulk established his rule over Hyderabad, “Every generation reinterprets it—through textiles, embroidery, and styling—but the soul of the Khada Dupatta remains untouched,” notes Jayanti Reddy, founder and designer of her eponymous label. And perhaps that is why it has endured—not just as a garment, but as what Reddy describes as “a cultural heirloom,” carrying within it “grace, dignity, and opulence that transcends time.” Its longevity lies not in resistance, but in its ability to evolve without losing its core. That core is held in the way the garment is crafted. The Khada Dupatta is defined by its heavily worked borders—often executed in As Karan Torani, founder and designer of the label Torani, notes, Indian clothing has never needed to chase relevance in the way many other fashion systems do. “The Khada Dupatta, in particular, speaks of layering, dignity and power dressing,” he explains. “Its upright drape frames the body with a kind of architectural elegance, giving it both restraint and presence.” For him, a bride who chooses this silhouette is someone who wants her wedding look to tell a story, and understands that fashion can also serve as an archive. Today, this narrative continues to unfold in both traditional and contemporary contexts. Celebrities like Rekha have long drawn from Hyderabadi codes of dressing, while Nita Ambani, Sania Mirza, and more recently Sobhita Dhulipala have reaffirmed its place within modern bridal imagination. Ultimately, the Khada Dupatta carries its power in both feeling and memory. For a bride, it can make the day feel larger, while also tying her to something older than the ceremony itself. That continuity is part of what keeps it alive across generations.

article_title: Hues of summer: This legacy jewellery brand brings natural gemstones to the forefront
sub_title: Hues by Tanishq redefines authentic, design-led jewellery with contemporary silhouettes for the modern women
article_content: Jewellery is no longer limited to occasions, it has now taken on the role of expression—one that is brighter, bolder, and more fun. Enter: the Hues collection. As the auspicious festival of Akshaya Tritiya approaches, Tanishq, the brand from the House of Tata, taps into the contemporary appeal of natural gemstone jewellery with its latest offering. The Hues collection marks a welcome shift away from the restraint that has dominated bijoux trends in recent years, reimagining how modern women experience and embrace natural gemstones across both everyday and occasion wear. Anchored in a selection of 100 per cent natural gemstones, this collection signals Tanishq’s intent to shape a space defined by authenticity and design-led aesthetics. At the heart of each piece is a gemstone, with contour, structure, and silhouette crafted to enhance its natural vibrance and depth. “The range draws from the richness of Indian summer—its lush landscapes and vivid colours—and translates these into jewellery through sculptural silhouettes and fluid compositions. The result is a collection that is expressive, contemporary, and crafted with a strong point of view on modern Indian design,” adds Garima Maheshwari, Head of Design at Tanishq. Modern women are increasingly seeking jewellery that embodies elegance, individuality, and a sense of youthfulness. Crafted exclusively in 18 kt gold, Hues challenges traditional perceptions of jewellery, favouring experimentation over convention. The collection explores a diverse play of cuts—from classic marquise and intricate tabiz to smooth cabochon finishes. Cabochon stones add sculpted luminosity, while layered colour compositions, enhanced by techniques such as bunching and slicing, bring depth, texture, and movement. Bringing together a selection of natural gemstones—including emeralds, amethysts, citrines, tourmalines, and tanzanites—the collection reimagines preciousness through the transformative power of colour, form, and character. Actor Triptii Dimri fronts the campaign, celebrating the joyful spirit of Hues by portraying jewellery as a natural extension of a woman’s mood, individuality, and personal style. “At a time when jewellery is becoming a true expression of self, gemstones—with their vibrant colour and inherent character—feel instinctively right as an expansion of our repertoire. Triptii brings this spirit to life with effortless modernity—grounded, yet distinctly her own—much like the woman we design for,” says Pelki Tshering, Chief Marketing Officer, Titan Company Limited. Positioning Hues as a reflection of the evolving Indian woman, Dimri shares how the collection allows her to feel rooted and unapologetically herself. Excerpts of the interview below. The collection highlights self-expression through colour. Earlier, jewellery was often seen as traditional, worn only on special occasions. Hues by Tanishq redefines this notion—it makes jewellery modern, allowing it to be less about the occasion and more about expressing who you are in the moment, in a way that feels effortless and personal. I feel confident, bold, and completely myself. The collection is so versatile that I can express myself in any way I want. You can pick a piece depending on your mood. I keep it real and style it according to how I’m feeling—whether I want to dress up or just go out casually, there’s a piece for every moment. What makes the collection special is that it elevates your look effortlessly. I'm particularly drawn towards green. It’s my favourite colour, and it makes me feel grounded and calm. Jewellery is constantly evolving, and people are experimenting more than ever. They’re no longer playing it safe—they’re layering, mixing colours, and exploring new styles. That’s what makes this shift so exciting to witness. I think she would be confident, unpredictable, evolving, and fresh. My favourite is the Blooming Orchard. When I first saw it, I thought, this is just like me—the blend of colours is so beautiful, and it reminds me of the different 'hues' of an Indian summer. It’s versatile, delicate, full of life, and has such a fine, intricate design. I’d probably put it in a box and keep it all for myself!

article_title: 7 Gen Z creatives on building wardrobes with real personality
sub_title: For these multi-hyphenates, the 9-to-5 was never really an option
article_content: How do you define a generation? How do you account for lived experiences that spill far beyond temporal boundaries? Oscar Wilde said that to define is to limit, and if there’s one thing I do know about Gen Z, it’s that we don’t like limits. In fact, we actively despise them. Whether it’s dismantling gender binaries or making increasingly loud democratic demands, this is a generation that refuses to sit still. And when it comes to bringing home the dough, the cookie-cutter career path is on the brink of extinction. Gen Z creatives are more amoeba than ladder-climbers; they’re constantly metamorphosing, adapting to whatever the world throws their way. And naturally, they’re doing it in style.

The border is detailed with zari and returns along the pallu. Sambalpuri patta saris, woven across Odisha’s Sambalpur, Bargarh and Sonepur regions, are known for their intricate ikat technique, in which both warp and weft threads are tie-dyed before weaving to create their characteristic feathered effect. Often featuring motifs such as conch shells, wheels, florals and temple-inspired forms, they carry the visual language of Odisha’s textile heritage. In Dixit’s sari, those motifs appeared in bold pink against an electric blue ground, giving the weave a particularly vivid finish. Styled by Sukriti Grover, Dixit paired the sari with temple jewellery from PNG Jewellers, including a layered rani haar, matching jhumkas, stacked kadas and rings. The beauty look paired warm peach-coral eyeshadow with liner, fresh skin and a pink lip.

article_title: 14 brands that prove handloom textiles can go beyond saris and kurtis
sub_title: Looking cute and saving the planet is easy, actually
article_content: Long before ‘sustainable’ became a marketing buzzword, it was simply the way things were done. Handloom textiles with cotton and silk were woven with care, yard by yard, often with techniques passed down over generations. They made Today, as the industry circles back to mindful consumption, a new generation of designers is revisiting these textiles with fresh eyes. Handloom textiles, once confined to familiar silhouettes, are being reimagined into pieces that feel current and yet everlasting—easygoing separates, fluid dresses and sharp tailoring. Here are 14 brands creating with handloom textiles in ways that feel anything but expected. Shweta Gupta’s work starts with handloom cottons and silks developed alongside weavers in Chanderi, but it rarely stays predictable. Techniques like smocking, faggoting and pleat tucks show up often, adding texture in ways that feel considered. There’s a touch of whimsy in the way it all comes together, just enough to keep the clothes feeling light, a little unusual and easy to wear. Known for its focus on indigenous cotton and 100% natural dyes, 11.11 works almost entirely within a hand-process ecosystem. The label brings together techniques like hand spinning, handloom weaving, hand painting, miniature tie-dyeing and quilting, often within a single garment. Founded in 2014 by Gauri Verma and Karuna Laungani, Jodi works with natural Indian textiles, bringing in techniques like hand block printing, Founded by Rina Singh, Eka approaches handloom with a mix of research, craft and a sense of storytelling. The brand often works with repurposed and archival fabrics, keeping production small-scale. It leans soft and introspective with layered silhouettes, pastel tones and a slightly vintage mood that feels pulled from the pages of a well-loved novel. Payal Pratap works closely with weaving clusters across India, including Banaras, Bhagalpur, West Bengal and Bhagaiya, developing fabrics in small handwoven batches. The brand uses a mix of cottons, linens, silks, and wools, often finished with patchwork, smocking, and embroidery. Founded in 2013, Hannah Khiangte centres her practice around indigenous Zo textiles, working with weavers across Founded in 2018 by Manjushree Saikia, Ura Maku works with handloom textiles from Assam. Working with regional weavers, the label develops fabrics that reflect local techniques while adapting them into modern silhouettes. The aesthetic is clean and functional. Founded in 2019 by Shweta Agarwal, Āroka keeps things minimal, but not plain. The focus is on handwoven materials developed with a small cooperative in Kalna, West Bengal, with subtle weaves layering doing most of the talking. The aesthetic stays clean and pared-back, but there’s enough texture and detail to keep it from feeling too straightforward. Kritika Murarka builds collections that foreground surface technique and material. The brand often incorporates elements like hand embroidery, appliqué and textural detailing into otherwise clean silhouettes. It's contemporary with a decorative edge, structured separates and occasion-leaning pieces. Harago works with artisans across India, developing handwoven textiles in regions such as West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, and Assam, while also collaborating with craft communities like Bagru near Jaipur. Urvashi Kaur works extensively with handloom textiles sourced from weaving clusters across India, including jamdani from Bengal, leheriya from Jaipur, khadi and Bhujodi from Kutch, and Chanderi, Maheshwari, and Kota doriya. The brand builds its collections around these region-specific fabrics, treating each as a starting point for design. Since its launch in 2015, Naushad Ali has focused on working with artisans across India, building collections around heritage fabrics and traditional techniques. It keeps things relaxed with loose silhouettes and easy layering. Embroidery and playful accents show up often, adding character without taking away from the overall laid-back feel. Margn approaches handloom through a lens of minimalism and structure, often working with naturally dyed fabrics and traditional weaves. The silhouettes are clean and architectural, with an emphasis on cut, proportion and finish. Founded in 2014 by Sreejith Jeevan and based in Kochi, the brand’s approach is shaped by its setting, drawing from Kerala’s textile traditions as well as Kochi’s more eclectic, urban sensibility. Its aesthetic moves between what the designer describes as a “modern old” and a “nostalgic new”, blending familiar weaves with updated silhouettes.

article_content: Knee stability exercises probably aren’t top of mind when you hit the gym. But having stable knees is super important in a bunch of different scenarios, from running a marathon to “Everybody could probably benefit from some sort of strengthening to improve stability of the knees,” Carrie Whitelam, a physical therapist at Hospital for Special Surgery in New York City, tells us. First though, what even is Knee stability can encompass a lot of different things, but to boil it down, it’s “the ability to maintain alignment and positioning of your knee during movement and activity,” Whitelam says. There are passive structures in the body that help with knee stability, which include certain ligaments, Whitelam explains, such as the ACL and MCL. And there are active structures that help out too, which include muscles such as the quads, hamstrings and hips, she adds. During a squat, for example, you need all three players firing and coordinating with each other to complete the movement correctly and prevent your knee from collapsing inward. Having good knee stability isn’t just about squatting with perfect form. It also helps reduce our chances of knee pain and injury as we exercise, participate in sports and move about our day-to-day. That’s because when our knees are stable (which happens when the quads, hamstrings and hips are all strong enough to do their job), our bones, cartilage and other stabilising ligaments, like ACL or MCL, don’t have to take on From a big picture perspective, good knee stability helps protect the joint as we perform a whole host of movements, which over the long haul, plays into our ability to stay independent and keep doing the activities that we love as we age. One easy yet effective way to improve knee stability is to incorporate moves that target the main muscles that support knee stability: the quads, hamstrings and Specifically, moves that require the quads and the hammies to work together at the knee and also involve hip steering and maintaining alignment as the knee bends and straightens are great “starter exercises” for better knee stability, Solie says. These types of movements “have a great crossover for helping build knee stability during functional things throughout the day, whether it’s carrying groceries up the stairs or carrying a child,” he explains. Below are three exercises that Solie recommends for better knee stability: the step-up, forward lunge and lateral These are common moves in many resistance training programs, so you may already be doing them regularly—in which case, great! But if not, give them a whirl in a mini circuit-style workout: do the moves in the order listed below, performing each for 30 seconds and then rest 30 seconds before moving onto the next exercise. Repeat for three to four total rounds. Once you’ve mastered good form and the moves feel easy, add external load (in the form of dumbbells or kettlebells, for example) to up the ante, Solie says. When you start using weights, he suggests switching the programming to three sets of 15 to 20 reps of each exercise. Solie is a big fan of this exercise because it encourages you to proactively stabilise your knee. article_title: How to care for your skin during a heatwave, according to dermatologists
sub_title: From lightweight hydration to smart sun protection, this is what truly works to cool down angry skin
article_content: Returning to Chennai after more than a year away was a visceral shock to the system. I expected the familiar embrace of home; I didn’t expect the air to feel like a convection oven. Being one of India’s hottest cities, the humidity here can really cling on and within forty-eight hours, my skin felt like it was burning. We all know the "drink more water and We spoke to the experts to break down how to pivot your routine when the heat cranks up. It comes down to thermoregulation. When the air is hotter than your body, your skin relies almost entirely on evaporation to stay cool. "For every degree's rise in skin temperature, sebum production can increase by approximately 10%," explains Dr Kiran Sethi, skin and longevity doctor. This surge in oil, mixed with sweat and dead skin cells creates a ‘pore-clogging cocktail’ that leads to the dreaded trifecta: When your face feels like a slip-and-slide, the first instinct is to scrub. Don’t. Over-cleansing strips your lipid bilayer (a thin, protective layer of fats and oils that helps lock in moisture), leading to reactive seborrhea—where your skin overproduces even But the biggest mistake we make is clinging to our heavy It’s tempting to jump into an ice-cold shower, but Dr Sethi warns against it. Cold water can trap core heat. Lukewarm water promotes vasodilation, which allows your body to dump heat more efficiently. Extreme heat often drives us toward sugary "cooling" drinks. However, high-glycemic loads trigger IGF-1 (a hormone that can increase oil production and stimulate acne-related skin cell activity). Synthetic fibres like polyester trap sweat, inviting fungal infections. Stick to linen or cotton to allow your skin to breathe. Limit outdoor exposure during peak UV hours (11:00 AM to 4:00 PM) when the "Heat Index" most severely challenges your skin’s ability to repair itself. In the end, the secret to weathering a heatwave is as much about minimising the body's heat load and respecting the skin's natural acid mantle as it is about the products you use. article_title: 7 new designer stores we’re excited to shop at this season
sub_title: Across Mumbai, Delhi and Bengaluru, these new boutiques turn retail into a more tactile experience
article_content: Shopping online is efficient. It is also, at times, a bit spiritually flat. You click, zoom, add to cart, and hope the fabric behaves in real life the way it did under studio lighting and a persuasive caption. The appeal of good designer stores lies elsewhere. It is in the atmosphere, the materiality, the way a Dhruv Kapoor opened its first flagship in New Delhi in January, taking the brand’s distinctive visual language into an immersive physical setting. Located in Chattarpur, the store pairs raw marble with micro-concrete floors and mirror-finish walls, creating a space that feels sleek without turning cold. Lighting, scent and sound have all been carefully calibrated, which sounds faintly like the setup for a futuristic spa but, in this case, works to elevate the experience. Alongside seasonal collections, the flagship houses the tailoring, separates, accessories and lifestyle pieces that make up the brand’s wider vocabulary. Amit Aggarwal launched the first dedicated store for AM:IT in Dhan Mill, returning to the label that first introduced his design language in a more everyday form. The 750 sq. ft. space carries forward the brand’s fascination with material transformation, with installations that place Banarasi jacquard cards alongside e-waste and electronic circuitry. It is an apt setting for a pret line built around reworked textiles, modular separates and couture-level construction techniques translated into pieces designed for daily life. OTT by Tarun Tahiliani opened its first Mumbai store at Phoenix Palladium, bringing the label’s India Modern take on ready-to-wear to the city. The space is warm and pared back, with clean lines, gold accents and digital screens that place the focus on the clothes. Inside, you’ll find the brand’s mix of kaftans, capes, gilets and separates, along with signature details like chikankari and jewel-toned prints designed for wardrobes that move easily from day to dinner. Farah Khan Ali’s flagship in Fort turns jewellery retail into something more atmospheric. Set inside Chemco House, the boutique is layered with apricot-amber tones, sculptural displays and softly modulated lighting, creating a space that feels intimate. Angel chandeliers, dragonfly-wing lamps and a central display detailed with birds and florals bring a sense of theatre, while the jewellery remains firmly at the centre. The result is part salon and part gallery. Shanti Banaras opened a new store at Ambawatta One in Mehrauli, with a format that shifts the way Banarasi textiles are usually encountered. Designed almost like a maze, the space reveals itself gradually, slowing the eye and asking visitors to look at each piece more closely. Metallic lehengas, real zari weaves and hand-embroidered saris are displayed individually rather than in the familiar gadda-style format, making their structure and finish easier to take in. Even the chandeliers nod to the craft, drawing on loom punch cards and turning a coded part of the weaving process into design. 11.11 / eleven eleven’s Lodhi Colony flagship is located within one of Delhi’s most characterful neighbourhoods. The space brings its seed-to-stitch philosophy into physical form through bamboo-clad details, indigo passages and hand-finished surfaces that foreground material and process. The architecture folds the garments into a larger narrative, giving the brand’s hand-spun khadi, natural dyes and indigenous craft practices a setting that feels immersive instead of instructional. Off-White has officially entered India with its flagship in Bengaluru, bringing Virgil Abloh’s luxury-meets-streetwear language to a physical retail space here for the first time. The store introduces a curated selection of apparel, footwear, accessories and lifestyle pieces, all housed within an environment that reflects the brand’s stripped-back, industrial-leaning aesthetic. For a label whose appeal has long travelled through images, hype and cultural cachet, this opening gives Indian shoppers an in-person way into the world of Off-White.

article_title: Jacqueline Fernandez’s Manish Malhotra ensemble is a pearl lover’s dream
sub_title: A pearl hair detail, glossy skin and a half-up hairstyle keep the styling in step with the sari’s finish
article_content: Jacqueline Fernandez arrived at a recent outing dressed in a blush Constructed in lace, the sari is worked through with pearl embellishment, extending from the scalloped border across the body of the fabric. The detailing is most concentrated along the edges, where pearls of varying sizes trace the hemline and pallu, creating a denser outline against the more lightly scattered field. Fernandez shifts the drape slightly, pulling the pallu across her back and letting it fall from one arm, which keeps the border in view for longer. The true showstopper of her ensemble is the blouse. A  departure from conventional codes, it is a silk bralette layered with a matching lace cropped cape. The cape is high-necked, with pearls applied with meticulous density at the scalloped hem and the neckline that almost mimics the effect of wearing a statement neckpiece. Lace and pearls have a lineage that stretches back to the Edwardian era, when gauzy lace-trimmed gowns defined the period's feminine ideal and pearls sets were among the most prized adornments a woman could wear. The pairing was revived and democratised in the early 20th century when Coco Chanel famously reimagined pearls as symbols of female independence rather than mere aristocratic status. That spirit has been revisited on international runways repeatedly. Dior has leaned into pearl accents across clothing and accessories, and then Simone Rocha and Vivienne Westwood played with subversive pearl styling. With Fernandez’s sari, Manish Malhotra has given this long-standing Western obsession an Indian occasion-wear translation. Fernandez keeps the accessories minimal, with diamond studs and a cocktail ring. A pearl hair detail is worked into her half-up hairstyle, while her makeup stays within a tonal range, with sheen concentrated on the eyes and skin to mirror the finish of the fabric.

article_title: The 400-year-old Khada Dupatta remains the soul of Hyderabadi bridal dressing
sub_title: From royal origins to contemporary brides, the Khada Dupatta endures—balancing heritage with personal expression
article_content: Every bride anticipates her wedding day—not just for the ceremony, but for what it allows her to become. It is a rare moment of expansiveness: to be seen, celebrated and, if only for a day, become the centre of it all. A wedding dress, then, is never just an outfit. It marks a transition, carrying meaning beyond fabric. In Hyderabad, that presence is often shaped by the Khada Dupatta, a signature The Khada Dupatta is a three-piece outfit, typically consisting of a kurta, a churidar and a six-yard dupatta. Its true essence, however, lies in the dupatta itself—the element that gives the ensemble its name, structure and cultural presence. Unlike more common styles of draping, it is worn in a distinctive manner that covers both shoulders and falls down the back. The term Worn across generations, the Khada Dupatta reflects a legacy spanning nearly 400 years, shaped by craft passed from one woman to another. Its history is often traced back to the Mughal era. Nur Jahan—widely regarded as a tastemaker of her time—is credited with influencing textiles and courtly dress, with As Mughal influence extended into the Deccan, this aesthetic evolved. When Nizam-ul-Mulk established his rule over Hyderabad, “Every generation reinterprets it—through textiles, embroidery, and styling—but the soul of the Khada Dupatta remains untouched,” notes Jayanti Reddy, founder and designer of her eponymous label. And perhaps that is why it has endured—not just as a garment, but as what Reddy describes as “a cultural heirloom,” carrying within it “grace, dignity, and opulence that transcends time.” Its longevity lies not in resistance, but in its ability to evolve without losing its core. That core is held in the way the garment is crafted. The Khada Dupatta is defined by its heavily worked borders—often executed in As Karan Torani, founder and designer of the label Torani, notes, Indian clothing has never needed to chase relevance in the way many other fashion systems do. “The Khada Dupatta, in particular, speaks of layering, dignity and power dressing,” he explains. “Its upright drape frames the body with a kind of architectural elegance, giving it both restraint and presence.” For him, a bride who chooses this silhouette is someone who wants her wedding look to tell a story, and understands that fashion can also serve as an archive. Today, this narrative continues to unfold in both traditional and contemporary contexts. Celebrities like Rekha have long drawn from Hyderabadi codes of dressing, while Nita Ambani, Sania Mirza, and more recently Sobhita Dhulipala have reaffirmed its place within modern bridal imagination. Ultimately, the Khada Dupatta carries its power in both feeling and memory. For a bride, it can make the day feel larger, while also tying her to something older than the ceremony itself. That continuity is part of what keeps it alive across generations.

The sari carries delicate buta work across its canvas, along with an embroidered scalloped border. “But it is the pallu that I wanted to be the centre of focus,” says designer Masaba Gupta, adding, “I wanted the sari to feel light, yet look heavy enough to be worn for important and elaborate occasions. The pallu showcases our signature patchwork technique and is finished with gold embroidery in ‘sitara’ and ‘dabka’ kaam, featuring House of Masaba motifs.” The Gulposh is about bringing three crafts together in one sari without one overpowering the other. The sari is complemented with a blouse featuring a sweetheart neckline and noodle-thin straps. “The same gold embroidery and buta work from the pallu are translated onto it. The cut of the blouse is unmistakably modern and fresh, while the sari is crafted using traditional techniques. It is exactly this contrast that House of Masaba has built its creative language on,” elaborates Gupta. The border is detailed with zari and returns along the pallu. Sambalpuri patta saris, woven across Odisha’s Sambalpur, Bargarh and Sonepur regions, are known for their intricate ikat technique, in which both warp and weft threads are tie-dyed before weaving to create their characteristic feathered effect. article_title: The humble vest might be the most versatile piece in your wardrobe
sub_title: Here are 10 ways to style a vest
article_content: The humble vest may be one of the most versatile pieces in your wardrobe. It moves easily between masculine and feminine, formal and off-duty, Indian and global. It is often the thing you reach for when everything else feels too predictable. A good vest can fix proportion, add shape and make familiar outfits feel interesting again. Right now, Indian designers are doing especially compelling work with the silhouette, from handwoven fabrics and old embroideries to cuts that feel just unexpected enough. Have fun playing with prints, textiles. Play with a singular colour hue or complementary colours and focus on contrast through fabric, from sheer to heavy, matte to shine, flat to textured. The effect is rich, fashion-literate and far more interesting than a straightforward set. Pair a soft, voluminous blouse (think French countryside) with an embroidered vest, ideally something that feels like it came from an heirloom trunk, borrowed from a grandparent, perhaps. Balance the volume and softness with structured culottes or tailored shorts, adding a bit of edge. Change the mood with footwear: boots add edge, while flats keep it lighter. Wear the vest on its own as a top, nothing layered underneath. Pair it with a bubble skirt or anything with a bit of volume to keep the proportions interesting. Let the colour story travel across the outfit, from shoes to jewellery. It is playful, dressed up and ready for a long lunch that rolls into evening drinks. article_title: From Priyanka Chopra Jonas to Rihanna—see every Met Gala look from the last decade
sub_title: Revisit the Met Gala red carpet’s most iconic style moments—and the ensembles you may have missed too.
article_content: Over the past 15 years, the This year’s Met Gala will celebrate the Costume Institute’s new exhibition, titled “ While we’ll all have to wait to see how that plays out, we can satisfy our craving for elaborate dressing by looking at past Met Gala events. Consider it prime time to refresh your memory of all the past iconic looks to grace the carpet—and also, brush up on the moments and themes that you may have missed or forgotten. (Take Helen Lasichanh’s 2017 Comme des Garçons shapely look, the Olsen twins’ unexpected take on the 2013 punk theme, and many more.) Below, Last year’s Met Gala theme, “Superfine: Tailoring Black Style,” focused on The 2024 Met Gala theme, “Sleeping Beauties: Reawakening Fashion,” spotlighted one-of-a-kind fashions of the past. Approximately 250 items were drawn from the Costume Institute’s permanent collection—some very rarely seen in public before—and were displayed in entirely new ways, thanks to video animation, light projection, soundscaping, AI, CGI, and other forms of sensory stimulation. It was co-hosted by Zendaya, Jennifer Lopez, Chris Hemsworth, Bad Bunny, and Anna Wintour. The dress code was “ The 2023 Met Gala theme, “Karl Lagerfeld: A Line of Beauty,” served as a celebration of Karl Lagerfeld—highlighting the late designer’s one-of-a-kind contributions to fashion while helming major fashion houses such as Chanel, Fendi, Balmain, and more. It was co-hosted by Michaela Coel, Penélope Cruz, Roger Federer, The 2022 Met Gala theme, “In America: An Anthology of Fashion,” kicked off the Costume Institute’s exhibition of the same name: It centered on the tenets of American style, and highlighted the anonymous and unsung heroes of U.S. design. On the red carpet, stars served up their best takes on the The 2019 Met Gala celebrated the Costume Institute’s newest exhibition, “ The theme for the 2018 Met Gala connected the holy with the haute. The exhibit explored Catholic iconography in fashion, from papal vestments to more inspired takes from Gianni Versace, Coco Chanel, and more. Guests embraced this focus, choosing ensembles with nods to crosses, crowns, and, in Rihanna’s case, cardinal hats. Paying homage to Rei Kawakubo, the 2017 Met Gala exhibition examined more than 100 pieces of the designer’s work at Comme des Garçons, spanning the brand’s history from the 1980s onward. While few stars wore Comme on the carpet, save for Rihanna in a fall 2016 look, many did embrace Kawakubo’s avant-garde spirit. “Manus x Machina” explored the role of technology in fashion, from the 20th century to the present. The exhibit spotlighted more than 170 ensembles, and on the carpet, many guests went along with the futuristic theme. It was a particularly strong year for couple moments: Kim Kardashian West and Kanye West showed up in metallic silver Balmain looks, while Gigi Hadid and Zayn Malik did his-and-hers bionic eveningwear. The 2015 Met Gala theme examined the influence of Chinese art, film, and pop culture on Western fashion, doing so through a collection of traditional artworks and more than 130 haute couture and ready-to-wear looks. The stars who won the red carpet were those who embraced Chinese designers: Rihanna’s much-meme’d yellow Guo Pei design is still talked about today. If you love sweeping gowns, this is the year for you. The 2014 exhibition acknowledged the work of designer Charles James, one of the biggest names in mid-20th-century American fashion, and whose work inspired countless names after him, including the couturier Christian Dior. As for the carpet dress code, stars embraced couture designs that evoked the spirit of his work (read: feminine dresses like Dakota Johnson’s Jason Wu and Florence Welch’s Valentino Haute Couture), and the men dressed in white tie. One of the wildest Met Galas in history, the 2013 theme focused on punk subculture and its influence on fashion. There were loads of safety pins, fishnet, and spike heels on the carpet. Sarah Jessica Parker even wore a mohawk headpiece by Philip Treacy. The 2012 Met Gala exhibition examined the striking similarities between the works of Elsa Schiaparelli and Miuccia Prada, and the push-and-pull tensions between their two aesthetics. On the carpet, many chose Prada for their evening attire, like Carey Mulligan, Jessica Biel, Amber Valletta, Gwyneth Paltrow, and Eva Mendes. This year’s theme was an ode to the incomparable work of the late Lee Alexander McQueen. Naomi Campbell, Sarah Jessica Parker, and many more paid homage to the designer by wearing his frocks that were heavy on the fantasy. While Beyoncé did not wear McQueen, she did steal the show that year in an embroidered Emilio Pucci number. The 2010 Met Gala exhibit showcased evolving perceptions of the modern American woman from 1890 to 1940, and how those perceptions have affected the way American women are seen today. A certain timelessness was maintained though the red carpet, though more daring stars, such as Katy Perry, took risks by wearing an LED-light gown.

article_title: 7 new designer stores we’re excited to shop at this season
sub_title: Across Mumbai, Delhi and Bengaluru, these new boutiques turn retail into a more tactile experience
article_content: Shopping online is efficient. It is also, at times, a bit spiritually flat. You click, zoom, add to cart, and hope the fabric behaves in real life the way it did under studio lighting and a persuasive caption. The appeal of good designer stores lies elsewhere. It is in the atmosphere, the materiality, the way a Dhruv Kapoor opened its first flagship in New Delhi in January, taking the brand’s distinctive visual language into an immersive physical setting. Located in Chattarpur, the store pairs raw marble with micro-concrete floors and mirror-finish walls, creating a space that feels sleek without turning cold. Lighting, scent and sound have all been carefully calibrated, which sounds faintly like the setup for a futuristic spa but, in this case, works to elevate the experience. Alongside seasonal collections, the flagship houses the tailoring, separates, accessories and lifestyle pieces that make up the brand’s wider vocabulary. Amit Aggarwal launched the first dedicated store for AM:IT in Dhan Mill, returning to the label that first introduced his design language in a more everyday form. The 750 sq. ft. space carries forward the brand’s fascination with material transformation, with installations that place Banarasi jacquard cards alongside e-waste and electronic circuitry. It is an apt setting for a pret line built around reworked textiles, modular separates and couture-level construction techniques translated into pieces designed for daily life. OTT by Tarun Tahiliani opened its first Mumbai store at Phoenix Palladium, bringing the label’s India Modern take on ready-to-wear to the city. The space is warm and pared back, with clean lines, gold accents and digital screens that place the focus on the clothes. Inside, you’ll find the brand’s mix of kaftans, capes, gilets and separates, along with signature details like chikankari and jewel-toned prints designed for wardrobes that move easily from day to dinner. Farah Khan Ali’s flagship in Fort turns jewellery retail into something more atmospheric. Set inside Chemco House, the boutique is layered with apricot-amber tones, sculptural displays and softly modulated lighting, creating a space that feels intimate. Angel chandeliers, dragonfly-wing lamps and a central display detailed with birds and florals bring a sense of theatre, while the jewellery remains firmly at the centre. The result is part salon and part gallery. Shanti Banaras opened a new store at Ambawatta One in Mehrauli, with a format that shifts the way Banarasi textiles are usually encountered. Designed almost like a maze, the space reveals itself gradually, slowing the eye and asking visitors to look at each piece more closely. Metallic lehengas, real zari weaves and hand-embroidered saris are displayed individually rather than in the familiar gadda-style format, making their structure and finish easier to take in. Even the chandeliers nod to the craft, drawing on loom punch cards and turning a coded part of the weaving process into design. 11.11 / eleven eleven’s Lodhi Colony flagship is located within one of Delhi’s most characterful neighbourhoods. The space brings its seed-to-stitch philosophy into physical form through bamboo-clad details, indigo passages and hand-finished surfaces that foreground material and process. The architecture folds the garments into a larger narrative, giving the brand’s hand-spun khadi, natural dyes and indigenous craft practices a setting that feels immersive instead of instructional. Off-White has officially entered India with its flagship in Bengaluru, bringing Virgil Abloh’s luxury-meets-streetwear language to a physical retail space here for the first time. The store introduces a curated selection of apparel, footwear, accessories and lifestyle pieces, all housed within an environment that reflects the brand’s stripped-back, industrial-leaning aesthetic. For a label whose appeal has long travelled through images, hype and cultural cachet, this opening gives Indian shoppers an in-person way into the world of Off-White.

article_title: Hues of summer: This legacy jewellery brand brings natural gemstones to the forefront
sub_title: Hues by Tanishq redefines authentic, design-led jewellery with contemporary silhouettes for the modern women
article_content: Jewellery is no longer limited to occasions, it has now taken on the role of expression—one that is brighter, bolder, and more fun. Enter: the Hues collection. As the auspicious festival of Akshaya Tritiya approaches, Tanishq, the brand from the House of Tata, taps into the contemporary appeal of natural gemstone jewellery with its latest offering. The Hues collection marks a welcome shift away from the restraint that has dominated bijoux trends in recent years, reimagining how modern women experience and embrace natural gemstones across both everyday and occasion wear. Anchored in a selection of 100 per cent natural gemstones, this collection signals Tanishq’s intent to shape a space defined by authenticity and design-led aesthetics. At the heart of each piece is a gemstone, with contour, structure, and silhouette crafted to enhance its natural vibrance and depth. “The range draws from the richness of Indian summer—its lush landscapes and vivid colours—and translates these into jewellery through sculptural silhouettes and fluid compositions. The result is a collection that is expressive, contemporary, and crafted with a strong point of view on modern Indian design,” adds Garima Maheshwari, Head of Design at Tanishq. Modern women are increasingly seeking jewellery that embodies elegance, individuality, and a sense of youthfulness. Crafted exclusively in 18 kt gold, Hues challenges traditional perceptions of jewellery, favouring experimentation over convention. The collection explores a diverse play of cuts—from classic marquise and intricate tabiz to smooth cabochon finishes. Cabochon stones add sculpted luminosity, while layered colour compositions, enhanced by techniques such as bunching and slicing, bring depth, texture, and movement. Bringing together a selection of natural gemstones—including emeralds, amethysts, citrines, tourmalines, and tanzanites—the collection reimagines preciousness through the transformative power of colour, form, and character. Actor Triptii Dimri fronts the campaign, celebrating the joyful spirit of Hues by portraying jewellery as a natural extension of a woman’s mood, individuality, and personal style. “At a time when jewellery is becoming a true expression of self, gemstones—with their vibrant colour and inherent character—feel instinctively right as an expansion of our repertoire. Triptii brings this spirit to life with effortless modernity—grounded, yet distinctly her own—much like the woman we design for,” says Pelki Tshering, Chief Marketing Officer, Titan Company Limited. Positioning Hues as a reflection of the evolving Indian woman, Dimri shares how the collection allows her to feel rooted and unapologetically herself. Excerpts of the interview below. The collection highlights self-expression through colour. Earlier, jewellery was often seen as traditional, worn only on special occasions. Hues by Tanishq redefines this notion—it makes jewellery modern, allowing it to be less about the occasion and more about expressing who you are in the moment, in a way that feels effortless and personal. I feel confident, bold, and completely myself. The collection is so versatile that I can express myself in any way I want. You can pick a piece depending on your mood. I keep it real and style it according to how I’m feeling—whether I want to dress up or just go out casually, there’s a piece for every moment. What makes the collection special is that it elevates your look effortlessly. I'm particularly drawn towards green. It’s my favourite colour, and it makes me feel grounded and calm. Jewellery is constantly evolving, and people are experimenting more than ever. They’re no longer playing it safe—they’re layering, mixing colours, and exploring new styles. That’s what makes this shift so exciting to witness. I think she would be confident, unpredictable, evolving, and fresh. My favourite is the Blooming Orchard. When I first saw it, I thought, this is just like me—the blend of colours is so beautiful, and it reminds me of the different 'hues' of an Indian summer. It’s versatile, delicate, full of life, and has such a fine, intricate design. I’d probably put it in a box and keep it all for myself!

article_title: How to treat rosacea on brown skin, according to dermatologists
sub_title: The signs to watch for, triggers that can worsen it and treatments that can help
article_content: For something so common, rosacea still has a remarkably good disguise. It is usually pictured in one particular way: visible redness, light skintone, flushed cheeks, a face announcing its distress. It's far more confusing on melanin-rich skin. The tenderness, stinging and bumps are there. What may not be there, at least not in the way we imagine it, is obvious redness. That misunderstanding changes the way people treat it. Skin gets labelled “reactive” or “sensitive” in the abstract, treated like acne or exfoliated into submission. We loaded up on products meant to fix texture or unclog pores, while the real issue keeps simmering underneath. Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory condition, shaped by a mix of genetics, immune response and environmental triggers, with symptoms that can include flushing, papules, pustules, visible vessels and eye irritation. “Your genetics predetermine whether you have rosacea–that’s the number one reason you get it,” dermatologist Dr Emma Craythorne That split between predisposition and provocation is part of what makes rosacea so maddening. The condition may be wired in, but it is often activated and aggravated by the habits of everyday life: heat, ultraviolet radiation, spicy food, alcohol, stress, vigorous exercise and irritating skincare. “Rosacea in deeper skin tones is less likely to be immediately identified because the colour cues are subtler,” says dermatologist and cosmetic formulator Dr Kavitha Arya. “Patients often describe burning, warmth, tenderness or breakouts that never quite look or behave like ‘typical’ acne. There is faint redness, but discoloration can also be more purple-toned." People spend months treating the wrong issue. If the skin is hot, reactive and bumpy, the instinct is often to reach for stronger acne products, exfoliating acids or foaming cleansers that promise to reset things. In practice, that can leave inflamed skin even more irritated. Rosacea can overlap with acne, seborrhoeic dermatitis, contact dermatitis and, in some cases, autoimmune conditions that need to be ruled out. Which is why the best treatment plan usually starts not with a miracle product but with some notes and a professional read of what the skin is actually doing. Dermatologists diagnose rosacea by examining the skin and eyes, asking questions about symptoms and triggers and, where needed, testing to exclude other conditions. Craythorne That immune reactivity is also why so many people with rosacea say their skin hates everything. Inflamed skin has a much lower tolerance for friction, fragrance, strong surfactants and strong exfoliants. Craythorne also name-checks demodex mites, which live in the skin’s sebaceous glands, as an inflammatory problem for those with rosacea. Once rosacea on brown skin is identified, treatment tends to be less flashy than the average skincare routine. Gentle cleanser, a plain moisturiser and daily sunscreen alongside medication tailored to the person's needs. “Topical prescriptions such as azelaic acid, metronidazole and ivermectin are among the standard options,” says Arya. “Treatment has to account not only for inflammation but for the pigment aftermath,” says Arya. “One-size-fits-all rosacea routines often fall short. You are treating the flare-up, but you are also trying not to create another problem while you do it.” Laser therapy can reduce rosacea-related colour changes, including the violet or brown-toned changes seen in darker skin, though energy-based treatment in skin of colour requires thoughtful device selection done by the right hands because of the risk of pigmentary change. For people with brown skin, the problem is not only rosacea itself but the lag between having it and having it recognised. When the condition is still largely imagined in one shade range, everyone else is left translating their symptoms alone.

sub_title: From lightweight hydration to smart sun protection, this is what truly works to cool down angry skin
article_content: Returning to Chennai after more than a year away was a visceral shock to the system. I expected the familiar embrace of home; I didn’t expect the air to feel like a convection oven. Being one of India’s hottest cities, the humidity here can really cling on and within forty-eight hours, my skin felt like it was burning. We all know the "drink more water and We spoke to the experts to break down how to pivot your routine when the heat cranks up. It comes down to thermoregulation. When the air is hotter than your body, your skin relies almost entirely on evaporation to stay cool. "For every degree's rise in skin temperature, sebum production can increase by approximately 10%," explains Dr Kiran Sethi, skin and longevity doctor. This surge in oil, mixed with sweat and dead skin cells creates a ‘pore-clogging cocktail’ that leads to the dreaded trifecta: When your face feels like a slip-and-slide, the first instinct is to scrub. Don’t. Over-cleansing strips your lipid bilayer (a thin, protective layer of fats and oils that helps lock in moisture), leading to reactive seborrhea—where your skin overproduces even But the biggest mistake we make is clinging to our heavy It’s tempting to jump into an ice-cold shower, but Dr Sethi warns against it. Cold water can trap core heat. Lukewarm water promotes vasodilation, which allows your body to dump heat more efficiently. Extreme heat often drives us toward sugary "cooling" drinks. However, high-glycemic loads trigger IGF-1 (a hormone that can increase oil production and stimulate acne-related skin cell activity). Synthetic fibres like polyester trap sweat, inviting fungal infections. Stick to linen or cotton to allow your skin to breathe. Limit outdoor exposure during peak UV hours (11:00 AM to 4:00 PM) when the "Heat Index" most severely challenges your skin’s ability to repair itself. In the end, the secret to weathering a heatwave is as much about minimising the body's heat load and respecting the skin's natural acid mantle as it is about the products you use. Consider it prime time to refresh your memory of all the past iconic looks to grace the carpet—and also, brush up on the moments and themes that you may have missed or forgotten. (Take Helen Lasichanh’s 2017 Comme des Garçons shapely look, the Olsen twins’ unexpected take on the 2013 punk theme, and many more.) Below, Last year’s Met Gala theme, “Superfine: Tailoring Black Style,” focused on The 2024 Met Gala theme, “Sleeping Beauties: Reawakening Fashion,” spotlighted one-of-a-kind fashions of the past. Approximately 250 items were drawn from the Costume Institute’s permanent collection—some very rarely seen in public before—and were displayed in entirely new ways, thanks to video animation, light projection, soundscaping, AI, CGI, and other forms of sensory stimulation. It was co-hosted by Zendaya, Jennifer Lopez, Chris Hemsworth, Bad Bunny, and Anna Wintour. The dress code was “ The 2023 Met Gala theme, “Karl Lagerfeld: A Line of Beauty,” served as a celebration of Karl Lagerfeld—highlighting the late designer’s one-of-a-kind contributions to fashion while helming major fashion houses such as Chanel, Fendi, Balmain, and more. It was co-hosted by Michaela Coel, Penélope Cruz, Roger Federer, The 2022 Met Gala theme, “In America: An Anthology of Fashion,” kicked off the Costume Institute’s exhibition of the same name: It centered on the tenets of American style, and highlighted the anonymous and unsung heroes of U.S. design. On the red carpet, stars served up their best takes on the The 2019 Met Gala celebrated the Costume Institute’s newest exhibition, “ The theme for the 2018 Met Gala connected the holy with the haute. The exhibit explored Catholic iconography in fashion, from papal vestments to more inspired takes from Gianni Versace, Coco Chanel, and more. Guests embraced this focus, choosing ensembles with nods to crosses, crowns, and, in Rihanna’s case, cardinal hats. Paying homage to Rei Kawakubo, the 2017 Met Gala exhibition examined more than 100 pieces of the designer’s work at Comme des Garçons, spanning the brand’s history from the 1980s onward. While few stars wore Comme on the carpet, save for Rihanna in a fall 2016 look, many did embrace Kawakubo’s avant-garde spirit. “Manus x Machina” explored the role of technology in fashion, from the 20th century to the present. The exhibit spotlighted more than 170 ensembles, and on the carpet, many guests went along with the futuristic theme. It was a particularly strong year for couple moments: Kim Kardashian West and Kanye West showed up in metallic silver Balmain looks, while Gigi Hadid and Zayn Malik did his-and-hers bionic eveningwear. The 2015 Met Gala theme examined the influence of Chinese art, film, and pop culture on Western fashion, doing so through a collection of traditional artworks and more than 130 haute couture and ready-to-wear looks. The stars who won the red carpet were those who embraced Chinese designers: Rihanna’s much-meme’d yellow Guo Pei design is still talked about today. If you love sweeping gowns, this is the year for you. The 2014 exhibition acknowledged the work of designer Charles James, one of the biggest names in mid-20th-century American fashion, and whose work inspired countless names after him, including the couturier Christian Dior. As for the carpet dress code, stars embraced couture designs that evoked the spirit of his work (read: feminine dresses like Dakota Johnson’s Jason Wu and Florence Welch’s Valentino Haute Couture), and the men dressed in white tie. One of the wildest Met Galas in history, the 2013 theme focused on punk subculture and its influence on fashion. There were loads of safety pins, fishnet, and spike heels on the carpet. Sarah Jessica Parker even wore a mohawk headpiece by Philip Treacy. The 2012 Met Gala exhibition examined the striking similarities between the works of Elsa Schiaparelli and Miuccia Prada, and the push-and-pull tensions between their two aesthetics. On the carpet, many chose Prada for their evening attire, like Carey Mulligan, Jessica Biel, Amber Valletta, Gwyneth Paltrow, and Eva Mendes. This year’s theme was an ode to the incomparable work of the late Lee Alexander McQueen. Naomi Campbell, Sarah Jessica Parker, and many more paid homage to the designer by wearing his frocks that were heavy on the fantasy. While Beyoncé did not wear McQueen, she did steal the show that year in an embroidered Emilio Pucci number. The 2010 Met Gala exhibit showcased evolving perceptions of the modern American woman from 1890 to 1940, and how those perceptions have affected the way American women are seen today. A certain timelessness was maintained though the red carpet, though more daring stars, such as Katy Perry, took risks by wearing an LED-light gown.

article_title: The 400-year-old Khada Dupatta remains the soul of Hyderabadi bridal dressing
sub_title: From royal origins to contemporary brides, the Khada Dupatta endures—balancing heritage with personal expression
article_content: Every bride anticipates her wedding day—not just for the ceremony, but for what it allows her to become. It is a rare moment of expansiveness: to be seen, celebrated and, if only for a day, become the centre of it all. A wedding dress, then, is never just an outfit. It marks a transition, carrying meaning beyond fabric. In Hyderabad, that presence is often shaped by the Khada Dupatta, a signature The Khada Dupatta is a three-piece outfit, typically consisting of a kurta, a churidar and a six-yard dupatta. Its true essence, however, lies in the dupatta itself—the element that gives the ensemble its name, structure and cultural presence. Unlike more common styles of draping, it is worn in a distinctive manner that covers both shoulders and falls down the back. The term Worn across generations, the Khada Dupatta reflects a legacy spanning nearly 400 years, shaped by craft passed from one woman to another. Its history is often traced back to the Mughal era. Nur Jahan—widely regarded as a tastemaker of her time—is credited with influencing textiles and courtly dress, with As Mughal influence extended into the Deccan, this aesthetic evolved. When Nizam-ul-Mulk established his rule over Hyderabad, “Every generation reinterprets it—through textiles, embroidery, and styling—but the soul of the Khada Dupatta remains untouched,” notes Jayanti Reddy, founder and designer of her eponymous label. And perhaps that is why it has endured—not just as a garment, but as what Reddy describes as “a cultural heirloom,” carrying within it “grace, dignity, and opulence that transcends time.” Its longevity lies not in resistance, but in its ability to evolve without losing its core. That core is held in the way the garment is crafted. The Khada Dupatta is defined by its heavily worked borders—often executed in As Karan Torani, founder and designer of the label Torani, notes, Indian clothing has never needed to chase relevance in the way many other fashion systems do. “The Khada Dupatta, in particular, speaks of layering, dignity and power dressing,” he explains. “Its upright drape frames the body with a kind of architectural elegance, giving it both restraint and presence.” For him, a bride who chooses this silhouette is someone who wants her wedding look to tell a story, and understands that fashion can also serve as an archive. Today, this narrative continues to unfold in both traditional and contemporary contexts. Celebrities like Rekha have long drawn from Hyderabadi codes of dressing, while Nita Ambani, Sania Mirza, and more recently Sobhita Dhulipala have reaffirmed its place within modern bridal imagination. Ultimately, the Khada Dupatta carries its power in both feeling and memory. For a bride, it can make the day feel larger, while also tying her to something older than the ceremony itself. That continuity is part of what keeps it alive across generations.

Jewellery from Kalyan Jewellers complements the sari's festive aesthetic. Braid the hair and add a few tassels of red and silver to the tip,” says Manglien Gangte, Vogue India fashion associate.

article_title: 7 new designer stores we’re excited to shop at this season
sub_title: Across Mumbai, Delhi and Bengaluru, these new boutiques turn retail into a more tactile experience
article_content: Shopping online is efficient. It is also, at times, a bit spiritually flat. You click, zoom, add to cart, and hope the fabric behaves in real life the way it did under studio lighting and a persuasive caption. The appeal of good designer stores lies elsewhere. It is in the atmosphere, the materiality, the way a Dhruv Kapoor opened its first flagship in New Delhi in January, taking the brand’s distinctive visual language into an immersive physical setting. Located in Chattarpur, the store pairs raw marble with micro-concrete floors and mirror-finish walls, creating a space that feels sleek without turning cold. Lighting, scent and sound have all been carefully calibrated, which sounds faintly like the setup for a futuristic spa but, in this case, works to elevate the experience. Alongside seasonal collections, the flagship houses the tailoring, separates, accessories and lifestyle pieces that make up the brand’s wider vocabulary. Amit Aggarwal launched the first dedicated store for AM:IT in Dhan Mill, returning to the label that first introduced his design language in a more everyday form. The 750 sq. ft. space carries forward the brand’s fascination with material transformation, with installations that place Banarasi jacquard cards alongside e-waste and electronic circuitry. It is an apt setting for a pret line built around reworked textiles, modular separates and couture-level construction techniques translated into pieces designed for daily life. OTT by Tarun Tahiliani opened its first Mumbai store at Phoenix Palladium, bringing the label’s India Modern take on ready-to-wear to the city. The space is warm and pared back, with clean lines, gold accents and digital screens that place the focus on the clothes. Inside, you’ll find the brand’s mix of kaftans, capes, gilets and separates, along with signature details like chikankari and jewel-toned prints designed for wardrobes that move easily from day to dinner. Farah Khan Ali’s flagship in Fort turns jewellery retail into something more atmospheric. Set inside Chemco House, the boutique is layered with apricot-amber tones, sculptural displays and softly modulated lighting, creating a space that feels intimate. Angel chandeliers, dragonfly-wing lamps and a central display detailed with birds and florals bring a sense of theatre, while the jewellery remains firmly at the centre. The result is part salon and part gallery. Shanti Banaras opened a new store at Ambawatta One in Mehrauli, with a format that shifts the way Banarasi textiles are usually encountered. Designed almost like a maze, the space reveals itself gradually, slowing the eye and asking visitors to look at each piece more closely. Metallic lehengas, real zari weaves and hand-embroidered saris are displayed individually rather than in the familiar gadda-style format, making their structure and finish easier to take in. Even the chandeliers nod to the craft, drawing on loom punch cards and turning a coded part of the weaving process into design. 11.11 / eleven eleven’s Lodhi Colony flagship is located within one of Delhi’s most characterful neighbourhoods. The space brings its seed-to-stitch philosophy into physical form through bamboo-clad details, indigo passages and hand-finished surfaces that foreground material and process. The architecture folds the garments into a larger narrative, giving the brand’s hand-spun khadi, natural dyes and indigenous craft practices a setting that feels immersive instead of instructional. Off-White has officially entered India with its flagship in Bengaluru, bringing Virgil Abloh’s luxury-meets-streetwear language to a physical retail space here for the first time. The store introduces a curated selection of apparel, footwear, accessories and lifestyle pieces, all housed within an environment that reflects the brand’s stripped-back, industrial-leaning aesthetic. For a label whose appeal has long travelled through images, hype and cultural cachet, this opening gives Indian shoppers an in-person way into the world of Off-White.

article_title: Hues of summer: This legacy jewellery brand brings natural gemstones to the forefront
sub_title: Hues by Tanishq redefines authentic, design-led jewellery with contemporary silhouettes for the modern women
article_content: Jewellery is no longer limited to occasions, it has now taken on the role of expression—one that is brighter, bolder, and more fun. Enter: the Hues collection. As the auspicious festival of Akshaya Tritiya approaches, Tanishq, the brand from the House of Tata, taps into the contemporary appeal of natural gemstone jewellery with its latest offering. The Hues collection marks a welcome shift away from the restraint that has dominated bijoux trends in recent years, reimagining how modern women experience and embrace natural gemstones across both everyday and occasion wear. Anchored in a selection of 100 per cent natural gemstones, this collection signals Tanishq’s intent to shape a space defined by authenticity and design-led aesthetics. At the heart of each piece is a gemstone, with contour, structure, and silhouette crafted to enhance its natural vibrance and depth. “The range draws from the richness of Indian summer—its lush landscapes and vivid colours—and translates these into jewellery through sculptural silhouettes and fluid compositions. The result is a collection that is expressive, contemporary, and crafted with a strong point of view on modern Indian design,” adds Garima Maheshwari, Head of Design at Tanishq. Modern women are increasingly seeking jewellery that embodies elegance, individuality, and a sense of youthfulness. Crafted exclusively in 18 kt gold, Hues challenges traditional perceptions of jewellery, favouring experimentation over convention. The collection explores a diverse play of cuts—from classic marquise and intricate tabiz to smooth cabochon finishes. Cabochon stones add sculpted luminosity, while layered colour compositions, enhanced by techniques such as bunching and slicing, bring depth, texture, and movement. Bringing together a selection of natural gemstones—including emeralds, amethysts, citrines, tourmalines, and tanzanites—the collection reimagines preciousness through the transformative power of colour, form, and character. Actor Triptii Dimri fronts the campaign, celebrating the joyful spirit of Hues by portraying jewellery as a natural extension of a woman’s mood, individuality, and personal style. “At a time when jewellery is becoming a true expression of self, gemstones—with their vibrant colour and inherent character—feel instinctively right as an expansion of our repertoire. Triptii brings this spirit to life with effortless modernity—grounded, yet distinctly her own—much like the woman we design for,” says Pelki Tshering, Chief Marketing Officer, Titan Company Limited. Positioning Hues as a reflection of the evolving Indian woman, Dimri shares how the collection allows her to feel rooted and unapologetically herself. Excerpts of the interview below. The collection highlights self-expression through colour. Earlier, jewellery was often seen as traditional, worn only on special occasions. Hues by Tanishq redefines this notion—it makes jewellery modern, allowing it to be less about the occasion and more about expressing who you are in the moment, in a way that feels effortless and personal. I feel confident, bold, and completely myself. The collection is so versatile that I can express myself in any way I want. You can pick a piece depending on your mood. I keep it real and style it according to how I’m feeling—whether I want to dress up or just go out casually, there’s a piece for every moment. What makes the collection special is that it elevates your look effortlessly. I'm particularly drawn towards green. It’s my favourite colour, and it makes me feel grounded and calm. Jewellery is constantly evolving, and people are experimenting more than ever. They’re no longer playing it safe—they’re layering, mixing colours, and exploring new styles. That’s what makes this shift so exciting to witness. I think she would be confident, unpredictable, evolving, and fresh. My favourite is the Blooming Orchard. When I first saw it, I thought, this is just like me—the blend of colours is so beautiful, and it reminds me of the different 'hues' of an Indian summer. It’s versatile, delicate, full of life, and has such a fine, intricate design. I’d probably put it in a box and keep it all for myself!
