article_title: How street markets in India trained a generation’s fashion eye
sub_title: In the absence of malls and flagship stores, pavement markets became unlikely classrooms where we learnt to recognise fabric, construction and design through the thrill of the hunt
article_content: From the blue tarp hangs a coiled wire powering a naked bulb. Its clinical white light bathes a narrow makeshift passage lined with rows of hangers holding clothes marked with labels you wouldn’t expect to find in any Indian shopping mall. The portly man in a white shirt, now the colour of weak tea after a full day of work, pulls a synthetic white-and-pink puff-sleeved frock from a large blue plastic bag behind the stall and thrusts it towards me and declares, “Aap par achha lagega ye (This would look good on you).” I turn to my 55-year-old aunt with horror. Is this what people think of me? She suppresses a giggle while holding up a pair of tiny cut-off denim shorts he has recommended for her. “Bershka hai ye, Spain se aaya hai (It's by Bershka, from Spain),” he says proudly. On this October afternoon in 2024 at Janpath in New Delhi, Bershka is still months away from officially launching in India. The vendor knows that only adds to the appeal. “Why don’t you show me things like that?” I ask, pointing to a rack behind him. “That’s for young people,” he replies dismissively. When we correct him, he glances at my aunt’s figure-hugging A-line dress that stops just above the knees, then at my own loose cotton kaftan from Nicobar and grins. “Yahan toh pata hi na chale kaun bada hai aur kaun chhota (You can't tell whose younger or older here).” We’re still laughing when I spot a long denim shift dress hanging behind him. The cut is curved rather than straight, with side slits that climb halfway up the thigh and a deep V-neckline. Its torn label reads Oasis, the UK brand that today survives mostly online. I can already see how I’d wear it, with Converse high tops. And I’m about to make our slightly smug shopkeeper pay for his jokes with a very generous discount. Scenes like this unfold every day in India’s street markets. Beneath corrugated roofs in Janpath, inside the humid press of Sarojini Nagar on a Saturday afternoon, along the pavement stretches of Colaba Causeway and Linking Road, shoppers rummage through piles of clothing that appear to have arrived from nowhere you can easily name. For many Indians growing up in the 1990s and early 2000s, these markets were the chaotic bargain zones where we often had our first encounter with global fashion. This informal pipeline expanded dramatically after India opened its economy in 1991. When Finance Minister Manmohan Singh dismantled the license raj and ushered in a wave of economic liberalisation, the garment export sector grew rapidly. Textile exports nearly doubled during the following decade, rising from roughly $5 billion to more than $12 billion. Factories across towns like Panipat, Bahadurgarh and Najafgarh began producing clothing for global brands including Zara, Mango, Gap, Primark and H&M. These factories overproduced by design, typically by 3 to 5 percent above each order, to account for inevitable quality rejections such as misaligned stitching, shade variations or slightly misplaced buttons. Pieces that do not make it through brand inspections are often sold off in bulk. In India, many of those garments eventually found their way to pavement stalls and market tables. Long before Zara or H&M opened stores in the country, their clothes were already circulating here, hanging from metal racks or piled in large plastic sacks. Retail access to those brands, however, would arrive much later. Zara would not open its first Indian store until 2010, and H&M would follow five years after that. For years in between, the closest many Indian shoppers came to these labels was in the crowded aisles of street markets which filled the gap. Many people learned to recognise good clothing there long before they could afford it. Saumyaa Vohra, a lifestyle journalist, remembers being 23 and newly working in fashion media, with very little money to spend. One day, digging through a pile at Sarojini Nagar, she found a sweater that immediately stood out. “It was unusual, substantial, the kind of thing you can’t quite explain but you know is right,” she recalls. She washed it several times and began wearing it to work. Soon colleagues started asking if it was vintage Ralph Lauren. The knit resembled something from a Ralph Lauren campaign from the early 1990s. For two years she allowed the assumption to stand. The sweater had cost ₹100. “It was a really interesting feeling,” she says now. “To be wearing something that was considered not just fashionable, but a unique vintage edit of something.” Kangkan Rabha, a model and photographer from Guwahati who runs a slow-curation project called Code Toru, had a similar revelation growing up in Assam. As a child, he often visited markets in Dudhnoi and Fancy Bazaar with his mother. At one shop, he found his first pair of Levi’s. “It felt special and earned,” he says, “not because of the label, but because of what it meant.” His mother taught him to assess garments differently. Fabric quality, stitching and construction mattered more than brand names. “I naturally gravitate towards worn-out pieces, slightly imperfect things, clothes that feel lived in,” he says. “That’s where the real charm is.” Over time he has discovered a Lanvin double-breasted blazer in brown herringbone tweed and even a Carven jacket, both with intact Woolmark tags. “Imagine finding a niche French brand in a small part of Assam,” he says. “The best finds happen when you don’t force it.” Karishma Sakhrani, a lifestyle content creator and development chef who divides her time between Mumbai and Dubai, describes street shopping as a kind of visual training. “When you’re surrounded by chaos, you learn to edit quickly,” she says. “You learn quality by touch. You learn proportion instinctively.” Among her favourite discoveries are River Island cover-ups from Hill Road that she later wore to resorts in the Maldives and a gold-studded crop top she paired with a sari at a wedding, all purchased for a few hundred rupees. “If something costs almost nothing, you’ll take a risk with it,” she says. “Sometimes those risks become the pieces you wear for years.” Yet the ecosystem that once produced these discoveries may be changing. Divya Balakrishnan, Vogue India’s associate fashion editor, remembers travelling across cities specifically to explore street markets. “I used to hunt like a hound,” she says. “I used to travel to Bengaluru, Mumbai, Delhi for the markets. I’ve found coats, sweaters and tees from Ralph Lauren, Vivienne Westwood, YSL. You could always tell authenticity by the stitch or the button.” Today, she notices a shift, with the markets lined with more of the same. “The same crop tops, the same oversized tees, the same floral maxis. It’s because they’re being made for the same brands, trends and people.” Quality has also changed, where earlier it was possible to uncover unusual pieces hidden among the piles, many stalls now prioritise quantity over craft. “You could really find treasures earlier,” she says. Even so, the markets continue to attract loyal shoppers. Vohra, who now lives in Goa, still returns regularly. Fast fashion holds little appeal for her. Rabha has grown more selective with age but still sees value in the experience. “I shop slower now,” he says. A self-described “mix shopper”, he believes neither in thrifting as identity nor in the false opposition between conscious consumption and supporting new designers. He has learnt that there is a distance between the garment and the label, and that path he is happy to explore. India, notably, still lacks a widespread vintage retail ecosystem comparable to the thrift stores of London or the curated vintage districts of Tokyo and Bangkok. For decades, street markets have filled that role informally. Their appeal lies not only in affordability but in the process itself. Searching through piles of garments, feeling fabrics between your fingers, spotting something unexpected in the middle of chaos. You cannot algorithm your way through Sarojini Nagar on a crowded weekend afternoon. No app can guide you through a slush pile. What you can develop instead is an instinct. The ability to recognise a good garment when you see one, to imagine how it might fit into your wardrobe, to bargain for it with confidence. “Street markets give you personality,” Sakhrani says, “not just product.”

article_title: From pashmina shawls to ajrakh prints: what climate change is doing to treasured Indian textiles
sub_title: How much longer until all we’re left with is nylon and polyester?
article_content: Assam’s muga silk comes from the cocoons of a silkworm species that cannot exist outside the specific climatic conditions of the Brahmaputra Valley. Unlike most silks, muga is not dyed—the luminous gold is inherent to the fibre itself. It even becomes glossier with wear. Traditionally, almost every household maintained small silk farms in its backyard, but that system is growing increasingly fragile. “One early morning last April, I received a call from one of our farmers,” recalls Jagrity Phukan, a designer and the founder of Way of Living Studio, whose Assam-based textile practice works primarily with muga, eri and Across India, this pattern repeats. When ecosystems collapse, so do livelihoods. When we talk about fashion and climate change, the conversation is usually unidirectional. Fast fashion creates waste, factories pollute rivers and supply chains are opaque. This is all true, but there’s another side of the story that rarely gets the same, if any, attention. What happens to indigenous textiles and crafts when the climate they depend on starts to collapse? Our country’s natural ecological diversity has gifted us a corresponding textile heritage. In the north, pashmina—so fine it can pass through a ring, yet warm enough to survive Himalayan winters—is under pressure. It comes from Changthangi goats, reared by nomadic Changpa herders at altitudes between 14,000 and 17,000 feet. These goats grow their exceptional wool as a biological response to extreme cold. As winters get warmer, the wool fibres are affected. Tariq Dar, founder of Pashmkaar, a brand dedicated to preserving traditional Kashmiri weaving and embroidery practices, explains that while the warmth of the shawls has remained consistent so far, “the quantity and the quality are slowly getting affected. Not in a way most consumers can yet feel, but enough for experts to notice.” Where fibres once measured just 13 to 14 microns, today the geographical indication standard permits a thickness of 16 to 17 microns. It’s a dilution of one of the world’s finest natural fibres, and of a livelihood that has sustained communities in Kashmir and Climate, however, is only part of the story. Abhilasha Bahuguna, founder of Looms of Ladakh—an ethical, herder- and artisan-led luxury brand—points out that ecology and geopolitics are inseparable. “For centuries, Changpa herders moved seasonally between Tibet and Ladakh in a transhumance cycle that allowed pastures time to regenerate. In the 1960s, when the Indo-China border closed, grazing patterns changed permanently.” Grass no longer had time to recover, and because these goats are entirely pasture-fed, fibre quality began to decline. In response, some Changpa herders are turning to yak wool, which, while quite warm, has much coarser fibres than pashmina. Yaks nibble grass from the top rather than pulling it out by the roots, making them gentler grazers. They also live at lower altitudes, closer to where younger Changpa herders want to be. With little infrastructure or support at 17,000 feet, many are migrating to villages nearer to Leh and Kargil. “What is actually required to protect pashmina is collaborative visioning [between the herders, artisans and governmental interventions],” adds Bahuguna. Unlike Kashmir, Ladakh does not have a long-established textile production ecosystem with different communities handling different processes, so change is not as tough. “Changpa herders want skills, institutional support, bargaining power and ownership within the industry.” Down south, Chendamangalam in Handloom weaving here is largely home-based. It depends on stability: dry floors, controlled humidity, sunlight and time. In spite of large-scale destruction of property and handlooms, many weavers were back at work within 110 days—not because conditions had improved, but because every day without a loom was a day without income. The revival narrative glosses over how vulnerable the cluster already was. Today, looms are raised off the ground, and equipment can be dismantled early when floods threaten. “Some brands [like 11.11/eleven eleven] are now also working on a seed-to-store model,” adds Menon, “intervening at every stage to preserve the integrity of hand-making.” The model stands for a transparent supply chain, tracing the journey of the textile from cotton seed to the customer’s hands, which faces instability from the very beginning. According to a 2010 study published in As Laila Tyabji, author, craft activist and cofounder of Dastkar, an NGO that works to revive traditional crafts in India, points out, “Craft is rooted in the geography of the land from where it originates.” Ajrakh, for instance, is the resist-dyed block-printed textile traditionally practised by Khatri communities in Kutch. It’s known for its deep indigos, rich reds and near-mathematical symmetry. It requires repeated washing and open-air drying at multiple stages, and the mineral balance of the water directly affects how natural dyes show up. “Ajrakh is an entire system of knowledge,” says designer Monica Shah of Jade by MK, whose brand consistently champions the craft clusters and artisans they work with. “You can’t rush it. It depends on water, weather and the artisan’s judgement more than any machine.” Historically, Kutch’s fresh groundwater made this possible. Today, the region faces rising salinity due to industrial overextraction and seawater intrusion, exacerbated by repeated drought cycles.“Even with utmost skill and care, there are black splotches and muddy tones due to the saline content. Is it a wonder that many traditional ajrakh printers are turning to chemical dyes?” shares Tyabji. Next door in Rajasthan, dabu printing tells a similar story. It relies on a resist paste made from local Construction and mining have altered the soil composition around many ajrakh and dabu craft clusters, forcing printers to travel further for materials or substitute them with inferior ones. “Some clusters have tried collective systems such as shared resources, better washing set-ups, filtration support and training the next generation, but it’s not enough,” adds Shah. In Assam’s silk farms, even when the crop survives, yields have declined significantly and cocoon thickness has reduced. “Earlier, my uncles who reared silkworms wouldn’t even shave during the rearing period. They washed their hands with ash water instead of soap because they believed even a trace of a chemical or oil could harm the worms,” shares Phukan. A far cry from soap, tar fumes from road development have destabilised these ecosystems today. Faced with unpredictable weather and shrinking returns, many families are switching to farming tea—already expanding into silk-growing regions, bringing pesticides and chemical residues with it. “Artisans adapt constantly because they’ve always worked with nature, not against it,” shares Shah. “They shift working hours, change drying methods, modify sequences and adjust dye behaviour depending on the climate.” But you can only adjust so much when faced with failing water systems and extreme heat. As Menon says, “we are perpetually reacting to disaster, not preventing it.” There’s a certain pride in wearing traditional textiles. Ajrakh printing dates back to the Indus Valley civilisation. With its saturated colours and geometric patterns, it carries centuries of knowledge in its folds. Muga silk, which flourished under the Ahom dynasty in the 13th century, has a sheen as inimitable as its softness. The next time you wear a muga silk

article_title: Matthieu Blazy's Chanel is built for the fashion nerds
sub_title: For an audience hungry for IYKYK  nuggets, Matthieu Blazy serves up an endless buffet
article_content: The first time I realised my partner was ‘The One’ was a moment so deceptively ordinary, you might actually roll your eyes upon reading this. We were exiting my apartment building in the afternoon when he doubled back and handed me his sunglasses. “It’s very bright, you’ll get a headache,” he said. A man’s act of remembering a throwaway detail shared casually months ago. A woman’s surprise at being seen and cared for in that wholly quotidian, impossibly real way. When I told my partner it was the most romantic thing anyone had ever done for me, he did actually roll his eyes. When I recounted the incident to my best friend, she understood immediately. Women are so used to shrinking themselves—in public, at the workplace, in marriages, at the gym—that when we are seen and remembered, strange quirks, weird medical conditions and all, well… we fall in love. Matthieu Blazy understands this simple truth that evades so many others of his sex. For Chanel’s celebrated Métiers d’art 2026 show last December, the house’s new creative director did not fly his audience to a tropical island or plop a Swedish iceberg (RIP Karl Lagerfeld) in the centre of the runway. Blazy made them schlep down to an unused subway station in New York. Hardly the epitome of glamour. Then, as a train rolled in and a cast of characters poured out in every direction, he forced us to look at, and fall for, the details like only a true fashion nerd can. The show made it clear that Blazy hadn’t just rabbit-holed into the Chanel archives. He’d also invested time in getting to know Coco Chanel, the woman. Everywhere you looked, there were cheeky references to her life, waiting to be identified. A red scarf slung low across the hips of a black co-ord set, styled like Mademoiselle herself. A tweed suit woven to look like leopard print, an ethical homage to her love for fur. A leather jacket hand-painted with ‘Tonight or Never’, recalling the 1931 film that marked Chanel’s debut as a Hollywood costume stylist. Then, the vocabulary expanded. The fashion nerd flexed. Intermingled with allusions to his chosen ancestor were everyday women Chanel might have met on her pit stop in New York. The off-duty showgirl waltzing home from Broadway, feathered fan in hand. The Upper East Side cat lady. The mob boss, dressed to kill. The end result felt cinematic to Margaret Zhang, filmmaker and the former head of editorial content at Vogue China. Though we watched the same show, she was seated further down the subway platform than me, giving her a completely different vantage point of the chaotic choreography. Zhang found Blazy’s approach to be more like a film director’s, “unafraid of people moving in cycles as opposed to bodies moving through a sterile space”. She points to the mutual creative respect Blazy has for his audience: “He is doing the work but he’s also asking us to do the work rather than just telling us exactly what he’s thinking. It takes confidence to invite people in, to allow for scrutiny like that and it’s such a luxury to be trusted as an audience.” Scrutiny of the microscopic kind is part of the package at a house like Chanel. It’s the double- edged sword that Sabyasachi Mukherjee knows intimately—his own maison boasts an equally loyal and opinionated following. Also a fashion nerd, the Indian couturier made the effort to attend Blazy’s sophomore effort in New York to see the vision for himself. Mukherjee notes that the industry is tentatively moving out of a phase of “corporate designers” to embrace the “young and idealistic” again, powered by a newfound confidence that the post-digital world has given the consumer. “That’s why personal style has come back, why research and nerdism is coming back,” he explains. Brands can no longer prey on people’s insecurities to sell a prohibitively expensive handbag; the craft has to speak for itself. Blazy’s democratic approach, one where the magic of the métiers is laid out on the table to be deduced and dissected, is shaking up the old guard but magnetising the next generation. A necessary reinvention to survive when our very understanding of luxury is being questioned. “For too long, men in suits were running fashion,” says Mukherjee. “But you can’t capture human desire or imagination on an excel sheet.”

article_title: Why a generation raised on screens is getting into watches
sub_title: Rado’s Adrian Bosshard shares what brands are learning from a new generation of collectors
article_content: I got my first real watch when I was about 10—a Casio F-91W that was a gift from my father. It was my introduction to ‘real’ watches as opposed to the cheap knockoffs I had worn before. It was only in my 20s that I bought a watch with my own money, a Tissot PR100 that required a serious squeeze from my wallet. But it was worth every penny. It turns out that story isn’t unique, with Gen Z collectors beginning their careers today and finding themselves in the same boat. Having been introduced to the watch world at a young age by the adults in their lives—or discovering it through its adjacency with their other interests—they are now beginning to build collections of their own. “The beginning of my obsession started when my grandfather passed on a Citizen Signature chronograph to me,” says 23-year-old Nirek Dembla, a student of business analytics. He adds, “I was instantly fascinated with its engineering and proportions; the dial taught me about the elegance of smaller dial sizes.” Archana Ajith, a 28-year-old journalist from Mumbai, credits her father for shaping her interest. “He has an extensive watch collection and began building it when he was around my age. Growing up, I watched him carefully choose each piece with a deep appreciation for its craftsmanship.” Twenty-eight-year-old Gladwin Menezes, however, developed his obsession independently. “[It’s] something I cultivated by watching tennis matches and sporting events where athletes would wear cool watches. Eventually, I grew curious about why their watches cost so much; despite the jokes about ‘time toh same hi dikhata hai’, I wanted to understand the craft, history and also a little about the mechanics.” That joke about watches has been around for decades. My X-rupee watch tells the same time as your a-lot-more-than-X-rupee one. And the response hasn’t changed either: a watch does more than tell time. It can speak volumes about whether you value attention to detail or vibes; prefer unabashed bling or stoic restraint; are interested in craft or technology, maybe both. A report from Chrono24 and Fratello from last year revealed that Gen Z watch owners around the world are drawn to vintage dress watches. Many of these have become familiar sights on social media feeds and red carpets alike, being sported by pop-culture figures from Zohran Mamdani with his Casio A1000MA-7VT to Saif Ali Khan’s Jaeger-LeCoultre Reverso Grande Taille and Paul Mescal’s Cartier Tank. For many young collectors, these pieces become entry points into watch history. “What particularly draws me to the Cartier Tank is its proportions, as it proves that a watch does not need to be massive to have a presence,” says Dembla. Menezes concurs: “The Tank has always been a favourite, and the Reverso is also one that I find really interesting.” India’s most famous defunct watchmaker also continues to attract Ajith. “I admire vintage HMT mechanical timepieces because they represent a period when India had its own watchmaking identity.” Luxury watch imports into India have been steadily rising in recent years, with a combined increase of 35% according to reports from Deloitte and Morgan Stanley-LuxeConsult. A new free-trade agreement between India and the EU will gradually reduce import duties on Swiss watches, potentially expanding the market further. Among the brands paying attention to this growing interest is Rado. I recently met CEO Adrian Bosshard, who was in the country for the launch of the True Round x Les Couleurs Le Corbusier collection at India Art Fair; the watchmaker has had a presence at the Delhi event for seven years. Bosshard (the perfect example of nominative determinism, if ever there was one) was eager to discuss what the company has observed among younger buyers, a target market that continues to grow. He reveals, “We’re seeing an important trend with young customers—of [them buying] long-term luxury goods. Today, young customers think and evaluate [their options]; they like to buy products with a long-term and sustainable relevancy.” When asked about timeless vintage designs, Bosshard points to the Anatom, a 40-year-old icon that was revived a few years ago. “It was a total revolution at the time [in 1983] because of its design. At a time when watches were round and steel, it was ‘Hardmetal’ (Rado’s proprietary tungsten-carbide alloy) and anatomical.” The curvature of the watch was designed to enhance its wrist-feel—one of the factors Bosshard considers when choosing a watch, alongside design, quality and reliability. Our Gen Z contributors seem to echo this list. “Proportions are very important; a watch has to sit well on my wrist and feel balanced,” Ajith says. Dembla concurs: “I mainly focus on sub-40mm watches as I think they provide the most balanced silhouette [for me],” adding, “I also look for clean, minimal designs that are backed by rich historical significance.” These criteria are mirrored in their collections and wishlists. Dembla says, “My most recent and significant piece is a Rado Captain Cook high-tech ceramic diver with a beautiful green dial. This watch in particular was the grail for me when I started collecting, because of its concave ceramic bezel and pure diver-watch DNA. As for what’s next in my collection, it’s a Jaeger-LeCoultre Reverso.” Ajith’s wish list also features names that will be instantly recognisable to collectors of any age: “Audemars Piguet and Cartier will probably always be on it. But realistically, what I’m eyeing right now is a 37mm Rado Captain Cook automatic.” For this new wave of collectors, the watches on their wish lists share one thing in common: longevity. While trends may ebb and flow, these are pieces chosen with the expectation that they will stay meaningful long after the novelty of purchase fades. As Dembla puts it, “In a time when we are surrounded by vast amounts of fleeting digital utility, a traditional timepiece acts as a rare island of permanence.”

article_title: Ananya Panday’s gold-thread Anamika Khanna couture and Priyanka Chopra Jonas’s layered Dior skirt lead this week’s best looks
sub_title: Texture and tailoring take the lead, with embroidery-heavy couture sitting alongside runway-driven silhouettes
article_content: Surface work, tailoring and silhouette shifts defined this week’s standout fashion moments. Embroidery dominated the Indian looks, from Ananya Panday’s densely worked Anamika Khanna couture to Mrunal Thakur’s paisley-laden sari by Mrunalini Rao. Elsewhere, international runways entered the mix: Alia Bhatt stepped out at Milan Fashion Week in a leather trench worn as a dress, while Priyanka Chopra Jonas attended Dior’s show in Jonathan Anderson’s layered skirt silhouette referencing Paul Poiret. Ananya Panday wore Anamika Khanna couture in the form of a mandarin-collar jacket and long skirt densely covered in gold floral embroidery. Vines, leaves and blossoms spread across the surface in layered threadwork with sequins and bead clusters stitched through the motifs, giving the garment a richly worked texture. Along the inner closure running down the front of the jacket, strings of white beads formed scalloped edges that introduced a lighter vertical line through the field of gold. From the jacket hem, long strands of fringe fell over the skirt and moved with each step, bringing motion to a surface otherwise packed with ornamentation. Stylist Priyanka Kapadia Badani paired the ensemble with a neckpiece built around fan-shaped motifs and stud earrings, but it is the pearl drops on the necklace that create continuity with the ensemble's surface work. Riviera Lynn created a luminous no-makeup makeup look, while hair by Sankalp Vilas Surve fell in loose waves that softened the sharp neckline of the mandarin collar. Sanya Malhotra chose an Aseem Kapoor ensemble built around a sculpted bra blouse embroidered with figurative motifs and geometric borders. The skirt extended the palette through vertical panels worked with resham thread, zari and marori embroidery, with bead tassels and small hanging details scattered across the surface. A printed dupatta in sheer silk introduced another layer of pattern to the mix of colour and texture. Styled by Manisha Melwani, the look included a gemstone choker and gold studs by Ritika Bhasin Gupta. Hair jewellery by Anupa Tulsi Jewellers threaded through the bun alongside fresh flowers. Trenches are the new dresses and Mrunal Thakur wore a black sari by Mrunalini Rao where the embroidery runs continuously from the blouse into the pallu border. Multicoloured threadwork, sequins and bead clusters form dense floral and paisley motifs across the blouse before extending into a broad embroidered band along the drape. The rest of the sari remains largely dark, interrupted only by small scattered motifs across the fabric. Styled by Tanishq Malhotra-Gulabani, the look included drop earrings from PMJ Jewels. Sleek straight hair and softly contoured makeup kept the attention on the sari's surface work. Keep scrolling for more of the best fashion looks of the week.

article_title: This high jewellery brand is crafting heritage in every heirloom
sub_title: At Raj Mahtani Couture Jewels, five generations of craftsmanship meet contemporary vision, creating pieces that honour legacy while embracing modern elegance
article_content: The true beauty of heirloom jewellery lies in the stories they carry—notes of love, history, and memory that lend an evocative depth to every look. Whether through elaborate necklaces rooted in age-old Indian craftsmanship or shoulder dusters with contemporary flair, Raj Mahtani has built a design language that honours heritage while embracing innovation. Founded in 1880, Raj Mahtani Couture Jewels draws on the legacy of his five-generation, family-run jewellery house. The eponymous label blends craft traditions with contemporary techniques, creating high jewellery that feels both timeless and forward-thinking. Over the years, the brand has become synonymous with pieces that celebrate milestones, define special moments, and evolve into treasured keepsakes. At the heart of the brand lies a distinct design philosophy: honour the past while designing for the present. A Raj Mahtani necklace—often the centrepiece of a bridal look—is created to stand the test of time. Mughal influences, old-world techniques, and classical stone settings are reinterpreted through a contemporary lens. The Raj Mahtani bride embodies this same sensibility: confident, globally aware, and appreciative of fine craftsmanship. Table-cut diamonds, Old-cut diamonds, New-cut diamonds, Colombian emeralds, Burmese rubies, and exceptional pearls are sourced and transformed into pieces that feel both opulent and statement-making. Perfect for heritage weddings, couture bridal styling, and cherished celebrations where timeless elegance is paramount. Raj Mahtani was the first in India to align fine jewellery with couture, recognising early on that jewels are integral to the fashion narrative. His collaborations with leading Indian designers such as Anamika Khanna, Tarun Tahiliani and Manish Malhotra, along with international names like Diane von Furstenberg and Roberto Cavalli, positioned his creations not as accessories but as defining elements of the fashion runway. With a discerning clientele across London, Singapore, Hong Kong, Sri Lanka, New York City and Dubai, the brand’s appeal lies in its balance of tradition and relevance. In a world where luxury can often feel transient, Mahtani’s creations offer a sense of permanence. Crafted with precision and guided by intention, Raj Mahtani Couture Jewels continues to define a distinctly modern expression of Indian high jewellery—one that is rooted in legacy yet confident in its global perspective.

article_title: The GI-tagged sari you probably haven't heard of
sub_title: In Pollachi, Tamil Nadu, Negamam’s weaving community continues to make its distinctive cotton sari by hand, one household at a time
article_content: I am sitting in the open verandah of Pollachi RiverHouse, watching palms sway along the Aliyar River and sipping fresh “This is a Negamam cotton sari from my village. We also call it the Village Cot Sari or Getti Ragam—thick variety in local lingo,” Shiva, the property manager tells me. In that moment, the fabric seems to hold Pollachi itself. The next day, almost impulsively, I decide to visit the Periya Negamam weaving cluster, located just 15 kilometres north of the property. If a single sari can hold such a story, I want to see where that story begins. In Periya Negamam, weaving is not confined to workshops. It lives inside homes. Inside one such house, I met Nagaraj, 50, a third-generation weaver whose pit loom sits half a metre below the floor level. The loom is built into the house itself. His wife, Anandhini, 45, sits nearby separating threads while his mother, Savitri, 60, winds yarn into bobbins. It takes an entire household to keep a loom running. “Moisture-laden winds flowing from the Western Ghats make weaving easier between June and November. The climate prevents the cotton threads from snapping, allowing the weavers to maintain the dense structure that defines a Negamam sari,” Muthu, my guide-translator, tells me. A traditional Negamam cotton sari is distinctive in ways that even an untrained eye can eventually recognise. It is thicker than most cotton saris, with around 86 to 90 picks per inch, giving the fabric durability and weight. The sari measures roughly 7.3-8.2 metres, longer than many standard saris, and is woven with 80s count cotton yarn in both warp and weft. The designs are simple: narrow borders in striking colours, checks and stripes across the body, and nature-inspired motifs decorating the pallu. Mustard against indigo, greens against maroons. Despite weaving a Negamam sari every other day, Anandhini, like many other weavers, owns only one Negamam sari, which she says she wore for her daughter’s wedding. A single sari takes anywhere from two to three days to complete, depending on the design's complexity. What sells for several thousand rupees in the retail market earns a weaver between ₹800 and ₹1,100. “We earn up to ₹15,000 a month, even though it takes the labour of four family members to complete all the work,” says Nagaraj. The process is far from small. The yarn is dried and prepared until it takes on a slightly stiff texture, ready for the loom. Then the weaving begins: pedal pressed, shuttle thrown, threads tightened. Nearly 300 families, in and around Periya Negamam, begin their day at 5am when the sound of looms starts to echo through the streets. It continues steadily until evening, broken only by meals and brief rests. In many cities across India, Negamam saris are now worn by entrepreneurs and office-goers who favour textiles that endure long hours and rising temperatures without losing their pleats or form. “Office wear,” laughs Mahendran Ajithan, 35, and his wife Ranjiphe, another weaver family I met later in the village. “Because they get softer and lighter after every wash.” But before a sari reaches that softness, it passes through a complex process that belongs to an entire village. Weaving is organised like a relay. Each street specialises in a different stage of production– yarn preparation, drawing cotton fibres and spinning them into thread. The yarn is dyed in multiple colours and laid out to dry under the sun for a few days, followed by warping, where loose threads are transformed into an organised structure for weaving. I watch Ajithan operating a large drum-like warping machine. Hundreds of threads stretch across the drum in perfect alignment, enough to produce about twelve saris. From there, the yarn travels to the paavupattarai, a workshop dedicated to sizing. This step gives strength to the cotton threads. A mixture of rice, maize or potato starch is brushed repeatedly over the stretched yarn. Two workers hold a large brush between them, walking briskly across the threads again and again until the starch settles evenly. The thick fabric can withstand years of washing, yet is breathable enough for Tamil Nadu’s heat. In March 2023, Negamam cotton saris received a Geographical Indication, or GI, tag, but the weavers say the recognition has not translated into higher incomes or better wages. The pressures remain much the same. The first threat comes from power looms. Machine-made saris cost half the price of handloom pieces. For buyers, affordability usually outweighs craft provenance, and then there is the generational challenge. “Nobody under forty wants to weave,” Dhandapani, 71, tells me. Earlier, children would spend afternoons learning the craft after school. Today, many families discourage it. Weaving is perceived as economically uncertain, labour-intensive and less profitable. Parents fear that becoming a weaver might limit marriage prospects. Many weavers have moved to silk weaving instead. Handloom weaving also relies on family collaboration. When younger people migrate to cities for education or employment, the chain breaks. Yet the story does not end in decline. Sustainable fashion brands such as Ethicus are trying to reshape the future of the craft through revival efforts, working with local weavers and continuing to produce textiles on the region’s traditional looms. “Earlier they thought weaving was ordinary,” says Kamatchi Sundram, 50, who handles dyeing. “Now when visitors come and take photos, they realise it’s something special,” adds his wife Dhanalakshmi, 45, as we pose for a picture. And back at Pollachi RiverHouse that evening, admiring the suspended drapes, I think again about how a Negamam sari carries more than utility. It carries climate, labour, habit and memory, all held in cotton sturdy enough for everyday life.

article_title: From trousseaus to runways, phulkari carries the stories of women’s lives
sub_title: Designer Pratima Pandey collaborated with The Nabha Foundation on Marzi, a collection that celebrates phulkari as living Punjabi heritage rather than a relic of the past
article_content: On an uncharacteristically pleasant March evening in Delhi, I braved the evening traffic to visit the National Crafts Museum & Hastkala Academy to discover more about phulkari. My Punjabi best friend would break out her mother’s phulkari bagh, a ceremonial dupatta with heavy floral embroidery, at every Diwali celebration in college, wistfully declaring every time (without fail) that she couldn’t wait to receive her own at her wedding. For a Budaun-Hyderabad hybrid family like mine, cultural artefacts being passed down generations were always a source of conflict in the household. The heirlooms passed down from my paternal grandmother (from Budaun, Uttar Pradesh) would act as a red cape being brandished in front of my maternal grandmother (from Hyderabad). The only thing in common between the two matriarchs was the belief that anything the other did was subpar, to put it politely. This made joint family functions a minefield to navigate with the finesse of the most seasoned of soldiers. So the sense of connection and belonging that a beautifully embroidered dupatta would evoke in my friend fascinated me. What is it like to see a As I observed a 26-year-old craftswoman, Sukhpreet, skilfully render a geometric floral pattern without any tracing or hesitation, my mind was filled with memories of the time I valiantly tried to fix a button on my dad’s shirt, only to end up attaching the button to my finger instead of the shirt’s placket and an acute sense of second-hand pride on seeing an age-old craft being passed down and celebrated by a younger lot. In his telling of the 18th-century classic Punjabi folk tragedy These records and poems might document it for cultural historians and enthusiasts, but phulkari has long existed as a quiet, coded language of women’s lives, carrying within its geometrical patterns stories of love, labour, migration and memory. It’s an intimate archive that has continued to live on in the trunks and Presented by The Nabha Foundation, a philanthropic organisation established for the preservation of the state’s cultural heritage, Phulkari of Punjab brought together archival textiles, displays, a moderated panel discussion and a runway presentation of designer Pratima Pandey’s phulkari-focused collection, Marzi. “Phulkari is no longer confined to nostalgia or museum spaces,” says Shubhra Singh, executive director, The Nabha Foundation. “It’s being recontextualised for contemporary audiences while retaining its essence. This dual movement of preservation and evolution has been critical to its renewed relevance.” Traditionally, phulkari textiles marked life-cycle events such as births and marriages. When a girl was born in a household, the grandmother and mother would start preparing her phulkari bagh, a style of the embroidery where the entire surface of the fabric is embroidered. Over time, however, shifts in the economy and lifestyle pushed the craft to the margin, threatening its continuity. Over the past few decades, concerted efforts have gone into preserving the craft; The Nabha Foundation itself supports over 400 artisans across Punjab who work towards making the practice of phulkari a sustainable endeavour. Artisans enrolled in the programme pass down the craft to a younger crop of women and draw a new wave of consumers by contemporising and recontextualising phulkari without losing its essence. A way to do this was to collaborate with designer Pratima Pandey on her collection. “Phulkari, at its core, is an act of agency with women choosing motifs, colours and stories without formal training or permission. Yet, many of these same women have lived within limited frameworks of choice. The collection grew from that tension. It became a way to honour the inherent freedom within the craft while acknowledging the boundaries around the maker,” says Pandey. With strains of singer Amira Gill’s rendition of ‘Ik Onkar’, the foundational faith principle of Sikhism, in the background, models walked down the brick-paved runway at the Crafts Museum in phulkari-adorned saris, cropped jackets, sheer chanderi skirts and dresses. Craft collaborations could risk becoming purely aesthetic exercises, but Pandey consciously tried to ensure this remained a dialogue rather than a one-sided reinterpretation. “We didn’t approach the artisans with fixed designs. The process involved unlearning, [and then] understanding their rhythm, decisions and instincts. There were moments when we stepped back entirely and let their way lead the outcome.” Singh echoes the sentiment, adding, “Phulkari is approached as a living, evolving language, not a static bank of motifs. The role of design is to contextualise, not overwrite. The artisans remain central to the process.” In the end, what remains is not just the surface of the textile but the many hands and the centuries of choices that shape it.

article_title: This legacy jewellery brand brings a fresh perspective on heirloom jewellery to the mix

article_content: Affectionately known as ‘bauji’ by both family and staff, Late Shri Hazoorilal Narang laid the foundation of Hazoorilal Legacy, a business rooted in trust, craftsmanship, and ambition. Narang’s brainchild, the jewellery house, is well known today for marrying international sensibilities with a proud traditional ethos. From Lahore to Delhi’s Chandni Chowk—where bauji opened the first store in 1952—to its home today in South Extention II, for over seven decades, Hazoorilal Legacy has remained steadfast in its pursuit of timeless design. It focuses on creating jewellery that enhances life’s meaningful occasions with elegance while upholding a reputation for integrity, artistry, and excellence. The Legacy Collection from The House of Hazoorilal Legacy embodies their constant pursuit of design excellence. It is an annual showcase that highlights the brand's one-of-a-kind pieces. This curation celebrates elegance with character, bringing together gold, polki, and a vibrant palette of carefully sourced natural gemstones—from deep emeralds to delicate morganites—illuminated by fine diamonds. This collection truely emerges as the brand’s defining statement—an ode to its storied heritage expressed through a distinctly modern lens. Anchored in the brand’s legacy of unparalleled craftsmanship and visionary design, their recent collection, ‘The Spring Edit 2026’ captures the essence of renewal, beauty, and sophistication. Each piece in the edit has been designed to balance modern elegance with timeless charm. Deeply rooted in Indian heritage and master craftsmanship, the brand continues to expand its vision of luxury from New Delhi to the global stage. Supported by a strong digital presence, influential brand ambassadors, and diverse collections ranging from the opulent Legacy Collection to the Zoori line with its playful designs and colourful gemstone jewellery, the brand is ready for the future. A significant chapter in this global journey has been the brand’s first year in the Dubai market, marked by strong growth and meaningful engagement. The brand’s distinctive blend of vintage inspiration and contemporary design—grounded in Indian workmanship—resonated strongly with Dubai’s cosmopolitan clientele. At its core, Hazoorilal Legacy represents a study in curated opulence. Every creation reveals an architectural sensibility, where gemstones—from emeralds and diamonds to rubellites—are placed with precision to achieve visual harmony. The result is jewellery that feels both powerful and poised: a sophisticated expression of contemporary luxury that resonates with a global audience.

article_title: An enduring legacy of craft, culture, and creativity

article_content: Tracing its origins to the 19th century, the legacy of Raniwala 1881 began to take shape when Rai Bahadur Champalal of Beawar, Rajasthan, was honoured by the British. A true connoisseur with a discerning eye for gemstones, his passion for refined Indian craftsmanship became the cornerstone of an enduring legacy. Inspired by the opulence of the Rajputana era, Raniwala 1881 has evolved into a distinguished jewellery house, standing today as a proud custodian of India’s rich cultural heritage. Heritage and innovation lie at the heart of Raniwala 1881. Designed for the woman of today, each creation reflects a harmonious blend of culture, confidence, and individuality. Every piece tells a story—evolving seamlessly from a treasured inheritance into an expression of effortless, everyday elegance. For Raniwala 1881, jewellery sits at the intersection of heritage, modernity, and individuality, defining its distinctive design philosophy. Rooted in Jaipur, the brand’s visual identity draws deeply from the historical grandeur of the Raniwala haveli, reflecting a rich legacy of craftsmanship while embracing a contemporary sensibility. The brand’s statement pieces imbue a delicate balance between structure and fluidity, designed to evolve with the wearer’s identity over time. Bold, collar-like compositions feature uncut diamonds set in high-carat gold, creating a sense of both strength and softness. Alongside these are multi-layered rani haars—cascading necklaces with an almost architectural presence. Strands of tourmalines, spinels, and pearls are punctuated with oversized gemstone plaques, adding depth, rhythm, and visual drama. Polki, celebrated for its raw, organic beauty, lies at the heart of the design language. Complementing this are vibrant coloured gemstones and finely crafted gold, coming together to create versatile, contemporary aesthetics. Think uncut diamonds that pair just as effortlessly with linen trousers as they do with a silk sari, and rubies and emeralds that move beyond festive occasions to add a subtle brilliance to everyday moments. Each piece is shaped by the hands of skilled karigars, preserving techniques that have been passed down through generations. Embodying identity and self-expression, jewellery becomes a medium through which heritage is not only retained but also worn, redefined, and made personal.

article_title: 7 Gen Z creatives on building wardrobes with real personality
sub_title: For these multi-hyphenates, the 9-to-5 was never really an option
article_content: How do you define a generation? How do you account for lived experiences that spill far beyond temporal boundaries? Oscar Wilde said that to define is to limit, and if there’s one thing I do know about Gen Z, it’s that we don’t like limits. In fact, we actively despise them. Whether it’s dismantling gender binaries or making increasingly loud democratic demands, this is a generation that refuses to sit still. And when it comes to bringing home the dough, the cookie-cutter career path is on the brink of extinction. Gen Z creatives are more amoeba than ladder-climbers; they’re constantly metamorphosing, adapting to whatever the world throws their way. And naturally, they’re doing it in style.

article_title: A closer look at a collection that brings Kapurthala’s past into everyday dressing
sub_title: The House of Valaya’s luxury prêt label JJV.Kapurthala introduces ATTH for Spring–Summer 2026, marking its eighth season, drawing on Kapurthala’s royal past and the house’s long-standing fascination with travel and Art Deco design
article_content: Some places leave a lasting impression. For JJ Valaya, the Delhi-based couturier known for building a world around Indian heritage, that place has always been Kapurthala. Often referred to as the Paris of Punjab, the princely state was shaped by the travels of Maharaja Jagatjit Singh, who brought back European influences that still echo in its architecture and cultural identity. Through JJV.Kapurthala, that world is reimagined in a way that feels lighter and more relaxed, translating the house’s distinctive style into clothing designed for everyday use. The label’s Spring–Summer 2026 collection, ATTH, continues this connection. The word means ‘eight’ in Punjabi, marking the eighth season of the line and continuing the brand’s tradition of naming collections through Punjabi numerology. Each season becomes a marker of time—an evolving chapter rooted in the culture and history that continue to inspire the house. Every JJV.Kapurthala collection is shaped by three directions that define the core ethos of the world of VALAYA—Royale, Nomade and Art Deco—and this season returns to them with subtle shifts. In the Royale chapter, Paisley appears, in a more restrained form. The motif is reworked and layered with jaali-inspired patterns; these two traditional elements sit together in a way that feels balanced. The Nomade story turns to ikat, a craft treasured for its organic qualities. The patterns retain their natural irregularity, bringing a sense of movement to the garments. For Art Deco, the collection adds an unexpected element—a monkey motif drawn from Eastern artistic traditions. Set against the structured geometry often associated with the Art Deco period, it introduces a playful note while maintaining the collection’s visuals. The collection moves away from the weight of intricate embroidery and instead embraces bold prints, fluid fabrics, and subtle antique touches. The aim is simple: pieces that embody the spirit of celebration while remaining easy to wear. For womenswear, the season brings in summer-friendly tops and tunics, along with modern skirt sets, kaftans, shararas, and relaxed co-ord ensembles—silhouettes that are ideal for travel, social gatherings, and everyday wear. Fabric is key to achieving this sense of ease. Cupro, satin, linen, Giza cotton, georgette, and modal feature throughout the collection, chosen for their lightness and drape in warmer weather. The colour palette echoes this balance. Ivory, crème, mustard, teal, and shades of pink and coral form the softer base of the season, complemented by deeper house signatures such as navy, plum, and black. The collection launches this March and will be available in JJV.Kapurthala stores nationwide and on the brand’s website. With ATTH, the house returns to the themes that have long defined its design language—heritage, craft, and a sense of discovery—presented in pieces that feel easy and expressive.

sub_title: If anything, the first Aizawl Design Project was a testament to that
article_content: For years, the narrative of fashion in Northeast India has been frustratingly narrow. The region’s relationship with style has often been flattened into three easy clichés: cultural shows, beauty pageants and the well-worn mythology of thrift culture. None of them are entirely false. But none of them capture the full picture either. The first Aizawl Design Project was proof of how outdated those assumptions have become. Its first public expression, the The collections, styled by Aizawl-born stylist James Lalthanzuala, brought together three distinct designers from Mizoram—Hannah Khiangte, Lapâr and Escape Engmoia—each working with the Zo The showcase was conceived and curated by Lal Moya, an event curator based in Washington DC. “As a Mizo creative, I have always believed our designers deserve the same level of staging and presentation that you see anywhere in the world. The talent has always been here. What we needed was the platform and the courage to present it properly,” he said. For decades, fashion from the Northeast has been expected to carry the duty of representation. Clothes had to signify something: tribe, tradition, identity, solidarity. Fashion, in the sense of experimentation or self-expression, was often treated as secondary. What the The designers are reworking indigenous textiles as living materials that can adapt to new forms, without treating them like inherited artefacts anymore. “My collection comes from the idea of Lapâr was established in 2017 by Patricia Zadeng. With a degree in textile design from the When asked why he named his brand This showcase did not erase the region’s cultural heritage. If anything, it situates the Zo Perhaps the most significant change is that fashion from the Northeast is no longer asking for validation using cultural tokens. Designers are building their own communities, creating their own platforms and shaping their own visual identities. The Northeast’s fashion scene has always had unbridled style. article_title: This family-run jewellery house has a legacy spanning nine decades
sub_title: Here’s how Bishan, a luxury jewellery house, reflects a legacy built on trust and timeless design
article_content: The year was 1933. The late Bishan Singh Chadha opened a jewellery store in Rawalpindi—then part of India, now in Pakistan—unaware that this modest beginning would lay the foundation for a 21st-century brand. Ninety years later, the jewellery house continues to honour his legacy and his affinity for creating pieces that go on to become heirloom jewellery. The brand’s deep respect for legacy is showcased on its website, where its first-ever sales bill from 1933 occupies a place of pride. The family-run jewellery house opened its first store in independent India in Chandni Chowk, Delhi. This was followed by another store in Delhi in 2000. Since then, the brand has found patrons outside India and now exports its handcrafted creations across the Middle East and beyond. The brand was first launched under the name Harnam Singh Bishan Singh Jewellers. Over the decades, the house evolved to 100% in-house manufacturing, gaining full creative control to craft bespoke pieces for discerning clients. In 2023, the brand was reintroduced as Bishan—a refined identity that honours its rich heritage while embracing the future of Indian jewellery. By 2010, it was serving over 2,000 clients across more than 10 countries. Today, with stores in Delhi, Dubai, and Qatar, Bishan is known for designs that honour the grandeur of traditional Indian craftsmanship while embracing a global aesthetic, making them equally suited for a Parisian soiree or a regal Indian wedding. More than mere adornment, Bishan jewellery celebrates exclusivity, individuality, and timeless elegance. Each creation is designed to become an heirloom—a delicate balance of classical influences and contemporary sophistication. Whether you seek a regal statement with emeralds, vintage charm with sapphires, or the serene elegance of rare diamonds, Bishan offers endless ways to infuse meaning, intention, and sophistication into your ensemble.

article_title: Are single-edition Banarasi saris the ultimate luxury flex?
sub_title: As rarity becomes part of the appeal, Swati & Sunaina Gold is betting that serious sari collectors want what cannot be repeated
article_content: It all started with a wild goose chase in Banaras (Varanasi),” recalls Swati Agarwal. One half of the label Swati & Sunaina Gold, the designer traces the brand’s origin story back a decade ago when, inspired by her Marwari family’s trove of heirloom saris, she set out to find a rangkaat (a complex weaving technique that interlocks silk with zari threads) drape for her brother’s wedding. The search was obsessive—calls to President’s Award– winning artisans, hours spent poring over Weaver Service Centre booklets, even a cold hunt through Varanasi’s bylanes. She never found the rangkaat she had dreamed of, but discovered a new calling instead. In a landscape crowded with Banarasi brocade brands, Agarwal and her sister-in-law Sunaina Jalan have conjured up an anomaly. Their focus is the single-edition sari, which means no two patrons will ever own the same piece. Exclusivity is taken so seriously that they do not even maintain a physical archive of their actual creations (they do chronicle through sketches and samples). Each collection is a capsule of just six design directions, with 12 to 18 pieces in singular colourways. With pieces starting at ₹3 lakh, these are not impulse buys. Since the beginning, the founders have worked exclusively with Banarasi textiles, drawing on dampach, kadua, jamdani, rangkaat and gyaser (their interpretation of the Indo-Tibetan textile). But each comes with interventions. Where others would settle for neat colour panels in rangkaat, they tied the blocks with woven bows. Their intervention in gyaser required looms that normally yielded only 23 inches to be adapted to accommodate an entire sari—a feat never attempted before. Their Vanya collection of 24 saris brought wild silks from the Northeast—eri, tussar, muga and mulberry—into the Banaras gharana. The kora or white nature of these silks was paired with motifs inspired by Indian white flowers (rajnigandha, juhi, bela, champa, aparajita and brahmakamal) as well as miniature Kangra paintings of Krishna in the night garden. What makes Swati & Sunaina Gold stand out in a competitive market is “their research vis-à-vis history, design and the technique applied in their collections,” explains textile curator Lavina Baldota. It’s little wonder that these saris, sans shiny embellishment or accoutrement, “demand a certain price”, she adds. This dedication to detail is evident in their collections. The pair took four trips to France and wrote a thesis on the India-France textile connection before releasing the newest Varanasi to Versailles line, which showcases a fine mix of brocade and French lace. As India experiences a revivalist moment, and formal contemporary textile museums remain rare, the role of individual designers and collectors becomes even more crucial. Agarwal shares that a young bride from Hyderabad commissioned a sari for her wedding. “She’d met her fiancé only a couple of months prior, but the connection felt cosmic, and she wanted her bridal look to reflect that.” The team created a piece that drew from the couple’s astrological signs, lucky numbers and intertwined names in a Telugu script. The bride archived the entire process, proving that collectors who buy refined textiles value the journey as deeply as the finished weave itself. To the sisters-in-law, as with other skill-led designers— Chinar Farooqui of Injiri and her quiet devotion to jamdani; Sanjay Garg of Raw Mango, who has expanded the handloom lexicon; Pankaj S with his luminous Murshidabad mul; and Aadyam Handwoven with its explorations in ikat—speaking about process and their long-term relationships with makers isn’t marketing. It’s a responsibility. Which is why conversations must shift beyond focusing on how many hours a weaver spent at the loom or which mythological character inspired a motif. The sharper question is whether stakeholders—not just the weaver but the yarn dyer, the spinner, the jacquard punch maker, even the loom maker—are compensated well enough to continue this work. Exhibitions that showcase skill, patronage that inspires continuity and above-market pay structures are what separate romanticism from real commitment. Agarwal and Jalan understand that difference. “I don’t think weaving is a dying art form, but it is certainly an ageing one,” Agarwal says, contemplatively. The renewed fascination with handlooms has helped both small ateliers and big brands, but she points to a new threat. “Many young weavers may not have the patience or focus like their forefathers did.” She notes many young practitioners’ attention spans have been hijacked by their phone while a power loom grunts on the side. For years, the fear was that the new hands would just not have the same agility. Now, it’s focus that is slipping away. And in that quiet fading of concentration lies the real fragility of the craft Agarwal and Jalan are trying so hard to protect.

article_title: In these fashion stores, the clothes are only part of the experience
sub_title: Indian designers are creating whimsical imaginariums where there’s much more to thrill than the swipe of a credit card
article_content: At the Sabyasachi store in Mumbai, an interesting statistic comes up in conversation with a sales associate. She mentions that on any given day, between 10 and 15 people walk in with no explicit intention of making a purchase. Many are international tourists, keen to see what’s been recommended to them as one of the most exquisite retail spaces in all of India. And for good reason. The store (and its many addresses across the country and in New York) offers an encounter with Indian maximalism where time feels suspended. Its curation of collectibles—heirloom furniture, treasured curios, antique rugs and the like—exists in a profusion that has to be seen first-hand to be truly understood. Naturally, then, visitors are sometimes confused to learn the artefacts aren’t for sale. A few lanes away, Gaurav Gupta’s three-storey flagship is an immediate visual foil: an all-white world of minimalist futurism. Architect Vishal K Dar created a space for the brand that is undulating and otherworldly—like a white-cube gallery in which the garments are presented as wearable art. Further south, Sanjay Garg’s Raw Mango store, designed by interior architect Ashiesh Shah and designer Isla Maria ‘Loulou’ Van Damme, is meditative, measured and almost anti-spectacle in its approach to Indian craft traditions. The layout, material palette and aesthetic elements draw from the tropical modernist philosophies of architects like Geoffrey Bawa and Charles Correa, culminating in a space of true repose: an 800-square-foot courtyard. In addition to the one-kilometre radius they inhabit, the retail spaces of Sabyasachi, Gaurav Gupta and Raw Mango share a strong common denominator: they each function as compelling, tangible extensions of their brands’ sartorial identities. Within South Mumbai’s Indo-Saracenic and neogothic streetscape, these fashion stores exist as micro-universes of craft. They’re evolving into a new version of the third space, where communities are formed, cross-collaboration is encouraged and creative programming feels entirely natural. Raw Mango’s famous baithaks come to mind, the most recent edition of which was hosted at the label’s Banjara Hills store last November. For designers who see themselves as being creators before entrepreneurs, the store is where their vision can be realised in full. At Delhi Vintage Co, the worldbuilding takes on an almost mythological nature. Their new 10,000-square-foot store in the capital, designed by Smita Singh of NoDoor, draws from the phases of a lunar eclipse interpreted as a series of archways. Founder Manish Chhabra’s soulful private collection of Indian art is displayed throughout the store, though one of his most significant pieces was a bespoke commission: a sculpture of a devi, seemingly suspended in motion at the very edge of a table and secured in position by threads, produced by Neil Ghose Balser and Doyel Joshi of How Are You Feeling Studio. “We worked very closely on every element—from artefacts to textures to spatial flow,” says Chhabra. “Even the fragrance in the store is custom-curated, because I wanted the experience to go beyond the visual. ” Another rendition of this ideology lies in the glittering new Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla store at Jio World Plaza in Mumbai. Quilted curtains finished with aabla embroidery, gold-leafed walls with AJSK patola motifs and mirrored ceilings are only a prelude to the brand’s take on opulence. The rapid growth of e-commerce feels almost directly proportional to a more resolute conviction that physical retail spaces are irreplicable. This is especially true in a luxury marketplace. The physical store is where a customer can best understand the difference between one house and the next beyond price points— where a brand is fully felt and where loyalty is earned, in a way a website never can. Brands are working hard to protect this distinction, ensuring the act of making an in-person purchase doesn’t exist in a vacuum. S howrooms now come with branded cafés and restaurants, and in some cases these hospitality outposts become their own attraction: in 2024, Mumbai got its first Armani/Caffè, with a menu comprising a selection of Giorgio Armani’s favourite dishes. Indian labels such as Nappa Dori routinely partner with coffee brands for their in-store cafés. When Moonray rebranded to Chorus last year, with a three-storey flagship in Kala Ghoda, it included a chic café and home-decor section, as well as a compelling selection of handcrafted soaps, body oils and candles. Among legacy brands, there is an increased focus on consumer literacy around craft processes and provenance. A few years ago, Hermès presented its ‘In Motion’ travelling exhibition in Mumbai, offering a rare and detailed insight into over a century of the house’s archive. In Jaipur, the House of Sunita Shekhawat, a family-run fine jewellery brand, established a permanent museum to celebrate the art of meenakari around two years ago. “People don’t walk in only to see objects; they walk in to understand where meenakari comes from and why it matters,” says Sunita Shekhawat. “Clients now arrive with a stronger emotional connect and a deeper respect for the craft. We’ve seen a clear shift towards mindful collecting rather than quick purchases.” Among brands that offer a more interactive understanding of craft processes, Basement, the concept store for clothing and lifestyle label 11.11/Eleven Eleven in Delhi, stands as a noteworthy example. A large brass vat filled with indigo dye is the pièce de résistance in the store. Customers are encouraged to dip raw fabric into the liquid and witness it take on the colour, in an experience they’re not likely to forget anytime soon. While it is a globally accepted fact that brick-and-mortar fashion stores are far more than sites for transactions, it feels most relevant in India, where so much of fashion’s foundation is intricate handwork, technique and generational—as well as regional— expertise. The store is where this foundation becomes truly intelligible; the delicacy of chikankari or the raised relief of zari can rarely be understood through an image alone. Gupta says, “A physical store allows for something that digital can never fully replicate—that is, presence. It allows clients to slow down, to feel the weight of a fabric, to understand proportion, to engage with craftsmanship.” Chhabra echoes this sentiment. “Luxury is deeply tied to human interaction,” he says. “The physical store allows for a slower, more immersive engagement, where stories are shared, textures are explored and relationships are built. In that sense, reinvention is essential.”

article_title: 5 ’90s trouser trends to supercharge your wardrobe in 2026
sub_title: From capri to cropped, here are the ’90s trousers we’ll be wearing again this summer.
article_content: We’ve always loved the ’90s – but, in 2026, we You’ve got a pair of strappy heels or block boots – but what else to wear on your bottom half? Below, five ’90s-inspired trouser trends we’ll be wearing in rotation this year. Capri pants, which had a moment in the 1950s and ’60s, and then again in the late ’90s and early 2000s, are one of those weird garments that shouldn’t work but somehow just do – especially with a little low-rise heel and a spaghetti strap top. article_title: This craft school in Kutch is in the business of forging confidence
sub_title: Somaiya Kala Vidya has helped artisans gain financial autonomy in a world where craft is a buzzword
article_content: Three girls sat on a I sat with the graduating batch as they prepared for the show—passing around mood boards, swatches, Somaiya Kala Vidya (SKV) was founded with a clear belief: If craft is to remain culturally honest and economically relevant, innovation must come from within. And that Today, SKV runs as a year-long residential programme for artisans of Kutch for craftspeople from various communities. There is no age limit and no literacy requirement. On the syllabus are design principles and business management skills. Some students are as young as 16 years old. Others are in their 30s, with children to raise and households to run. The institute spends Rs 3-4 lakh per student. Men pay ₹12,000, women ₹6,000. When asked why as most artisan courses are free, Nishit Sangomla, director of SKV replied: “Deliberately so, to instil ownership without creating barriers.” The shift in gender participation is palpable. For years, women’s applications had been sporadic—none at all up till 2019, as the women had to stay on campus for the duration of the year. Elder brothers, uncles and other men would do the course but not the women. Post-pandemic, the outreach in weaving villages like Bhujodi, Gamthara and Sarli has changed that balance. On graduation night, a generation of women who had woven for years without recognition now spoke as designers, some for the first time. Some women were the first to ever practice the craft, such as The next day, I set out to meet some alumni from the school, curious to see the ripples the classroom had on their craft post completing the course. In Ajrakhpur, I met Zaid Khatri, a 10th-generation What stayed with him most vividly from the course were the drawing classes. “This was the first time I was allowed to draw, just draw,” he told me. Colour studies gave language to instincts he had always carried—grayscale, chromatic balance, colour placement. The shift was not easy. Zaid admits he struggled in school, and geometry-based modules done by hand were difficult. Yet it was through that process that his practice expanded. During market visits to Ahmedabad, including a stop at Anokhi, he began to understand customers not as abstract buyers but as individuals with their own visual worlds. In one home filled with For his final collection, he explored the idea of the eternal within Ajrakh, moving away from the traditional A similar shift appeared in the story of Kanchan, a 24-year-old carpet weaver and a graduate of the 2024 batch. Unlike many others, she was the first weaver in her family. Her father works as a driver; she first learned weaving from an aunt before training in carpet making in Bhujodi. Representatives from the school encountered her work during a village visit. They admired the carpet she had woven but asked her something she had never considered: how would she explain the design to a customer? What were its elements? What colours had she chosen and why? At the school, the first colour theory class puzzled her. “Why are we working on paper?” she wondered. Slowly the exercises revealed a different way of seeing—repeat patterns, motif abstraction. For the first time she experimented with brick repeats, drop repeats and figurative motifs like birds or camels, moving beyond the geometric forms she had always used. It also introduced collaboration. Though she is a weaver, she began working with a friend who practises Bandhani, incorporating Bandhani elements into her carpets. That year was also her first time living away from home, travelling later to Mumbai for an exhibition where she learned how customers respond to craft. The same language of design reshaped the practice of Pachan Suji, an 11th-generation Bhujodi weaver in his 40s and, at the institute, the eternal backbencher. He began weaving at 13 and spent years working simply as a karigar. “Kaam tha,” he said. There was work. When he finally enrolled in the programme—after much resistance—one classroom exercise changed his perspective. He was asked to deconstruct one of his own woven pieces and identify its design elements: positive and negative space, rhythm and repetition. “Magic,” he said.
