article_title: Why fashion illustrations will always be on our moodboards
sub_title: As artificial intelligence accelerates what can be produced cheaply, there is a call to return to the nuance and imperfection of whathumans create
article_content: Stepping out of my London hotel, Harvey Nichols. I had expected the familiar grammar of luxury retail: mannequins frozen mid-gesture, campaign faces enlarged to abstraction. Instead, drawings darted across the glass—Jacky Blue’s sketches animated on screen, stretched beyond scale, rendered in thick, confident strokes that simultaneously had a doodle-like charm. I was not new to the vocabulary of illustration. Fashion did not enter my life through proximity. It arrived obliquely, through cinema. Audrey Hepburn led me to Givenchy and Dior, and from there to Edith Head. What stayed were not only the finished garments, but the drawings that preceded them. I sketched obsessively through my years of science education, mostly in the­ margins of textbooks, copying silhouettes I could not access in any other way. When fashion felt unreachable, I drew it closer. Fashion illustrations have long functioned as a form of access for buyers and enthusiasts alike. From early costume books at 19th-century couture ateliers to campaigns in Vogue, this language was how designers and their patrons communicated. When the industry accelerated and photography made the process of creating images instant, illustration seemed to slip from the centre. Yet, a single held-back line can sometimes contain more feeling than an entire campaign. The legendary Italian fashion illustrator René Gruau understood this instinctively. His work for Dior, beginning with Miss Dior in 1947, did not merely advertise the clothing but conjured up an immersive world for the brand. A ballerina in a tutu; an ingenue’s hand resting lightly on a leopard’s paw; a woman, as seen from behind, hugging a huge bouquet of flowers—you could almost smell it. Gruau’s 20th-century drawings for Dior, Balenciaga, Schiaparelli and Givenchy shaped how modern luxury learned to look at itself. That sensibility carries forward most clearly today in the work of the English fashion illustrator David Downton. He built his reputation on drawings made fresh from Paris couture fittings each season, as well as on his live portrayals of illustrious figures—from Cate Blanchett to Linda Evangelista—rendered in his signature,­ watercolour lines that convey an air of impenetrable glamour. His art has circulated so widely that it sits pinned to moodboards and framed in private homes, absorbed into the collective visual memory of fashion. Downton arrived in Paris in 1996, just as John Galliano and Alexander McQueen were taking up their posts at Dior and Givenchy. “There was electricity in the air. I felt like I had entered Narnia and I knew I had found my métier,” says Downton. His work remains committed to being present, standing up, pacing, making decisions that cannot be undone. Downton muses, “It is an intimate experience. A mini love affair. Today, it takes an army to produce a portrait or a fashion photograph. But with a drawing, it is just you and the subject: time arrested.” Milan-based Jenny Walton, trained in real-time observation, translates that energy into her own work, sketching runway shows not to record but to respond, creating images that are as much personal impression as reportage. Which is what the major brands, from Bergdorf Goodman to Elsewhere in the world of fashion illustration, the tone shifts. New York–based Julie Houts approaches drawing not as reverence but as satire. Her images are populated by rats and fashion girls collapsed in fetal positions. Emotions spill and absurdity reigns. She sketched the industry’s contradictions, exposing its anxieties and excesses through witty text scrawled onto these illustrations. “Because fashion illustration is so limitless, it easily lends itself to pushing ideas to their most absurd, exaggerated conclusion.” At the National Institute of Design in Ahmedabad, designer David Abraham was tau­ght to emphasise drawing for its own sake—learning proportion, perspective, ratios and how to render material. How granite behaves differently from wood, chiffon from silk. These principles, he explains, are what make a drawing work. One half of the duo behind the label Abraham & Thakore, At their label, sketches are iterative and ongoing. A doodle might lead to the development of a weave in Telangana, which then returns altered through material and technique. When the fabric Illustration was my portal into the fashion industry, but you rarely see it anywhere anymore. But, it appears, the countertrend is already underway. As artificial intelligence accelerates what can be produced cheaply, there is a call to return to the nuance and imperfection of what Recently, I came across a post by a young Germany-based illustrator and motion designer, Haojing Simota: “When I was a kid, I dreamed of designing clothes and watching models strut down a runway in my creations. Then life happened, bills happened and that dream quietly packed itself away in a drawer. [But] recently I realised: dreams don’t disappear—they change shape. With drawing and animation, why not build the runway I once imagined, brush by brush, frame by frame?” It is heartening to see the return of wonder to fashion. “Because we have all become so accustomed to digital images, there is an indescribable energy in seeing an illustrator’s hand in an image,” says Houts, insisting that “ideas can feel more distilled or potent” when communicated this way. article_title: 14 brands that prove handloom textiles can go beyond saris and kurtis
sub_title: Looking cute and saving the planet is easy, actually
article_content: Long before ‘sustainable’ became a marketing buzzword, it was simply the way things were done. Handloom textiles with cotton and silk were woven with care, yard by yard, often with techniques passed down over generations. They made Today, as the industry circles back to mindful consumption, a new generation of designers is revisiting these textiles with fresh eyes. Handloom textiles, once confined to familiar silhouettes, are being reimagined into pieces that feel current and yet everlasting—easygoing separates, fluid dresses and sharp tailoring. Here are 14 brands creating with handloom textiles in ways that feel anything but expected. Shweta Gupta’s work starts with handloom cottons and silks developed alongside weavers in Chanderi, but it rarely stays predictable. Techniques like smocking, faggoting and pleat tucks show up often, adding texture in ways that feel considered. There’s a touch of whimsy in the way it all comes together, just enough to keep the clothes feeling light, a little unusual and easy to wear. Known for its focus on indigenous cotton and 100% natural dyes, 11.11 works almost entirely within a hand-process ecosystem. The label brings together techniques like hand spinning, handloom weaving, hand painting, miniature tie-dyeing and quilting, often within a single garment. Founded in 2014 by Gauri Verma and Karuna Laungani, Jodi works with natural Indian textiles, bringing in techniques like hand block printing, Founded by Rina Singh, Eka approaches handloom with a mix of research, craft and a sense of storytelling. The brand often works with repurposed and archival fabrics, keeping production small-scale. It leans soft and introspective with layered silhouettes, pastel tones and a slightly vintage mood that feels pulled from the pages of a well-loved novel. Payal Pratap works closely with weaving clusters across India, including Banaras, Bhagalpur, West Bengal and Bhagaiya, developing fabrics in small handwoven batches. The brand uses a mix of cottons, linens, silks, and wools, often finished with patchwork, smocking, and embroidery. Founded in 2013, Hannah Khiangte centres her practice around indigenous Zo textiles, working with weavers across Founded in 2018 by Manjushree Saikia, Ura Maku works with handloom textiles from Assam. Working with regional weavers, the label develops fabrics that reflect local techniques while adapting them into modern silhouettes. The aesthetic is clean and functional. Founded in 2019 by Shweta Agarwal, Āroka keeps things minimal, but not plain. The focus is on handwoven materials developed with a small cooperative in Kalna, West Bengal, with subtle weaves layering doing most of the talking. The aesthetic stays clean and pared-back, but there’s enough texture and detail to keep it from feeling too straightforward. Kritika Murarka builds collections that foreground surface technique and material. The brand often incorporates elements like hand embroidery, appliqué and textural detailing into otherwise clean silhouettes. It's contemporary with a decorative edge, structured separates and occasion-leaning pieces. Harago works with artisans across India, developing handwoven textiles in regions such as West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, and Assam, while also collaborating with craft communities like Bagru near Jaipur. Urvashi Kaur works extensively with handloom textiles sourced from weaving clusters across India, including jamdani from Bengal, leheriya from Jaipur, khadi and Bhujodi from Kutch, and Chanderi, Maheshwari, and Kota doriya. The brand builds its collections around these region-specific fabrics, treating each as a starting point for design. Since its launch in 2015, Naushad Ali has focused on working with artisans across India, building collections around heritage fabrics and traditional techniques. It keeps things relaxed with loose silhouettes and easy layering. Embroidery and playful accents show up often, adding character without taking away from the overall laid-back feel. Margn approaches handloom through a lens of minimalism and structure, often working with naturally dyed fabrics and traditional weaves. The silhouettes are clean and architectural, with an emphasis on cut, proportion and finish. Founded in 2014 by Sreejith Jeevan and based in Kochi, the brand’s approach is shaped by its setting, drawing from Kerala’s textile traditions as well as Kochi’s more eclectic, urban sensibility. Its aesthetic moves between what the designer describes as a “modern old” and a “nostalgic new”, blending familiar weaves with updated silhouettes.

article_title: How designers are reinterpreting Banarasi weaves beyond the traditional sari
sub_title: From reworked blouse constructions and unconventional styling to shawls and separates, labels are finding new ways to extend the vocabulary of Banarasi textiles
article_content: Banarasi weaves are among India’s most enduring textile traditions, their history shaped by centuries of craftsmanship, patronage and technical refinement. If the This weaving legacy stretches back centuries. Varanasi has long been associated with textile production, while the Banarasi brocade tradition, as we know it today, flourished under Mughal patronage. Over time, motifs such as kalga, bel and jaal came to define the visual language of the weave, along with intricate zari work and richly patterned silk textiles that became closely associated with ceremonial dressing and heirloom saris. Each technique on the loom offers its own refinement. From the labour-intensive Kadhwa which stands as the gold standard, each motif is woven individually into the fabric. In contrast, Fekwa introduces a lighter and more fluid structure through continuous weft work. Tanchoi, with Chinese roots that came to India by Parsi traders, favours intricately patterned silk over zari, creating an almost embossed texture. On the other hand, Jangla unveils in sweeping floral vines, while delicate Booti scatters motifs across the surface. What has changed in recent years is not the value of the weave, but the forms in which it appears. As India grows into a global fashion powerhouse, the looms of Varanasi have begun to hum to a slightly different rhythm. While tradition still shapes the craft, a new generation of designers and weavers are reimagining this textile. Designers are keeping their textile language intact while expanding where and how Banarasi can be worn. While the classic vermilion, rani pink and emerald green palette remains, the same silk and zari craftsmanship has newer interpretations which have introduced muted ivories, pistachios and metallic charcoals. Think Raw Mango’s tailored jackets, Ekaya’s breezy kaftans or Tasuvure’s relaxed Banarasi co-ord sets. “At Ekaya, there’s a lot of constant learning involved, from experimenting with scale, reworking classic patterns or exploring lighter constructions that fit better into modern wardrobes,” says Palak Shah, founder and CEO of Ekaya Banaras. This has manifested in the brand’s Silk Dialogue collection, which brought together East Asian design references and Banarasi craftsmanship. “Our silhouettes rooted in Banarasi weaving are sculpted into gowns or modern drapes, and have been met with a great deal of love from our patrons over the years,” says Amit Aggarwal, whose evolving design language at AM:IT reimagines the craft through pieces including bibs, jackets, skirts and modular separates. Weavers and artisans remain central to the story of the craft. In Varanasi, weaving is not merely an occupation but a practice passed through generations, sustaining families while preserving an aesthetic vocabulary that has long defined Indian couture. Kamya Tandon, creative director at Ushnakmal-Moolchand Banaras, says that Varanasi’s weavers meet new ideas with curiosity rather than resistance. Working with a broad community of weavers and artisans, Ushnakmal-Moolchand Banaras recently translated contemporary patterns such as houndstooth, zig-zags and checks into “For collaborations with craft clusters and artisans to translate into meaningful empowerment, they need to move beyond sporadic interventions. Crafts like Banarasi weaving support entire communities, creative empowerment also comes from engaging with the craft in a long-term manner from a place of knowledge and respect,” observes Aditi Chand, co-founder of Tilfi Banaras. Tilfi engages with artisans and craftsmen all year round rather than through seasonal inspiration or one-off collections, and artisans are involved in the ideation process as they best understand the relationship between motif and loom technique. That long-view approach isn't just about speaking to a globally informed audience; it matters in a fashion landscape shaped by shifting tastes, a desire for sustainability, and pressure to create wardrobes with longer life. For some designers, that has also meant working with existing textiles rather than only producing new ones. Aggarwal, who has been working with Banarasi weaves since 2016, believes it is his role to create a bridge between heritage craftsmanship and contemporary relevance. “In our practice, this philosophy also extends to working with pre-loved Banarasi saris, which we source and rework to give them a renewed life. By transforming textiles that already carry history and emotion, the process honours both the original craftsmanship and the artisan legacy embedded within them. These ensembles were a part of our runway collection ‘Orizon’ at Lakmē Fashion Week recently." The future of Banarasi weaving will include the sari, but no longer exclusively so. What designers are doing is not a break from tradition, but a creating a broader vocabulary for it, one that allows Banarasi textiles to travel across garments, generations and uses while remaining tied to the craft history that made them distinctive in the first place. “For me, the sari is essentially like a blank canvas,” says Shah. “The way you drape it, style it and accessorise it can completely transform how it feels. I think the future of Banarasi lies in that freedom.”

article_title: What I learnt about fashion growing up in small-town India
sub_title: What if fashion’s most original references are not imported at all?
article_content: It was a regular weeknight—the groaning of construction cranes and Mumbai’s refusal to pause playing in the back- ground as the doorbell announced the arrival of my “Looking back, it was the idea of dressing up to feel like you weren’t in something, or not part of something. It was almost a fantasy act,” he said, speaking about his I reacted to that sentiment like a Pavlovian dog, spiralling right back to my childhood. That early itch for a different world, that vague, stubborn hope that being a little odd is the point. I grew up in Lamka, Manipur, part of the wider landscape of small-town India, which is far from anything deemed “fashion”. Tin-roofed houses climbed uneven slopes, mornings smelled of Long before I saw a runway show on FashionTV, which many of the townsfolk tabooed because of the “half-naked women”, I watched my mother thrift clothes, always a size larger so they’d last me longer. One such piece was a ruby-red pair of jeans that I often paired with a black jacket boasting the deepest pockets. Now, those pockets could actually be better used for lugging around Janice, my cousin, was the first person I knew who appeared to exist in two different worlds. At least 15 years older than me, she was already living in Delhi at this point, and would come home during vacations with jewellery gathered from the city. Oxidised earrings that must have been bought in Sarojini Nagar, scarves that smelt faintly of city air. My favourite was a three-tiered beaded necklace from her Naga friend, which she hung on the wall of her bedroom. Everything she spoke about was laced with such a sense of flourish that one couldn’t help but admire her. On a bus ride to Imphal, she spoke of when she worked part-time at a perfume shop. I remember her talking about an apple-shaped It’s a sentiment I shared with designer Alan Alexander, who grew up in Thiruvananthapuram in Kerala. Far from any formal fashion ecosystem, he recounted to me how getting his first computer at 12 had expanded his worldview overnight. “I used to obsessively read articles and blogs from across the world—about fashion, costumes, art, books, culture, music, socio-political struggles, food recipes, everything under the sun,” he said. “I would download international music in languages I didn’t even speak, just to experience things unknown. All of this was information I absorbed simply for the sake of it.” “In fact,” he added, “fashion wasn’t even my first choice of career. I studied applied electronics and instrumentation before switching.” I remember a conversation I had with photographer Tenzing Dakpa, with whom I have collaborated a couple of times in the past. A second-generation Tibetan, he was raised in Gangtok, “Fashion as a personification came from adopting musical influences and style as a way to identify yourself with a certain temperament.” At another point, almost apologetically, he added, “It’s photography and description that I’m interested in. Fashion almost becomes a by-product of that process.” Fashion, for many of us growing up in small-town India, doesn’t begin with proximity to its industry or access to its institutions, but with a desire to imagine another life, or to make sense of the one you’re already in. By the time the episode ended, the city was still grumbling outside. But so was my mind. Who actually gets to shape fashion’s language? It struck me how often we look outward for inspiration, building moodboards with borrowed references from Pinterest when the original vocabulary was already formed around us. Long before we even knew what to call it.

article_title: Is Gen Z's personal style in its copy-paste era?
sub_title: Everyone wants to stand out using the same references
article_content: We have all seen that photograph of young women posed against an autumn backdrop in The skinny jean has since been declared over, and the Katniss Everdeen Enter the baby tee and cargo pants. Or the cropped white T-shirt with wide-leg jeans, slick bun, tiny shoulder bag and trainers that have been aggressively workshopped to look accidental. This outfit would like you to believe it came together instinctually, that you simply got dressed and happened to emerge looking like a fully formed aesthetic. Curious, then, how so many other people had the same spontaneous thought. Blindfold yourself and throw a pebble in any direction in Bandra or Hauz Khas. Your next five strawberry matchas are on me if you don’t hit at least three people wearing some version of this look. A ten-minute scroll on Instagram will confirm it just as efficiently. This isn’t the death of personal style so much as its outsourcing. Fashion has always been tied to the desire to feel distinct, to look like yourself and not like everyone else. It gives you a feeling of control over your identity. Now that anyone can copy anything instantly, that urge to assert individuality has only grown stronger. The more style starts to look the same, the more people want to stand out. As What someone wears no longer comes only from what they genuinely like. It increasingly has to look deliberate, as though every choice was made on purpose. And some people deal with this by sticking to a uniform. When you’re constantly being exposed to new ‘cores’ and aesthetics, the easiest response is to stop playing along and stick to basics. And even this “uniform” is not outside of the system; it is a result of it. Either way, there is no clean way out of that loop. What emerges instead is a version of personal style that feels increasingly formulaic. Originality may still exist, but in a culture of endless reference and instant replication, it has become harder to recognise and even harder to prove.

article_title: This one-of-a-kind bejewelled angrakha blouse is a tribute to Jaipur's Johri Bazaar
sub_title: Rooted in Abhishek Raniwala’s childhood memories of Johri Bazaar, Raniwala 1881 reimagines the angrakha as a wearable heirloom shaped by multiple specialised artisans
article_content: Back in the 18th century, Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II envisioned a city that would serve as the heart of trade in Northern India. At the heart of it all was “I used to accompany my grandfather to Johri Bazaar as a child,” recalls Raniwala. “I’d observe how he’d meet all kinds of people and how much respect they gave him. We’d walk and spend hours in the market just visiting different workshops and talking about jewellery. Johri Bazaar became like an office for us. It is not a confined unit, it’s one large office where everyone plays their part.” The jewellery house’s newest creation, the Bejewelled Rani Ratna Angrakha, emerges from this memory. Crafted using approximately 840 grams of gold and But why the form of an angrakha? For Raniwala, the reasoning was twofold: First, to demonstrate that Johri Bazar and Rajasthan’s jewellery and sartorial traditions are not relics but living, evolving practices that have continually adapted to new silhouettes and techniques. This, he says, is the energy he wants Angrakha to embody for the next 100 years. At the same time, the house was determined to move beyond the conventional boundaries of jewellery and create something fluid and wearable. By choosing a garment-inspired form, The convergence of jewellery and garments has been a catalyst for iconic fashion moments throughout history: from Paco Rabanne’s legacy of bags from metallic discs, chainmail and even 18-carat gold medallions, to Alexander McQueen and British jewellery designer Shaun Leane’s ‘Coiled Corset’ in the ’90s, to modern-day labels like Misho that have extended sculptural metalwork into corsets and The team at Raniwala 1881 drew on their collective knowledge of jewellery crafts, archives and modern software to conceptualise the Angrakha. Despite being a part of the ecosystem since his formative years, Raniwala found himself surprised at the intricacies of balancing different crafts in one piece. “Every craft has its own hand movement and flow. A meenakari artisan cannot perform jadau. A stone cutter cannot perform meenakari. If a piece is half-done by one artisan and given to another mid-process, the difference will show. Coordinating all of that was tedious. There was a lot of planning, mapping and timing involved.” The Bejewelled Rani Ratna Angrakha is currently on display at the Raniwala 1881 Atelier in Jaipur, and Raniwala hopes it will travel in the coming years. “This is a little contribution from our design house that celebrates Johri Bazaar and Jaipur and helps young people feel connected to this legacy even years from now.”

article_title: 5 Vogue-approved tips on method dressing for the job you want
sub_title: Dress for the job you want
article_content: While the common focus is, of course, what to wear for an interview, there’s also a case to be made for how you wear it being just as important. You can’t control what people choose to fixate on, but you can make sure your outfit isn’t the thing pulling focus from your ideas. That tension has resurfaced lately thanks to the rise of “method dressing” on the red carpet. Celebrities like And that applies just as much in places without photographers. The interview room. The lobby waiting area. The Michelle Obama recently spoke on a podcast about how her outfits often received more attention than her ideas, especially in interviews. It’s a sharp reminder of something many people already know instinctively: what you wear and how you turn up can shape how your ideas are received, sometimes before you’ve even spoken. So consider this your permission slip to method dress for an interview. Better still, most of the smartest interview styling choices aren’t about buying something new but editing what you already own, and wearing it like you mean it. Below, five of the most wearable method dressing “roles” for what to wear for an interview. If you’re confused, start here. This combination works across almost every industry because it looks polished without trying too hard. Wear it with a fitted tee or shirt, tailored bottoms and closed-toe mules. It works because it looks serious without feeling stiff. Add a pair of dainty silver earrings, just enough to complete the look without taking focus away from it. The sweet spot is to look interesting without making that the only thing you are all about. Try tonal separates and add one point of tension: a sharply framed pair of glasses, an architectural bag or a “personality” shoe. If you hate shirts, don’t force it. A fine knit top can look just as sharp, and often more modern. There’s a particular kind of drip in looking like you’re not fighting your outfit. The main trick? Nothing should need constant adjusting. If you’re interviewing for a senior role or a job that’s client-facing, you want to look like the person they’d trust in a room that matters. This isn’t about going overly corporate; it’s about looking grounded. Think sharp tailoring, elevated basics and a great coat if the weather allows. The energy should be: “I can represent this company without trying too hard.” Video interviews are their own genre. Your outfit needs to work in a tight frame and under lighting that can be unkind. Clean necklines will always look more composed than anything overly dressed up. The biggest trick is avoiding too casual from the waist up: if you look like you’re on a coffee run, it changes how you’re received, even if your answers are brilliant.

article_title: Ananti: Inside a label built on craft and longevity
sub_title: A closer look at the thinking, process, and influences behind the brand
article_content: Getting dressed once meant saving your most elaborate outfit for a single, standout moment. Today, it’s about finding pieces that feel worth returning to. Ananti designs with that sensibility, creating ethnic wear that balances occasion dressing with longevity. Working within the framework of classical Indian silhouettes—anarkalis, lehengas, kurta sets, shararas—the brand refines tradition through a contemporary lens, preserving familiar forms while subtly updating how they look, feel, and move today. Founded with a deep respect for Indian craft, Ananti approaches design as a layered, thoughtful process. Each garment begins with detailed hand-drawn sketches that guide both embroidery and silhouette together. The outcome is clothing that feels considered and complete, where every element has a purpose, and nothing feels excessive. Across its collections, embroidery is treated with precision and intent. About 10-15 handwork techniques come together within a single piece, creating depth through careful placement rather than density. The brand works with minimalist embellishment materials—ranging from 0 mm to 2 mm—using fine Japanese katdana, kora, dabka, badla, sequins, and resham in balanced proportions. Motifs emerge gradually, revealing themselves up close rather than announcing themselves at first glance. Inspiration flows from a wide cultural vocabulary. Indian architecture forms a foundation, with patterns drawn from jharokhas, vintage glasswork, hand-painted walls, and traditional flooring patterns, as well as heritage jewellery and classical art forms. Even classical music plays a role with ragas often used to set the emotional tone of a collection, and whether it’s going to be serene, regal or celebratory. This philosophy is inseparable from its founder, whose years working closely with artisans and ateliers continue to shape the brand’s approach. D: I come from a small town called Jetpur in Gujarat, where both my parents were government school principals. I was initially drawn to interior design, but later discovered my passion for fashion and moved to Bombay to pursue it. After graduating in fashion design in 2009, I worked in export houses, particularly as an embroidery designer under the mentorship of Shamina Talyarkhan. Working on projects for designers like Karl Lagerfeld, Dolce & Gabbana, Zuhair Murad, and Armani shaped my understanding of embroidery techniques, motifs, and silhouettes. After nine years in the industry, I felt ready to build my own label and bring my design philosophy to life. D: We’re focusing on strengthening our digital presence, curated exhibitions, and building meaningful relationships with our clients. The goal is steady, thoughtful growth—aligned with our design philosophy. At a moment when occasionwear often leans toward visual excess, Ananti proposes a more measured approach. Defined by precision, heritage, and clarity of design, the label places its faith in craft and form and allows restraint to become its signature, rather than embellishment.

article_title: Sonam Kapoor’s lime Shehlaa Khan ensemble reworked Mughal florals in paint and zardozi
sub_title: Rhea Kapoor styled the look with layers of jewellery
article_content: In February 2026, Sonam Ahuja Kapoor celebrated her second pregnancy with a godh bharai ceremony, hosted by her family. For the occasion, the mother-to-be opted for a bespoke outfit by friend and designer Shehlaa Khan. The lime look was conceived in close collaboration with Kapoor’s sister and stylist Rhea Kapoor. “We wanted to do something special and still use a signature style of my label,” Khan shares. What they arrived at was a silhouette that is thoughtful and comfortable, featuring a bubble skirt, a contoured blouse and a flowing kimono cape, defined by a classic Indian-style dupatta. “Given that it's an Indian godh bharai, the only thing contemporary about the outfit was its silhouette,” explains Khan. Despite that deliberate modernity of form, the overall impression is traditional. On Kapoor, the structure of the blouse and the volume of the bubble skirt introduced a sculptural quality, whereas the kimono cape softened the look with fluid movement. The starting point for the look’s embellishment was unambiguous in its ambition. “The idea was to resemble a Mughal style painting, and therefore we used the signature hand-painting technique as the base of the embellishment on a Chanderi silk fabric. which is rich yet represents a vintage Indian aesthetic.” Mughal miniature painting, which flourished as a courtly artform between the 16th and 18th centuries, is defined by vibrant mineral pigments and an obvious synthesis of Indian, Persian and European influences. The paintings are celebrated for their realistic portraiture and naturalistic depictions of flora and fauna, and this is the exact visual language that Khan has translated onto fabric. The hand-painted crimson blossoms and brushed-gold leaves were elevated through zardozi embroidery worked in nakshi and saadi materials. “The festive nature of the event required some sparkles, to give the look of Zari work used in extensive garments of women from royalty in the Mughal era," Khan adds. “The outfit was a very intricate yet heartfelt tribute to the relationship Sonam holds with the brand since its early years," adds Khan. “It took a long time and several hours of handwork of various artisans to bring this outfit together.” Colour, too, Khan says, played a defining role in shaping the mood. “We chose lime because Sonam loves green but yet wanted it to be a bright and a happy shade for the joyous occasion.” Rhea styled her look with jewellery that blended heirloom sentiment with artisanal charm. The necklace and earrings were from Kapoor’s personal collection, while the ring and gucha came from Amrapali Jewels, the hathphool, waist belt and pearl kadas from Sheetal Zaveri, and additional kadas from Maalka By Varun Haria and Falguni Mehta.

article_title: How to style a red dress without looking like a walking Valentine’s Day card
sub_title: Vogue's guide on how to wear the world’s most high-maintenance colour
article_content: Whether it’s bombshell dressing for This isn’t about reinventing your wardrobe or saving red exclusively for evenings out. Instead, it’s about subtle shifts in styling: unexpected pairings, pared-back accessories and a willingness to let contrast do the work. Red doesn’t need help commanding attention; it needs grounding. The mood now is about seeing bold pieces through a cooler, offbeat lens. Keep reading for Vogue’s guide on how to style a red dress in ways that feel current and entirely your own. A red dress is already doing most of the talking. Rather than competing with it, keep accessories minimal: a single gold cuff, black leather heels, or a metallic mini bag will add polish without distraction. Red-on-red styling can easily tip into literal territory; neutrals and metals keep things sharp. If there’s one styling choice that can instantly recalibrate a red dress, it’s footwear. Classic heels will always work, but they also reinforce red’s reputation as an evening-only colour. Instead, grounding the look with flatter, more pragmatic shoes makes the dress feel wearable and modern. The safest route is a boxy blazer or a clean trench to keep it chic. For contrast, an oversized denim jacket or a leather trench works well, adding just enough friction to stop the look from feeling too “done.” Think of outerwear as something to steady the look. For daytime or transitional weather, layering is key. Wear a red dress over a crisp white shirt or a fitted t-shirt to instantly make it feel less dressy. This approach pulls red firmly into everyday territory, away from its eveningwear reputation. Skip the red lip cliché, go for bronzed skin, nude lips with a softly smoked eye. If you must go red, make it deep and matte. Keep your hair sleek and straight, or tousled and undone for that effortless contrast to the high-impact colour.

article_title: Femininity, functionality, sensuality: Maria Grazia Chiuri on her return to Fendi
sub_title: Maria Grazia Chiuri was announced Chief Creative Officer of Fendi six months after her exit from Dior. It's where she began her career in 1989.
article_content: Staring down the barrel of Maria Grazia Chiuri’s kohl-framed gaze, I feel suddenly uneasy. “Designers who are men can do womenswear,” she says with heavy irony. “But designers who are women cannot do menswear.” I’ve just delivered a question about what will, in June, be her first menswear show as Warming up, she raises an eyebrow, smiles, and leans forward. “Because geniuses are only men! Creative people, only men!” She pauses, as if to consider: “ What about Wait. What about Chiuri’s own record of changemaking? In 2016 she became Christian Dior’s first-ever female Creative Director (of womenswear, haute couture, and accessories, but not menswear). Over the next nine years her feminocentric, feminist, collaborative approach to design and storytelling at the French house surely changed that discourse: because while yes, her collections sometimes divided the critics, they nearly always entranced the clients. And along the way, by the way, she close-to quadrupled revenues. “Yes, and everybody remembers me because I did the big number in Dior! When a male designer does a big number, [it is because] he has a sense of business. But if a woman designer does a big number, it is because she is In the face of friendly fire, it’s time to deflect. Let’s bring it back to Fendi, where Chiuri was announced Chief Creative Officer last October, six months after her departure from Dior. Fendi is where, aged 24, Chiuri takes control. “The Fendi sisters too. Everybody speaks only about Karl Lagerfeld, like they did nothing. I’m sorry, eh.” She laughs a full laugh, and the balloon is punctured. “I’m sorry eh! Boring possibly, but also tangibly true: just run a comparison of the number of female creative directors in top fashion houses as compared to male. And as Chiuri says, however, that she has not rejoined Fendi to prove any personal point. “I’m here to give back what they gave to me.” She adds: “I worked here for a long time, in another time, when fashion was completely different. This was a very small company, a family company. I learned so much at Fendi. I think for my generation it was incredible to work with the founders.” She is still full of admiration for the Fendi sisters, under whom she worked so long. “These were five women from Rome who called Karl Lagerfeld in Paris, before he was at Chanel, in 1965. I think that was not so normal, to maintain your tradition and background but at the same time to have a conversation with someone who is completely innovative and from a completely different camp. They were great visionaries.” Chiuri departed Fendi in 1999, shortly before it was acquired by LVMH. She left with Nearly 30 years after leaving it, the Fendi she has returned to, she says: “is different like all the brands today are different. The organization is different and the dimensions are different. And when I left, Fendi was a family company.” Which is not to say, of course, that the culture of Fendi’s present owner LVMH is unfamiliar to her: Dior is one of its subsidiaries, and leading that great French house for so long has given her another layer of experience and learning. Now the sum of all her experience is being applied to shaping a new phase for Fendi. Her arrival, she believes, coincides with the dawn of a broader period of evolution in the luxury fashion arena. “We are moving into another moment. I think the big impact in this system was about the new media. Everybody started to speak about fashion. Because fashion became more popular, there were not only the journalists and the people that know about fashion speaking about fashion. The impact of all these voices was very strong, but not all the time positive. I think part of it became an entertainment. But in the end, it [fashion] is not that.” She continues: “I think we have an idea that is more the narrative of this job, and less the reality of this job. Sometimes the narrative is that you [the designer] are there, like a light from the sky, and you just make a sketch… The reality is more complex. It is really teamwork. There are so many different technical skills.” But doesn’t she acknowledge that this complexity, even if true, is challenging to digest for those who prefer to enjoy the fantasy and image of fashion? “Yes. And we arrive at a point that could be more crucial to have a name for something, or a narrative, and you don’t see if someone Tomorrow’s fall 2026 show in Milan will be the first opportunity to transmit the energy of Chiuri’s new formula of desire at Fendi outside the closed circuit of her team. Asked to sell the essence of that formula, Chiuri again raises an eyebrow. “I am probably not a good seller! But I synthesize my vision for Fendi in this show. In the silhouette. In the accessories. In the shoes. For women and for men also—there will be some men in the show too, absolutely, because we did the collections together. I work in parallel with the two teams like they are the same team.” As previously established, however, Chiuri will also present a show during the menswear week in June. What about the accessories, traditionally alongside fur the core of the house’s offer? “Accessories are very important. We are working on every single category: sunglasses, jewelry, everything. I am trying to define all the iconic elements of the house and to put them all in order, these codes. This is very important. Sometimes—and not just for Fendi—the idea to communicate Chiuri says she is moving away from the recent orthodoxy to use branding as decoration through monograms, to return instead towards presenting a range of embroidered and other applied materials that can reflect the individual personalities of the clients. She says, “that was part of the story with the Baguette and the Peekaboo too.” She adds: “The logo is a signature. It is not decorative.” In order to clarify that signature, she recruited Leonardo Sonnoli to “renovate” the house Double-F logo and font. “I think we have to use it only with products that are right for the logo,” she adds: “not for all.” Instead of via the branding of its logo, Chiuri plans for Fendi to communicate itself through the substance of its silhouette. “Because I think we are now working in another time in the fashion industry, my point of view is very focused on the silhouette. It is important to define the silhouette of Fendi. And really that is the silhouette of the coat. The coat, the jacket. That is my job. And also what kind of women and men are the references.” Before Fendi became so famous for its accessories (an achievement of which Chiuri was a part) it was most renowned for the sophistication and richness of its furs. These were predominantly worn as coats and jackets. Each Fendi sister was responsible for a different element of their development and presentation, and Chiuri considered the core characteristics of the sisters while shaping this new silhouette. She says, “the reference is the sisters. They were very creative, but also pragmatic: they worked. So the way they were was very… functional. Then sensuality is very important also, because the element of fur is about something soft, light, and very close to sensuality. For Fendi, fur and feeling are the same.” To hear Chiuri mention fur unprompted is something of a surprise. While the house has never ceased producing its In 2021, during his four year period as Fendi’s Artistic Director of ready-to-wear, Kim Jones began showing couture beyond fourrure in Paris. Chiuri indicates she plans to continue it, without disclosing exactly when. She says, “It’s not possible to define everything at the beginning. You have to go step by step. I really want to do couture, but only when we are ready. Because it is very important to work on the global project, and the global vision. I’m happy because this first collection is the first step.” Another key step will be the simultaneous release of Chiuri’s first campaign for the house created with Jo Ann Callis, an artist whose lens of subversive honesty and self-possession seems finely aligned with that of the designer. These steps begin a journey Chiuri had neither any obligation nor need to embark upon. We are speaking in the Teatro della Cometa, the jewel-like 1950s theatre at the foot of Rome’s Capitoline hill that Chiuri bought and “For me Fendi is very important,” she says, and repeats: “so it’s very important to give back what they gave to me.” Then she leans forward again, gaze fixed. “Between us, I really have love for all the fashion brands. Not only Fendi. I really Before luxury’s recruitment consultants reach en masse for their phones, there is no doubt that for the foreseeable future Chiuri’s studies will remain solely focused upon the founders she knows most intimately: the Fendis. Chiuri demurs at the suggestion that her work ahead might also contain some autobiographical elements, drawn from her memories of arriving here for her first job, aged 24. “It’s difficult for me now to see myself then,” she says, shaking her head. And yet comparing her conversation today with her characterization of the sisters—as creatively imaginative yet pragmatically orderly, as hard-working yet passionate—suggests powerfully that Fendi’s new phase will also hew true to the soul of Maria Grazia Chiuri.

article_title: Is the male gaze evolving?
sub_title: Sometimes I dress like a boy, but my straight boyfriend still thinks I look cute
article_content: My Fast-forward 18 months, and my style has only become more ‘tomboy femme’. My jeans are baggier than ever. I own more vests and structured tops than I need. And yet, my skirt collection is at an all-time high (I now own four). If you happen to rummage through my wardrobe, you'll see lace and frills peeking through. I dress based on how I’m feeling—whether that’s a basic tank top and Which raises the question: are men evolving? Is the male gaze loosening its grip on the deep cleavage and hip-hugging silhouette? Or have some men simply learned to see fashion as expression, an extension of the women they love? “I’m not really going to change myself to make someone I’m dating more comfortable,” shares New York–based creator Teo Marcella. Marcella, who is in a four-year relationship with their boyfriend, admits there was temptation in the beginning to lean into dressing a certain way, but they pushed against it. “I held my own ground in what I knew was comfortable for me. And I think, honestly, that authenticity has allowed us to develop a really strong foundation.” Marcella grew up with a very specific kind of femininity. “As a kid, I was very girly, looking at the stars of Disney Channel. It was all very feminine.” But with time, they realised they felt “so much more comfortable and so much more in my body dressing androgynously. I still like to have a feminine face, but I love a masc outfit,” shares Marcella. Interestingly, they notice how the world responds. “When I’m dressed more masculine, there’s less chivalry from people around. People might hold doors for me less [often], but I’ll hold doors [open] for people. I’ll help people out of cars. Something interesting happens with my energy there.” Aastha Gaur, a Los Angeles–based creator and senior director of design at Google, describes her style as existing between chill and commanding, rather than feminine or masculine. “Imagine a T-shirt and jeans,” she says. “More chill would be wearing a cardigan. More commanding would be wearing a Growing up in India, Gaur identified as a tomboy early on. “I had this sense of boys having more freedom than girls. Later, as a postgraduate student in LA, she swung hard in the opposite direction with frills, dresses and hyperfemininity before realising it wasn’t her. “Eventually, I settled into a place where it’s not masculine, it’s not feminine. It’s somewhere in the middle. That feels better.” In high school, a senior once warned her, “You dress like a boy. You should know that men are not attracted to that.” The comment lodged itself somewhere in her brain. Years later, when she started dating her now husband, she briefly tried to course-correct. “I went shopping and bought this grey frilly dress. I don’t think I wore it more than once. I was like, OK, I cannot do this. It’s just not me.” “I do think overall he is very secure in his masculinity and who he is,” she says. “So he doesn’t feel like his wife has to be feminine or look feminine to project a certain kind of image.” It helps that he’s a designer. “If he likes something, he’ll just say, ‘Oh wow, that looks cool, babe.’ It’s not limited to any specific kind of outfit. He sees the colour composition, the shapes.” In other words, he has taste. Marcella echoes that dynamic. “He absolutely loves it,” they say of their partner’s reaction to their personal style. “He’s very fashion-forward himself and it’s been great because we get to share closets.” Which, quite frankly, is the final frontier of any relationship. I see it in my own relationship, too. I’ll show my boyfriend pieces I’m considering buying and genuinely take his opinion on my outfits into account, which, to my perpetual shock, often improve the look. He runs his clothes by me, loves going shopping together, sends me reels of clothes he thinks I'll like and always has a new pair of Of course, not all responses are enlightened. Gaur points out that when she receives hate from men, it often stems from discomfort. “It can be threatening to see a woman showing up in a powerful way. Because in those minds, masculinity equals power. Men expect women to dress a certain way because I think they’re explicitly looking for softness, which to them is weakness.” Which brings us back to the original question: are men evolving? Maybe some are. Maybe the male gaze is splintering. Maybe there’s a growing cohort of men who find autonomy attractive, who are secure in their own masculinity and their femininity. They understand design, appreciate shape and proportion and find any well-put-together outfit as compelling as a body-con gown. Or maybe, it’s just really hot when a woman dresses like a man.

article_title: Priyanka Chopra Jonas returns to the Oscars 2026 in a white Dior gown with a feather-trimmed slit
sub_title: A sculpted bodice and diagonal draping through the waist shape the white gown’s streamlined silhouette
article_content: Priyanka Chopra Jonas returned to the Oscars red carpet in a white Dior gown that moves from a sharply cut bodice into a fluid skirt. The strapless neckline curves into an angular sweetheart shape, while the bodice holds firm through the waist. Below, the dress changes direction as fabric gathers diagonally across the hips, drawing the eye toward one side before falling into the skirt. That shift introduces movement through the midsection and breaks the straight line of the bodice. A high slit runs through the skirt, edged with feather trimming along the opening. The feathers sit only along that cut of the fabric rather than across the entire skirt, forming a narrow band of texture against the white base. As Chopra Jonas walked the carpet and later stepped on stage to present, the feathered edge lifted and settled with her stride. She wore high jewellery from Bvlgari’s Eclecttica collection, including a diamond necklace set with a vivid blue centre stone and matching rings. Her hair was worn long and sleek with a side part, brushed over one shoulder. The makeup followed a warm, muted palette: softly smoked eyes, bronzed skin and a nude lip. Her return this year favoured clean tailoring and controlled texture over elaborate embellishment, allowing the silhouette and the feathered movement of the skirt to register from a distance. “Rethink the white gown for a corporate outing, opt for a white suit and if you want to add a little bit of play, you can don a suit with a feather trim on the sleeve hem. The sleekness or sharpness of the look depends on the cut of the suit and the clean lines. Opt for trousers that are straight, slim-legged, and fall over your stilettos. A clean watch and an ear cuff to complete the look,” says Divya Balakrishnan, Vogue India fashion associate.

article_content: As something of a maestro when it comes to setting colour trends, Interestingly, this creamy note somewhat preempted But, of course, what might be a succour to one person, enabling them to feel cool, calm and collected, could simply be, well, slightly boring to someone else, who perhaps feels invisible or even sad in stealth-wealth neutrals. Luckily, the spring/summer 2026 collections didn’t just cater to one school of thought but, instead, offered up multiple colour theories for contemplation. Prada’s show contained typically “off” gradations, including, but not limited to, canary yellow, lime green and turquoise blue. Naturally, they did the job of making certain garments – fluid knee-length skirts attached to a set of braces or, equally, knickers with a pair of pockets on either side – look even more outlandish (and brilliant, obviously). Elsewhere, bold colour-blocking was interspersed with easy-to-wear shades like black, white and chocolate. This was very much present and correct at It would also be remiss not to consider the most recent autumn/winter 2026 runways, which confirmed that bold colour will be everywhere at the tail end of the year too. It’s one thing to appreciate a colour as it comes down the catwalk. But, as easy as it might be to get swept up in a designer’s singular vision, recasting your wardrobe in electrically-charged hues as opposed to basic navy or beige, it will first pay to consider what colours feel like “you”. To help, we’ve dissected 10 colour trends that you could add to your roster ahead of the new season. Fuchsia made its presence felt on the catwalk at Alaïa, where a knitted skirt, falling in asymmetric pleats that zig-zagged up one calf, was the definition of “hot pink.” And it didn't stop there. At Chloé, puff-sleeved fuchsia crop tops were somewhat neutralised by sensible khaki skirts. Meanwhile over at Conner Ives, the shade was practically top-to-toe, with one outfit comprising a collar-popped tracksuit top, a fringed skirt and toe-thong Prada is always one-to-watch for what trends will cut through over the next six months, not least because of the way Ms. Prada manages to make any colour an interesting proposition (even the brand’s actual runway was a glossed clementine orange). Despite the profusion of shades, it was this particular Jil Sander’s spring/summer 26 collection was a lesson in “less is more”, with a focus on Klein Blue, a saturated primary-coloured shade that appeared on single-breasted coats, soft-power dresses and cropped jumpers. Eye-popping in some ways, but grounded in others, you won’t regret inviting its exuberance into your wardrobe, as long as it’s tempered by opaque black tights or a wool skirt in white. Tomato is a non-mover when it comes to colour trends – but for spring/summer 26, there’s a twist. At We’ve already discussed the relevance of Pantone’s “ For one of the most exciting debuts at Paris Fashion Week, Loewe’s creative-director duo, Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, delivered something of a wham-bam colour palette featuring searing primary shades. This green – or more accurately emerald – was particularly head-turning, especially when rendered as this clean take on While navy has long been a mainstay of the modern wardrobe, the autumn/winter 2026 collections offered elevated new interpretations of the shade. At Burberry, it appeared across an entire spectrum of textures, from plissé taffeta to buttery leather accessories, proving how much depth a single hue can hold. Ferragamo and If fuchsia is the grown-up way to wear pink, bubble gum is its playful younger sibling. Designers embraced the saccharine shade in glossy fabrics and sharply-cut silhouettes, giving the Barbie-approved hue a fresh dose of fashion credibility. At A softer alternative to navy, powder blue emerged as a key transitional shade across both seasons. At Chanel, it softened the house’s signature tweeds and polished accessories, while Erdem applied it to fluid silks adorned with delicate embroidery and embellishment. There’s an inherent calmness to powder blue, but in 2026, it feels far from sleepy. Styled alongside deeper blues, rich reds, chocolate browns or flashes of pink, the shade becomes quietly powerful. At Marni, Meryll Rogge’s highly anticipated debut as creative director set the tone with a palette of pastels punctuated by bursts of brightness. Among the standouts was butter yellow, a shade that has been steadily gaining traction for several seasons. Look out for creamy-toned variations rather than acidic brights. When styled with chocolate brown, navy or cream, butter yellow behaves almost like a neutral, which is precisely what makes it one of the most wearable colour trends of the year.

article_content: When Sonali Bendre arrived at filmmaker Sooraj Barjatya’s daughter’s wedding reception, she set the tone for the summer with a vibrant kurta set. Dressed in a colourful ensemble by Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla, the actor embraced a vibrant palette that brought together craft and comfort. Featuring a straight, pheran-style kurta, the actor’s look is composed of striking multi-coloured panels in shades of orange, aquamarine and yellow. It was rounded off with coordinated palazzo pants and an airy orange dupatta. The interplay of colour blocking and traditional craft lent the outfit a bohemian spirit, yet its tailored structure ensured it remained Reception-ready. According to Abu Jani and Sandeep Khosla, the set belongs to their ‘Banjara’ repertoire, a line that celebrates nomadic craft traditions through contemporary silhouettes. “Sonali Bendre is a joyous vision in Banjara by Abu Sandeep,” the designer duo shared. “The freshest peach, blue and yellow pastel hues come alive to create the perfect sartorial welcome to spring. The patchwork kali kurta, crafted in silk, features multicolour resham embroidery punctuated with mirror work.” The designers also note that the piece draws inspiration from their vintage’ Rabadi’ collection, translating heritage techniques into a modern context. The result is what they describe as “bohemian grace reinvented for the 21st century woman, where craft, art and attitude converge in spirited harmony.” A memoni and organza dupatta adds a wispy contrast to the rich fabric and intricate embroidered surface of the kurta. Bendre styled the look with a sculptural gold choker with matching drop earrings and stacked kadas. Metallic stilettos and a clutch served as the finishing touches. For glam, she went with a matte base and smoky eyes in shades of burnt orange that complemented the palette of the outfit, along with a nude pink lipstick. article_content: Minimalist, elegant, powerful: When we think about the heel trends and While the Of course, going vintage should be a top priority, but there’s also plenty of cool-girl brands articulating their own fresh takes on the ’90s stompers. Here are the six key heel trends shining this season. The two-tone heeled shoes are so back, all thanks to The Nostalgia really is the name of the game among shoe designers, but many are adding a more modern edge, too. Last season, Gucci reinvented its iconic red Ancora If there is one pair of heels that screams ’90s, it’s the mule. article_title: Sharvari’s Torani lehenga showcased 2,000 hours of zardozi, dapka and marodi handwork
sub_title: The actor’s lotus pink and sage lehenga was paired with jewellery by Sunita Shekhawat
article_content: At a wedding reception where moody and metallic tones typically dominate after dark, Sharvari made a case for the softer side of eveningwear. The actor's pastel lehenga by Torani is proof that powdery palettes can hold their own. The lehenga is crafted in raw silk and complemented with a scalloped blouse with full sleeves and a translucent sage organza dupatta. For designer Karan Torani, the inspiration lies deep within Indian mythological storytelling. “This ensemble draws its spirit from the eternal poetry of Raas Leela, the divine dance of Radha and Krishna that has lived for centuries in Indian miniature paintings, temple murals and oral folklore,” he says. “I was imagining Radha standing quietly by the banks of the Yamuna in Vrindavan, a figure suspended between devotion and romance, surrounded by blooming gardens, peacocks and the music of the flute.” That imagery informed the soft lotus pink and sage colours of the garment. Torani envisioned the outfit “to feel almost like an Indian figurine coming to life,” he explains. The silhouette, too, borrows from historical Indian dress forms. “The choli draws from the classic angiya, a form that has existed in Indian dress traditions for centuries, interpreted with gentle, sculpted cuts to give it a contemporary elegance while retaining its modest, full-sleeved romanticism.” Across the lehenga, Torani’s signature visual language appears through scalloped borders, chintz florals and the Airavata elephant motif. Equally compelling is the surface ornamentation on the lehenga. “The entire surface is enriched with traditional hand techniques–zardozi, dapka, marodi, badla and kinari work–each painstakingly layered by artisans who have inherited these skills across generations. When these techniques come together, the garment begins to feel less like fabric and more like a tapestry,” Torani reveals. The process required more than 2,000 hours of handwork, with every scallop and motif positioned deliberately. “A small detail that brings it all together is the heart-shaped ‘Dilbar’ potli.” Styled by Tanya Ghavri, Sharvari’s lehenga was completed with jewellery from Sunita Shekhawat. Pieces from the Jaipur-based label’s Padmapriya collection brought in lotus and parrot motifs inspired by Goddess Lakshmi. Her chandbalis with kaan phool showcased intricate champlevé and delicate gulabi meenakari and they were paired with a ring from the label’s Heritage collection.

article_title: Sharvari’s Aditi Gupta lehenga puts its weight in a scallop-edged blouse
sub_title: The skirt carries pattern through panels and borders, leaving the heaviest surface work at the top
article_content: Sharvari chose a pearl-gold lehenga by Aditi Gupta for Up close, the lehenga reveals a careful layering of textiles. Panels of silk, zari tissue and jacquard Banarasi are pieced together in vertical sections, broken up by jharokha-inspired motifs and elongated paisley embroidery. The patterning moves downward rather than outward, giving the skirt weight without getting weighed down. The blouse introduces the most visual interest. Cut with a deep plunge neckline and scalloped edges, it is densely embroidered with paisley motifs that continue around the back. The embroidery shifts from compact geometry at the bodice to looser bead and pearl detailing along the straps and edges. At the back, tassel ties and beadwork added movement, making the blouse as considered from behind as it was from the front. Stylist Tanya Ghavri accessorises Sharvari's look with heritage jewellery by Razwada Jewels, featuring a statement choker, earrings and bangles worked in gold and stones. Hair is pulled back in a no-makeup makeup beauty look. “Pull the look away from overt bridal territory by editing it down rather than adding more. Skip the heavy necklace, soften the hair into a loose, low tie or knot, and let the blouse and skirt do the work. Drape the dupatta in a classic shoulder throw and secure it to the blouse with a brooch above the left side of the bust; let the ends fall. Keep jewellery minimal to one element at a time, lose the polki necklace to let the earrings breathe,” says Vogue India fashion associate Manglien Gangte.

For the occasion, the south star wore heritage on her sleeves, turning to a revival Banarasi Iktara weave from the Label Sourav Das. Rendered in a pistachio green that looks time-honoured yet freshly calibrated for now, the sari breaks from the primary jewel tones typically associated with Banarasi drapes. The silk canvas is scattered with gold woven buttis, while a rich border and pallu elevates it. “Samantha’s is wearing a quintessential Hazar Buiti Asharfi Sikka revival Banarasi sari with a bygone angri border woven in finer counts of mulberry silk. It also has konias on either side of the pallu. The sari is woven with Kaduwa method in Iktara style with hand-beaten patua zari,” shares Sourav Das. The Iktara, also known as single thread, technique offers not just strength and smoothness but also a fluid fall and a resilient life that’s prized by connoisseurs. Banarasi saris have long occupied a rarefied place in Indian wardrobes. Their lineage traces back centuries of royal patronage and painstaking craftsmanship. One weave can take weeks, sometimes months, to complete, with master weavers translating complex designs onto looms that demand memory and muscle. What makes them singular is not just the silk or the zari, but the varied motifs, from florals nodding to abundance, to paisley border, signifying fertility and eternity. In the actor’s sari, the geometric buttis, which speaks of cosmic order, feels particularly resonant. It serves an emblem of continuity for a woman who has repeatedly chosen longevity over trend. She completed the look with an open-setting diamond and emerald choker, complemented by matching stud earrings and a statement ring from Golecha’s Jewels. Her hair was worn in a sleek, middle-parted half-up, half-down style, while her makeup stayed understated and refined with a matte, skin-like base, softly smoked eyes and a nude lip that let the jewellery and weave take the spotlight. A pistachio sari and jewels, like hers, is a smart trousseau investment. While it is timeless in spirit, it is refreshingly modern and versatile enough to move seamlessly from intimate family ceremonies to landmark events for years to come.

article_title: A life beautifully lived—Hamish Bowles remembers Valentino
sub_title: Valentino Garavani conquered the worlds of fashion and style, bringing a certain idea of beauty to all he touched
article_content: Valentino Clemente Ludovico Garavani—known, simply and powerfully, as Valentino—was born on May 11th, 1932, in Voghera, a rather quiet place lost somewhere between Milan and Genoa. But by the time he died, aged 93, on January 19, he had conquered the worlds of fashion and style, bringing a “I love beauty—it’s not my fault,” Valentino famously said with a shrug, and in fashion, he saw a way to captivate and ensnare women (his only clients when starting out, before he widened the purview of his well-dressed net). He trained at the Accademia dell’Arte in Milan, studying both French and fashion, and then, aged 17, moved to Paris, to the École des Beaux-Arts and the Chambre Syndicale de la Couture, before securing an apprenticeship in 1951 with the Athenian couturier Jean Dessès, who dressed royalty and high society ladies in his immaculately draped and vividly colored evening gowns. Jacqueline, the Comtesse de Ribes, dressed with Dessès, and when she was asked by Oleg Cassini to design some dresses for him in Paris, she mentioned it to Dessès, telling the designer that “I don’t know how to draw in a chic way.” Dessès was amused. “I have an Italian illustrator,” he told her, “who would be very happy to earn a little more money after working-hours doing the drawings for you”, and a friendship between Valentino and Jacqueline was born. When he was When Guy Laroche, Dessès’s assistant, departed to start his own couture house, Valentino joined him for a few years before leaving to work briefly with the Russian-Georgian Princess Irene Galitzine (Galitzine had made palazzo pyjamas a thing, amidst opulent evening clothes). Then, in 1959, Valentino started his own house with backing from his father and a family friend. In the meantime, someone had come into his life. Giancarlo Giammetti recently recalled their first meeting, with Giammetti seated alone in a Roman cafe. “A kind person came and said, ‘Are you alone?’ I said, ‘Yes.’ ‘Do you mind if me and my friend can sit here?’ Of course,” Giammetti remembered. “And Valentino sat next to me—I remember very deeply.” A whoosh of dark hair framed Valentino’s tanned face, with its sultry features and his arresting blue eyes. “Then Valentino started to speak to me in French. I said, ‘Sorry?’ ‘Oh, sorry—I just arrived from Paris after seven years, my mind goes French, and I was hoping that you speak French…’” Giammetti, it turns out, had studied French for most of his life. “He said, ‘From now on, if I see you again, we speak French.’ And we still do. Incredibly.” The two would speak French to each other—as lovers, and then as intimate friends and business partners—for the rest of Valentino’s life. Valentino soon found a lavish, frescoed apartment in the fashionable Via Condotti, but less than a year later, he was facing bankruptcy. (Though Valentino threw the blame at his “champagne tastes,” someone had not been paying the rent.) He and Giammetti simply moved the salon to a 16th-century palazzo on the Via Gregoriana. (Incidentally, Giammetti acquired the Via Condotti apartment recently and has had it transformed into his offices by Studio Peregalli’s Laura Sartori Rimini. It’s a sumptuous series of rooms, the walls now hung with silver tissue or silk velvet—though some still have their original frescoes—and filled with Hervé van der Straten furniture and antiques. What may have been “Champagne tastes” in 1959 are now sublime and defining.) Valentino gradually began to make his mark on fashion. His flashing good looks easily summoned the press, to be sure, but it was his clothes that had an allure for the stars who would pass through Rome. And when Elizabeth Taylor, there to shoot Suddenly, his work was appearing in As Valentino became a name to watch, with ladies—Audrey Hepburn, Sophia Loren, any number of princesses, Jaqueline Kennedy Onassis, Nan Kempner, Lynn Wyatt, and Susan Gutfreund, among so many more, flocking to dress with him—so his residences became exponentially more impressive. His Roman base—a penthouse apartment with Persian miniatures on the fabric-covered walls and banquettes fit for a Turkish salon, had been transformed into a house on the Appian Way, decorated by Renzo Mongiardino, the When I first went to Rome for the couture in the mid-’80s, long before my Appian Way adventure, I plucked up all my courage and walked into Valentino’s intimidating couture salon just off the top of the Spanish steps—two small-ish rooms that positively oozed with Of course, this pair of elegantly finished rooms opened onto a positive hive of industry occupying five floors of a vast palazzo. Here were the couture ateliers: room after room of industrious ladies and a smattering of men—hundreds of them—applied to the task at hand in light-flooded rooms. (Some years after my first adventure with the couture salon, the place was subtly transformed by the English architects and designers Peter Moore and Peter Kent—there were silvered bannisters, acres of pale grey marble in the hallways, and paintings by Julian Schnabel, Keith Haring, and Francesco Clemente, and it was all very, very chic.) Valentino’s show then always finished with music just before the In 1991, I had an appointment with Valentino to discuss his entire career, and met with him in an elegant room looking over the Piazza Mignanelli, filled with antiques and lush draperies that lent it a Cécile Sorel sort of look. It was not easy getting him to speak. Next door in a vast room—and I mean Of course, Valentino had a number of other properties: in Capri, in New York, in London. But in 1995, I was invited to the 17th century chateau of brick and stone he had acquired—a house that was revealed to me only after I had followed a drive and dramatically turned a corner: There, plunging downhill, and glimmering below, was the Chateau de Wideville, once home to Madame de la Valliere, mistress of Louis XIV (Versailles is conveniently near). In the evening’s light, I explored the breathtaking Jacques Wirtz gardens, where brilliant violet rosemary stretched across the field and cut through the forests, while roses and scented high-summer flowers filled the walled garden. And then: the breathtaking house itself. Valentino worked with Henri Samuel on the interiors, which—with their emerald silk-velvet armchairs and a sort of Chinoiserie motif, which gave the house a sort of fanciful Palm Beach air—brought a level of comfort to the splendidly austere exterior. I was amused to see that the enormous Francis Bacon in Valentino’s sitting room depicted an abstracted man sitting on a carpet of bunches of roses, quite unlike anything I had seen before in his work—as Valentino-ish as it was possible for a Bacon to be. As I headed in for dinner, rather moved by the exquisite gardens and the ravishing interiors—by everything that Giancarlo and Valentino had done in life—I said to Valentino, “What you’ve done is to create beauty.” He clasped my hand and, weeping, said, “It

Designs with elegant plaid motifs, ideal for an event or a day at work; in sophisticated shades such as brown, military green and steel grey. We will also see them in all types of outfits, from the most sophisticated to the most daring. Whether in a corporate look, with a romantic touch, librarian as in 2022 or in a modern key with tight blouses and normcore shoes. In winter they kept silent, but in summer they will be the object of desire of all, ready to make you feel attractive and spring everywhere. Louis Vuitton caught with a tailored design with a folded hem, a detail that lowers the seriousness of the garment. Isabel Marant pushes the Safari girl aesthetic through capri pants with functional pockets in military green. And Saint Laurent proposes an opaque green design in parachute fabric to face the high temperatures with style and elegance. For Spring-Summer 2026, harem pants become the competition of capri and bermuda shorts. Michael Kors adds them to his collection for the season in a vaporous fabric suitable for wearing with strappy blouses and heeled sandals. Balmain takes the style level up a notch by showing them in a satin and olive green version, ideal for creating 2000s-inspired outfits with button heels. Louis Vuitton made it clear that airy designs will be a basic to formulate minimalist or monochrome styles. Michael Kors chose XXL designs in chocolate-coloured cotton, perfect to wear in a tropical setting or simply to ornament the silhouette. Finally, Zimmermann pairs them with an elegant brown jumpsuit to look spectacular from day to night. Although everything seems to indicate that skinny pants will be the kings of the season, in reality, there is also room for baggy designs that have been on the radar for more than three (consecutive) years. Loewe, Calvin Klein, Stella McCartney, Zimmermann and Ami, to name a few, included them on their runways this season as one of the favourites. From traditional black models to electronic tones that go with the season. We will see them with elegant details such as darts, low rise, classic prints and the classic middle line that office workers love. The high waist below the ribs, which is always essential to seal an Which designs to invest in? Puddle pants in pastel shades, if it is in a suit, the better. Also in linen fabrics with a bluish dye (if you are looking for a modern garment), bootcut, cigarette and even straight. Which confirms that there is an infinity of options for every woman, the signal to take a break from the usual mini-dresses. Yes, Yes, palazzo pants - or also known as elephant leg - will define spring elegance in 2026. Celine confirmed that they can become more modern and less sober by combining them in an effortless look with sportswear and white sneakers. Ralph Lauren proposes them in a bright red sartorial ensemble with slatted espadrilles, the bold yet personality-driven outfit to keep in your favorites. Boss combined classic black pieces in an oversize style with satin blouses and pointed shoes. Lastly, Ulla Johnson suggests plaid print designs to embrace a lady-like-modern aesthetic for 2026. Favourites to invest in? Plains in neutral tones, loud ones like solid red and even modern prints, from plaid to retro '80s stripes. What are the favourite fabrics that will go from runway to street style? Last year linen and lace dominated the streets, now it's the turn of satin pants. These were positioned as the number one option that shone in more than one fashion show of the season. Ami opted for a low rise model with XL belt to play with the silhouette and build casual daytime outfits. Ferragamo revived the skort-skirt of the 2000s, but in an elegant, modern and functional version. Tom Ford gives a nod to the pajama looks that celebrities like Angelina Jolie popularized in the past. An evening blue ensemble to look glamorous with metallic pumps on a special evening. Khaite showed them in a cylindrical version, ideal to increase volume or to go out of the traditional in terms of style. Finally, Toteme enchants with straight satin pants that we will see in minimalist or one-tone styles. It seems that everything points to leather effect pants going from fall to summer, a glamorous piece that is worth continuing to wear. Especially for those days of unpredictable weather or summer showers that appear without warning. Bottega Veneta and Versace are adding braided leather or crocodile-effect designs to give a reptile touch to the outfit. article_title: Diana Penty’s red Mahima Mahajan sari finds an unexpected hasli moment
sub_title: A corset-style blouse alters the balance of the Mahima Mahajan sari, concentrating detail at the bodice and letting the drape fall uninterrupted
article_content: Diana Penty’s Mahima Mahajan sari is densely worked from edge to edge. Fine gold butti embroidery is distributed evenly across the red silk. The embroidery becomes heavier and more concentrated, marking the outline of the drape as it falls from shoulder to hem and giving the sari a clearer finish. It is paired with a corset-style blouse, hand-embroidered and cut to sit close. The shaping is visible in the seams and structure of the blouse, setting it apart from a conventional sari blouse while keeping the drape itself unchanged. By concentrating embroidery on the blouse and along the sari’s edges, the look avoids feeling scattered, even with extensive surface work. Stylist Namita Alexander accessorised Penty with a diamond choker, matching earrings and stacked bangles that sit comfortably alongside the sari’s detailing. The standout is a beige mini bag by Özel from the Özel x Mortantra collaboration. The bag is embroidered with zardozi paisley motifs and finished with metallic detailing. The handle, crafted from a traditional hasli neckpiece, gives the bag a distinct identity and ties it back to the jewellery worn with the sari. Hair is worn in loose, side-parted waves. Makeup by Séverine Perina stays warm and natural, with softly lined eyes and a neutral lip that sit comfortably alongside the richness of the sari and accessories. “Reimagine this red look for a day wandering a gallery. Ditch the heavy jewellery and pair a simple silk or georgette red and cream polka sari with a cropped blouse. article_title: Nita Ambani’s Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla sari frames lace through borders and blouse
