article_content: Nita Ambani wears an Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla sari from the Burano collection, a reference to the needle lace made on the island of Burano, Italy, in a pale rose-pink georgette that reads light on the body but detailed at the edges. The colour stays even across the drape, setting up the lace embroidery as the defining feature. Embellishment is concentrated along the borders, pallu edge and blouse where lace motifs are meticulously hand embroidered in silk threads with sequins and pearls. The blouse mirrors the border pattern exactly, creating a visual loop that keeps the eye moving across the look rather than settling in one place. The Burano reference draws from the island’s lace-making tradition, particularly the openwork language associated with The jewellery comes from her own collection of distinct pieces: a lotus-shaped diamond choker surrounded by Basra pearls and a Basra pearl bracelet. With the drape kept spare and the colour understated, the sari’s impact comes from where the work is placed, not how much of it appears “Re-think this dreamy pink colour in a '50s evening look. Work with a pink silk structured gown, an off-the-shoulder and cinched at the waist. Pair it with jewellery akin to Nita Ambani working with pearls and diamonds, set in a traditional Hyderabad pearl design or French style. Ditch the jewellery on the arms and opt for a high-heeled pair of pumps,” says Vogue India fashion associate Divya Balakrishnan.

article_title: Tara Sutaria’s floral skirt set is a comfortable alternative to heavy lehengas
sub_title: The actor went the minimal route to accessorise her Gauri & Nainika look
article_content: For her intimate Christmas celebrations at home, Tara Sutaria chose a look that straddled intimacy with high drama. Though technically a modern co-ord set, Sutaria’s look by Gauri & Nainika reads as something far more versatile. Inching towards a compelling alternative to an ornate lehenga, it appears equally suited to a destination wedding soirée where modernity is prized as much as tradition. At first glance, the ensemble feels like a modern-day lehenga reimagined through a contemporary lens. Comprising a high-waisted, billowing, floor-grazing skirt and a sculpted bralette, the set is lifted by painterly florals that bloom against a noir base. The ensemble is drawn from Gauri & Nainika’s Lakmē Fashion Week x FDCI Spring–Summer 2026 showcase, where the designer duo unveiled a collection rooted in wearable artistry. Inspired by painted canvases, dark roses and moody still lifes, the line translated romance into tactile form using organza, tulle and silk mikado, shaping silhouettes defined by volume, bows, ruffles and drama. On Sutaria, these themes distilled into a maximalist floral piece that felt opulent and of-the-moment. Black punctuated with bold florals has long held fashion’s imagination, from the late '30s’ bias-cut evening gowns to the lacquered rose prints of the ‘50s. This lineage is mirrored on her look. The high-waisted skirt elongates the frame, offering a sleek, cinched foundation, while the bralette’s open back introduces a sensual counterpoint. A sleek, centre-parted bun was adorned with red roses, complemented by a deep crimson lip, together conjuring a Frida Kahlo-esque romanticism. A pair of drop chandelier earrings added the final flourish, letting the noir florals take centre stage. With thoughtful styling, a skirt set, like hers, can seamlessly shift from a formal evening affair to a festive sangeet night. Swap the diamonds for polkis, dial up the drama with the makeup and you have a versatile statement that can be reworked and returned to, time and again.

article_title: The digital Vintage Casio watch is bending time in 2025
sub_title: From a certain NYC mayor to your style influencer cousin, simple 20th-century timepieces like Casio’s A1000MA series have become everyone’s go-to accessories.
article_content: As I stand on an uneven platform for the next train, I am presented with my current favourite fashion show—the New York subway. You can spot a fall/winter ’25 And this isn’t just a New York thing. Over the last two months, I’ve started noticing the same glint everywhere I go. In Tokyo, it’s the clear-resin variants; in Seoul, the retro golds; in Mumbai cafés, the classic F91W that refuses to retire. One September afternoon in Bandra, outside a tiny post-production studio, a filmmaking student waited for his auto wearing a block-printed kurta and a gold-toned Casio LA670. A week later in Delhi, during a quick coffee run in Meherchand Market, a If you glance around, you’ll also spot the odd Seiko Rotocall and Q Timex, but somehow, it is vintage Casio watches that are dominating the conversation. Especially, the A1000MA-7—and somehow the entire Casio Vintage family has found itself back in the cultural spotlight. History was first made with the release of the Casiotron (QW02-10) in 1974—the world’s first fully digital wristwatch with an automatic calendar—but it was never just a timekeeper. Over the years, Casio digital watches have become pop-culture fixtures, appearing everywhere from on-screen sci-fi fantasies including They remain a staple of This lineage, from the pioneering Casiotron to the cult-classic F-91W of the 1990s, leads directly to today’s A1000 models. They carry the same retro credibility and matte-metal minimalism, now elevated with polished stainless steel and a Milanese strap. It’s this blend of historic tech cool and modern refinement that makes wearing the watch both disarmingly ordinary and unexpectedly iconic. “It’s one of the few timepieces that slips into anyone’s life without demanding a costume change,” says stylist Ayesha Amin Nigam, who has been spotting them on shoots across Delhi and Mumbai. She tells me that, in the last year alone, she’s seen them on interns, models, production assistants, even accountants who wander on set in between takes. “It shapeshifts into whatever the outfit needs—grounding streetwear, sharpening suiting or sitting quietly against a The variants alone could fill a moodboard: the brushed-steel A1000MA, its gold-toned MG counterpart, the pastel-tinted MPR editions, the ultra-slim LA670s, and even the resin-cased F-series that collectors love for its purist ’80s silhouette. And unlike many vintage icons, most of these models are still in production and available directly at brand stores, while a handful of discontinued colourways and older A1000 batches quietly trade hands on resale platforms like My Almari and Luxepolis for those seeking a deeper There is another reality that also exists: Christie’s Geneva Luxury Week reported sales of 21,641,435 Swiss francs (approximately ₹242 crores) in rare watches, with a significant 34% of the bidders being millennials and Gen Z’ers. If younger consumers are willing to spend big at auction, why are modest, sub-₹20,000 digital Casios suddenly the cultural touchstone? Part of the answer lies in accessibility, nostalgia and the social currency of effortless style. “Casio democratised digital timekeeping long before it was fashionable,” explains Sarosh Mody, founder of Luxury Watch Works, an after-sales boutique based in Mumbai. “The G-Shock, for example, became—and remains—a cultural icon. Its popularity reflects the people’s choice, not marketing, not snob value. Casio understood utility decades before smartwatches were conceived. The calculator, TV, radio and camera watches were made by them way before the Swiss even thought about them. The brand has blurred the line between Today, reissues and collaborations like the Timex T80 x Maison Margiela and Omega x Swatch drops show that design credibility doesn’t need a luxury price tag. Together, these watches have become a global shorthand for personality, nostalgia and style that crosses generations and geographies. And style icons and collectors continue the trend: Casio watches were a mainstay of But why this watch and why now? I suspect that it’s because it is fundamentally reminiscent of a simpler time. The only complication in the watch is an alarm, just like the one you would wear in school, beeping at the end of an exam. It’s something you perhaps spotted on your father back in the day, and till today, it rings a bell. A personal connection in your wardrobe that tells a story: perhaps that’s the ultimate style flex.

article_title: Sorry, body positivity—the Ozempic era is officially upon us
sub_title: From size 000 to naked dresses, the silhouette is shifting. If you grew up in the nineties, you've seen this story before.
article_content: Fashion has a message for you. It is written in cut-outs and sheer panels and dresses engineered to pull taut across a torso. If you grew up in the nineties, the message feels familiar. For a beautiful, chaotic decade, the industry genuinely seemed to be making space. Runways got a little wider, brands stocked sizes beyond S-L. Body positivity, neutrality and midsize creators built communities out of the radical act of existing at a size beyond 10 and dressing well. Progress, fitful and incomplete, but pointing somewhere new. The cultural moment that produced all of that was also running out of road, and GLP-1s like The algorithm noticed before most of us did. One search, one article, and within days the advertisements followed: telehealth, semaglutide, before and afters. Red carpet appearances and celebrity transformations did the rest. Somewhere between the prescription pad for medical conditions and the paparazzi shot, GLP-1s became something else; thinness shifted from aspirational to 'easily' attainable. Fashion, as it always does, paid close attention. According to the The body the clothes are designed for is, increasingly, a very specific one. And the designs make no secret of it. A dress built around a torso cut-out doesn't reveal the body; it requires a particular body type. Remove the specific body it assumes and the whole thing falls apart. But the Ozempic era didn't invent fashion's preference for a narrow silhouette. That preference is old and stubborn and has survived every cultural correction aimed at it, including the body positivity movement, which, at its peak, briefly made the industry blink. What the Ozempic era did was make that preference clearly visible once again. And visibility, as the last decade proved, is where change begins. The millennial women standing in changing rooms right now—going looking for a cap sleeve and coming home empty-handed—have been here before. We lived through the first version of this story, written in low-rise jeans, diet culture and the tyranny of the bandage dress. We're also the same women who drove the body positivity movement in the first place. Not always from the outside, throwing stones, but from inside the industry: the editors, stylists, creators, customers whose spending made inclusive sizing commercially viable. They got loud about it, spent their money differently, demanded more, and the industry—slowly, grudgingly, genuinely—moved. Not because fashion had a change of heart. Because the woman in the changing room did, and she took her debit card with her. Fashion moves in cycles no one fully controls and everyone partially creates. The industry follows culture; culture follows the industry; somewhere in the middle, a woman tries something on and decides how she feels about herself that day. The cycle that produced one shift can produce another. And in the meantime, there is something to be said for getting dressed anyway, finding the thing you love in this season, this particular cultural weather, and wearing it like you were always meant to.

article_title: John Galliano returns to fashion via a creative partnership with Zara
sub_title: The Spanish retailer Zara has signed John Galliano to a two-year creative partnership which will see him “re-author” the brand’s archives.
article_content: John Galliano is back in the atelier: The Spanish retailer “I’ve been curating some of Zara’s recent archives,” Since Ortega Perez was named chair in 2022, Zara has collaborated with other high fashion designers, among them “I’m super excited, because it’s not something I’ve done before, so that kind of tickles me—the newness, the excitement, the actual process,” Galliano noted. “Even with my team, I have to keep reminding them daily: In January, Galliano was seen front row at Jonathan Anderson’s haute couture debut for Dior. Before his Galliano has spent the two years since his exit from Margiela—having gotten off “the crazy merry-go-round,” as he called it—“going to museums, walking through the woods without my phone, getting lost but not being afraid to get lost, and relying on instinct again, reconnecting with instinct, like breathing correctly.” He went on: “It’s been precious time to just really think about what I would like to do next. You think, He’s been secretly working in an atelier “somewhere around Paris” since January. “It’s early days at the moment, but I’ve launched quite a few toiles, and when we see them back, we’ll be able to see how far I can push it safely, if you know what I mean.” Though he doesn’t want to give away too much about the work in progress, he will say it’s “informed by form and proportion [without] falling into any categories. One could safely say it’s beyond gender and beyond seasons.” The first collection will arrive in stores in September. And of course, the thought that his clothes could suddenly be accessible to a whole new range of people tickles him too: “To deliver fashion through that enormous platform—that, of course, that’s thrilling. And to be able to work with the kind of resources they have as well, that’s equally thrilling,” he said. So, how does he feel about getting back on the merry-go-round? “They say act three of your life is the most important,” Galliano mused, “and can be the most fun.”

article_title: The next chapter of cocktail dressing is moodier, sharper and far more considered
sub_title: Through their collection Abyssal, Rohit Gandhi + Rahul Khanna explore mood over metallics and tailoring that holds its own
article_content: Cocktail dressing at Indian weddings has reached the saturation point. For the past few seasons, it’s been a game of high shine and impact: sequinned gowns engineered for flash photography, sherwanis and tuxedos dialled up with surface drama. It worked: it photographed beautifully and filled Instagram grids. But somewhere along the way, it also became predictable. You could almost guess the look before the invite arrived. And when something becomes predictable, it stops feeling personal. And somewhere between brides designing meticulous mood boards and building multi-chapter wedding wardrobes, the want for something new is at its height, exactly where Abyssal, the Spring Summer Couture 2026 collection by Rohit Gandhi + Rahul Khanna steps in–a house that has, for over two decades, built its reputation on structure over sensationalism. The collection is inspired by the ocean’s deeper zones, not the obvious turquoise surface, but the layers beneath, where light behaves differently and colour begins to dissolve. The palette moves through oceanic shades that feel atmospheric; pearls, metallic florals and crystals are hand-embroidered like artefacts recovered from the ocean floor, embedded beautifully into the fabric. “For Abyssal, we took one step further to look at the science and architecture at the depths of the ocean where light doesn’t pass through and colour begins to disappear for the human eye. There is a sense of poetry older than time that reveals itself every thousand feet. That is the magic we’re capturing, like a message in a bottle, with this collection,” say the designer duo. The modern wedding wardrobe is no longer built around one defining outfit. It’s a welcome dinner that feels intimate, a cocktail evening that sets the tone and an afterparty that relaxes the rules. Each look needs to carry its own identity without feeling like a costume. Especially today when brides and grooms aren’t going after the next trendy thing. Instead, they’re on the search for pieces that elevate their style while allowing restyling and rewear beyond the wedding week. They want couture to justify itself in construction, detailing and how it sits on the body. If you’re getting married in 2026, here’s the reality: your cocktail look can rightly get its own spotlight, courtesy of Rahul Gandhi+Rahul Khanna. Let’s detail the specifics: First, colour. Instead of the predictable jewel tones or safe metallics, the collection leans into abyssal blues, frost whites and deep charcoals. These aren’t statement colours in the obvious sense. They’re mood colours. They photograph differently; softer in daylight, sharper under evening lights. For a bride, that means a cocktail dressing that is classy, chic and just the right amount of edgy. For a groom, it means stepping away from the default black and into tonal greys or inky blues that turn heads. Then, texture, and this is the real highlight. With this collection, the designers don’t use pearls, crystals, and metallic florals as afterthought embellishments. They build garments around them. Pearls are embedded into the surface like something organic—almost geological—unearthed from the ocean floor, sitting against the oceanic hues that make them feel modern. Then you have the crystals and the metallic floral accents, too, that are designed and handworked to catch the light just right, move along with you as you dance the night away, to make a beautiful case for the magic of Indian craftsmanship. For couples tired of heavy embroidery that weighs both the garment and the moment down, this is a discerning way to do embellishment. You still get the details and craftsmanship. But the structure of the silhouette leads the conversation. And perhaps that’s why Abyssal feels relevant, because it understands that the most compelling things aren’t always the ones floating at the surface.

article_title: Every original has a story. The best ones are written in denim
sub_title: With Alia Bhatt at the forefront, Levi's brings its global Behind Every Original campaign to India, spotlighting authenticity, reinvention and individuality
article_content: The Levi’s jean revolution was a pivotal moment in fashion history. Like many Americans in the mid-1800s, Levi Strauss wasn’t looking to strike gold when he headed west to California to innovate durable denim workwear for labourers—but he struck it anyway. Levi’s has always been known for disrupting the apparel industry with its jeanswear. Today, the brand’s inherent pioneering spirit exemplifies American style, while its ability to tailor its offerings beyond borders, turns the Levi’s legacy into a generational love affair. It's difficult to imagine that a single piece of clothing could connect actors, artists, pop stars and hip-hop icons. Yet Levi’s jeans are the original blank canvas—from straight and slouchy to baggy, embroidered and distressed, people have taken these jeans and truly made them their own. Behind Every Original builds on that legacy, celebrating the mindset behind originality—the curiosity, conviction and courage to see the world differently. This time around, the brand brings its 2026 vision, Behind Every Original, to India, starring global brand ambassador Alia Bhatt. Bhatt’s evolution mirrors that of a generation that values authenticity over perfection, making her a natural embodiment of Levi's global narrative. “I’ve always been a curious mind, wanting to know the why behind the what,” she shares. Off-screen, her personal style reflects that same ease and self-expression. She gravitates toward relaxed denim, effortless tees and silhouettes that feel lived in. “For me, it was never about checking every box or doing what was expected. I’d rather be myself than anyone I’m told to be. You don’t wait for permission to shake things up—you make your own rules. Being original is messy, imperfect and completely your own,” she says. Every frame celebrates Bhatt’s denim-clad individuality—strutting, dancing, moving and, above all, living in Levi’s. Looking for a jean that fits comfortably at the waist but feels loose and easy through the thighs without looking too baggy? Enter: the Cinch Waist Jean. This season, Levi’s builds on its offering of relaxed fits, designed with an adjustable back detail that creates a customisable, waist-defining shape while maintaining a wide-leg silhouette. Rooted in Levi’s heritage of authentic, well-crafted denim and driven by innovation, the Cinch collection offers a fresh approach to everyday denim—sculpted, adaptable, and designed to move with you. Reinforcing the brand’s leadership in fit innovation and its commitment to designing denim that adapts to different bodies, moods, and ways of wearing, the collection introduces three versatile styles: the Cinch Wide-Leg Jeans, an effortless and fluid option for off-duty days; the Cinch Baggy Jeans, relaxed with a contemporary edge that makes them perfect for a casual brunch or day out; and the Cinch Barrel Jeans, fit for occasions when you want to dress things up without sacrificing comfort. You can also opt for the Levi’s Loose Boot—a modern, laid-back take on the classic bootcut. With its relaxed fit and subtle flare, it strikes the perfect balance between structure and ease (think of it as the ideal in-between). With Behind Every Original, Levi’s reaffirms what it has always stood for: denim is more than what you wear—it’s a part of your story worth telling.

article_title: Women in arts take to the runway for Carolina Herrera Fall 2026 show
sub_title: Wes Gordon returns to his home turf, translating his artistic lineage into a collection defined by sculptural silhouettes, graphic clarity, and lived-in ease
article_content: Pick a theme for the season so far, and it might as well be ceremonial glamour—particularly at Carolina Herrera, the quintessential New York brand led by creative director Wes Gordon. Here, Gordon positions himself as the architect of a maison mid-renovation, offering a front-row seat to a bold, free-spirited approach to fashion and beauty—one that is rooted in cultural exchange, a vision that feels both timely and enduring. It’s hardly Carolina Herrera’s first brush with the art world. The house’s close ties with renowned artists like Andy Warhol and Robert Mapplethorpe paved the way for the Women in the Arts initiative, which has encouraged and supported female creatives since 2022. Gordon’s inspiration for the latest collection, too, drew from the artistic realm, reflecting the confidence of a brand comfortably operating at the intersection of fashion and art. Functioning almost like a modern canvas, New York’s historic setting hosted Carolina Herrera’s Fall 2026 showcase, celebrating a diverse community of women—past and present—whose work and influence have shaped the artistic landscape. The collection imagines women in motion—creating and moving through the world with conviction. True to that sentiment, strength and volume appear in exaggerated shoulders, cocoon coats, puff-sleeve blazers, and streamlined pencil skirts. The crisp Herrera signature button-down is reimagined as an artist’s smock, relaxed in spirit and rendered in black and white, while a procession of embellished, diaphanous dresses brings a mix of sheer drama to the presentation. As any Carolina Herrera runway regular knows, leopard print and floral motifs play a pivotal role in each collection. This season, a hand-painted, vibrant red calla lily print sets a bold tone. Embroidered eveningwear enters the collection with paillette knits and gold coats and dresses. The ensembles are constructed from sequins that recall the muted gold tones of artist Agnes Martin’s Gordon’s tribute didn’t stop at the collection. The showcase unfolded in an expansive venue in New York’s Meatpacking District, illuminated by a mural created by set designer Sarah Oliphant. Among the models walking the runway was a multigenerational community of contemporary curators, patrons, gallerists, and collectors—each a real-life muse in their own right. The show featured painter Amy Sherald; artists Anh Duong and Eliza Douglas; sculptor Rachel Feinstein and her daughter, Flora Currin; photographer Ming Smith; gallerist Hannah Traore; and more, all of whom were handpicked by Gordon to help bring the collection’s inspiration to life. With handbags, Gordon revisits signature styles like the Mimi and Karlita. The Mimi is reimagined with an all-over black-and-white graphic leopard print, with a bow detail at the strap. The Karlita, the season’s ideal evening bag, is rendered in the collection’s palette and includes a striking chilli red. Statement jewellery completes the narrative, with calla lily brooches, gold necklaces and earrings. House codes return through print: bold leopard jacquard, painterly calla lily motifs, and poppy florals rendered on organza. Colour sharpens with a bold palette of ceramic nude, forest green, plum, celeste blue, and chilli red. A hand-drawn print of the heel—a nod to the iconic bottle of Carolina Herrera’s bestselling Good Girl perfume—introduces a note of contemporary playfulness on blouses and skirts, marking its 10-year anniversary with a touch of wit. On the occasion of International Women’s Day, Carolina Herrera reaffirmed its commitment to supporting female creativity by unveiling Good Girl Murano—a one-of-a-kind artistic tribute crafted entirely in Murano glass. Conceived as a collector’s piece, the fragrance is limited to ten bottles worldwide, reimagining artisan tradition through a modern lens. After months of experimentation, Venetian designer Lucia Massari chose borosilicate glass for the body, developed in collaboration with Ash Polzer, an American artist who built her practice within Murano’s traditionally male-dominated glassmaking world. For the finishing touch, Massari turned to Luigi Varagnolo, one of the last artisans specialising in Venetian mirror ornamentation. His contribution—a delicate glass flower crowning the stiletto—introduces a note of fragility, almost irony, to the silhouette’s sharpness. Jasmine—Carolina Herrera’s favourite flower—takes centre stage, in the fragrance. Enriched with indulgent notes of tonka bean, cacao, almond, and coffee, this Eau de Parfum, crafted by perfumers Louise Turner and Quentin Bisch, is a celebration of elegance, creativity, and artistic audacity.

Or take a cue from Gigi’s everyday formula and throw on a matching leather bomber, a simple white T-shirt and ballet flats. Play with texture and opt for sumptuous silk and plush faux-fur to counteract the polish of a classic pair of kick-flare leather trousers à la Chloé. Matte leather is a popular choice, but coated leather comes a close second. Patent trouser styles look best when they’re a slouchy fit or barrel-leg, especially when in a glossy cherry red hue. sub_title: A Vogue writer gets to the bottom of the trendiest supplements and the answer might be a tough pill to swallow
article_content: I am sitting in a small room painted emerald green as a nurse counts vials she will need to fill with my warm Like most 30-somethings, I have the nagging feeling that I should be more committed to achieving optimal health. And like most 30-somethings who have stacked obligations like Jenga blocks, there is a limit to how much I am willing to do. I have not come to this place to be told to Me, and most people you know. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, more than half of adults (and more women than men) take a supplement and the proportion is trending upward. There are now around 100,000 different supplements (which the FDA defines in vague terms as ingestible products meant to augment the diet) on the market. Such interventions run the gamut from familiar add-ons like the humble vitamin to witchier formulations: microbiome ‘boosters,’ sleep chews, tablets meant to reduce stress, bloat and ‘toxins’ in the bloodstream and capsules formulated to But not even the sober and sensible among us are immune to their quick-fix promises. An acquaintance (the daughter of two doctors) told me she turned to vitamin gummies after gobs of her hair fell out postpartum. She trawled the drugstore aisles for a product high in follicle-boosting This friend did her research on the ground, reading labels in an actual store—a quaint approach, according to The Lanby’s cofounder Chloe Harrouche. “Most people are sourcing their supplements through Instagram,” she explains. “They’re like, 'Well, if it worked for them....’” Many people report getting health information from I have never missed an annual checkup, but I still wonder about the potions and pastilles I scroll past. article_title: How to treat rosacea on brown skin, according to dermatologists
sub_title: The signs to watch for, triggers that can worsen it and treatments that can help
article_content: For something so common, rosacea still has a remarkably good disguise. It is usually pictured in one particular way: visible redness, light skintone, flushed cheeks, a face announcing its distress. It's far more confusing on melanin-rich skin. The tenderness, stinging and bumps are there. What may not be there, at least not in the way we imagine it, is obvious redness. That misunderstanding changes the way people treat it. Skin gets labelled “reactive” or “sensitive” in the abstract, treated like acne or exfoliated into submission. We loaded up on products meant to fix texture or unclog pores, while the real issue keeps simmering underneath. Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory condition, shaped by a mix of genetics, immune response and environmental triggers, with symptoms that can include flushing, papules, pustules, visible vessels and eye irritation. “Your genetics predetermine whether you have rosacea–that’s the number one reason you get it,” dermatologist Dr Emma Craythorne That split between predisposition and provocation is part of what makes rosacea so maddening. The condition may be wired in, but it is often activated and aggravated by the habits of everyday life: heat, ultraviolet radiation, spicy food, alcohol, stress, vigorous exercise and irritating skincare. “Rosacea in deeper skin tones is less likely to be immediately identified because the colour cues are subtler,” says dermatologist and cosmetic formulator Dr Kavitha Arya. “Patients often describe burning, warmth, tenderness or breakouts that never quite look or behave like ‘typical’ acne. There is faint redness, but discoloration can also be more purple-toned." People spend months treating the wrong issue. If the skin is hot, reactive and bumpy, the instinct is often to reach for stronger acne products, exfoliating acids or foaming cleansers that promise to reset things. In practice, that can leave inflamed skin even more irritated. Rosacea can overlap with acne, seborrhoeic dermatitis, contact dermatitis and, in some cases, autoimmune conditions that need to be ruled out. Which is why the best treatment plan usually starts not with a miracle product but with some notes and a professional read of what the skin is actually doing. Dermatologists diagnose rosacea by examining the skin and eyes, asking questions about symptoms and triggers and, where needed, testing to exclude other conditions. Craythorne That immune reactivity is also why so many people with rosacea say their skin hates everything. Inflamed skin has a much lower tolerance for friction, fragrance, strong surfactants and strong exfoliants. Craythorne also name-checks demodex mites, which live in the skin’s sebaceous glands, as an inflammatory problem for those with rosacea. Once rosacea on brown skin is identified, treatment tends to be less flashy than the average skincare routine. Gentle cleanser, a plain moisturiser and daily sunscreen alongside medication tailored to the person's needs. “Topical prescriptions such as azelaic acid, metronidazole and ivermectin are among the standard options,” says Arya. “Treatment has to account not only for inflammation but for the pigment aftermath,” says Arya. “One-size-fits-all rosacea routines often fall short. You are treating the flare-up, but you are also trying not to create another problem while you do it.” Laser therapy can reduce rosacea-related colour changes, including the violet or brown-toned changes seen in darker skin, though energy-based treatment in skin of colour requires thoughtful device selection done by the right hands because of the risk of pigmentary change. For people with brown skin, the problem is not only rosacea itself but the lag between having it and having it recognised. When the condition is still largely imagined in one shade range, everyone else is left translating their symptoms alone.

The next day, I mixed three drops of almond oil into my face cream, along with a silent prayer, and braced for a “Since most face oils are occlusive, when used on slightly damp skin or layered over a serum or moisturiser, they help to seal in hydration,” explains Dr Jaishree Sharad, cosmetic dermatologist. “Typically, 2-4 drops are enough. What they do is reduce transepidermal water loss, essentially acting like a sealant over existing hydration. Over time, I realised face oils come bearing both promises and perils. They play a supportive role, sealing in moisture, reducing water loss and supporting the For most people, a well-formulated moisturiser is enough. Face oil is not mandatory. But in the right context — dry skin, cold weather, barrier repair — a few carefully chosen drops can make a visible difference. As for me, I no longer hear imaginary dermatologists wailing when I reach for oil. But I also don’t treat it as a necessary step if I'm too tired or my skin is in a good place. Because of its ability to decelerate digestion, soluble fibre has a knack for slowing or lessening the absorption of several substances that can have negative effects on our health if they build up too fast or rise too high. For instance, soluble fibre puts the brakes on the rate at which carbohydrates enter into the bloodstream, according to the FDA, which helps prevent spikes in blood glucose (blood sugar) after eating. “It’s going to ‘trap’ sugar molecules so that they’re absorbed more slowly, which is helpful for keeping blood sugar levels more regular,” Linsenmeyer explains. If you drink a glass of pure orange juice, for instance, that sugar gets metabolised pretty much immediately, causing your blood sugar to climb rapidly. But if you eat a whole orange, which contains soluble fibre, the sugar uptake is more gradual, Linsenmeyer says. This can help lower the level of LDL cholesterol (the ‘bad’ kind) in your blood and in turn, potentially lessen the risk of heart disease. In fact, “consuming adequate soluble fibre is associated with healthy Soluble fibre can also boost your gut microbiome (the vast population of bacteria and other microorganisms that live in your digestive tract and mediate multiple aspects of your health) in a big way. Rather, it has pretty much the opposite effect. Unlike its soluble sister, this kind of fibre passes right through us and exits virtually unchanged, speeding the movement of food through the digestive system and adding bulk to our stool. Yet another difference: It’s also not fermentable. In contrast to soluble fibre, which is inherently fermentable, insoluble fibre typically isn’t, so it won’t do much to act as a prebiotic or promote a Instead, “you can think of insoluble fibre as the broom that sweeps the gut clear,” Nielsen says. “It helps to increase motility and it helps to promote the turnover of gut cells.” Insoluble fibre can also be beneficial for various digestive conditions associated with sluggish or irregular bowel movements. For instance, the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) advises people with diverticulosis (a disease in which little sacs bulge out of the weak areas of your colon wall) to incorporate more fibre into their diets. Of course, if you have any other digestive condition, always speak with your doctor to find out what the best diet is for you before making any radical changes. In some cases, doubling down on fibre could cause digestive discomfort. Certain fibrous foods like The added volume in your stomach provided by insoluble fibre can also help enhance the sensation of fullness you get after eating, Linsenmeyer says. In fact, both soluble and insoluble fibre can help sustain post-meal fullness for longer. Insoluble fibre’s main claim to fame is its power to push waste along. Because of this, insoluble fibre beats out soluble fibre for While both kinds of fibre are needed for a balanced, well-functioning digestive system, insoluble fibre is especially critical for keeping you from getting backed up (or for getting things moving again). Not only does insoluble fibre encourage consistent bowel movements to help you stay regular, it also helps create softer stools that are easier to pass, Christine Lee, a gastroenterologist at the Cleveland Clinic, explains. Fibre is generally awesome and in most cases, it’s not So while all of this fibre info is fascinating and useful, it’s not like you need to be tallying up how much insoluble versus soluble fibre you’re getting (that’d be pretty difficult to do, given that many nutrition labels don’t list them separately). And again, while it’s common for foods to have more of one kind than the other, most Now that you know getting enough total fibre is generally more crucial than getting a certain amount of either type, you might be wondering what ‘enough’ looks like. As with many nutrients, the optimal amount per day depends on your individual body: your And in case you were wondering, there aren’t any ‘good clear-cut guidelines’ for soluble versus insoluble One final thing to keep in mind here: while eating fibre is important, there’s no need to dial it up and overload on the nutrient. In fact, going too hard on fibre (especially by abruptly increasing your intake or relying too heavily on fibre supplements or fibre-fortified foods) can end up causing bloating, cramps and gas, according to the Mayo Clinic. In that case, your gut “isn't habituated to a higher-fibre diet,” Nielsen explains. It is usually pictured in one particular way: visible redness, light skintone, flushed cheeks, a face announcing its distress. It's far more confusing on melanin-rich skin. The tenderness, stinging and bumps are there. What may not be there, at least not in the way we imagine it, is obvious redness. That misunderstanding changes the way people treat it. Skin gets labelled “reactive” or “sensitive” in the abstract, treated like acne or exfoliated into submission. We loaded up on products meant to fix texture or unclog pores, while the real issue keeps simmering underneath. Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory condition, shaped by a mix of genetics, immune response and environmental triggers, with symptoms that can include flushing, papules, pustules, visible vessels and eye irritation. “Your genetics predetermine whether you have rosacea–that’s the number one reason you get it,” dermatologist Dr Emma Craythorne That split between predisposition and provocation is part of what makes rosacea so maddening. The condition may be wired in, but it is often activated and aggravated by the habits of everyday life: heat, ultraviolet radiation, spicy food, alcohol, stress, vigorous exercise and irritating skincare. “Rosacea in deeper skin tones is less likely to be immediately identified because the colour cues are subtler,” says dermatologist and cosmetic formulator Dr Kavitha Arya. “Patients often describe burning, warmth, tenderness or breakouts that never quite look or behave like ‘typical’ acne. There is faint redness, but discoloration can also be more purple-toned." People spend months treating the wrong issue. If the skin is hot, reactive and bumpy, the instinct is often to reach for stronger acne products, exfoliating acids or foaming cleansers that promise to reset things. In practice, that can leave inflamed skin even more irritated. Rosacea can overlap with acne, seborrhoeic dermatitis, contact dermatitis and, in some cases, autoimmune conditions that need to be ruled out. Which is why the best treatment plan usually starts not with a miracle product but with some notes and a professional read of what the skin is actually doing. Dermatologists diagnose rosacea by examining the skin and eyes, asking questions about symptoms and triggers and, where needed, testing to exclude other conditions. Craythorne That immune reactivity is also why so many people with rosacea say their skin hates everything. Inflamed skin has a much lower tolerance for friction, fragrance, strong surfactants and strong exfoliants. Craythorne also name-checks demodex mites, which live in the skin’s sebaceous glands, as an inflammatory problem for those with rosacea. Once rosacea on brown skin is identified, treatment tends to be less flashy than the average skincare routine. Gentle cleanser, a plain moisturiser and daily sunscreen alongside medication tailored to the person's needs. “Topical prescriptions such as azelaic acid, metronidazole and ivermectin are among the standard options,” says Arya. “Treatment has to account not only for inflammation but for the pigment aftermath,” says Arya. “One-size-fits-all rosacea routines often fall short. You are treating the flare-up, but you are also trying not to create another problem while you do it.” Laser therapy can reduce rosacea-related colour changes, including the violet or brown-toned changes seen in darker skin, though energy-based treatment in skin of colour requires thoughtful device selection done by the right hands because of the risk of pigmentary change. For people with brown skin, the problem is not only rosacea itself but the lag between having it and having it recognised. When the condition is still largely imagined in one shade range, everyone else is left translating their symptoms alone.

article_title: Ashwaghanda, magnesium and vitamin D: do we all really need to take these supplements?
sub_title: A Vogue writer gets to the bottom of the trendiest supplements and the answer might be a tough pill to swallow
article_content: I am sitting in a small room painted emerald green as a nurse counts vials she will need to fill with my warm Like most 30-somethings, I have the nagging feeling that I should be more committed to achieving optimal health. And like most 30-somethings who have stacked obligations like Jenga blocks, there is a limit to how much I am willing to do. I have not come to this place to be told to Me, and most people you know. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, more than half of adults (and more women than men) take a supplement and the proportion is trending upward. There are now around 100,000 different supplements (which the FDA defines in vague terms as ingestible products meant to augment the diet) on the market. Such interventions run the gamut from familiar add-ons like the humble vitamin to witchier formulations: microbiome ‘boosters,’ sleep chews, tablets meant to reduce stress, bloat and ‘toxins’ in the bloodstream and capsules formulated to But not even the sober and sensible among us are immune to their quick-fix promises. An acquaintance (the daughter of two doctors) told me she turned to vitamin gummies after gobs of her hair fell out postpartum. She trawled the drugstore aisles for a product high in follicle-boosting This friend did her research on the ground, reading labels in an actual store—a quaint approach, according to The Lanby’s cofounder Chloe Harrouche. “Most people are sourcing their supplements through Instagram,” she explains. “They’re like, 'Well, if it worked for them....’” Many people report getting health information from I have never missed an annual checkup, but I still wonder about the potions and pastilles I scroll past. Should I be subscribing to the brand of “superfood gummies” that purports to combine a multivitamin with adaptogens, herbs, antioxidants, prebiotics, ‘super mushrooms’ and the nutritional equivalent of whole vegetables and fruits? Could I live to be 100 and nimble on AG1, a greens powder endorsed by neuroscientist and podcaster Andrew Huberman? Should I actually read one of the dozens of articles I’ve glimpsed about While I wait for the medical professionals to interpret the blood sacrifice I left in Midtown, I end up in a back-and-forth with another friend who, a few months ago, in the lead-up to running a Perhaps for the best. Observing data from 63 hospitals over the course of a decade, researchers have found that adverse effects from supplements are responsible for around 23,000 ER visits nationwide each year. “Supplements are supposed to do just that: supplement,” adds Jillian O’Neil, a dietitian and a fitness coach at Equinox. “They’re for what you’re not getting on your plate and to fill in what isn’t realistic for you to consume.” She would scream it from the rooftops if she could: none are a replacement for fundamental good habits— And for some people, supplements—​because of their actual efficacy or thanks to the almighty placebo effect—do make a real difference. article_title: Kiara Advani’s House of Masaba sari centres patchwork, buta work and gold embroidery
sub_title: The actor accessorised her look with fresh water and Baroque pearls
article_content: April in Mumbai calls for fabrics that breathe and colours that do not fight the heat. Kiara Advani arrived with the answer for the Nita Mukesh Ambani Cultural Centre’s third anniversary. For the evening, she stepped out wearing House of Masaba’s ‘Gulposh’ In the fresh colours of spring, sage green and soft pink, the sari, crafted in crepe silk, is characterised by its fluid fall, subtle sheen and featherlight quality. The sari carries delicate buta work across its canvas, along with an embroidered scalloped border. “But it is the pallu that I wanted to be the centre of focus,” says designer Masaba Gupta, adding, “I wanted the sari to feel light, yet look heavy enough to be worn for important and elaborate occasions. The pallu showcases our signature patchwork technique and is finished with gold embroidery in ‘sitara’ and ‘dabka’ kaam, featuring House of Masaba motifs.” The Gulposh is about bringing three crafts together in one sari without one overpowering the other. The sari is complemented with a blouse featuring a sweetheart neckline and noodle-thin straps. “The same gold embroidery and buta work from the pallu are translated onto it. The cut of the blouse is unmistakably modern and fresh, while the sari is crafted using traditional techniques. It is exactly this contrast that House of Masaba has built its creative language on,” elaborates Gupta. For jewellery, Advani reached for the fine jewellery collection from House of Masaba x Amrapali Jewels, called the ‘Maharani Maker’ choker. A coin in 18-carat gold, featuring the brand’s iconic ‘Son Chidiya’ motif, is nestled within a multi-layered pearl choker that combines freshwater and baroque pearls in various shapes and sizes. The actor’s beauty look was kept in the same soft register as the sari. Rose-toned eye shadow, a soft contour, a flush of blush and a nude-pink lip made up her makeup, while her hair was kept open in tousled curls.

article_content: Madhuri Dixit Nene wore a royal blue and rani pink Sambalpuri patta silk The drape features an all-over interplay of large-scale florals and geometric motifs. The border is detailed with zari and returns along the pallu. Sambalpuri patta saris, woven across Odisha’s Sambalpur, Bargarh and Sonepur regions, are known for their intricate ikat technique, in which both warp and weft threads are tie-dyed before weaving to create their characteristic feathered effect. Often featuring motifs such as conch shells, wheels, florals and temple-inspired forms, they carry the visual language of Odisha’s textile heritage. In Dixit’s sari, those motifs appeared in bold pink against an electric blue ground, giving the weave a particularly vivid finish. Styled by Sukriti Grover, Dixit paired the sari with temple jewellery from PNG Jewellers, including a layered rani haar, matching jhumkas, stacked kadas and rings. The beauty look paired warm peach-coral eyeshadow with liner, fresh skin and a pink lip.

article_title: 14 brands that prove handloom textiles can go beyond saris and kurtis
sub_title: Looking cute and saving the planet is easy, actually
article_content: Long before ‘sustainable’ became a marketing buzzword, it was simply the way things were done. Handloom textiles with cotton and silk were woven with care, yard by yard, often with techniques passed down over generations. They made Today, as the industry circles back to mindful consumption, a new generation of designers is revisiting these textiles with fresh eyes. Handloom textiles, once confined to familiar silhouettes, are being reimagined into pieces that feel current and yet everlasting—easygoing separates, fluid dresses and sharp tailoring. Here are 14 brands creating with handloom textiles in ways that feel anything but expected. Shweta Gupta’s work starts with handloom cottons and silks developed alongside weavers in Chanderi, but it rarely stays predictable. Techniques like smocking, faggoting and pleat tucks show up often, adding texture in ways that feel considered. There’s a touch of whimsy in the way it all comes together, just enough to keep the clothes feeling light, a little unusual and easy to wear. Known for its focus on indigenous cotton and 100% natural dyes, 11.11 works almost entirely within a hand-process ecosystem. The label brings together techniques like hand spinning, handloom weaving, hand painting, miniature tie-dyeing and quilting, often within a single garment. Founded in 2014 by Gauri Verma and Karuna Laungani, Jodi works with natural Indian textiles, bringing in techniques like hand block printing, Founded by Rina Singh, Eka approaches handloom with a mix of research, craft and a sense of storytelling. The brand often works with repurposed and archival fabrics, keeping production small-scale. It leans soft and introspective with layered silhouettes, pastel tones and a slightly vintage mood that feels pulled from the pages of a well-loved novel. Payal Pratap works closely with weaving clusters across India, including Banaras, Bhagalpur, West Bengal and Bhagaiya, developing fabrics in small handwoven batches. The brand uses a mix of cottons, linens, silks, and wools, often finished with patchwork, smocking, and embroidery. Founded in 2013, Hannah Khiangte centres her practice around indigenous Zo textiles, working with weavers across Founded in 2018 by Manjushree Saikia, Ura Maku works with handloom textiles from Assam. Working with regional weavers, the label develops fabrics that reflect local techniques while adapting them into modern silhouettes. The aesthetic is clean and functional. Founded in 2019 by Shweta Agarwal, Āroka keeps things minimal, but not plain. The focus is on handwoven materials developed with a small cooperative in Kalna, West Bengal, with subtle weaves layering doing most of the talking. The aesthetic stays clean and pared-back, but there’s enough texture and detail to keep it from feeling too straightforward. Kritika Murarka builds collections that foreground surface technique and material. The brand often incorporates elements like hand embroidery, appliqué and textural detailing into otherwise clean silhouettes. It's contemporary with a decorative edge, structured separates and occasion-leaning pieces. Harago works with artisans across India, developing handwoven textiles in regions such as West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, and Assam, while also collaborating with craft communities like Bagru near Jaipur. Urvashi Kaur works extensively with handloom textiles sourced from weaving clusters across India, including jamdani from Bengal, leheriya from Jaipur, khadi and Bhujodi from Kutch, and Chanderi, Maheshwari, and Kota doriya. The brand builds its collections around these region-specific fabrics, treating each as a starting point for design. Since its launch in 2015, Naushad Ali has focused on working with artisans across India, building collections around heritage fabrics and traditional techniques. It keeps things relaxed with loose silhouettes and easy layering. Embroidery and playful accents show up often, adding character without taking away from the overall laid-back feel. Margn approaches handloom through a lens of minimalism and structure, often working with naturally dyed fabrics and traditional weaves. The silhouettes are clean and architectural, with an emphasis on cut, proportion and finish. Founded in 2014 by Sreejith Jeevan and based in Kochi, the brand’s approach is shaped by its setting, drawing from Kerala’s textile traditions as well as Kochi’s more eclectic, urban sensibility. Its aesthetic moves between what the designer describes as a “modern old” and a “nostalgic new”, blending familiar weaves with updated silhouettes.

article_title: Is Gen Z's personal style in its copy-paste era?
sub_title: Everyone wants to stand out using the same references
article_content: We have all seen that photograph of young women posed against an autumn backdrop in The skinny jean has since been declared over, and the Katniss Everdeen Enter the baby tee and cargo pants. Or the cropped white T-shirt with wide-leg jeans, slick bun, tiny shoulder bag and trainers that have been aggressively workshopped to look accidental. This outfit would like you to believe it came together instinctually, that you simply got dressed and happened to emerge looking like a fully formed aesthetic. Curious, then, how so many other people had the same spontaneous thought. Blindfold yourself and throw a pebble in any direction in Bandra or Hauz Khas. Your next five strawberry matchas are on me if you don’t hit at least three people wearing some version of this look. A ten-minute scroll on Instagram will confirm it just as efficiently. This isn’t the death of personal style so much as its outsourcing. Fashion has always been tied to the desire to feel distinct, to look like yourself and not like everyone else. It gives you a feeling of control over your identity. Now that anyone can copy anything instantly, that urge to assert individuality has only grown stronger. The more style starts to look the same, the more people want to stand out. As What someone wears no longer comes only from what they genuinely like. It increasingly has to look deliberate, as though every choice was made on purpose. And some people deal with this by sticking to a uniform. When you’re constantly being exposed to new ‘cores’ and aesthetics, the easiest response is to stop playing along and stick to basics. And even this “uniform” is not outside of the system; it is a result of it. Either way, there is no clean way out of that loop. What emerges instead is a version of personal style that feels increasingly formulaic. Originality may still exist, but in a culture of endless reference and instant replication, it has become harder to recognise and even harder to prove.

article_title: Malaika Arora steps onto the accessible luxury scene with her latest venture
sub_title: From a range of handbags to lab-grown diamond jewellery, Malaika Arora’s Maejoy is an elevated lifestyle brand that blends accessibility with aspirational design
article_content: There are some luxury products reserved for special occasions—the ones that help you celebrate milestones and pass on as heirlooms. But then there are those that make everyday feel special—a necklace or a matching bag that elevates your outfit. These pieces have their own charm, making those long, tiring days a little easier to get through. Centred on this idea of everyday luxury is actress Malaika Arora’s new brand, Maejoy. An elevated lifestyle accessories brand, Maejoy, along with Exceed Entertainment and Myntra Jabong, adds over 250 designs of handbags and lab-grown diamond jewellery to the portfolio. Fashion today is less about imitation and more about expressing yourself. Everyone’s personal style is varied; a kaleidoscope of their own character traits and quirks. Everything you choose to wear—from a basic graphic t-shirt to a vintage bag you thrifted becomes a statement of your individuality, confidence and self-expression. Maejoy is a celebration of this kind of modern fashion, guided by the philosophy of The Joy of Being Me. Through a vast range of products, the brand aims to make high-fashion designs and silhouettes accessible to everyone. “Maejoy is a labour of love. Throughout my career, whether on screen, in business, or through my personal style, I’ve championed the idea that fashion should be empowering yet effortless,” shares Arora about her latest venture. Translating the vision behind the brand into a business was its collaboration with Myntra Jabong, the fashion and lifestyle e-commerce company. The brand launches a contemporary collection of bags; everything from practical workwear and casual backpacks to ornamental clutches. These come in a variety of materials and finishes, such as sturdy synthetic leather and versatile raffia, edgy metallic and rhinestone embellishments. The structured shoulder bags are a highlight of the collection; elegant, versatile and ideal for the kind of days that start with 10 am meetings and end with eventful evenings stretching long into the night. Crossbody and tote bags stand out, too, with their ability to be fashionably practical. Maejoy's jewellery line features rings, earrings, pendants, and bracelets in silver, gold and rose-gold tones. article_title: From trousseaus to runways, phulkari carries the stories of women’s lives
sub_title: Designer Pratima Pandey collaborated with The Nabha Foundation on Marzi, a collection that celebrates phulkari as living Punjabi heritage rather than a relic of the past
article_content: On an uncharacteristically pleasant March evening in Delhi, I braved the evening traffic to visit the National Crafts Museum & Hastkala Academy to discover more about phulkari. My Punjabi best friend would break out her mother’s phulkari bagh, a ceremonial dupatta with heavy floral embroidery, at every Diwali celebration in college, wistfully declaring every time (without fail) that she couldn’t wait to receive her own at her wedding. For a Budaun-Hyderabad hybrid family like mine, cultural artefacts being passed down generations were always a source of conflict in the household. The heirlooms passed down from my paternal grandmother (from Budaun, Uttar Pradesh) would act as a red cape being brandished in front of my maternal grandmother (from Hyderabad). The only thing in common between the two matriarchs was the belief that anything the other did was subpar, to put it politely. This made joint family functions a minefield to navigate with the finesse of the most seasoned of soldiers. So the sense of connection and belonging that a beautifully embroidered dupatta would evoke in my friend fascinated me. What is it like to see a As I observed a 26-year-old craftswoman, Sukhpreet, skilfully render a geometric floral pattern without any tracing or hesitation, my mind was filled with memories of the time I valiantly tried to fix a button on my dad’s shirt, only to end up attaching the button to my finger instead of the shirt’s placket and an acute sense of second-hand pride on seeing an age-old craft being passed down and celebrated by a younger lot. In his telling of the 18th-century classic Punjabi folk tragedy These records and poems might document it for cultural historians and enthusiasts, but phulkari has long existed as a quiet, coded language of women’s lives, carrying within its geometrical patterns stories of love, labour, migration and memory. It’s an intimate archive that has continued to live on in the trunks and Presented by The Nabha Foundation, a philanthropic organisation established for the preservation of the state’s cultural heritage, Phulkari of Punjab brought together archival textiles, displays, a moderated panel discussion and a runway presentation of designer Pratima Pandey’s phulkari-focused collection, Marzi. “Phulkari is no longer confined to nostalgia or museum spaces,” says Shubhra Singh, executive director, The Nabha Foundation. “It’s being recontextualised for contemporary audiences while retaining its essence. This dual movement of preservation and evolution has been critical to its renewed relevance.” Traditionally, phulkari textiles marked life-cycle events such as births and marriages. When a girl was born in a household, the grandmother and mother would start preparing her phulkari bagh, a style of the embroidery where the entire surface of the fabric is embroidered. Over time, however, shifts in the economy and lifestyle pushed the craft to the margin, threatening its continuity. Over the past few decades, concerted efforts have gone into preserving the craft; The Nabha Foundation itself supports over 400 artisans across Punjab who work towards making the practice of phulkari a sustainable endeavour. Artisans enrolled in the programme pass down the craft to a younger crop of women and draw a new wave of consumers by contemporising and recontextualising phulkari without losing its essence. A way to do this was to collaborate with designer Pratima Pandey on her collection. “Phulkari, at its core, is an act of agency with women choosing motifs, colours and stories without formal training or permission. Yet, many of these same women have lived within limited frameworks of choice. The collection grew from that tension. It became a way to honour the inherent freedom within the craft while acknowledging the boundaries around the maker,” says Pandey. With strains of singer Amira Gill’s rendition of ‘Ik Onkar’, the foundational faith principle of Sikhism, in the background, models walked down the brick-paved runway at the Crafts Museum in phulkari-adorned saris, cropped jackets, sheer chanderi skirts and dresses. Craft collaborations could risk becoming purely aesthetic exercises, but Pandey consciously tried to ensure this remained a dialogue rather than a one-sided reinterpretation. “We didn’t approach the artisans with fixed designs. The process involved unlearning, [and then] understanding their rhythm, decisions and instincts. There were moments when we stepped back entirely and let their way lead the outcome.” Singh echoes the sentiment, adding, “Phulkari is approached as a living, evolving language, not a static bank of motifs. The role of design is to contextualise, not overwrite. The artisans remain central to the process.” In the end, what remains is not just the surface of the textile but the many hands and the centuries of choices that shape it.

sub_title: An sweep of emerald along the lower lash line extended the colour story
article_content: At a recent awards ceremony in Mumbai, Kriti Sanon wore a vivid green Nensi Dojaka gown as she picked up an award for her performance in Cut in lustrous green satin, the floor-length gown skimmed the body before falling into a fluid, floor-length hem. Fine criss-cross straps run across the bodice and gather at the centre, where the fabric is drawn in and released into a softer drape below. Side cutouts break up the surface, while the open back pushes the look further into eveningwear territory. Dojaka's work often revisits the codes of ‘90s minimalism, with intricate cutouts, sheer panels and lingerie-like elements. The resurgence of lingerie-inspired fashion has been steadily gaining ground on international runways. From spring collections to winter styling narratives, designers, like her, have reimagined intimate wear as outerwear, shifting it from the private to the public sphere. The trend’s appeal lies in its duality–it is at once delicate and assertive. Sanon leaned into the colour story with layered jewellery. article_title: This is the best beachwear for a summer wardrobe with personality
sub_title: Maximalism at its best, these beachwear pieces are here to help you beat the heat in style
article_content: Beach outfits are usually among the first things we think about when summer is around the corner. Before the holidays are booked, before the first long weekend by the sea, before the city has fully surrendered to heat, the mood begins to shift. Suddenly, everything feels a little more sun-soaked in the imagination. Melting ice cream, salt-stiff hair, glasses of something cold sweating onto tabletops, the conviction that life would improve if only you were near a beach. Summer sells the same fantasy every year, and to be fair, it remains extremely effective. Somewhere between reruns of This year, fashion is in the mood to indulge that impulse. A few easy pieces can do most of the work. Stripes and spots still hold up, printed swimwear adds colour fast and a strong cover-up can pull the whole look together. Add a roomy bag, flats or a piece of jewellery, and the rest takes care of itself.

article_title: This legacy jewellery brand brings a fresh perspective on heirloom jewellery to the mix
sub_title: Hazoorilal Legacy finds new expression in a curated selection that bridges tradition and modern elegance with polki, gold, diamonds and precious stones
article_content: Affectionately known as ‘bauji’ by both family and staff, Late Shri Hazoorilal Narang laid the foundation of Hazoorilal Legacy, a business rooted in trust, craftsmanship, and ambition. Narang’s brainchild, the jewellery house, is well known today for marrying international sensibilities with a proud traditional ethos. From Lahore to Delhi’s Chandni Chowk—where bauji opened the first store in 1952—to its home today in South Extention II, for over seven decades, Hazoorilal Legacy has remained steadfast in its pursuit of timeless design. It focuses on creating jewellery that enhances life’s meaningful occasions with elegance while upholding a reputation for integrity, artistry, and excellence. The Legacy Collection from The House of Hazoorilal Legacy embodies their constant pursuit of design excellence. It is an annual showcase that highlights the brand's one-of-a-kind pieces. This curation celebrates elegance with character, bringing together gold, polki, and a vibrant palette of carefully sourced natural gemstones—from deep emeralds to delicate morganites—illuminated by fine diamonds. This collection truely emerges as the brand’s defining statement—an ode to its storied heritage expressed through a distinctly modern lens. Anchored in the brand’s legacy of unparalleled craftsmanship and visionary design, their recent collection, ‘The Spring Edit 2026’ captures the essence of renewal, beauty, and sophistication. Each piece in the edit has been designed to balance modern elegance with timeless charm. Deeply rooted in Indian heritage and master craftsmanship, the brand continues to expand its vision of luxury from New Delhi to the global stage. Supported by a strong digital presence, influential brand ambassadors, and diverse collections ranging from the opulent Legacy Collection to the Zoori line with its playful designs and colourful gemstone jewellery, the brand is ready for the future. A significant chapter in this global journey has been the brand’s first year in the Dubai market, marked by strong growth and meaningful engagement. The brand’s distinctive blend of vintage inspiration and contemporary design—grounded in Indian workmanship—resonated strongly with Dubai’s cosmopolitan clientele. At its core, Hazoorilal Legacy represents a study in curated opulence. Every creation reveals an architectural sensibility, where gemstones—from emeralds and diamonds to rubellites—are placed with precision to achieve visual harmony. The result is jewellery that feels both powerful and poised: a sophisticated expression of contemporary luxury that resonates with a global audience.

article_title: 7 Gen Z creatives on building wardrobes with real personality
sub_title: For these multi-hyphenates, the 9-to-5 was never really an option
article_content: How do you define a generation? How do you account for lived experiences that spill far beyond temporal boundaries? Oscar Wilde said that to define is to limit, and if there’s one thing I do know about Gen Z, it’s that we don’t like limits. In fact, we actively despise them. Whether it’s dismantling gender binaries or making increasingly loud democratic demands, this is a generation that refuses to sit still. And when it comes to bringing home the dough, the cookie-cutter career path is on the brink of extinction. Gen Z creatives are more amoeba than ladder-climbers; they’re constantly metamorphosing, adapting to whatever the world throws their way. And naturally, they’re doing it in style.

article_title: This family-run jewellery house has a legacy spanning nine decades
sub_title: Here’s how Bishan, a luxury jewellery house, reflects a legacy built on trust and timeless design
article_content: The year was 1933. The late Bishan Singh Chadha opened a jewellery store in Rawalpindi—then part of India, now in Pakistan—unaware that this modest beginning would lay the foundation for a 21st-century brand. Ninety years later, the jewellery house continues to honour his legacy and his affinity for creating pieces that go on to become heirloom jewellery. The brand’s deep respect for legacy is showcased on its website, where its first-ever sales bill from 1933 occupies a place of pride. The family-run jewellery house opened its first store in independent India in Chandni Chowk, Delhi. This was followed by another store in Delhi in 2000. Since then, the brand has found patrons outside India and now exports its handcrafted creations across the Middle East and beyond. The brand was first launched under the name Harnam Singh Bishan Singh Jewellers. Over the decades, the house evolved to 100% in-house manufacturing, gaining full creative control to craft bespoke pieces for discerning clients. In 2023, the brand was reintroduced as Bishan—a refined identity that honours its rich heritage while embracing the future of Indian jewellery. By 2010, it was serving over 2,000 clients across more than 10 countries. Today, with stores in Delhi, Dubai, and Qatar, Bishan is known for designs that honour the grandeur of traditional Indian craftsmanship while embracing a global aesthetic, making them equally suited for a Parisian soiree or a regal Indian wedding. More than mere adornment, Bishan jewellery celebrates exclusivity, individuality, and timeless elegance. Each creation is designed to become an heirloom—a delicate balance of classical influences and contemporary sophistication. Whether you seek a regal statement with emeralds, vintage charm with sapphires, or the serene elegance of rare diamonds, Bishan offers endless ways to infuse meaning, intention, and sophistication into your ensemble.
