article_title: A closer look at a collection that brings Kapurthala’s past into everyday dressing
sub_title: The House of Valaya’s luxury prêt label JJV.Kapurthala introduces ATTH for Spring–Summer 2026, marking its eighth season, drawing on Kapurthala’s royal past and the house’s long-standing fascination with travel and Art Deco design
article_content: Some places leave a lasting impression. For JJ Valaya, the Delhi-based couturier known for building a world around Indian heritage, that place has always been Kapurthala. Often referred to as the Paris of Punjab, the princely state was shaped by the travels of Maharaja Jagatjit Singh, who brought back European influences that still echo in its architecture and cultural identity. Through JJV.Kapurthala, that world is reimagined in a way that feels lighter and more relaxed, translating the house’s distinctive style into clothing designed for everyday use. The label’s Spring–Summer 2026 collection, ATTH, continues this connection. The word means ‘eight’ in Punjabi, marking the eighth season of the line and continuing the brand’s tradition of naming collections through Punjabi numerology. Each season becomes a marker of time—an evolving chapter rooted in the culture and history that continue to inspire the house. Every JJV.Kapurthala collection is shaped by three directions that define the core ethos of the world of VALAYA—Royale, Nomade and Art Deco—and this season returns to them with subtle shifts. In the Royale chapter, Paisley appears, in a more restrained form. The motif is reworked and layered with jaali-inspired patterns; these two traditional elements sit together in a way that feels balanced. The Nomade story turns to ikat, a craft treasured for its organic qualities. The patterns retain their natural irregularity, bringing a sense of movement to the garments. For Art Deco, the collection adds an unexpected element—a monkey motif drawn from Eastern artistic traditions. Set against the structured geometry often associated with the Art Deco period, it introduces a playful note while maintaining the collection’s visuals. The collection moves away from the weight of intricate embroidery and instead embraces bold prints, fluid fabrics, and subtle antique touches. The aim is simple: pieces that embody the spirit of celebration while remaining easy to wear. For womenswear, the season brings in summer-friendly tops and tunics, along with modern skirt sets, kaftans, shararas, and relaxed co-ord ensembles—silhouettes that are ideal for travel, social gatherings, and everyday wear. Fabric is key to achieving this sense of ease. Cupro, satin, linen, Giza cotton, georgette, and modal feature throughout the collection, chosen for their lightness and drape in warmer weather. The colour palette echoes this balance. Ivory, crème, mustard, teal, and shades of pink and coral form the softer base of the season, complemented by deeper house signatures such as navy, plum, and black. The collection launches this March and will be available in JJV.Kapurthala stores nationwide and on the brand’s website. With ATTH, the house returns to the themes that have long defined its design language—heritage, craft, and a sense of discovery—presented in pieces that feel easy and expressive.

article_title: Fashion in Northeast India is bigger than beauty pageants and thrift clichés
sub_title: If anything, the first Aizawl Design Project was a testament to that
article_content: For years, the narrative of fashion in Northeast India has been frustratingly narrow. The region’s relationship with style has often been flattened into three easy clichés: cultural shows, beauty pageants and the well-worn mythology of thrift culture. None of them are entirely false. But none of them capture the full picture either. The first Aizawl Design Project was proof of how outdated those assumptions have become. Its first public expression, the The collections, styled by Aizawl-born stylist James Lalthanzuala, brought together three distinct designers from Mizoram—Hannah Khiangte, Lapâr and Escape Engmoia—each working with the Zo The showcase was conceived and curated by Lal Moya, an event curator based in Washington DC. “As a Mizo creative, I have always believed our designers deserve the same level of staging and presentation that you see anywhere in the world. The talent has always been here. What we needed was the platform and the courage to present it properly,” he said. For decades, fashion from the Northeast has been expected to carry the duty of representation. Clothes had to signify something: tribe, tradition, identity, solidarity. Fashion, in the sense of experimentation or self-expression, was often treated as secondary. What the The designers are reworking indigenous textiles as living materials that can adapt to new forms, without treating them like inherited artefacts anymore. “My collection comes from the idea of Lapâr was established in 2017 by Patricia Zadeng. With a degree in textile design from the When asked why he named his brand This showcase did not erase the region’s cultural heritage. If anything, it situates the Zo Perhaps the most significant change is that fashion from the Northeast is no longer asking for validation using cultural tokens. Designers are building their own communities, creating their own platforms and shaping their own visual identities. The Northeast’s fashion scene has always had unbridled style. What it’s finally gaining now is the space to experiment, to fail, to evolve and to exist beyond the narrow scripts it was once written into.

article_title: Are single-edition Banarasi saris the ultimate luxury flex?
sub_title: As rarity becomes part of the appeal, Swati & Sunaina Gold is betting that serious sari collectors want what cannot be repeated
article_content: It all started with a wild goose chase in Banaras (Varanasi),” recalls Swati Agarwal. One half of the label Swati & Sunaina Gold, the designer traces the brand’s origin story back a decade ago when, inspired by her Marwari family’s trove of heirloom saris, she set out to find a rangkaat (a complex weaving technique that interlocks silk with zari threads) drape for her brother’s wedding. The search was obsessive—calls to President’s Award– winning artisans, hours spent poring over Weaver Service Centre booklets, even a cold hunt through Varanasi’s bylanes. She never found the rangkaat she had dreamed of, but discovered a new calling instead. In a landscape crowded with Banarasi brocade brands, Agarwal and her sister-in-law Sunaina Jalan have conjured up an anomaly. Their focus is the single-edition sari, which means no two patrons will ever own the same piece. Exclusivity is taken so seriously that they do not even maintain a physical archive of their actual creations (they do chronicle through sketches and samples). Each collection is a capsule of just six design directions, with 12 to 18 pieces in singular colourways. With pieces starting at ₹3 lakh, these are not impulse buys. Since the beginning, the founders have worked exclusively with Banarasi textiles, drawing on dampach, kadua, jamdani, rangkaat and gyaser (their interpretation of the Indo-Tibetan textile). But each comes with interventions. Where others would settle for neat colour panels in rangkaat, they tied the blocks with woven bows. Their intervention in gyaser required looms that normally yielded only 23 inches to be adapted to accommodate an entire sari—a feat never attempted before. Their Vanya collection of 24 saris brought wild silks from the Northeast—eri, tussar, muga and mulberry—into the Banaras gharana. The kora or white nature of these silks was paired with motifs inspired by Indian white flowers (rajnigandha, juhi, bela, champa, aparajita and brahmakamal) as well as miniature Kangra paintings of Krishna in the night garden. What makes Swati & Sunaina Gold stand out in a competitive market is “their research vis-à-vis history, design and the technique applied in their collections,” explains textile curator Lavina Baldota. It’s little wonder that these saris, sans shiny embellishment or accoutrement, “demand a certain price”, she adds. This dedication to detail is evident in their collections. The pair took four trips to France and wrote a thesis on the India-France textile connection before releasing the newest Varanasi to Versailles line, which showcases a fine mix of brocade and French lace. As India experiences a revivalist moment, and formal contemporary textile museums remain rare, the role of individual designers and collectors becomes even more crucial. Agarwal shares that a young bride from Hyderabad commissioned a sari for her wedding. “She’d met her fiancé only a couple of months prior, but the connection felt cosmic, and she wanted her bridal look to reflect that.” The team created a piece that drew from the couple’s astrological signs, lucky numbers and intertwined names in a Telugu script. The bride archived the entire process, proving that collectors who buy refined textiles value the journey as deeply as the finished weave itself. To the sisters-in-law, as with other skill-led designers— Chinar Farooqui of Injiri and her quiet devotion to jamdani; Sanjay Garg of Raw Mango, who has expanded the handloom lexicon; Pankaj S with his luminous Murshidabad mul; and Aadyam Handwoven with its explorations in ikat—speaking about process and their long-term relationships with makers isn’t marketing. It’s a responsibility. Which is why conversations must shift beyond focusing on how many hours a weaver spent at the loom or which mythological character inspired a motif. The sharper question is whether stakeholders—not just the weaver but the yarn dyer, the spinner, the jacquard punch maker, even the loom maker—are compensated well enough to continue this work. Exhibitions that showcase skill, patronage that inspires continuity and above-market pay structures are what separate romanticism from real commitment. Agarwal and Jalan understand that difference. “I don’t think weaving is a dying art form, but it is certainly an ageing one,” Agarwal says, contemplatively. The renewed fascination with handlooms has helped both small ateliers and big brands, but she points to a new threat. “Many young weavers may not have the patience or focus like their forefathers did.” She notes many young practitioners’ attention spans have been hijacked by their phone while a power loom grunts on the side. For years, the fear was that the new hands would just not have the same agility. Now, it’s focus that is slipping away. And in that quiet fading of concentration lies the real fragility of the craft Agarwal and Jalan are trying so hard to protect.

article_title: In these fashion stores, the clothes are only part of the experience
sub_title: Indian designers are creating whimsical imaginariums where there’s much more to thrill than the swipe of a credit card
article_content: At the Sabyasachi store in Mumbai, an interesting statistic comes up in conversation with a sales associate. She mentions that on any given day, between 10 and 15 people walk in with no explicit intention of making a purchase. Many are international tourists, keen to see what’s been recommended to them as one of the most exquisite retail spaces in all of India. And for good reason. The store (and its many addresses across the country and in New York) offers an encounter with Indian maximalism where time feels suspended. Its curation of collectibles—heirloom furniture, treasured curios, antique rugs and the like—exists in a profusion that has to be seen first-hand to be truly understood. Naturally, then, visitors are sometimes confused to learn the artefacts aren’t for sale. A few lanes away, Gaurav Gupta’s three-storey flagship is an immediate visual foil: an all-white world of minimalist futurism. Architect Vishal K Dar created a space for the brand that is undulating and otherworldly—like a white-cube gallery in which the garments are presented as wearable art. Further south, Sanjay Garg’s Raw Mango store, designed by interior architect Ashiesh Shah and designer Isla Maria ‘Loulou’ Van Damme, is meditative, measured and almost anti-spectacle in its approach to Indian craft traditions. The layout, material palette and aesthetic elements draw from the tropical modernist philosophies of architects like Geoffrey Bawa and Charles Correa, culminating in a space of true repose: an 800-square-foot courtyard. In addition to the one-kilometre radius they inhabit, the retail spaces of Sabyasachi, Gaurav Gupta and Raw Mango share a strong common denominator: they each function as compelling, tangible extensions of their brands’ sartorial identities. Within South Mumbai’s Indo-Saracenic and neogothic streetscape, these fashion stores exist as micro-universes of craft. They’re evolving into a new version of the third space, where communities are formed, cross-collaboration is encouraged and creative programming feels entirely natural. Raw Mango’s famous baithaks come to mind, the most recent edition of which was hosted at the label’s Banjara Hills store last November. For designers who see themselves as being creators before entrepreneurs, the store is where their vision can be realised in full. At Delhi Vintage Co, the worldbuilding takes on an almost mythological nature. Their new 10,000-square-foot store in the capital, designed by Smita Singh of NoDoor, draws from the phases of a lunar eclipse interpreted as a series of archways. Founder Manish Chhabra’s soulful private collection of Indian art is displayed throughout the store, though one of his most significant pieces was a bespoke commission: a sculpture of a devi, seemingly suspended in motion at the very edge of a table and secured in position by threads, produced by Neil Ghose Balser and Doyel Joshi of How Are You Feeling Studio. “We worked very closely on every element—from artefacts to textures to spatial flow,” says Chhabra. “Even the fragrance in the store is custom-curated, because I wanted the experience to go beyond the visual. ” Another rendition of this ideology lies in the glittering new Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla store at Jio World Plaza in Mumbai. Quilted curtains finished with aabla embroidery, gold-leafed walls with AJSK patola motifs and mirrored ceilings are only a prelude to the brand’s take on opulence. The rapid growth of e-commerce feels almost directly proportional to a more resolute conviction that physical retail spaces are irreplicable. This is especially true in a luxury marketplace. The physical store is where a customer can best understand the difference between one house and the next beyond price points— where a brand is fully felt and where loyalty is earned, in a way a website never can. Brands are working hard to protect this distinction, ensuring the act of making an in-person purchase doesn’t exist in a vacuum. S howrooms now come with branded cafés and restaurants, and in some cases these hospitality outposts become their own attraction: in 2024, Mumbai got its first Armani/Caffè, with a menu comprising a selection of Giorgio Armani’s favourite dishes. Indian labels such as Nappa Dori routinely partner with coffee brands for their in-store cafés. When Moonray rebranded to Chorus last year, with a three-storey flagship in Kala Ghoda, it included a chic café and home-decor section, as well as a compelling selection of handcrafted soaps, body oils and candles. Among legacy brands, there is an increased focus on consumer literacy around craft processes and provenance. A few years ago, Hermès presented its ‘In Motion’ travelling exhibition in Mumbai, offering a rare and detailed insight into over a century of the house’s archive. In Jaipur, the House of Sunita Shekhawat, a family-run fine jewellery brand, established a permanent museum to celebrate the art of meenakari around two years ago. “People don’t walk in only to see objects; they walk in to understand where meenakari comes from and why it matters,” says Sunita Shekhawat. “Clients now arrive with a stronger emotional connect and a deeper respect for the craft. We’ve seen a clear shift towards mindful collecting rather than quick purchases.” Among brands that offer a more interactive understanding of craft processes, Basement, the concept store for clothing and lifestyle label 11.11/Eleven Eleven in Delhi, stands as a noteworthy example. A large brass vat filled with indigo dye is the pièce de résistance in the store. Customers are encouraged to dip raw fabric into the liquid and witness it take on the colour, in an experience they’re not likely to forget anytime soon. While it is a globally accepted fact that brick-and-mortar fashion stores are far more than sites for transactions, it feels most relevant in India, where so much of fashion’s foundation is intricate handwork, technique and generational—as well as regional— expertise. The store is where this foundation becomes truly intelligible; the delicacy of chikankari or the raised relief of zari can rarely be understood through an image alone. Gupta says, “A physical store allows for something that digital can never fully replicate—that is, presence. It allows clients to slow down, to feel the weight of a fabric, to understand proportion, to engage with craftsmanship.” Chhabra echoes this sentiment. “Luxury is deeply tied to human interaction,” he says. “The physical store allows for a slower, more immersive engagement, where stories are shared, textures are explored and relationships are built. In that sense, reinvention is essential.”

sub_title: As artificial intelligence accelerates what can be produced cheaply, there is a call to return to the nuance and imperfection of whathumans create
article_content: Stepping out of my London hotel, Harvey Nichols. I had expected the familiar grammar of luxury retail: mannequins frozen mid-gesture, campaign faces enlarged to abstraction. Instead, drawings darted across the glass—Jacky Blue’s sketches animated on screen, stretched beyond scale, rendered in thick, confident strokes that simultaneously had a doodle-like charm. I was not new to the vocabulary of illustration. Fashion did not enter my life through proximity. It arrived obliquely, through cinema. Audrey Hepburn led me to Givenchy and Dior, and from there to Edith Head. What stayed were not only the finished garments, but the drawings that preceded them. I sketched obsessively through my years of science education, mostly in the­ margins of textbooks, copying silhouettes I could not access in any other way. When fashion felt unreachable, I drew it closer. Fashion illustrations have long functioned as a form of access for buyers and enthusiasts alike. From early costume books at 19th-century couture ateliers to campaigns in Vogue, this language was how designers and their patrons communicated. When the industry accelerated and photography made the process of creating images instant, illustration seemed to slip from the centre. Yet, a single held-back line can sometimes contain more feeling than an entire campaign. The legendary Italian fashion illustrator René Gruau understood this instinctively. His work for Dior, beginning with Miss Dior in 1947, did not merely advertise the clothing but conjured up an immersive world for the brand. A ballerina in a tutu; an ingenue’s hand resting lightly on a leopard’s paw; a woman, as seen from behind, hugging a huge bouquet of flowers—you could almost smell it. Gruau’s 20th-century drawings for Dior, Balenciaga, Schiaparelli and Givenchy shaped how modern luxury learned to look at itself. That sensibility carries forward most clearly today in the work of the English fashion illustrator David Downton. He built his reputation on drawings made fresh from Paris couture fittings each season, as well as on his live portrayals of illustrious figures—from Cate Blanchett to Linda Evangelista—rendered in his signature,­ watercolour lines that convey an air of impenetrable glamour. His art has circulated so widely that it sits pinned to moodboards and framed in private homes, absorbed into the collective visual memory of fashion. Downton arrived in Paris in 1996, just as John Galliano and Alexander McQueen were taking up their posts at Dior and Givenchy. “There was electricity in the air. I felt like I had entered Narnia and I knew I had found my métier,” says Downton. His work remains committed to being present, standing up, pacing, making decisions that cannot be undone. Downton muses, “It is an intimate experience. A mini love affair. Today, it takes an army to produce a portrait or a fashion photograph. But with a drawing, it is just you and the subject: time arrested.” Milan-based Jenny Walton, trained in real-time observation, translates that energy into her own work, sketching runway shows not to record but to respond, creating images that are as much personal impression as reportage. Her images are populated by rats and fashion girls collapsed in fetal positions. Emotions spill and absurdity reigns. She sketched the industry’s contradictions, exposing its anxieties and excesses through witty text scrawled onto these illustrations. “Because fashion illustration is so limitless, it easily lends itself to pushing ideas to their most absurd, exaggerated conclusion.” At the National Institute of Design in Ahmedabad, designer David Abraham was tau­ght to emphasise drawing for its own sake—learning proportion, perspective, ratios and how to render material. How granite behaves differently from wood, chiffon from silk. These principles, he explains, are what make a drawing work. article_title: This craft school in Kutch is in the business of forging confidence
sub_title: Somaiya Kala Vidya has helped artisans gain financial autonomy in a world where craft is a buzzword
article_content: Three girls sat on a I sat with the graduating batch as they prepared for the show—passing around mood boards, swatches, Somaiya Kala Vidya (SKV) was founded with a clear belief: If craft is to remain culturally honest and economically relevant, innovation must come from within. And that Today, SKV runs as a year-long residential programme for artisans of Kutch for craftspeople from various communities. There is no age limit and no literacy requirement. On the syllabus are design principles and business management skills. Some students are as young as 16 years old. Others are in their 30s, with children to raise and households to run. The institute spends Rs 3-4 lakh per student. Men pay ₹12,000, women ₹6,000. When asked why as most artisan courses are free, Nishit Sangomla, director of SKV replied: “Deliberately so, to instil ownership without creating barriers.” The shift in gender participation is palpable. For years, women’s applications had been sporadic—none at all up till 2019, as the women had to stay on campus for the duration of the year. Elder brothers, uncles and other men would do the course but not the women. Post-pandemic, the outreach in weaving villages like Bhujodi, Gamthara and Sarli has changed that balance. On graduation night, a generation of women who had woven for years without recognition now spoke as designers, some for the first time. Some women were the first to ever practice the craft, such as The next day, I set out to meet some alumni from the school, curious to see the ripples the classroom had on their craft post completing the course. In Ajrakhpur, I met Zaid Khatri, a 10th-generation What stayed with him most vividly from the course were the drawing classes. “This was the first time I was allowed to draw, just draw,” he told me. Colour studies gave language to instincts he had always carried—grayscale, chromatic balance, colour placement. The shift was not easy. Zaid admits he struggled in school, and geometry-based modules done by hand were difficult. Yet it was through that process that his practice expanded. During market visits to Ahmedabad, including a stop at Anokhi, he began to understand customers not as abstract buyers but as individuals with their own visual worlds. Unlike many others, she was the first weaver in her family. Her father works as a driver; she first learned weaving from an aunt before training in carpet making in Bhujodi. Representatives from the school encountered her work during a village visit. They admired the carpet she had woven but asked her something she had never considered: how would she explain the design to a customer? What were its elements? What colours had she chosen and why? At the school, the first colour theory class puzzled her. “Why are we working on paper?” she wondered. Slowly the exercises revealed a different way of seeing—repeat patterns, motif abstraction. For the first time she experimented with brick repeats, drop repeats and figurative motifs like birds or camels, moving beyond the geometric forms she had always used. It also introduced collaboration. Though she is a weaver, she began working with a friend who practises Bandhani, incorporating Bandhani elements into her carpets. That year was also her first time living away from home, travelling later to Mumbai for an exhibition where she learned how customers respond to craft. article_title: Jacqueline Fernandez’s Manish Malhotra ensemble is a pearl lover’s dream
sub_title: A pearl hair detail, glossy skin and a half-up hairstyle keep the styling in step with the sari’s finish
article_content: Jacqueline Fernandez arrived at a recent outing dressed in a blush Constructed in lace, the sari is worked through with pearl embellishment, extending from the scalloped border across the body of the fabric. The detailing is most concentrated along the edges, where pearls of varying sizes trace the hemline and pallu, creating a denser outline against the more lightly scattered field. Fernandez shifts the drape slightly, pulling the pallu across her back and letting it fall from one arm, which keeps the border in view for longer. The true showstopper of her ensemble is the blouse. A  departure from conventional codes, it is a silk bralette layered with a matching lace cropped cape. The cape is high-necked, with pearls applied with meticulous density at the scalloped hem and the neckline that almost mimics the effect of wearing a statement neckpiece. Lace and pearls have a lineage that stretches back to the Edwardian era, when gauzy lace-trimmed gowns defined the period's feminine ideal and pearls sets were among the most prized adornments a woman could wear. The pairing was revived and democratised in the early 20th century when Coco Chanel famously reimagined pearls as symbols of female independence rather than mere aristocratic status. That spirit has been revisited on international runways repeatedly. Dior has leaned into pearl accents across clothing and accessories, and then Simone Rocha and Vivienne Westwood played with subversive pearl styling. With Fernandez’s sari, Manish Malhotra has given this long-standing Western obsession an Indian occasion-wear translation. Fernandez keeps the accessories minimal, with diamond studs and a cocktail ring. A pearl hair detail is worked into her half-up hairstyle, while her makeup stays within a tonal range, with sheen concentrated on the eyes and skin to mirror the finish of the fabric.

article_title: From Priyanka Chopra Jonas to Rihanna—see every Met Gala look from the last decade

article_content: Over the past 15 years, the This year’s Met Gala will celebrate the Costume Institute’s new exhibition, titled “ While we’ll all have to wait to see how that plays out, we can satisfy our craving for elaborate dressing by looking at past Met Gala events. Consider it prime time to refresh your memory of all the past iconic looks to grace the carpet—and also, brush up on the moments and themes that you may have missed or forgotten. (Take Helen Lasichanh’s 2017 Comme des Garçons shapely look, the Olsen twins’ unexpected take on the 2013 punk theme, and many more.) Below, Last year’s Met Gala theme, “Superfine: Tailoring Black Style,” focused on The 2024 Met Gala theme, “Sleeping Beauties: Reawakening Fashion,” spotlighted one-of-a-kind fashions of the past. Approximately 250 items were drawn from the Costume Institute’s permanent collection—some very rarely seen in public before—and were displayed in entirely new ways, thanks to video animation, light projection, soundscaping, AI, CGI, and other forms of sensory stimulation. It was co-hosted by Zendaya, Jennifer Lopez, Chris Hemsworth, Bad Bunny, and Anna Wintour. The dress code was “ The 2023 Met Gala theme, “Karl Lagerfeld: A Line of Beauty,” served as a celebration of Karl Lagerfeld—highlighting the late designer’s one-of-a-kind contributions to fashion while helming major fashion houses such as Chanel, Fendi, Balmain, and more. It was co-hosted by Michaela Coel, Penélope Cruz, Roger Federer, The 2022 Met Gala theme, “In America: An Anthology of Fashion,” kicked off the Costume Institute’s exhibition of the same name: It centered on the tenets of American style, and highlighted the anonymous and unsung heroes of U.S. design. On the red carpet, stars served up their best takes on the The 2019 Met Gala celebrated the Costume Institute’s newest exhibition, “ The theme for the 2018 Met Gala connected the holy with the haute. The exhibit explored Catholic iconography in fashion, from papal vestments to more inspired takes from Gianni Versace, Coco Chanel, and more. Guests embraced this focus, choosing ensembles with nods to crosses, crowns, and, in Rihanna’s case, cardinal hats. Paying homage to Rei Kawakubo, the 2017 Met Gala exhibition examined more than 100 pieces of the designer’s work at Comme des Garçons, spanning the brand’s history from the 1980s onward. While few stars wore Comme on the carpet, save for Rihanna in a fall 2016 look, many did embrace Kawakubo’s avant-garde spirit. “Manus x Machina” explored the role of technology in fashion, from the 20th century to the present. The exhibit spotlighted more than 170 ensembles, and on the carpet, many guests went along with the futuristic theme. It was a particularly strong year for couple moments: Kim Kardashian West and Kanye West showed up in metallic silver Balmain looks, while Gigi Hadid and Zayn Malik did his-and-hers bionic eveningwear. The 2015 Met Gala theme examined the influence of Chinese art, film, and pop culture on Western fashion, doing so through a collection of traditional artworks and more than 130 haute couture and ready-to-wear looks. The stars who won the red carpet were those who embraced Chinese designers: Rihanna’s much-meme’d yellow Guo Pei design is still talked about today. If you love sweeping gowns, this is the year for you. The 2014 exhibition acknowledged the work of designer Charles James, one of the biggest names in mid-20th-century American fashion, and whose work inspired countless names after him, including the couturier Christian Dior. As for the carpet dress code, stars embraced couture designs that evoked the spirit of his work (read: feminine dresses like Dakota Johnson’s Jason Wu and Florence Welch’s Valentino Haute Couture), and the men dressed in white tie. One of the wildest Met Galas in history, the 2013 theme focused on punk subculture and its influence on fashion. There were loads of safety pins, fishnet, and spike heels on the carpet. Sarah Jessica Parker even wore a mohawk headpiece by Philip Treacy. The 2012 Met Gala exhibition examined the striking similarities between the works of Elsa Schiaparelli and Miuccia Prada, and the push-and-pull tensions between their two aesthetics. On the carpet, many chose Prada for their evening attire, like Carey Mulligan, Jessica Biel, Amber Valletta, Gwyneth Paltrow, and Eva Mendes. This year’s theme was an ode to the incomparable work of the late Lee Alexander McQueen. Naomi Campbell, Sarah Jessica Parker, and many more paid homage to the designer by wearing his frocks that were heavy on the fantasy. While Beyoncé did not wear McQueen, she did steal the show that year in an embroidered Emilio Pucci number. The 2010 Met Gala exhibit showcased evolving perceptions of the modern American woman from 1890 to 1940, and how those perceptions have affected the way American women are seen today. A certain timelessness was maintained though the red carpet, though more daring stars, such as Katy Perry, took risks by wearing an LED-light gown.

article_title: The 400-year-old Khada Dupatta remains the soul of Hyderabadi bridal dressing
sub_title: From royal origins to contemporary brides, the Khada Dupatta endures—balancing heritage with personal expression
article_content: Every bride anticipates her wedding day—not just for the ceremony, but for what it allows her to become. It is a rare moment of expansiveness: to be seen, celebrated and, if only for a day, become the centre of it all. A wedding dress, then, is never just an outfit. It marks a transition, carrying meaning beyond fabric. In Hyderabad, that presence is often shaped by the Khada Dupatta, a signature The Khada Dupatta is a three-piece outfit, typically consisting of a kurta, a churidar and a six-yard dupatta. Its true essence, however, lies in the dupatta itself—the element that gives the ensemble its name, structure and cultural presence. Unlike more common styles of draping, it is worn in a distinctive manner that covers both shoulders and falls down the back. The term Worn across generations, the Khada Dupatta reflects a legacy spanning nearly 400 years, shaped by craft passed from one woman to another. Its history is often traced back to the Mughal era. Nur Jahan—widely regarded as a tastemaker of her time—is credited with influencing textiles and courtly dress, with As Mughal influence extended into the Deccan, this aesthetic evolved. When Nizam-ul-Mulk established his rule over Hyderabad, “Every generation reinterprets it—through textiles, embroidery, and styling—but the soul of the Khada Dupatta remains untouched,” notes Jayanti Reddy, founder and designer of her eponymous label. And perhaps that is why it has endured—not just as a garment, but as what Reddy describes as “a cultural heirloom,” carrying within it “grace, dignity, and opulence that transcends time.” Its longevity lies not in resistance, but in its ability to evolve without losing its core. That core is held in the way the garment is crafted. The Khada Dupatta is defined by its heavily worked borders—often executed in As Karan Torani, founder and designer of the label Torani, notes, Indian clothing has never needed to chase relevance in the way many other fashion systems do. “The Khada Dupatta, in particular, speaks of layering, dignity and power dressing,” he explains. “Its upright drape frames the body with a kind of architectural elegance, giving it both restraint and presence.” For him, a bride who chooses this silhouette is someone who wants her wedding look to tell a story, and understands that fashion can also serve as an archive. Today, this narrative continues to unfold in both traditional and contemporary contexts. Celebrities like Rekha have long drawn from Hyderabadi codes of dressing, while Nita Ambani, Sania Mirza, and more recently Sobhita Dhulipala have reaffirmed its place within modern bridal imagination. Ultimately, the Khada Dupatta carries its power in both feeling and memory. For a bride, it can make the day feel larger, while also tying her to something older than the ceremony itself. That continuity is part of what keeps it alive across generations.

article_title: 7 new designer stores we’re excited to shop at this season
sub_title: Across Mumbai, Delhi and Bengaluru, these new boutiques turn retail into a more tactile experience
article_content: Shopping online is efficient. It is also, at times, a bit spiritually flat. You click, zoom, add to cart, and hope the fabric behaves in real life the way it did under studio lighting and a persuasive caption. The appeal of good designer stores lies elsewhere. It is in the atmosphere, the materiality, the way a Dhruv Kapoor opened its first flagship in New Delhi in January, taking the brand’s distinctive visual language into an immersive physical setting. Located in Chattarpur, the store pairs raw marble with micro-concrete floors and mirror-finish walls, creating a space that feels sleek without turning cold. Lighting, scent and sound have all been carefully calibrated, which sounds faintly like the setup for a futuristic spa but, in this case, works to elevate the experience. Alongside seasonal collections, the flagship houses the tailoring, separates, accessories and lifestyle pieces that make up the brand’s wider vocabulary. Amit Aggarwal launched the first dedicated store for AM:IT in Dhan Mill, returning to the label that first introduced his design language in a more everyday form. The 750 sq. ft. space carries forward the brand’s fascination with material transformation, with installations that place Banarasi jacquard cards alongside e-waste and electronic circuitry. It is an apt setting for a pret line built around reworked textiles, modular separates and couture-level construction techniques translated into pieces designed for daily life. OTT by Tarun Tahiliani opened its first Mumbai store at Phoenix Palladium, bringing the label’s India Modern take on ready-to-wear to the city. The space is warm and pared back, with clean lines, gold accents and digital screens that place the focus on the clothes. Inside, you’ll find the brand’s mix of kaftans, capes, gilets and separates, along with signature details like chikankari and jewel-toned prints designed for wardrobes that move easily from day to dinner. Farah Khan Ali’s flagship in Fort turns jewellery retail into something more atmospheric. Set inside Chemco House, the boutique is layered with apricot-amber tones, sculptural displays and softly modulated lighting, creating a space that feels intimate. Angel chandeliers, dragonfly-wing lamps and a central display detailed with birds and florals bring a sense of theatre, while the jewellery remains firmly at the centre. The result is part salon and part gallery. Shanti Banaras opened a new store at Ambawatta One in Mehrauli, with a format that shifts the way Banarasi textiles are usually encountered. Designed almost like a maze, the space reveals itself gradually, slowing the eye and asking visitors to look at each piece more closely. Metallic lehengas, real zari weaves and hand-embroidered saris are displayed individually rather than in the familiar gadda-style format, making their structure and finish easier to take in. Even the chandeliers nod to the craft, drawing on loom punch cards and turning a coded part of the weaving process into design. 11.11 / eleven eleven’s Lodhi Colony flagship is located within one of Delhi’s most characterful neighbourhoods. The space brings its seed-to-stitch philosophy into physical form through bamboo-clad details, indigo passages and hand-finished surfaces that foreground material and process. The architecture folds the garments into a larger narrative, giving the brand’s hand-spun khadi, natural dyes and indigenous craft practices a setting that feels immersive instead of instructional. Off-White has officially entered India with its flagship in Bengaluru, bringing Virgil Abloh’s luxury-meets-streetwear language to a physical retail space here for the first time. The store introduces a curated selection of apparel, footwear, accessories and lifestyle pieces, all housed within an environment that reflects the brand’s stripped-back, industrial-leaning aesthetic. For a label whose appeal has long travelled through images, hype and cultural cachet, this opening gives Indian shoppers an in-person way into the world of Off-White.

article_title: Hues of summer: This legacy jewellery brand brings natural gemstones to the forefront
sub_title: Hues by Tanishq redefines authentic, design-led jewellery with contemporary silhouettes for the modern women
article_content: Jewellery is no longer limited to occasions, it has now taken on the role of expression—one that is brighter, bolder, and more fun. Enter: the Hues collection. As the auspicious festival of Akshaya Tritiya approaches, Tanishq, the brand from the House of Tata, taps into the contemporary appeal of natural gemstone jewellery with its latest offering. The Hues collection marks a welcome shift away from the restraint that has dominated bijoux trends in recent years, reimagining how modern women experience and embrace natural gemstones across both everyday and occasion wear. Anchored in a selection of 100 per cent natural gemstones, this collection signals Tanishq’s intent to shape a space defined by authenticity and design-led aesthetics. At the heart of each piece is a gemstone, with contour, structure, and silhouette crafted to enhance its natural vibrance and depth. “The range draws from the richness of Indian summer—its lush landscapes and vivid colours—and translates these into jewellery through sculptural silhouettes and fluid compositions. The result is a collection that is expressive, contemporary, and crafted with a strong point of view on modern Indian design,” adds Garima Maheshwari, Head of Design at Tanishq. Modern women are increasingly seeking jewellery that embodies elegance, individuality, and a sense of youthfulness. Crafted exclusively in 18 kt gold, Hues challenges traditional perceptions of jewellery, favouring experimentation over convention. The collection explores a diverse play of cuts—from classic marquise and intricate tabiz to smooth cabochon finishes. Cabochon stones add sculpted luminosity, while layered colour compositions, enhanced by techniques such as bunching and slicing, bring depth, texture, and movement. Bringing together a selection of natural gemstones—including emeralds, amethysts, citrines, tourmalines, and tanzanites—the collection reimagines preciousness through the transformative power of colour, form, and character. Actor Triptii Dimri fronts the campaign, celebrating the joyful spirit of Hues by portraying jewellery as a natural extension of a woman’s mood, individuality, and personal style. “At a time when jewellery is becoming a true expression of self, gemstones—with their vibrant colour and inherent character—feel instinctively right as an expansion of our repertoire. Triptii brings this spirit to life with effortless modernity—grounded, yet distinctly her own—much like the woman we design for,” says Pelki Tshering, Chief Marketing Officer, Titan Company Limited. Positioning Hues as a reflection of the evolving Indian woman, Dimri shares how the collection allows her to feel rooted and unapologetically herself. Excerpts of the interview below. The collection highlights self-expression through colour. Earlier, jewellery was often seen as traditional, worn only on special occasions. Hues by Tanishq redefines this notion—it makes jewellery modern, allowing it to be less about the occasion and more about expressing who you are in the moment, in a way that feels effortless and personal. I feel confident, bold, and completely myself. The collection is so versatile that I can express myself in any way I want. You can pick a piece depending on your mood. I keep it real and style it according to how I’m feeling—whether I want to dress up or just go out casually, there’s a piece for every moment. What makes the collection special is that it elevates your look effortlessly. I'm particularly drawn towards green. It’s my favourite colour, and it makes me feel grounded and calm. Jewellery is constantly evolving, and people are experimenting more than ever. They’re no longer playing it safe—they’re layering, mixing colours, and exploring new styles. That’s what makes this shift so exciting to witness. I think she would be confident, unpredictable, evolving, and fresh. My favourite is the Blooming Orchard. When I first saw it, I thought, this is just like me—the blend of colours is so beautiful, and it reminds me of the different 'hues' of an Indian summer. It’s versatile, delicate, full of life, and has such a fine, intricate design. I’d probably put it in a box and keep it all for myself!

article_title: What I learnt about fashion growing up in small-town India
sub_title: What if fashion’s most original references are not imported at all?
article_content: It was a regular weeknight—the groaning of construction cranes and Mumbai’s refusal to pause playing in the back- ground as the doorbell announced the arrival of my “Looking back, it was the idea of dressing up to feel like you weren’t in something, or not part of something. It was almost a fantasy act,” he said, speaking about his I reacted to that sentiment like a Pavlovian dog, spiralling right back to my childhood. That early itch for a different world, that vague, stubborn hope that being a little odd is the point. I grew up in Lamka, Manipur, part of the wider landscape of small-town India, which is far from anything deemed “fashion”. Tin-roofed houses climbed uneven slopes, mornings smelled of Long before I saw a runway show on FashionTV, which many of the townsfolk tabooed because of the “half-naked women”, I watched my mother thrift clothes, always a size larger so they’d last me longer. One such piece was a ruby-red pair of jeans that I often paired with a black jacket boasting the deepest pockets. Now, those pockets could actually be better used for lugging around Janice, my cousin, was the first person I knew who appeared to exist in two different worlds. At least 15 years older than me, she was already living in Delhi at this point, and would come home during vacations with jewellery gathered from the city. Oxidised earrings that must have been bought in Sarojini Nagar, scarves that smelt faintly of city air. My favourite was a three-tiered beaded necklace from her Naga friend, which she hung on the wall of her bedroom. Everything she spoke about was laced with such a sense of flourish that one couldn’t help but admire her. On a bus ride to Imphal, she spoke of when she worked part-time at a perfume shop. I remember her talking about an apple-shaped It’s a sentiment I shared with designer Alan Alexander, who grew up in Thiruvananthapuram in Kerala. Far from any formal fashion ecosystem, he recounted to me how getting his first computer at 12 had expanded his worldview overnight. “I used to obsessively read articles and blogs from across the world—about fashion, costumes, art, books, culture, music, socio-political struggles, food recipes, everything under the sun,” he said. “I would download international music in languages I didn’t even speak, just to experience things unknown. All of this was information I absorbed simply for the sake of it.” “In fact,” he added, “fashion wasn’t even my first choice of career. I studied applied electronics and instrumentation before switching.” I remember a conversation I had with photographer Tenzing Dakpa, with whom I have collaborated a couple of times in the past. A second-generation Tibetan, he was raised in Gangtok, “Fashion as a personification came from adopting musical influences and style as a way to identify yourself with a certain temperament.” At another point, almost apologetically, he added, “It’s photography and description that I’m interested in. Fashion almost becomes a by-product of that process.” Fashion, for many of us growing up in small-town India, doesn’t begin with proximity to its industry or access to its institutions, but with a desire to imagine another life, or to make sense of the one you’re already in. By the time the episode ended, the city was still grumbling outside. But so was my mind. Who actually gets to shape fashion’s language? It struck me how often we look outward for inspiration, building moodboards with borrowed references from Pinterest when the original vocabulary was already formed around us. Long before we even knew what to call it.

article_title: The best places to shop for jewellery in Jaipur
sub_title: From sixth-generation gemstone ateliers to contemporary studios crafting everyday silver and costume pieces
article_content: Jaipur has long been India’s gemstone capital. Walk through Johri Bazaar and you’ll see why: vitrines glowing with uncut emeralds, trays of The story began in the 18th century, when Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II invited skilled artisans to settle in the newly built city, establishing Jaipur as a thriving hub for coloured gemstones and jewellery. And that he did, so much so that today, you’ll find many top jewellery labels being headlined by the sixth, even seventh generation jewellers who’ve inherited the trade and know-how from their ancestors, mastering age-old jewellery techniques and forms. And then there’s the city’s next-gen jewellers crafting fun, throw-on-and-go pieces meant to be lived-in, rather than locked up in your tijoris. If you’re looking for the best jewellery stores in Jaipur, the city offers a spectrum that spans heirloom polki and kundan sets, festive gemstone statements, demi-fine silver and playful costume pieces. Below, we’ve rounded up the best jewellery stores in Jaipur for bridal, festive, demi-fine and everyday shopping. What began as an exploration of India’s fine crafts in 1980 is now a globally acclaimed brand featuring timeless high jewellery inspired by Mughal, Rajput, Victorian, and Temple styles. From gemstone to diamond, pearls to polki–expect anything and everything. Strong since 1921, The House of Rambhajos beautifully marries traditional techniques like kundan and polki with modern design sensibilities to create heirloom-worthy pieces, think larger-than-life bridal necklaces, gemstone satladas, cocktail rings and kundan kadas. One of the oldest and most prominent jewellery stores in Jaipur on the buzzing MI Road, The Gem Palace has crafted pieces for celebrities and leaders from around the world. An unmissable for those who appreciate rare, never-before-seen jewels. Our favourites? An ornamented choti encrusted with diamonds, a fidget spinner of a ring and a candy-esque string of stones. Ghatiwala Jewellers has been mastering the traditional, fit-for-the-royalty Jadau jewellery for decades. And now, they’ve introduced a fresh line of playful rose-cut jewellery using coloured gemstones fit for cocktails, festivals and pre-wedding celebrations. An atelier best-known for their meenakari, kundan and polki creations since 1951, GK Chudiwalas celebrates Rajasthan’s motifs and designs in their creations. Their latest collaboration with architect Shantanu Garg, called ‘Araaish’, draws inspiration from Jaipur’s stepwells and palaces, and is a must-visit for those on the lookout for something unique. With a century’s worth of experience under their belt, BG 1930 is a fine jewellery house creating heirloom gemstone, polki and diamond pieces. What caught our attention is a three-layered necklace with a whopping centre stone, as seen on Ashley Graham and Isha Ambani’s pearl belt. With stores in Mumbai, Jaipur, Hong Kong and Dubai, Entice displays an array of gemstone and diamond jewellery that is equal parts classic and contemporary. Bookmark for statement diamond pieces, everyday dainty jewels and luxe gifting. Should you have eyes for the most distinctive of jewels, a visit to Umrao Jewels in the gorgeous Narain Niwas Palace is imperative. The collection is a masterclass in Edwardian, Byzantine, Mughal-Kundan Meena, Housed inside the Tholia Building on MI Road–the family’s generational home–the atelier is filled with many heirloom pieces and believes in creating the same for generations to come. Check in for timeless polki and jadau pieces, futuristic gemstone brooches and Victorian style pieces. Designed between Italy and India, Tallin’s collections are a melange of Indian maximalism and Italian design sensibilities. What jumps out the most is their mixing of unusual stones and cuts to create gentle forms featuring floral patterns, and sharp form pieces with striking enamelling and angular designs. An offspring of the prominent legacy brand Jain Jewellers, Gyan Jaipur draws immensely from Jaipur, its arches, latticework and the Aravalis. You get beautifully set precious and semi-precious Monikered as ‘The Modern Meenakar’, Sunita Shekhawat champions the centuries-old craft of meenakari or enamelling jewellery with expertly paired gemstones. Favoured by the likes of the Ambani family, Maharani Gayatri Devi of Jaipur and Kareena Kapoor Khan, among others, Shekhawat makes a case for enamelling like never before. If your jewellery memo reads wearable art, Jewel Saga is an unmissable. Vibrant enamelling, coloured gemstones, luminous pearls and Jaipur-inspired motifs are ingeniously paired to bring about one-of-a-kind styles fit for the bride and her tribe alike. With stores in Delhi, Noida and now Jaipur, the jewellery house boasts a collection of polki, diamond and gemstone jewels. Worth checking out on your visit are their gemstone-encrusted brooches, and the ‘Raina’ collection ft. luxurious pink tourmalines, rubies, emeralds, peridots and diamonds. If your jewellery moodboard looks right out of a royal period drama, PCT’s Navratan range should be on your radar. Bijoux boxes are flooding with classic emerald, ruby, tanzanite, yellow sapphire, polki and pearl pieces. Remember those colourful jelly candies from your childhood? That’s what Mina’s jewels look like. Fun, colourful and oh so delicious. With enamelling as the beating heart of the brand, they create stackable bracelets, versatile earrings and vibrant necklaces fit for your everyday shenanigans. Tucked in the bustling Johri Bazaar, Noor draws you in with its striking 92.5 silver everything–necklaces, larger-than-life cocktail rings, regal payals and dual-toned jewels set with semi-precious stones. What’s equally noteworthy are their silver potlis, purses and parandas. Inspired by French fashion and India’s rich tribal culture, Diane Singh produces minimalist pieces in silver that go on to become one with you. Think toi et moi rings featuring customisable semi-precious gemstones, sleek stackable bangles, necklaces fit for layering, dainty anklets and then some. From the house of Amrapali, Tribe dived deep into Indian folklore and tribal life to craft casual and occasionwear jewels in silver. Their latest collaboration with The Palace Atelier champions the city’s Pachranga (five-coloured) flag in earpieces, neckchains, charms, lapel pins and more. For gold-plated silver jewels with Indian-inspired motifs, Devi Jaipur must be on your itinerary. From elegant jhumkas to baalis enamelled in vibrant hues, motif rings to gemstone necklaces–Devi is for those who like their jewels elegant yet elevated. Check out tribal-inspired silver necklaces, fuss-free everyday baubles and coloured stone rings and pendants. As seen on actor Jaideep Ahlawat, their braided bracelets, as well as charm pendants for men, are second to none. Expertly championing the enamelling technique of For a vast collection of silver and alloy jewellery that looks like fine occasionwear pieces, minus the hefty price tag. Also find sterling silver bridal necklace sets, sheeshphools and statement hathphools. Mirasa has created what they call ‘destination fine jewellery.’ Think polki, diamond and gemstone jewellery of your dreams–all in 92.5 silver, gold plating and immaculate finish. Edgy, angular and avant-garde unisex silver jewels. Expect everything from quirky character pendants and statement studs to enamelled, gemstone rings and ombre tennis bracelets. What looks like a tiny atelier from its facade opens into a world of majestic brooches, lapel pins and gemstone cufflinks–all an ode to Jaipur. Their signature Jaipur pin is inspired by the maze of bazaars in the walled city of Jaipur. Tucked in the lush lawns of Hotel Narain Niwas Palace, Kassa does sculpted brass pendants, earrings, rings and cuffs that can easily zhuzh up any everyday fit. One of the best jewellery stores in Jaipur if easywear molten-gold-looking jewellery is your thing. An eclectic mix of silver and brass jewels fit for festivities and casual wear. KESYA’s enamelled bangles featuring tiny hearts, multi-coloured hydro-quartz studs and bracelets, and polki-inspired pieces can easily become mainstays in your jewellery box. For timepieces that celebrate Rajasthan’s intricate architecture, art and workmanship. Their work features genuine coins from 1950s India, postal stamps dating pre-independence and jaali or latticework as seen in Rajasthan’s architecture. Reimagining traditional Indian jewellery with quirky charms is Kichu. Look out for fierce animal-inspired necklaces, statement signet rings and uniquely-shaped earrings. Stocked at Jaipur Modern

article_content: When you’re tired, decision fatigue is real. On mornings when you’re running on Over time, I’ve realised that looking put together has very little to do with effort. The best low-effort style hacks aren’t about buying more; they’re about building a system you can rely on when your brain refuses to cooperate. Build a uniform wardrobe with a neutral palette (or any other colour scheme that works for you), one ‘personality piece’ and a signature scent to seal it. For me, that’s a pair of wide-fit Uniqlo trousers from the women’s section that I have in three colours, ribbed tanks in black and white and a rotation of button-downs, shackets, kimonos and tang jackets, topped off with a baseball cap and a few spritzes of Another 13 by Le Labo. I could pick anything from this pile blindfolded and they’d appear just as thought out because these are all foundational pieces that have helped me create an OOTD stencil for mornings that just aren’t it. Here's a list of 5 very low-effort styling hacks that will make you look undeniably tasteful. Hair accessories are the easiest form of maximalism and are your best friends for days you don't have the time or energy to wash or dress it up. One large, colourful scrunchie instantly shifts the energy of an outfit. If you don't have the hair length for a scrunchie, throw a baseball cap on. You can wear the simplest outfit in the world, jeans and a white shirt or a simple A-line dress that doesn't need ironing and still look like a style savant if you do your hair right. Metallic accents are the tired girl’s shortcut to looking awake. Think of metal as Even if you've spent hours putting your look together, the wrong choice of footwear can flush it all down the drain. A pair of well-made shoes, whether they're sneakers or a pair of embroidered Nothing screams tired and busy (and stylish) girlie than a bag that holds your entire universe in it. Call it the Jane Birkin-fication of your low-effort look. Step out in your pyjamas if you have, carry the right arm candy and you're set. Just say, “Claire, it's French!” Sometimes, the best beauty hack for a tired face is to cover up the eyes. And if you're anything like me, your patience disintegrates the more tired you are. And to be honest, it is smarter to hide those tired glares before it becomes occupational hazard.

article_title: This one-of-a-kind bejewelled angrakha blouse is a tribute to Jaipur's Johri Bazaar
sub_title: Rooted in Abhishek Raniwala’s childhood memories of Johri Bazaar, Raniwala 1881 reimagines the angrakha as a wearable heirloom shaped by multiple specialised artisans
article_content: Back in the 18th century, Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II envisioned a city that would serve as the heart of trade in Northern India. At the heart of it all was “I used to accompany my grandfather to Johri Bazaar as a child,” recalls Raniwala. “I’d observe how he’d meet all kinds of people and how much respect they gave him. We’d walk and spend hours in the market just visiting different workshops and talking about jewellery. Johri Bazaar became like an office for us. It is not a confined unit, it’s one large office where everyone plays their part.” The jewellery house’s newest creation, the Bejewelled Rani Ratna Angrakha, emerges from this memory. Crafted using approximately 840 grams of gold and But why the form of an angrakha? For Raniwala, the reasoning was twofold: First, to demonstrate that Johri Bazar and Rajasthan’s jewellery and sartorial traditions are not relics but living, evolving practices that have continually adapted to new silhouettes and techniques. This, he says, is the energy he wants Angrakha to embody for the next 100 years. At the same time, the house was determined to move beyond the conventional boundaries of jewellery and create something fluid and wearable. By choosing a garment-inspired form, The convergence of jewellery and garments has been a catalyst for iconic fashion moments throughout history: from Paco Rabanne’s legacy of bags from metallic discs, chainmail and even 18-carat gold medallions, to Alexander McQueen and British jewellery designer Shaun Leane’s ‘Coiled Corset’ in the ’90s, to modern-day labels like Misho that have extended sculptural metalwork into corsets and The team at Raniwala 1881 drew on their collective knowledge of jewellery crafts, archives and modern software to conceptualise the Angrakha. Despite being a part of the ecosystem since his formative years, Raniwala found himself surprised at the intricacies of balancing different crafts in one piece. “Every craft has its own hand movement and flow. A meenakari artisan cannot perform jadau. A stone cutter cannot perform meenakari. If a piece is half-done by one artisan and given to another mid-process, the difference will show. Coordinating all of that was tedious. There was a lot of planning, mapping and timing involved.” The Bejewelled Rani Ratna Angrakha is currently on display at the Raniwala 1881 Atelier in Jaipur, and Raniwala hopes it will travel in the coming years. “This is a little contribution from our design house that celebrates Johri Bazaar and Jaipur and helps young people feel connected to this legacy even years from now.”

article_title: Every original has a story. The best ones are written in denim
sub_title: With Alia Bhatt at the forefront, Levi's brings its global Behind Every Original campaign to India, spotlighting authenticity, reinvention and individuality
article_content: The Levi’s jean revolution was a pivotal moment in fashion history. Like many Americans in the mid-1800s, Levi Strauss wasn’t looking to strike gold when he headed west to California to innovate durable denim workwear for labourers—but he struck it anyway. Levi’s has always been known for disrupting the apparel industry with its jeanswear. Today, the brand’s inherent pioneering spirit exemplifies American style, while its ability to tailor its offerings beyond borders, turns the Levi’s legacy into a generational love affair. It's difficult to imagine that a single piece of clothing could connect actors, artists, pop stars and hip-hop icons. Yet Levi’s jeans are the original blank canvas—from straight and slouchy to baggy, embroidered and distressed, people have taken these jeans and truly made them their own. Behind Every Original builds on that legacy, celebrating the mindset behind originality—the curiosity, conviction and courage to see the world differently. This time around, the brand brings its 2026 vision, Behind Every Original, to India, starring global brand ambassador Alia Bhatt. Bhatt’s evolution mirrors that of a generation that values authenticity over perfection, making her a natural embodiment of Levi's global narrative. “I’ve always been a curious mind, wanting to know the why behind the what,” she shares. Off-screen, her personal style reflects that same ease and self-expression. She gravitates toward relaxed denim, effortless tees and silhouettes that feel lived in. “For me, it was never about checking every box or doing what was expected. I’d rather be myself than anyone I’m told to be. You don’t wait for permission to shake things up—you make your own rules. Being original is messy, imperfect and completely your own,” she says. Every frame celebrates Bhatt’s denim-clad individuality—strutting, dancing, moving and, above all, living in Levi’s. Looking for a jean that fits comfortably at the waist but feels loose and easy through the thighs without looking too baggy? Enter: the Cinch Waist Jean. This season, Levi’s builds on its offering of relaxed fits, designed with an adjustable back detail that creates a customisable, waist-defining shape while maintaining a wide-leg silhouette. Rooted in Levi’s heritage of authentic, well-crafted denim and driven by innovation, the Cinch collection offers a fresh approach to everyday denim—sculpted, adaptable, and designed to move with you. Reinforcing the brand’s leadership in fit innovation and its commitment to designing denim that adapts to different bodies, moods, and ways of wearing, the collection introduces three versatile styles: the Cinch Wide-Leg Jeans, an effortless and fluid option for off-duty days; the Cinch Baggy Jeans, relaxed with a contemporary edge that makes them perfect for a casual brunch or day out; and the Cinch Barrel Jeans, fit for occasions when you want to dress things up without sacrificing comfort. You can also opt for the Levi’s Loose Boot—a modern, laid-back take on the classic bootcut. With its relaxed fit and subtle flare, it strikes the perfect balance between structure and ease (think of it as the ideal in-between). With Behind Every Original, Levi’s reaffirms what it has always stood for: denim is more than what you wear—it’s a part of your story worth telling.

article_title: Sorry, body positivity—the Ozempic era is officially upon us
sub_title: From size 000 to naked dresses, the silhouette is shifting. If you grew up in the nineties, you've seen this story before.
article_content: Fashion has a message for you. It is written in cut-outs and sheer panels and dresses engineered to pull taut across a torso. If you grew up in the nineties, the message feels familiar. For a beautiful, chaotic decade, the industry genuinely seemed to be making space. Runways got a little wider, brands stocked sizes beyond S-L. Body positivity, neutrality and midsize creators built communities out of the radical act of existing at a size beyond 10 and dressing well. Progress, fitful and incomplete, but pointing somewhere new. The cultural moment that produced all of that was also running out of road, and GLP-1s like The algorithm noticed before most of us did. One search, one article, and within days the advertisements followed: telehealth, semaglutide, before and afters. Red carpet appearances and celebrity transformations did the rest. Somewhere between the prescription pad for medical conditions and the paparazzi shot, GLP-1s became something else; thinness shifted from aspirational to 'easily' attainable. Fashion, as it always does, paid close attention. According to the The body the clothes are designed for is, increasingly, a very specific one. And the designs make no secret of it. A dress built around a torso cut-out doesn't reveal the body; it requires a particular body type. Remove the specific body it assumes and the whole thing falls apart. But the Ozempic era didn't invent fashion's preference for a narrow silhouette. That preference is old and stubborn and has survived every cultural correction aimed at it, including the body positivity movement, which, at its peak, briefly made the industry blink. What the Ozempic era did was make that preference clearly visible once again. And visibility, as the last decade proved, is where change begins. The millennial women standing in changing rooms right now—going looking for a cap sleeve and coming home empty-handed—have been here before. We lived through the first version of this story, written in low-rise jeans, diet culture and the tyranny of the bandage dress. We're also the same women who drove the body positivity movement in the first place. Not always from the outside, throwing stones, but from inside the industry: the editors, stylists, creators, customers whose spending made inclusive sizing commercially viable. They got loud about it, spent their money differently, demanded more, and the industry—slowly, grudgingly, genuinely—moved. Not because fashion had a change of heart. Because the woman in the changing room did, and she took her debit card with her. Fashion moves in cycles no one fully controls and everyone partially creates. The industry follows culture; culture follows the industry; somewhere in the middle, a woman tries something on and decides how she feels about herself that day. The cycle that produced one shift can produce another. And in the meantime, there is something to be said for getting dressed anyway, finding the thing you love in this season, this particular cultural weather, and wearing it like you were always meant to.

article_title: John Galliano returns to fashion via a creative partnership with Zara
sub_title: The Spanish retailer Zara has signed John Galliano to a two-year creative partnership which will see him “re-author” the brand’s archives.
article_content: John Galliano is back in the atelier: The Spanish retailer “I’ve been curating some of Zara’s recent archives,” Since Ortega Perez was named chair in 2022, Zara has collaborated with other high fashion designers, among them “I’m super excited, because it’s not something I’ve done before, so that kind of tickles me—the newness, the excitement, the actual process,” Galliano noted. “Even with my team, I have to keep reminding them daily: In January, Galliano was seen front row at Jonathan Anderson’s haute couture debut for Dior. Before his Galliano has spent the two years since his exit from Margiela—having gotten off “the crazy merry-go-round,” as he called it—“going to museums, walking through the woods without my phone, getting lost but not being afraid to get lost, and relying on instinct again, reconnecting with instinct, like breathing correctly.” He went on: “It’s been precious time to just really think about what I would like to do next. You think, He’s been secretly working in an atelier “somewhere around Paris” since January. “It’s early days at the moment, but I’ve launched quite a few toiles, and when we see them back, we’ll be able to see how far I can push it safely, if you know what I mean.” Though he doesn’t want to give away too much about the work in progress, he will say it’s “informed by form and proportion [without] falling into any categories. One could safely say it’s beyond gender and beyond seasons.” The first collection will arrive in stores in September. And of course, the thought that his clothes could suddenly be accessible to a whole new range of people tickles him too: “To deliver fashion through that enormous platform—that, of course, that’s thrilling. And to be able to work with the kind of resources they have as well, that’s equally thrilling,” he said. So, how does he feel about getting back on the merry-go-round? “They say act three of your life is the most important,” Galliano mused, “and can be the most fun.”

article_title: The next chapter of cocktail dressing is moodier, sharper and far more considered
sub_title: Through their collection Abyssal, Rohit Gandhi + Rahul Khanna explore mood over metallics and tailoring that holds its own
article_content: Cocktail dressing at Indian weddings has reached the saturation point. For the past few seasons, it’s been a game of high shine and impact: sequinned gowns engineered for flash photography, sherwanis and tuxedos dialled up with surface drama. It worked: it photographed beautifully and filled Instagram grids. But somewhere along the way, it also became predictable. You could almost guess the look before the invite arrived. And when something becomes predictable, it stops feeling personal. And somewhere between brides designing meticulous mood boards and building multi-chapter wedding wardrobes, the want for something new is at its height, exactly where Abyssal, the Spring Summer Couture 2026 collection by Rohit Gandhi + Rahul Khanna steps in–a house that has, for over two decades, built its reputation on structure over sensationalism. The collection is inspired by the ocean’s deeper zones, not the obvious turquoise surface, but the layers beneath, where light behaves differently and colour begins to dissolve. The palette moves through oceanic shades that feel atmospheric; pearls, metallic florals and crystals are hand-embroidered like artefacts recovered from the ocean floor, embedded beautifully into the fabric. “For Abyssal, we took one step further to look at the science and architecture at the depths of the ocean where light doesn’t pass through and colour begins to disappear for the human eye. There is a sense of poetry older than time that reveals itself every thousand feet. That is the magic we’re capturing, like a message in a bottle, with this collection,” say the designer duo. The modern wedding wardrobe is no longer built around one defining outfit. It’s a welcome dinner that feels intimate, a cocktail evening that sets the tone and an afterparty that relaxes the rules. Each look needs to carry its own identity without feeling like a costume. Especially today when brides and grooms aren’t going after the next trendy thing. Instead, they’re on the search for pieces that elevate their style while allowing restyling and rewear beyond the wedding week. They want couture to justify itself in construction, detailing and how it sits on the body. If you’re getting married in 2026, here’s the reality: your cocktail look can rightly get its own spotlight, courtesy of Rahul Gandhi+Rahul Khanna. Let’s detail the specifics: First, colour. Instead of the predictable jewel tones or safe metallics, the collection leans into abyssal blues, frost whites and deep charcoals. These aren’t statement colours in the obvious sense. They’re mood colours. They photograph differently; softer in daylight, sharper under evening lights. For a bride, that means a cocktail dressing that is classy, chic and just the right amount of edgy. For a groom, it means stepping away from the default black and into tonal greys or inky blues that turn heads. Then, texture, and this is the real highlight. With this collection, the designers don’t use pearls, crystals, and metallic florals as afterthought embellishments. They build garments around them. Pearls are embedded into the surface like something organic—almost geological—unearthed from the ocean floor, sitting against the oceanic hues that make them feel modern. Then you have the crystals and the metallic floral accents, too, that are designed and handworked to catch the light just right, move along with you as you dance the night away, to make a beautiful case for the magic of Indian craftsmanship. For couples tired of heavy embroidery that weighs both the garment and the moment down, this is a discerning way to do embellishment. You still get the details and craftsmanship. But the structure of the silhouette leads the conversation. And perhaps that’s why Abyssal feels relevant, because it understands that the most compelling things aren’t always the ones floating at the surface.

article_title: Priyanka Chopra Jonas returns to the Oscars 2026 in a white Dior gown with a feather-trimmed slit
sub_title: A sculpted bodice and diagonal draping through the waist shape the white gown’s streamlined silhouette
article_content: Priyanka Chopra Jonas returned to the Oscars red carpet in a white Dior gown that moves from a sharply cut bodice into a fluid skirt. The strapless neckline curves into an angular sweetheart shape, while the bodice holds firm through the waist. Below, the dress changes direction as fabric gathers diagonally across the hips, drawing the eye toward one side before falling into the skirt. That shift introduces movement through the midsection and breaks the straight line of the bodice. A high slit runs through the skirt, edged with feather trimming along the opening. The feathers sit only along that cut of the fabric rather than across the entire skirt, forming a narrow band of texture against the white base. As Chopra Jonas walked the carpet and later stepped on stage to present, the feathered edge lifted and settled with her stride. She wore high jewellery from Bvlgari’s Eclecttica collection, including a diamond necklace set with a vivid blue centre stone and matching rings. Her hair was worn long and sleek with a side part, brushed over one shoulder. The makeup followed a warm, muted palette: softly smoked eyes, bronzed skin and a nude lip. Nick Jonas accompanied her in a Ralph Lauren tuxedo jacket with a white shirt and black bow tie. Chopra Jonas last attended the Oscars nearly a decade ago. Her return this year favoured clean tailoring and controlled texture over elaborate embellishment, allowing the silhouette and the feathered movement of the skirt to register from a distance. “Rethink the white gown for a corporate outing, opt for a white suit and if you want to add a little bit of play, you can don a suit with a feather trim on the sleeve hem. The sleekness or sharpness of the look depends on the cut of the suit and the clean lines. Opt for trousers that are straight, slim-legged, and fall over your stilettos. A clean watch and an ear cuff to complete the look,” says Divya Balakrishnan, Vogue India fashion associate.
