article_title: Women in arts take to the runway for Carolina Herrera Fall 2026 show
sub_title: Wes Gordon returns to his home turf, translating his artistic lineage into a collection defined by sculptural silhouettes, graphic clarity, and lived-in ease
article_content: Pick a theme for the season so far, and it might as well be ceremonial glamour—particularly at Carolina Herrera, the quintessential New York brand led by creative director Wes Gordon. Here, Gordon positions himself as the architect of a maison mid-renovation, offering a front-row seat to a bold, free-spirited approach to fashion and beauty—one that is rooted in cultural exchange, a vision that feels both timely and enduring. It’s hardly Carolina Herrera’s first brush with the art world. The house’s close ties with renowned artists like Andy Warhol and Robert Mapplethorpe paved the way for the Women in the Arts initiative, which has encouraged and supported female creatives since 2022. Gordon’s inspiration for the latest collection, too, drew from the artistic realm, reflecting the confidence of a brand comfortably operating at the intersection of fashion and art. Functioning almost like a modern canvas, New York’s historic setting hosted Carolina Herrera’s Fall 2026 showcase, celebrating a diverse community of women—past and present—whose work and influence have shaped the artistic landscape. The collection imagines women in motion—creating and moving through the world with conviction. True to that sentiment, strength and volume appear in exaggerated shoulders, cocoon coats, puff-sleeve blazers, and streamlined pencil skirts. The crisp Herrera signature button-down is reimagined as an artist’s smock, relaxed in spirit and rendered in black and white, while a procession of embellished, diaphanous dresses brings a mix of sheer drama to the presentation. As any Carolina Herrera runway regular knows, leopard print and floral motifs play a pivotal role in each collection. This season, a hand-painted, vibrant red calla lily print sets a bold tone. Embroidered eveningwear enters the collection with paillette knits and gold coats and dresses. The ensembles are constructed from sequins that recall the muted gold tones of artist Agnes Martin’s Gordon’s tribute didn’t stop at the collection. The showcase unfolded in an expansive venue in New York’s Meatpacking District, illuminated by a mural created by set designer Sarah Oliphant. Among the models walking the runway was a multigenerational community of contemporary curators, patrons, gallerists, and collectors—each a real-life muse in their own right. The show featured painter Amy Sherald; artists Anh Duong and Eliza Douglas; sculptor Rachel Feinstein and her daughter, Flora Currin; photographer Ming Smith; gallerist Hannah Traore; and more, all of whom were handpicked by Gordon to help bring the collection’s inspiration to life. With handbags, Gordon revisits signature styles like the Mimi and Karlita. The Mimi is reimagined with an all-over black-and-white graphic leopard print, with a bow detail at the strap. The Karlita, the season’s ideal evening bag, is rendered in the collection’s palette and includes a striking chilli red. Statement jewellery completes the narrative, with calla lily brooches, gold necklaces and earrings. House codes return through print: bold leopard jacquard, painterly calla lily motifs, and poppy florals rendered on organza. Colour sharpens with a bold palette of ceramic nude, forest green, plum, celeste blue, and chilli red. A hand-drawn print of the heel—a nod to the iconic bottle of Carolina Herrera’s bestselling Good Girl perfume—introduces a note of contemporary playfulness on blouses and skirts, marking its 10-year anniversary with a touch of wit. On the occasion of International Women’s Day, Carolina Herrera reaffirmed its commitment to supporting female creativity by unveiling Good Girl Murano—a one-of-a-kind artistic tribute crafted entirely in Murano glass. Conceived as a collector’s piece, the fragrance is limited to ten bottles worldwide, reimagining artisan tradition through a modern lens. After months of experimentation, Venetian designer Lucia Massari chose borosilicate glass for the body, developed in collaboration with Ash Polzer, an American artist who built her practice within Murano’s traditionally male-dominated glassmaking world. For the finishing touch, Massari turned to Luigi Varagnolo, one of the last artisans specialising in Venetian mirror ornamentation. His contribution—a delicate glass flower crowning the stiletto—introduces a note of fragility, almost irony, to the silhouette’s sharpness. Jasmine—Carolina Herrera’s favourite flower—takes centre stage, in the fragrance. Enriched with indulgent notes of tonka bean, cacao, almond, and coffee, this Eau de Parfum, crafted by perfumers Louise Turner and Quentin Bisch, is a celebration of elegance, creativity, and artistic audacity.

article_title: Sharvari’s Torani lehenga showcased 2,000 hours of zardozi, dapka and marodi handwork
sub_title: The actor’s lotus pink and sage lehenga was paired with jewellery by Sunita Shekhawat
article_content: At a wedding reception where moody and metallic tones typically dominate after dark, Sharvari made a case for the softer side of eveningwear. The actor's pastel lehenga by Torani is proof that powdery palettes can hold their own. The lehenga is crafted in raw silk and complemented with a scalloped blouse with full sleeves and a translucent sage organza dupatta. For designer Karan Torani, the inspiration lies deep within Indian mythological storytelling. “This ensemble draws its spirit from the eternal poetry of Raas Leela, the divine dance of Radha and Krishna that has lived for centuries in Indian miniature paintings, temple murals and oral folklore,” he says. “I was imagining Radha standing quietly by the banks of the Yamuna in Vrindavan, a figure suspended between devotion and romance, surrounded by blooming gardens, peacocks and the music of the flute.” That imagery informed the soft lotus pink and sage colours of the garment. Torani envisioned the outfit “to feel almost like an Indian figurine coming to life,” he explains. The silhouette, too, borrows from historical Indian dress forms. “The choli draws from the classic angiya, a form that has existed in Indian dress traditions for centuries, interpreted with gentle, sculpted cuts to give it a contemporary elegance while retaining its modest, full-sleeved romanticism.” Across the lehenga, Torani’s signature visual language appears through scalloped borders, chintz florals and the Airavata elephant motif. Equally compelling is the surface ornamentation on the lehenga. “The entire surface is enriched with traditional hand techniques–zardozi, dapka, marodi, badla and kinari work–each painstakingly layered by artisans who have inherited these skills across generations. When these techniques come together, the garment begins to feel less like fabric and more like a tapestry,” Torani reveals. The process required more than 2,000 hours of handwork, with every scallop and motif positioned deliberately. “A small detail that brings it all together is the heart-shaped ‘Dilbar’ potli.” Styled by Tanya Ghavri, Sharvari’s lehenga was completed with jewellery from Sunita Shekhawat. Pieces from the Jaipur-based label’s Padmapriya collection brought in lotus and parrot motifs inspired by Goddess Lakshmi. Her chandbalis with kaan phool showcased intricate champlevé and delicate gulabi meenakari and they were paired with a ring from the label’s Heritage collection.

article_content: As something of a maestro when it comes to setting colour trends, Interestingly, this creamy note somewhat preempted But, of course, what might be a succour to one person, enabling them to feel cool, calm and collected, could simply be, well, slightly boring to someone else, who perhaps feels invisible or even sad in stealth-wealth neutrals. Eye-popping in some ways, but grounded in others, you won’t regret inviting its exuberance into your wardrobe, as long as it’s tempered by opaque black tights or a wool skirt in white. Tomato is a non-mover when it comes to colour trends – but for spring/summer 26, there’s a twist. At We’ve already discussed the relevance of Pantone’s “ For one of the most exciting debuts at Paris Fashion Week, Loewe’s creative-director duo, Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, delivered something of a wham-bam colour palette featuring searing primary shades. This green – or more accurately emerald – was particularly head-turning, especially when rendered as this clean take on While navy has long been a mainstay of the modern wardrobe, the autumn/winter 2026 collections offered elevated new interpretations of the shade. At Burberry, it appeared across an entire spectrum of textures, from plissé taffeta to buttery leather accessories, proving how much depth a single hue can hold. Ferragamo and If fuchsia is the grown-up way to wear pink, bubble gum is its playful younger sibling. Designers embraced the saccharine shade in glossy fabrics and sharply-cut silhouettes, giving the Barbie-approved hue a fresh dose of fashion credibility. article_title: Why a generation raised on screens is getting into watches
sub_title: Rado’s Adrian Bosshard shares what brands are learning from a new generation of collectors
article_content: I got my first real watch when I was about 10—a Casio F-91W that was a gift from my father. It was my introduction to ‘real’ watches as opposed to the cheap knockoffs I had worn before. It was only in my 20s that I bought a watch with my own money, a Tissot PR100 that required a serious squeeze from my wallet. But it was worth every penny. It turns out that story isn’t unique, with Gen Z collectors beginning their careers today and finding themselves in the same boat. Having been introduced to the watch world at a young age by the adults in their lives—or discovering it through its adjacency with their other interests—they are now beginning to build collections of their own. “The beginning of my obsession started when my grandfather passed on a Citizen Signature chronograph to me,” says 23-year-old Nirek Dembla, a student of business analytics. He adds, “I was instantly fascinated with its engineering and proportions; the dial taught me about the elegance of smaller dial sizes.” Archana Ajith, a 28-year-old journalist from Mumbai, credits her father for shaping her interest. “He has an extensive watch collection and began building it when he was around my age. Growing up, I watched him carefully choose each piece with a deep appreciation for its craftsmanship.” Twenty-eight-year-old Gladwin Menezes, however, developed his obsession independently. “[It’s] something I cultivated by watching tennis matches and sporting events where athletes would wear cool watches. Eventually, I grew curious about why their watches cost so much; despite the jokes about ‘time toh same hi dikhata hai’, I wanted to understand the craft, history and also a little about the mechanics.” That joke about watches has been around for decades. My X-rupee watch tells the same time as your a-lot-more-than-X-rupee one. And the response hasn’t changed either: a watch does more than tell time. It can speak volumes about whether you value attention to detail or vibes; prefer unabashed bling or stoic restraint; are interested in craft or technology, maybe both. A report from Chrono24 and Fratello from last year revealed that Gen Z watch owners around the world are drawn to vintage dress watches. Many of these have become familiar sights on social media feeds and red carpets alike, being sported by pop-culture figures from Zohran Mamdani with his Casio A1000MA-7VT to Saif Ali Khan’s Jaeger-LeCoultre Reverso Grande Taille and Paul Mescal’s Cartier Tank. For many young collectors, these pieces become entry points into watch history. “What particularly draws me to the Cartier Tank is its proportions, as it proves that a watch does not need to be massive to have a presence,” says Dembla. Menezes concurs: “The Tank has always been a favourite, and the Reverso is also one that I find really interesting.” India’s most famous defunct watchmaker also continues to attract Ajith. “I admire vintage HMT mechanical timepieces because they represent a period when India had its own watchmaking identity.” Luxury watch imports into India have been steadily rising in recent years, with a combined increase of 35% according to reports from Deloitte and Morgan Stanley-LuxeConsult. A new free-trade agreement between India and the EU will gradually reduce import duties on Swiss watches, potentially expanding the market further. Among the brands paying attention to this growing interest is Rado. I recently met CEO Adrian Bosshard, who was in the country for the launch of the True Round x Les Couleurs Le Corbusier collection at India Art Fair; the watchmaker has had a presence at the Delhi event for seven years. Bosshard (the perfect example of nominative determinism, if ever there was one) was eager to discuss what the company has observed among younger buyers, a target market that continues to grow. He reveals, “We’re seeing an important trend with young customers—of [them buying] long-term luxury goods. Today, young customers think and evaluate [their options]; they like to buy products with a long-term and sustainable relevancy.” When asked about timeless vintage designs, Bosshard points to the Anatom, a 40-year-old icon that was revived a few years ago. “It was a total revolution at the time [in 1983] because of its design. At a time when watches were round and steel, it was ‘Hardmetal’ (Rado’s proprietary tungsten-carbide alloy) and anatomical.” The curvature of the watch was designed to enhance its wrist-feel—one of the factors Bosshard considers when choosing a watch, alongside design, quality and reliability. Our Gen Z contributors seem to echo this list. “Proportions are very important; a watch has to sit well on my wrist and feel balanced,” Ajith says. Dembla concurs: “I mainly focus on sub-40mm watches as I think they provide the most balanced silhouette [for me],” adding, “I also look for clean, minimal designs that are backed by rich historical significance.” These criteria are mirrored in their collections and wishlists. Dembla says, “My most recent and significant piece is a Rado Captain Cook high-tech ceramic diver with a beautiful green dial. This watch in particular was the grail for me when I started collecting, because of its concave ceramic bezel and pure diver-watch DNA. As for what’s next in my collection, it’s a Jaeger-LeCoultre Reverso.” Ajith’s wish list also features names that will be instantly recognisable to collectors of any age: “Audemars Piguet and Cartier will probably always be on it. But realistically, what I’m eyeing right now is a 37mm Rado Captain Cook automatic.” For this new wave of collectors, the watches on their wish lists share one thing in common: longevity. While trends may ebb and flow, these are pieces chosen with the expectation that they will stay meaningful long after the novelty of purchase fades. As Dembla puts it, “In a time when we are surrounded by vast amounts of fleeting digital utility, a traditional timepiece acts as a rare island of permanence.”

article_title: How street markets in India trained a generation’s fashion eye
sub_title: In the absence of malls and flagship stores, pavement markets became unlikely classrooms where we learnt to recognise fabric, construction and design through the thrill of the hunt
article_content: From the blue tarp hangs a coiled wire powering a naked bulb. Its clinical white light bathes a narrow makeshift passage lined with rows of hangers holding clothes marked with labels you wouldn’t expect to find in any Indian shopping mall. The portly man in a white shirt, now the colour of weak tea after a full day of work, pulls a synthetic white-and-pink puff-sleeved frock from a large blue plastic bag behind the stall and thrusts it towards me and declares, “Aap par achha lagega ye (This would look good on you).” I turn to my 55-year-old aunt with horror. Is this what people think of me? She suppresses a giggle while holding up a pair of tiny cut-off denim shorts he has recommended for her. “Bershka hai ye, Spain se aaya hai (It's by Bershka, from Spain),” he says proudly. On this October afternoon in 2024 at Janpath in New Delhi, Bershka is still months away from officially launching in India. The vendor knows that only adds to the appeal. “Why don’t you show me things like that?” I ask, pointing to a rack behind him. “That’s for young people,” he replies dismissively. When we correct him, he glances at my aunt’s figure-hugging A-line dress that stops just above the knees, then at my own loose cotton kaftan from Nicobar and grins. “Yahan toh pata hi na chale kaun bada hai aur kaun chhota (You can't tell whose younger or older here).” We’re still laughing when I spot a long denim shift dress hanging behind him. The cut is curved rather than straight, with side slits that climb halfway up the thigh and a deep V-neckline. Its torn label reads Oasis, the UK brand that today survives mostly online. I can already see how I’d wear it, with Converse high tops. And I’m about to make our slightly smug shopkeeper pay for his jokes with a very generous discount. Scenes like this unfold every day in India’s street markets. Beneath corrugated roofs in Janpath, inside the humid press of Sarojini Nagar on a Saturday afternoon, along the pavement stretches of Colaba Causeway and Linking Road, shoppers rummage through piles of clothing that appear to have arrived from nowhere you can easily name. For many Indians growing up in the 1990s and early 2000s, these markets were the chaotic bargain zones where we often had our first encounter with global fashion. This informal pipeline expanded dramatically after India opened its economy in 1991. When Finance Minister Manmohan Singh dismantled the license raj and ushered in a wave of economic liberalisation, the garment export sector grew rapidly. Textile exports nearly doubled during the following decade, rising from roughly $5 billion to more than $12 billion. Factories across towns like Panipat, Bahadurgarh and Najafgarh began producing clothing for global brands including Zara, Mango, Gap, Primark and H&M. These factories overproduced by design, typically by 3 to 5 percent above each order, to account for inevitable quality rejections such as misaligned stitching, shade variations or slightly misplaced buttons. Pieces that do not make it through brand inspections are often sold off in bulk. In India, many of those garments eventually found their way to pavement stalls and market tables. Long before Zara or H&M opened stores in the country, their clothes were already circulating here, hanging from metal racks or piled in large plastic sacks. Retail access to those brands, however, would arrive much later. Zara would not open its first Indian store until 2010, and H&M would follow five years after that. For years in between, the closest many Indian shoppers came to these labels was in the crowded aisles of street markets which filled the gap. Many people learned to recognise good clothing there long before they could afford it. Saumyaa Vohra, a lifestyle journalist, remembers being 23 and newly working in fashion media, with very little money to spend. One day, digging through a pile at Sarojini Nagar, she found a sweater that immediately stood out. “It was unusual, substantial, the kind of thing you can’t quite explain but you know is right,” she recalls. She washed it several times and began wearing it to work. Soon colleagues started asking if it was vintage Ralph Lauren. The knit resembled something from a Ralph Lauren campaign from the early 1990s. For two years she allowed the assumption to stand. The sweater had cost ₹100. “It was a really interesting feeling,” she says now. “To be wearing something that was considered not just fashionable, but a unique vintage edit of something.” Kangkan Rabha, a model and photographer from Guwahati who runs a slow-curation project called Code Toru, had a similar revelation growing up in Assam. As a child, he often visited markets in Dudhnoi and Fancy Bazaar with his mother. At one shop, he found his first pair of Levi’s. “It felt special and earned,” he says, “not because of the label, but because of what it meant.” His mother taught him to assess garments differently. Fabric quality, stitching and construction mattered more than brand names. “I naturally gravitate towards worn-out pieces, slightly imperfect things, clothes that feel lived in,” he says. “That’s where the real charm is.” Over time he has discovered a Lanvin double-breasted blazer in brown herringbone tweed and even a Carven jacket, both with intact Woolmark tags. “Imagine finding a niche French brand in a small part of Assam,” he says. “The best finds happen when you don’t force it.” Karishma Sakhrani, a lifestyle content creator and development chef who divides her time between Mumbai and Dubai, describes street shopping as a kind of visual training. “When you’re surrounded by chaos, you learn to edit quickly,” she says. “You learn quality by touch. You learn proportion instinctively.” Among her favourite discoveries are River Island cover-ups from Hill Road that she later wore to resorts in the Maldives and a gold-studded crop top she paired with a sari at a wedding, all purchased for a few hundred rupees. “If something costs almost nothing, you’ll take a risk with it,” she says. “Sometimes those risks become the pieces you wear for years.” Yet the ecosystem that once produced these discoveries may be changing. Divya Balakrishnan, Vogue India’s associate fashion editor, remembers travelling across cities specifically to explore street markets. “I used to hunt like a hound,” she says. “I used to travel to Bengaluru, Mumbai, Delhi for the markets. I’ve found coats, sweaters and tees from Ralph Lauren, Vivienne Westwood, YSL. You could always tell authenticity by the stitch or the button.” Today, she notices a shift, with the markets lined with more of the same. “The same crop tops, the same oversized tees, the same floral maxis. It’s because they’re being made for the same brands, trends and people.” Quality has also changed, where earlier it was possible to uncover unusual pieces hidden among the piles, many stalls now prioritise quantity over craft. “You could really find treasures earlier,” she says. Even so, the markets continue to attract loyal shoppers. Vohra, who now lives in Goa, still returns regularly. Fast fashion holds little appeal for her. Rabha has grown more selective with age but still sees value in the experience. “I shop slower now,” he says. A self-described “mix shopper”, he believes neither in thrifting as identity nor in the false opposition between conscious consumption and supporting new designers. He has learnt that there is a distance between the garment and the label, and that path he is happy to explore. India, notably, still lacks a widespread vintage retail ecosystem comparable to the thrift stores of London or the curated vintage districts of Tokyo and Bangkok. For decades, street markets have filled that role informally. Their appeal lies not only in affordability but in the process itself. Searching through piles of garments, feeling fabrics between your fingers, spotting something unexpected in the middle of chaos. You cannot algorithm your way through Sarojini Nagar on a crowded weekend afternoon. No app can guide you through a slush pile. What you can develop instead is an instinct. The ability to recognise a good garment when you see one, to imagine how it might fit into your wardrobe, to bargain for it with confidence. “Street markets give you personality,” Sakhrani says, “not just product.”

article_title: From pashmina shawls to ajrakh prints: what climate change is doing to treasured Indian textiles
sub_title: How much longer until all we’re left with is nylon and polyester?
article_content: Assam’s muga silk comes from the cocoons of a silkworm species that cannot exist outside the specific climatic conditions of the Brahmaputra Valley. Unlike most silks, muga is not dyed—the luminous gold is inherent to the fibre itself. It even becomes glossier with wear. Traditionally, almost every household maintained small silk farms in its backyard, but that system is growing increasingly fragile. “One early morning last April, I received a call from one of our farmers,” recalls Jagrity Phukan, a designer and the founder of Way of Living Studio, whose Assam-based textile practice works primarily with muga, eri and Across India, this pattern repeats. When ecosystems collapse, so do livelihoods. When we talk about fashion and climate change, the conversation is usually unidirectional. Fast fashion creates waste, factories pollute rivers and supply chains are opaque. This is all true, but there’s another side of the story that rarely gets the same, if any, attention. What happens to indigenous textiles and crafts when the climate they depend on starts to collapse? Our country’s natural ecological diversity has gifted us a corresponding textile heritage. In the north, pashmina—so fine it can pass through a ring, yet warm enough to survive Himalayan winters—is under pressure. It comes from Changthangi goats, reared by nomadic Changpa herders at altitudes between 14,000 and 17,000 feet. These goats grow their exceptional wool as a biological response to extreme cold. As winters get warmer, the wool fibres are affected. Tariq Dar, founder of Pashmkaar, a brand dedicated to preserving traditional Kashmiri weaving and embroidery practices, explains that while the warmth of the shawls has remained consistent so far, “the quantity and the quality are slowly getting affected. Not in a way most consumers can yet feel, but enough for experts to notice.” Where fibres once measured just 13 to 14 microns, today the geographical indication standard permits a thickness of 16 to 17 microns. It’s a dilution of one of the world’s finest natural fibres, and of a livelihood that has sustained communities in Kashmir and Climate, however, is only part of the story. Abhilasha Bahuguna, founder of Looms of Ladakh—an ethical, herder- and artisan-led luxury brand—points out that ecology and geopolitics are inseparable. “For centuries, Changpa herders moved seasonally between Tibet and Ladakh in a transhumance cycle that allowed pastures time to regenerate. In the 1960s, when the Indo-China border closed, grazing patterns changed permanently.” Grass no longer had time to recover, and because these goats are entirely pasture-fed, fibre quality began to decline. In response, some Changpa herders are turning to yak wool, which, while quite warm, has much coarser fibres than pashmina. Yaks nibble grass from the top rather than pulling it out by the roots, making them gentler grazers. They also live at lower altitudes, closer to where younger Changpa herders want to be. With little infrastructure or support at 17,000 feet, many are migrating to villages nearer to Leh and Kargil. “What is actually required to protect pashmina is collaborative visioning [between the herders, artisans and governmental interventions],” adds Bahuguna. Unlike Kashmir, Ladakh does not have a long-established textile production ecosystem with different communities handling different processes, so change is not as tough. “Changpa herders want skills, institutional support, bargaining power and ownership within the industry.” Down south, Chendamangalam in Handloom weaving here is largely home-based. It depends on stability: dry floors, controlled humidity, sunlight and time. In spite of large-scale destruction of property and handlooms, many weavers were back at work within 110 days—not because conditions had improved, but because every day without a loom was a day without income. The revival narrative glosses over how vulnerable the cluster already was. Today, looms are raised off the ground, and equipment can be dismantled early when floods threaten. “Some brands [like 11.11/eleven eleven] are now also working on a seed-to-store model,” adds Menon, “intervening at every stage to preserve the integrity of hand-making.” The model stands for a transparent supply chain, tracing the journey of the textile from cotton seed to the customer’s hands, which faces instability from the very beginning. According to a 2010 study published in As Laila Tyabji, author, craft activist and cofounder of Dastkar, an NGO that works to revive traditional crafts in India, points out, “Craft is rooted in the geography of the land from where it originates.” Ajrakh, for instance, is the resist-dyed block-printed textile traditionally practised by Khatri communities in Kutch. It’s known for its deep indigos, rich reds and near-mathematical symmetry. It requires repeated washing and open-air drying at multiple stages, and the mineral balance of the water directly affects how natural dyes show up. “Ajrakh is an entire system of knowledge,” says designer Monica Shah of Jade by MK, whose brand consistently champions the craft clusters and artisans they work with. “You can’t rush it. It depends on water, weather and the artisan’s judgement more than any machine.” Historically, Kutch’s fresh groundwater made this possible. Today, the region faces rising salinity due to industrial overextraction and seawater intrusion, exacerbated by repeated drought cycles.“Even with utmost skill and care, there are black splotches and muddy tones due to the saline content. Is it a wonder that many traditional ajrakh printers are turning to chemical dyes?” shares Tyabji. Next door in Rajasthan, dabu printing tells a similar story. It relies on a resist paste made from local Construction and mining have altered the soil composition around many ajrakh and dabu craft clusters, forcing printers to travel further for materials or substitute them with inferior ones. “Some clusters have tried collective systems such as shared resources, better washing set-ups, filtration support and training the next generation, but it’s not enough,” adds Shah. In Assam’s silk farms, even when the crop survives, yields have declined significantly and cocoon thickness has reduced. “Earlier, my uncles who reared silkworms wouldn’t even shave during the rearing period. They washed their hands with ash water instead of soap because they believed even a trace of a chemical or oil could harm the worms,” shares Phukan. A far cry from soap, tar fumes from road development have destabilised these ecosystems today. Faced with unpredictable weather and shrinking returns, many families are switching to farming tea—already expanding into silk-growing regions, bringing pesticides and chemical residues with it. “Artisans adapt constantly because they’ve always worked with nature, not against it,” shares Shah. “They shift working hours, change drying methods, modify sequences and adjust dye behaviour depending on the climate.” But you can only adjust so much when faced with failing water systems and extreme heat. As Menon says, “we are perpetually reacting to disaster, not preventing it.” There’s a certain pride in wearing traditional textiles. Ajrakh printing dates back to the Indus Valley civilisation. With its saturated colours and geometric patterns, it carries centuries of knowledge in its folds. article_title: Rashmika Mandanna's rainbow mehendi ensemble took over 4,000 hours of artisanal craftsmanship to make
sub_title: The Torani look served as a kaleidoscope of artisanal techniques and devotional art rooted in culture

article_title: Matthieu Blazy's Chanel is built for the fashion nerds
sub_title: For an audience hungry for IYKYK  nuggets, Matthieu Blazy serves up an endless buffet
article_content: The first time I realised my partner was ‘The One’ was a moment so deceptively ordinary, you might actually roll your eyes upon reading this. We were exiting my apartment building in the afternoon when he doubled back and handed me his sunglasses. “It’s very bright, you’ll get a headache,” he said. A man’s act of remembering a throwaway detail shared casually months ago. A woman’s surprise at being seen and cared for in that wholly quotidian, impossibly real way. When I told my partner it was the most romantic thing anyone had ever done for me, he did actually roll his eyes. When I recounted the incident to my best friend, she understood immediately. Women are so used to shrinking themselves—in public, at the workplace, in marriages, at the gym—that when we are seen and remembered, strange quirks, weird medical conditions and all, well… we fall in love. Matthieu Blazy understands this simple truth that evades so many others of his sex. For Chanel’s celebrated Métiers d’art 2026 show last December, the house’s new creative director did not fly his audience to a tropical island or plop a Swedish iceberg (RIP Karl Lagerfeld) in the centre of the runway. Blazy made them schlep down to an unused subway station in New York. Hardly the epitome of glamour. Then, as a train rolled in and a cast of characters poured out in every direction, he forced us to look at, and fall for, the details like only a true fashion nerd can. The show made it clear that Blazy hadn’t just rabbit-holed into the Chanel archives. He’d also invested time in getting to know Coco Chanel, the woman. Everywhere you looked, there were cheeky references to her life, waiting to be identified. A red scarf slung low across the hips of a black co-ord set, styled like Mademoiselle herself. A tweed suit woven to look like leopard print, an ethical homage to her love for fur. A leather jacket hand-painted with ‘Tonight or Never’, recalling the 1931 film that marked Chanel’s debut as a Hollywood costume stylist. Then, the vocabulary expanded. The fashion nerd flexed. Intermingled with allusions to his chosen ancestor were everyday women Chanel might have met on her pit stop in New York. The off-duty showgirl waltzing home from Broadway, feathered fan in hand. The Upper East Side cat lady. The mob boss, dressed to kill. The end result felt cinematic to Margaret Zhang, filmmaker and the former head of editorial content at Vogue China. Though we watched the same show, she was seated further down the subway platform than me, giving her a completely different vantage point of the chaotic choreography. Zhang found Blazy’s approach to be more like a film director’s, “unafraid of people moving in cycles as opposed to bodies moving through a sterile space”. She points to the mutual creative respect Blazy has for his audience: “He is doing the work but he’s also asking us to do the work rather than just telling us exactly what he’s thinking. It takes confidence to invite people in, to allow for scrutiny like that and it’s such a luxury to be trusted as an audience.” Scrutiny of the microscopic kind is part of the package at a house like Chanel. It’s the double- edged sword that Sabyasachi Mukherjee knows intimately—his own maison boasts an equally loyal and opinionated following. Also a fashion nerd, the Indian couturier made the effort to attend Blazy’s sophomore effort in New York to see the vision for himself. Mukherjee notes that the industry is tentatively moving out of a phase of “corporate designers” to embrace the “young and idealistic” again, powered by a newfound confidence that the post-digital world has given the consumer. “That’s why personal style has come back, why research and nerdism is coming back,” he explains. Brands can no longer prey on people’s insecurities to sell a prohibitively expensive handbag; the craft has to speak for itself. Blazy’s democratic approach, one where the magic of the métiers is laid out on the table to be deduced and dissected, is shaking up the old guard but magnetising the next generation. A necessary reinvention to survive when our very understanding of luxury is being questioned. “For too long, men in suits were running fashion,” says Mukherjee. “But you can’t capture human desire or imagination on an excel sheet.”

article_title: This high jewellery brand is crafting heritage in every heirloom
sub_title: At Raj Mahtani Couture Jewels, five generations of craftsmanship meet contemporary vision, creating pieces that honour legacy while embracing modern elegance
article_content: The true beauty of heirloom jewellery lies in the stories they carry—notes of love, history, and memory that lend an evocative depth to every look. Whether through elaborate necklaces rooted in age-old Indian craftsmanship or shoulder dusters with contemporary flair, Raj Mahtani has built a design language that honours heritage while embracing innovation. Founded in 1880, Raj Mahtani Couture Jewels draws on the legacy of his five-generation, family-run jewellery house. The eponymous label blends craft traditions with contemporary techniques, creating high jewellery that feels both timeless and forward-thinking. Over the years, the brand has become synonymous with pieces that celebrate milestones, define special moments, and evolve into treasured keepsakes. At the heart of the brand lies a distinct design philosophy: honour the past while designing for the present. A Raj Mahtani necklace—often the centrepiece of a bridal look—is created to stand the test of time. Mughal influences, old-world techniques, and classical stone settings are reinterpreted through a contemporary lens. The Raj Mahtani bride embodies this same sensibility: confident, globally aware, and appreciative of fine craftsmanship. Table-cut diamonds, Old-cut diamonds, New-cut diamonds, Colombian emeralds, Burmese rubies, and exceptional pearls are sourced and transformed into pieces that feel both opulent and statement-making. Perfect for heritage weddings, couture bridal styling, and cherished celebrations where timeless elegance is paramount. Raj Mahtani was the first in India to align fine jewellery with couture, recognising early on that jewels are integral to the fashion narrative. His collaborations with leading Indian designers such as Anamika Khanna, Tarun Tahiliani and Manish Malhotra, along with international names like Diane von Furstenberg and Roberto Cavalli, positioned his creations not as accessories but as defining elements of the fashion runway. With a discerning clientele across London, Singapore, Hong Kong, Sri Lanka, New York City and Dubai, the brand’s appeal lies in its balance of tradition and relevance. In a world where luxury can often feel transient, Mahtani’s creations offer a sense of permanence. Crafted with precision and guided by intention, Raj Mahtani Couture Jewels continues to define a distinctly modern expression of Indian high jewellery—one that is rooted in legacy yet confident in its global perspective.

article_title: Madhuri Dixit Nene’s painterly ensemble proves great tailoring can multitask

Designer Dipti Advait behind the label shares, “This collection is a new take on structure and fluidity, grounded in sharp cuts, easy layering and defined by bold prints. These are versatile staples perfect to create a capsule wardrobe that can go from a Sunday brunch to a pool party at a destination wedding.” That philosophy is evident in the interplay of tailored shirting and the fluid draping of the ensemble. At first glance, the set reads as a conventional coordinated shirt and skirt combination. Look closer and the construction reveals its innovation. “The tie-up drape skirt reimagines the classic sarong through a contemporary lens. The skirt’s versatile design allows it to be tied up in multiple ways, ensuring a flattering look for all body types,” says Advait. What catches your eye the most is its painterly print. “Sweeping brushstroke forms in crimson, deep terracotta and burnt sienna cut across an ivory cotton satin base, lending the look an artful edge. The composition channels the raw energy of Abstract Expressionism and yet remains wearable. The idea was to imagine strokes that are gestural and spontaneous, as though the cotton satin fabric itself was laid flat and painted by hand in a single, fluid motion,” the designer shares. The print did not originate digitally. “It was first born on paper, drawn entirely by hand before being translated onto fabric. Each brushstroke you see is a deliberate mark made by a human hand, later rendered onto the cloth to preserve every raw, imperfect edge of the original artwork.”

article_title: Sonam Kapoor’s lime Shehlaa Khan ensemble reworked Mughal florals in paint and zardozi
sub_title: Rhea Kapoor styled the look with layers of jewellery
article_content: In February 2026, Sonam Ahuja Kapoor celebrated her second pregnancy with a godh bharai ceremony, hosted by her family. For the occasion, the mother-to-be opted for a bespoke outfit by friend and designer Shehlaa Khan. The lime look was conceived in close collaboration with Kapoor’s sister and stylist Rhea Kapoor. “We wanted to do something special and still use a signature style of my label,” Khan shares. What they arrived at was a silhouette that is thoughtful and comfortable, featuring a bubble skirt, a contoured blouse and a flowing kimono cape, defined by a classic Indian-style dupatta. “Given that it's an Indian godh bharai, the only thing contemporary about the outfit was its silhouette,” explains Khan. Despite that deliberate modernity of form, the overall impression is traditional. On Kapoor, the structure of the blouse and the volume of the bubble skirt introduced a sculptural quality, whereas the kimono cape softened the look with fluid movement. The starting point for the look’s embellishment was unambiguous in its ambition. “The idea was to resemble a Mughal style painting, and therefore we used the signature hand-painting technique as the base of the embellishment on a Chanderi silk fabric. which is rich yet represents a vintage Indian aesthetic.” Mughal miniature painting, which flourished as a courtly artform between the 16th and 18th centuries, is defined by vibrant mineral pigments and an obvious synthesis of Indian, Persian and European influences. The paintings are celebrated for their realistic portraiture and naturalistic depictions of flora and fauna, and this is the exact visual language that Khan has translated onto fabric. The hand-painted crimson blossoms and brushed-gold leaves were elevated through zardozi embroidery worked in nakshi and saadi materials. “The festive nature of the event required some sparkles, to give the look of Zari work used in extensive garments of women from royalty in the Mughal era," Khan adds. “The outfit was a very intricate yet heartfelt tribute to the relationship Sonam holds with the brand since its early years," adds Khan. “It took a long time and several hours of handwork of various artisans to bring this outfit together.” Colour, too, Khan says, played a defining role in shaping the mood. “We chose lime because Sonam loves green but yet wanted it to be a bright and a happy shade for the joyous occasion.” Rhea styled her look with jewellery that blended heirloom sentiment with artisanal charm. The necklace and earrings were from Kapoor’s personal collection, while the ring and gucha came from Amrapali Jewels, the hathphool, waist belt and pearl kadas from Sheetal Zaveri, and additional kadas from Maalka By Varun Haria and Falguni Mehta.

article_title: How to style a red dress without looking like a walking Valentine’s Day card
sub_title: Vogue's guide on how to wear the world’s most high-maintenance colour
article_content: Whether it’s bombshell dressing for This isn’t about reinventing your wardrobe or saving red exclusively for evenings out. Instead, it’s about subtle shifts in styling: unexpected pairings, pared-back accessories and a willingness to let contrast do the work. Red doesn’t need help commanding attention; it needs grounding. The mood now is about seeing bold pieces through a cooler, offbeat lens. Keep reading for Vogue’s guide on how to style a red dress in ways that feel current and entirely your own. A red dress is already doing most of the talking. Rather than competing with it, keep accessories minimal: a single gold cuff, black leather heels, or a metallic mini bag will add polish without distraction. Red-on-red styling can easily tip into literal territory; neutrals and metals keep things sharp. If there’s one styling choice that can instantly recalibrate a red dress, it’s footwear. Classic heels will always work, but they also reinforce red’s reputation as an evening-only colour. Instead, grounding the look with flatter, more pragmatic shoes makes the dress feel wearable and modern. The safest route is a boxy blazer or a clean trench to keep it chic. For contrast, an oversized denim jacket or a leather trench works well, adding just enough friction to stop the look from feeling too “done.” Think of outerwear as something to steady the look. For daytime or transitional weather, layering is key. Wear a red dress over a crisp white shirt or a fitted t-shirt to instantly make it feel less dressy. This approach pulls red firmly into everyday territory, away from its eveningwear reputation. Skip the red lip cliché, go for bronzed skin, nude lips with a softly smoked eye. If you must go red, make it deep and matte. Keep your hair sleek and straight, or tousled and undone for that effortless contrast to the high-impact colour.

article_title: 5 Vogue-approved tips on method dressing for the job you want
sub_title: Dress for the job you want
article_content: While the common focus is, of course, what to wear for an interview, there’s also a case to be made for how you wear it being just as important. You can’t control what people choose to fixate on, but you can make sure your outfit isn’t the thing pulling focus from your ideas. That tension has resurfaced lately thanks to the rise of “method dressing” on the red carpet. Celebrities like And that applies just as much in places without photographers. The interview room. The lobby waiting area. The Michelle Obama recently spoke on a podcast about how her outfits often received more attention than her ideas, especially in interviews. It’s a sharp reminder of something many people already know instinctively: what you wear and how you turn up can shape how your ideas are received, sometimes before you’ve even spoken. So consider this your permission slip to method dress for an interview. Better still, most of the smartest interview styling choices aren’t about buying something new but editing what you already own, and wearing it like you mean it. Below, five of the most wearable method dressing “roles” for what to wear for an interview. If you’re confused, start here. This combination works across almost every industry because it looks polished without trying too hard. Wear it with a fitted tee or shirt, tailored bottoms and closed-toe mules. It works because it looks serious without feeling stiff. Add a pair of dainty silver earrings, just enough to complete the look without taking focus away from it. The sweet spot is to look interesting without making that the only thing you are all about. Try tonal separates and add one point of tension: a sharply framed pair of glasses, an architectural bag or a “personality” shoe. If you hate shirts, don’t force it. A fine knit top can look just as sharp, and often more modern. There’s a particular kind of drip in looking like you’re not fighting your outfit. The main trick? Nothing should need constant adjusting. If you’re interviewing for a senior role or a job that’s client-facing, you want to look like the person they’d trust in a room that matters. This isn’t about going overly corporate; it’s about looking grounded. Think sharp tailoring, elevated basics and a great coat if the weather allows. The energy should be: “I can represent this company without trying too hard.” Video interviews are their own genre. Your outfit needs to work in a tight frame and under lighting that can be unkind. Clean necklines will always look more composed than anything overly dressed up. The biggest trick is avoiding too casual from the waist up: if you look like you’re on a coffee run, it changes how you’re received, even if your answers are brilliant.

article_title: Sreeleela's tartan ensemble shifts shape at the waist
sub_title: From AFEW Rahul Mishra’s Silk Route collection showcased at Lakmē Fashion Week and shaped by cross-cultural exchange
article_content: Sreeleela’s plaid look from AFEW Rahul Mishra Fall–Winter 2025 shifted attention away from the body’s usual lines. Instead of narrowing at the waist, the silhouette widened there, using volume as its defining move. Cut in Scottish tartan, the fabric brought familiarity to an otherwise unconventional shape. The bustier opens with a dramatic pannier-like expansion at the waist. The volume sat firmly at the midsection, while the lower half dropped straight, allowing the interruption in shape to stand on its own. Seen within AFEW Rahul Mishra’s Silk Route collection at Lakmē Fashion Week, the ensemble pushes proportions at a time when many silhouettes remain cautious. The emphasis here was not accents or ornamentation, but shape as structure. Malkit J Gill keeps the accessories limited to black pumps, drop earrings from Outhouse that mirror the rounded volume introduced at the waist. Raashika Shetty kept the eyes as the focus of the beauty look with fluttery lashes, a natural flush on the cheeks and a nude lip. “Lean into the drama of the silhouette by adding a Napoleon bolero to accentuate the pannier and balance its structure. article_title: Is the male gaze evolving?
sub_title: Sometimes I dress like a boy, but my straight boyfriend still thinks I look cute
article_content: My Fast-forward 18 months, and my style has only become more ‘tomboy femme’. My jeans are baggier than ever. I own more vests and structured tops than I need. And yet, my skirt collection is at an all-time high (I now own four). If you happen to rummage through my wardrobe, you'll see lace and frills peeking through. I dress based on how I’m feeling—whether that’s a basic tank top and Which raises the question: are men evolving? Is the male gaze loosening its grip on the deep cleavage and hip-hugging silhouette? Or have some men simply learned to see fashion as expression, an extension of the women they love? “I’m not really going to change myself to make someone I’m dating more comfortable,” shares New York–based creator Teo Marcella. Marcella, who is in a four-year relationship with their boyfriend, admits there was temptation in the beginning to lean into dressing a certain way, but they pushed against it. “I held my own ground in what I knew was comfortable for me. And I think, honestly, that authenticity has allowed us to develop a really strong foundation.” Marcella grew up with a very specific kind of femininity. “As a kid, I was very girly, looking at the stars of Disney Channel. It was all very feminine.” But with time, they realised they felt “so much more comfortable and so much more in my body dressing androgynously. I still like to have a feminine face, but I love a masc outfit,” shares Marcella. Interestingly, they notice how the world responds. “When I’m dressed more masculine, there’s less chivalry from people around. People might hold doors for me less [often], but I’ll hold doors [open] for people. I’ll help people out of cars. Something interesting happens with my energy there.” Aastha Gaur, a Los Angeles–based creator and senior director of design at Google, describes her style as existing between chill and commanding, rather than feminine or masculine. “Imagine a T-shirt and jeans,” she says. “More chill would be wearing a cardigan. More commanding would be wearing a Growing up in India, Gaur identified as a tomboy early on. “I had this sense of boys having more freedom than girls. Later, as a postgraduate student in LA, she swung hard in the opposite direction with frills, dresses and hyperfemininity before realising it wasn’t her. “Eventually, I settled into a place where it’s not masculine, it’s not feminine. It’s somewhere in the middle. That feels better.” In high school, a senior once warned her, “You dress like a boy. You should know that men are not attracted to that.” The comment lodged itself somewhere in her brain. Years later, when she started dating her now husband, she briefly tried to course-correct. “I went shopping and bought this grey frilly dress. I don’t think I wore it more than once. I was like, OK, I cannot do this. It’s just not me.” “I do think overall he is very secure in his masculinity and who he is,” she says. “So he doesn’t feel like his wife has to be feminine or look feminine to project a certain kind of image.” It helps that he’s a designer. “If he likes something, he’ll just say, ‘Oh wow, that looks cool, babe.’ It’s not limited to any specific kind of outfit. He sees the colour composition, the shapes.” In other words, he has taste. Marcella echoes that dynamic. “He absolutely loves it,” they say of their partner’s reaction to their personal style. “He’s very fashion-forward himself and it’s been great because we get to share closets.” Which, quite frankly, is the final frontier of any relationship. I see it in my own relationship, too. I’ll show my boyfriend pieces I’m considering buying and genuinely take his opinion on my outfits into account, which, to my perpetual shock, often improve the look. He runs his clothes by me, loves going shopping together, sends me reels of clothes he thinks I'll like and always has a new pair of Of course, not all responses are enlightened. Gaur points out that when she receives hate from men, it often stems from discomfort. “It can be threatening to see a woman showing up in a powerful way. Because in those minds, masculinity equals power. Men expect women to dress a certain way because I think they’re explicitly looking for softness, which to them is weakness.” Which brings us back to the original question: are men evolving? Maybe some are. Maybe the male gaze is splintering. Maybe there’s a growing cohort of men who find autonomy attractive, who are secure in their own masculinity and their femininity. They understand design, appreciate shape and proportion and find any well-put-together outfit as compelling as a body-con gown. Or maybe, it’s just really hot when a woman dresses like a man.

article_title: Samantha Ruth Prabhu’s pistachio Banarasi silk sari is hand-beaten patua zari
sub_title: The actor paired her Label Sourav Das drape with emerald jewellery
article_content: On Republic Day, Samantha Ruth Prabhu made her way to the Rashtrapati Bhavan for the At Home reception after receiving an invite from President Droupadi Murmu. For the occasion, the south star wore heritage on her sleeves, turning to a revival Banarasi Iktara weave from the Label Sourav Das. Rendered in a pistachio green that looks time-honoured yet freshly calibrated for now, the sari breaks from the primary jewel tones typically associated with Banarasi drapes. The silk canvas is scattered with gold woven buttis, while a rich border and pallu elevates it. “Samantha’s is wearing a quintessential Hazar Buiti Asharfi Sikka revival Banarasi sari with a bygone angri border woven in finer counts of mulberry silk. It also has konias on either side of the pallu. The sari is woven with Kaduwa method in Iktara style with hand-beaten patua zari,” shares Sourav Das. The Iktara, also known as single thread, technique offers not just strength and smoothness but also a fluid fall and a resilient life that’s prized by connoisseurs. Banarasi saris have long occupied a rarefied place in Indian wardrobes. Their lineage traces back centuries of royal patronage and painstaking craftsmanship. One weave can take weeks, sometimes months, to complete, with master weavers translating complex designs onto looms that demand memory and muscle. What makes them singular is not just the silk or the zari, but the varied motifs, from florals nodding to abundance, to paisley border, signifying fertility and eternity. In the actor’s sari, the geometric buttis, which speaks of cosmic order, feels particularly resonant. It serves an emblem of continuity for a woman who has repeatedly chosen longevity over trend. She completed the look with an open-setting diamond and emerald choker, complemented by matching stud earrings and a statement ring from Golecha’s Jewels. Her hair was worn in a sleek, middle-parted half-up, half-down style, while her makeup stayed understated and refined with a matte, skin-like base, softly smoked eyes and a nude lip that let the jewellery and weave take the spotlight. A pistachio sari and jewels, like hers, is a smart trousseau investment. While it is timeless in spirit, it is refreshingly modern and versatile enough to move seamlessly from intimate family ceremonies to landmark events for years to come.

article_title: Keerthy Suresh’s lime-green velvet kurta is adorned with a mélange of zardozi, resham and metal work
sub_title: The south star styled her RajiRamniq look with a pair of jeans
article_content: For a recent press tour, Keerthy Suresh stepped out in a styling choice that reflects a larger shift in Indian occasion wear. She opted for a velvet kurta by RajiRamniq with blue At the centre of her look is a lime-green kurta from RajiRamniq’s ‘Nisbat’ collection, which draws from the idea of connection between craft and contemporary life. According to designers Raji Sharma and Ramniq Tangri Khatri, “crafted in a luminous velvet fabric, the kurta features a fluid straight silhouette with side slits for movement and modernity. The rich lime-green hue brings depth and royalty, while the relaxed structure keeps it breathable, wearable and celebration-ready.” A closer look at the kurta reveals its dense and layered craftsmanship. “The piece comes alive through an amalgamation of traditional embellishment like pearls, zardozi, Resham and metal coins in a modern, contemporary design,” the designers explain. “In the Nisbat collection, each element is applied through a carefully staged, hand-led process. Resham embroidery frames the borders and establishes definition. Zardozi adds architectural depth. Pearl work introduces softness and a subtle sheen, while mirror work is intentionally restrained to enhance light and movement. Metal coins at the neckline function as a tactile, heritage-inspired detail,” the duo elaborates about the surface ornamentation that took approximately 48 to 60 artisanal hours. “One of the understated strengths of the kurta lies in its versatility. While the craftsmanship gives it a ceremonial presence, the silhouette is intentionally balanced to move easily across contexts. It can be paired with a velvet sharara for formal settings or worn effortlessly with denims for a relaxed, contemporary look, much like Keerthy Suresh did,” they add. Leaning fully into the bohemian mood, the actor extended the aesthetic through her accessories, opting for a choker and earrings from Binni, a floral silver ring from Abhilasha Jewelry Collection, and another from Keiyura Jewelry. Her hippy fishtail braid was finished with oxidised accents from Rubans Jewellery, while smoky kohled eyes and nude lips completed the look. For footwear, she picked a pair of heels from Fizzy Goblet, adorned with embroidery that mirrored the crafts on her kurta.

article_title: A life beautifully lived—Hamish Bowles remembers Valentino
sub_title: Valentino Garavani conquered the worlds of fashion and style, bringing a certain idea of beauty to all he touched
article_content: Valentino Clemente Ludovico Garavani—known, simply and powerfully, as Valentino—was born on May 11th, 1932, in Voghera, a rather quiet place lost somewhere between Milan and Genoa. But by the time he died, aged 93, on January 19, he had conquered the worlds of fashion and style, bringing a “I love beauty—it’s not my fault,” Valentino famously said with a shrug, and in fashion, he saw a way to captivate and ensnare women (his only clients when starting out, before he widened the purview of his well-dressed net). He trained at the Accademia dell’Arte in Milan, studying both French and fashion, and then, aged 17, moved to Paris, to the École des Beaux-Arts and the Chambre Syndicale de la Couture, before securing an apprenticeship in 1951 with the Athenian couturier Jean Dessès, who dressed royalty and high society ladies in his immaculately draped and vividly colored evening gowns. Jacqueline, the Comtesse de Ribes, dressed with Dessès, and when she was asked by Oleg Cassini to design some dresses for him in Paris, she mentioned it to Dessès, telling the designer that “I don’t know how to draw in a chic way.” Dessès was amused. “I have an Italian illustrator,” he told her, “who would be very happy to earn a little more money after working-hours doing the drawings for you”, and a friendship between Valentino and Jacqueline was born. When he was When Guy Laroche, Dessès’s assistant, departed to start his own couture house, Valentino joined him for a few years before leaving to work briefly with the Russian-Georgian Princess Irene Galitzine (Galitzine had made palazzo pyjamas a thing, amidst opulent evening clothes). Then, in 1959, Valentino started his own house with backing from his father and a family friend. In the meantime, someone had come into his life. Giancarlo Giammetti recently recalled their first meeting, with Giammetti seated alone in a Roman cafe. “A kind person came and said, ‘Are you alone?’ I said, ‘Yes.’ ‘Do you mind if me and my friend can sit here?’ Of course,” Giammetti remembered. “And Valentino sat next to me—I remember very deeply.” A whoosh of dark hair framed Valentino’s tanned face, with its sultry features and his arresting blue eyes. “Then Valentino started to speak to me in French. I said, ‘Sorry?’ ‘Oh, sorry—I just arrived from Paris after seven years, my mind goes French, and I was hoping that you speak French…’” Giammetti, it turns out, had studied French for most of his life. “He said, ‘From now on, if I see you again, we speak French.’ And we still do. Incredibly.” The two would speak French to each other—as lovers, and then as intimate friends and business partners—for the rest of Valentino’s life. Valentino soon found a lavish, frescoed apartment in the fashionable Via Condotti, but less than a year later, he was facing bankruptcy. (Though Valentino threw the blame at his “champagne tastes,” someone had not been paying the rent.) He and Giammetti simply moved the salon to a 16th-century palazzo on the Via Gregoriana. (Incidentally, Giammetti acquired the Via Condotti apartment recently and has had it transformed into his offices by Studio Peregalli’s Laura Sartori Rimini. It’s a sumptuous series of rooms, the walls now hung with silver tissue or silk velvet—though some still have their original frescoes—and filled with Hervé van der Straten furniture and antiques. What may have been “Champagne tastes” in 1959 are now sublime and defining.) Valentino gradually began to make his mark on fashion. His flashing good looks easily summoned the press, to be sure, but it was his clothes that had an allure for the stars who would pass through Rome. And when Elizabeth Taylor, there to shoot Suddenly, his work was appearing in As Valentino became a name to watch, with ladies—Audrey Hepburn, Sophia Loren, any number of princesses, Jaqueline Kennedy Onassis, Nan Kempner, Lynn Wyatt, and Susan Gutfreund, among so many more, flocking to dress with him—so his residences became exponentially more impressive. His Roman base—a penthouse apartment with Persian miniatures on the fabric-covered walls and banquettes fit for a Turkish salon, had been transformed into a house on the Appian Way, decorated by Renzo Mongiardino, the When I first went to Rome for the couture in the mid-’80s, long before my Appian Way adventure, I plucked up all my courage and walked into Valentino’s intimidating couture salon just off the top of the Spanish steps—two small-ish rooms that positively oozed with Of course, this pair of elegantly finished rooms opened onto a positive hive of industry occupying five floors of a vast palazzo. Here were the couture ateliers: room after room of industrious ladies and a smattering of men—hundreds of them—applied to the task at hand in light-flooded rooms. (Some years after my first adventure with the couture salon, the place was subtly transformed by the English architects and designers Peter Moore and Peter Kent—there were silvered bannisters, acres of pale grey marble in the hallways, and paintings by Julian Schnabel, Keith Haring, and Francesco Clemente, and it was all very, very chic.) Valentino’s show then always finished with music just before the In 1991, I had an appointment with Valentino to discuss his entire career, and met with him in an elegant room looking over the Piazza Mignanelli, filled with antiques and lush draperies that lent it a Cécile Sorel sort of look. It was not easy getting him to speak. Next door in a vast room—and I mean Of course, Valentino had a number of other properties: in Capri, in New York, in London. But in 1995, I was invited to the 17th century chateau of brick and stone he had acquired—a house that was revealed to me only after I had followed a drive and dramatically turned a corner: There, plunging downhill, and glimmering below, was the Chateau de Wideville, once home to Madame de la Valliere, mistress of Louis XIV (Versailles is conveniently near). In the evening’s light, I explored the breathtaking Jacques Wirtz gardens, where brilliant violet rosemary stretched across the field and cut through the forests, while roses and scented high-summer flowers filled the walled garden. And then: the breathtaking house itself. Valentino worked with Henri Samuel on the interiors, which—with their emerald silk-velvet armchairs and a sort of Chinoiserie motif, which gave the house a sort of fanciful Palm Beach air—brought a level of comfort to the splendidly austere exterior. I was amused to see that the enormous Francis Bacon in Valentino’s sitting room depicted an abstracted man sitting on a carpet of bunches of roses, quite unlike anything I had seen before in his work—as Valentino-ish as it was possible for a Bacon to be. As I headed in for dinner, rather moved by the exquisite gardens and the ravishing interiors—by everything that Giancarlo and Valentino had done in life—I said to Valentino, “What you’ve done is to create beauty.” He clasped my hand and, weeping, said, “It

article_title: Shanaya Kapoor’s Anita Dongre lehenga is brought to life with hand-painted Pichhwai
sub_title: Hand-painted flora and fauna move across the surface, layered with antique work that gives the piece a tactile richness
article_content: When it comes to occasionwear, Shanaya Kapoor consistently returns to pieces designed to last. Her latest pick, an Featuring a strappy blouse and a billowing skirt, the ensemble’s silk base lends a diaphanousness that mirrors Kapoor’s pared-back approach to ceremonial dressing. Set against a distinctive meadow greenish-yellow, the lehenga immediately stands apart for its nature-inspired hue. Motifs take centre stage in the look, in sync with Dongre's signature design language. The hand-painted Pichhwai artwork unfolds across the lehenga like a living landscape, populated with blooming florals, foliage, wildlife and fluttering birds. The blouse reflects the same story and is further elevated with intricate surface techniques. A delicate organza dupatta brings the ensemble together, offering a gentler counterpoint to the richly detailed lehenga. The ensemble draws its soul from the art of Pichhwai painting, a 400-year-old craft that originated in Rajasthan in the 16th century. Traditionally created as devotional backdrops depicting tales of Shrinathji, Pichhwai paintings were also deeply inspired by the rhythms of nature, from seasons to flora and fauna. In the lehenga, this heritage is reinterpreted with each motif meticulously hand-painted by skilled artisans and delicately enhanced with sequins. The lehenga took close to 90 days to create, a timeline that honours the patience and attention this craft demands. The piece is animated by an in-house master painter, whose deep-rooted Pichhwai lineage informs every brushstroke. As the designer shared, this lehenga is part of the House of Anita Dongre’s larger effort to ensure that art forms like Pichhwai continue to thrive within a contemporary language. She accessorised with intricate temple jewellery from Indinoor. A gold necklace adorned with bird motifs carried on the lehenga’s avian motifs, paired with statement jhumkas and kaan chains that were attached to her loose braid. For her beauty look, she stuck with dewy makeup in warm copper tones for a soft, sun-kissed finish.

article_content: Nostalgia runs through Tara Sutaria’s recent sartorial pick, an ivory georgette The hero of her look is undoubtedly the blouse. Featuring elbow-length sleeves, it is densely embroidered with pearls, crystals and sequins. The thoughtful embellishments give the effect of jewellery worn on the body. The mirror work is structured to resemble a choker at the neckline, moving into what looks like layered, multi-string pearl necklaces draped across her torso. This trompe-l’oeil effect blurs the line between garment and adornment, making the blouse feel almost ceremonial. The high neckline further heightens its vintage appeal. Given the strength of the blouse, stylist Tanya Ghavri took a measured step back when it came to accessorising the look with jewellery. Thanks to the high neckline, she gave a necklace a rain check. She opted for a ring and stud earrings from Mohar by Priyanka and Nakul along with classic kadas by Diamantina Fine Jewels and Raj Diamonds. Soft glam defined the makeup, with a dewy base, gentle smoky eyes and glossy pink lips to keep things fresh. The sleek updo, too, felt inspired by yesteryears, completing the nostalgia-led narrative. What makes a look, like Sutaria’s sari, enduring is its versatility. The ivory palette acts as a blank canvas, allowing it to shift seamlessly across seasons and occasions. For daytime pheras, it feels serene and ceremonial, while a switch to a bold red pout, gemstone jewellery or sharper eye makeup can instantly take it into cocktail territory.

article_title: Sharvari’s Aditi Gupta lehenga puts its weight in a scallop-edged blouse
sub_title: The skirt carries pattern through panels and borders, leaving the heaviest surface work at the top
article_content: Sharvari chose a pearl-gold lehenga by Aditi Gupta for Up close, the lehenga reveals a careful layering of textiles. Panels of silk, zari tissue and jacquard Banarasi are pieced together in vertical sections, broken up by jharokha-inspired motifs and elongated paisley embroidery. The patterning moves downward rather than outward, giving the skirt weight without getting weighed down. The blouse introduces the most visual interest. Cut with a deep plunge neckline and scalloped edges, it is densely embroidered with paisley motifs that continue around the back. The embroidery shifts from compact geometry at the bodice to looser bead and pearl detailing along the straps and edges. At the back, tassel ties and beadwork added movement, making the blouse as considered from behind as it was from the front. Stylist Tanya Ghavri accessorises Sharvari's look with heritage jewellery by Razwada Jewels, featuring a statement choker, earrings and bangles worked in gold and stones. Hair is pulled back in a no-makeup makeup beauty look. “Pull the look away from overt bridal territory by editing it down rather than adding more. Skip the heavy necklace, soften the hair into a loose, low tie or knot, and let the blouse and skirt do the work. Drape the dupatta in a classic shoulder throw and secure it to the blouse with a brooch above the left side of the bust; let the ends fall. Keep jewellery minimal to one element at a time, lose the polki necklace to let the earrings breathe,” says Vogue India fashion associate Manglien Gangte.

article_title: Shanaya Kapoor's Gaurav Gupta sari makes a case for all-sequins everything
sub_title: The couture flows onto the body in a way that feels less like fabric and more like sculpture
article_content: Shanaya Kapoor wears a Gaurav Gupta The sari moves in a silver-to-charcoal gradient, its Drop earrings and hand chains from Indinoor, co-created by Kapoor, are worn with slicked-back hair, a flush of blush and winged liner. With its dense sequin surface, this sari sits best in evening settings that allow light and stillness to do their thing. “The takeaway from Shanaya Kapoor's look is the sculptural blouse. One that takes focus over the sari, to create such a look, work with a blouse or crop top that is detailed with pleats, surface embroidery techniques, made of interesting materials or holds a unique shape. Then work with a sari in a similar tonality or a complementary colour scheme.  Accessorise minimally, keeping the blouse as your main statement,” says Vogue India fashion associate Divya Balakrishnan.

article_title: Janhvi Kapoor’s scarlet Miu Miu mini stands on its cut
sub_title: The colour sets the tempo here, with everything else scaled back against it
article_content: Janhvi Kapoor steps out in a scarlet Miu Miu mini that plays with the familiarity of a cheongsam before cutting it short. The mandarin collar sits high and closed, the torso is held close and then the hem rises sharply, shifting what could have read as historic into something unmistakably current. The fabric blossoms in lily-inspired motifs across its surface, pale against red, spaced so the print never overtakes the colour. A small tie at the waist pulls the fabric slightly off-centre, introducing a looseness that keeps the silhouette from feeling sealed. She pairs the dress with white Rene Caovilla sandals, adding rings and drop earrings as the only adornment. Hair is worn up, leaving the collar and print unobstructed. "Lean into the oriental preppy tone of the outfit with lace socks and a pair of glossy Mary-Janes. A coin purse or a sculptural mini handbag in white would add the right amount of character without overdoing the character. think "in the mood for love", but slightly edgier," says Vogue India fashion associate Manglien Gangte.

article_title: Nita Ambani’s Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla sari frames lace through borders and blouse
sub_title: A lotus-shaped diamond choker and Basra pearls from her personal collection introduce a floral counterpoint to the lace
article_content: Nita Ambani wears an Abu Jani Sandeep Khosla sari from the Burano collection, a reference to the needle lace made on the island of Burano, Italy, in a pale rose-pink georgette that reads light on the body but detailed at the edges. The colour stays even across the drape, setting up the lace embroidery as the defining feature. Embellishment is concentrated along the borders, pallu edge and blouse where lace motifs are meticulously hand embroidered in silk threads with sequins and pearls. The blouse mirrors the border pattern exactly, creating a visual loop that keeps the eye moving across the look rather than settling in one place. The Burano reference draws from the island’s lace-making tradition, particularly the openwork language associated with The jewellery comes from her own collection of distinct pieces: a lotus-shaped diamond choker surrounded by Basra pearls and a Basra pearl bracelet. With the drape kept spare and the colour understated, the sari’s impact comes from where the work is placed, not how much of it appears “Re-think this dreamy pink colour in a '50s evening look. Work with a pink silk structured gown, an off-the-shoulder and cinched at the waist. Pair it with jewellery akin to Nita Ambani working with pearls and diamonds, set in a traditional Hyderabad pearl design or French style. Ditch the jewellery on the arms and opt for a high-heeled pair of pumps,” says Vogue India fashion associate Divya Balakrishnan.

Designs with elegant plaid motifs, ideal for an event or a day at work; in sophisticated shades such as brown, military green and steel grey. We will also see them in all types of outfits, from the most sophisticated to the most daring. Whether in a corporate look, with a romantic touch, librarian as in 2022 or in a modern key with tight blouses and normcore shoes. In winter they kept silent, but in summer they will be the object of desire of all, ready to make you feel attractive and spring everywhere. Louis Vuitton caught with a tailored design with a folded hem, a detail that lowers the seriousness of the garment. Isabel Marant pushes the Safari girl aesthetic through capri pants with functional pockets in military green. And Saint Laurent proposes an opaque green design in parachute fabric to face the high temperatures with style and elegance. For Spring-Summer 2026, harem pants become the competition of capri and bermuda shorts. Michael Kors adds them to his collection for the season in a vaporous fabric suitable for wearing with strappy blouses and heeled sandals. Balmain takes the style level up a notch by showing them in a satin and olive green version, ideal for creating 2000s-inspired outfits with button heels. Louis Vuitton made it clear that airy designs will be a basic to formulate minimalist or monochrome styles. Michael Kors chose XXL designs in chocolate-coloured cotton, perfect to wear in a tropical setting or simply to ornament the silhouette. Finally, Zimmermann pairs them with an elegant brown jumpsuit to look spectacular from day to night. Although everything seems to indicate that skinny pants will be the kings of the season, in reality, there is also room for baggy designs that have been on the radar for more than three (consecutive) years. Loewe, Calvin Klein, Stella McCartney, Zimmermann and Ami, to name a few, included them on their runways this season as one of the favourites. From traditional black models to electronic tones that go with the season. We will see them with elegant details such as darts, low rise, classic prints and the classic middle line that office workers love. The high waist below the ribs, which is always essential to seal an Which designs to invest in? Puddle pants in pastel shades, if it is in a suit, the better. Also in linen fabrics with a bluish dye (if you are looking for a modern garment), bootcut, cigarette and even straight. Which confirms that there is an infinity of options for every woman, the signal to take a break from the usual mini-dresses. Yes, Yes, palazzo pants - or also known as elephant leg - will define spring elegance in 2026. Celine confirmed that they can become more modern and less sober by combining them in an effortless look with sportswear and white sneakers. Ralph Lauren proposes them in a bright red sartorial ensemble with slatted espadrilles, the bold yet personality-driven outfit to keep in your favorites. Favourites to invest in? Plains in neutral tones, loud ones like solid red and even modern prints, from plaid to retro '80s stripes. What are the favourite fabrics that will go from runway to street style? Last year linen and lace dominated the streets, now it's the turn of satin pants. Ami opted for a low rise model with XL belt to play with the silhouette and build casual daytime outfits.
