It seems that everything points to leather effect pants going from fall to summer, a glamorous piece that is worth continuing to wear. Especially for those days of unpredictable weather or summer showers that appear without warning. Bottega Veneta and Versace are adding braided leather or crocodile-effect designs to give a reptile touch to the outfit. While Hermès, Ami and Zimmermann choose plain models in classic shades ranging from matte black to variations of brown.

article_title: Alaya F’s JJ Valaya ensemble puts its weight in the blouse, not the drape
sub_title: The belt cuts across the sari mid-fall, interrupting its usual vertical flow
article_content: Alaya F’s JJ Valaya sari centres its weight at the torso. The midnight-blue silk is densely worked, but it’s the velvet blouse, fully embroidered and cut with a deep neckline and open back, that establishes the look’s gravity. Instead of acting as a support act to the sari, the blouse holds visual dominance, allowing the rest of the ensemble to fall into place around it. The loosely draped pallu showcases a dense botanical jaal of delicate vines that sprout small blossoms, tendrils, and leafy motifs. This bold yet delicate contrast casts the entire ensemble in a new light. Stylist Sheefa J Gilani gives a modern spin to the traditionals by adding a gold belt to, cutting horizontally across the sari rather than pulling it inward. The placement interrupts the vertical movement of the fabric and shifts attention back to the blouse and border work, changing how the proportions of the look are read. Statement teardrop earrings from MR Jewels complement her soft-glam makeup, with subtly smoked eyes, a flush of pink “The inky indigo, the metallic embroidery and the hardware accessories together carry the statement of the look. Sharpen that mood by belting the sari a little lower, to give it that effortless low-waist feel. Amp up the gloss and add shimmery highlights to the lid to give it that dewy and soft touch to an otherwise heavy look. Keep the hair slick and straight, away from the face,” says Vogue fashion associate Manglien Gangte.

sub_title: The actor wore navratna jewellery to complement the vibrancy of her look.
article_content: Worn to a friend’s destination wedding, Khushi Kapoor’s The ivory skirt reveals a mélange of colours, featuring pinks, purples and verdant greens, woven together as varied prints and patterns. Architectural patterns sit alongside delicate Micro floral embroidery, scattered across the surface in multicoloured threads, lends a romantic delicacy to the blouse. But what elevates it is the ornate detailing at the hem and cuffs, both bejewelled bands encrusted with red and green gemstones, crystals, intricate embroidery and finishing pearl drops. The Kapoor’s stylist Mohit Rai tied the look together with a navratna choker and matching stud earrings from Golecha’s Jewels. Their pieces’ palette mirrored the gemstones on her blouse. A sleek, centre-parted bun kept the focus firmly on the craftsmanship, making it an ideal choice for festive celebrations. Her makeup stayed in sync with smoky eyes paired with nude pink lips. A multicoloured heart-shaped clutch from Doux Amour added a touch of whimsy. Ivory does not equate to pared down. A lehenga, like Kapoor’s, can become a conversation starter. With a different take on the accessories, it can transition seamlessly from a daytime beach wedding to a glam sangeet with diamonds swapped in for a fresh, after-dark edge.

article_title: Diana Penty’s red Mahima Mahajan sari finds an unexpected hasli moment
sub_title: A corset-style blouse alters the balance of the Mahima Mahajan sari, concentrating detail at the bodice and letting the drape fall uninterrupted
article_content: Diana Penty’s Mahima Mahajan sari is densely worked from edge to edge. Fine gold butti embroidery is distributed evenly across the red silk. The embroidery becomes heavier and more concentrated, marking the outline of the drape as it falls from shoulder to hem and giving the sari a clearer finish. It is paired with a corset-style blouse, hand-embroidered and cut to sit close. The shaping is visible in the seams and structure of the blouse, setting it apart from a conventional sari blouse while keeping the drape itself unchanged. By concentrating embroidery on the blouse and along the sari’s edges, the look avoids feeling scattered, even with extensive surface work. Stylist Namita Alexander accessorised Penty with a diamond choker, matching earrings and stacked bangles that sit comfortably alongside the sari’s detailing. The standout is a beige mini bag by Özel from the Özel x Mortantra collaboration. The bag is embroidered with zardozi paisley motifs and finished with metallic detailing. The handle, crafted from a traditional hasli neckpiece, gives the bag a distinct identity and ties it back to the jewellery worn with the sari. Hair is worn in loose, side-parted waves. Makeup by Séverine Perina stays warm and natural, with softly lined eyes and a neutral lip that sit comfortably alongside the richness of the sari and accessories. “Reimagine this red look for a day wandering a gallery. Ditch the heavy jewellery and pair a simple silk or georgette red and cream polka sari with a cropped blouse. Try an off-white lace blouse with a small puff sleeve for a romantic, vintage edge or a boxy crop top with reverse polka to play with pattern. Finish with simple kolhapuris or keds and pull your hair into a clean top knot,” says Vogue India's fashion associate Divya Balakrishnan.

article_title: The digital Vintage Casio watch is bending time in 2025
sub_title: From a certain NYC mayor to your style influencer cousin, simple 20th-century timepieces like Casio’s A1000MA series have become everyone’s go-to accessories.
article_content: As I stand on an uneven platform for the next train, I am presented with my current favourite fashion show—the New York subway. You can spot a fall/winter ’25 And this isn’t just a New York thing. Over the last two months, I’ve started noticing the same glint everywhere I go. In Tokyo, it’s the clear-resin variants; in Seoul, the retro golds; in Mumbai cafés, the classic F91W that refuses to retire. One September afternoon in Bandra, outside a tiny post-production studio, a filmmaking student waited for his auto wearing a block-printed kurta and a gold-toned Casio LA670. A week later in Delhi, during a quick coffee run in Meherchand Market, a If you glance around, you’ll also spot the odd Seiko Rotocall and Q Timex, but somehow, it is vintage Casio watches that are dominating the conversation. Especially, the A1000MA-7—and somehow the entire Casio Vintage family has found itself back in the cultural spotlight. History was first made with the release of the Casiotron (QW02-10) in 1974—the world’s first fully digital wristwatch with an automatic calendar—but it was never just a timekeeper. Over the years, Casio digital watches have become pop-culture fixtures, appearing everywhere from on-screen sci-fi fantasies including They remain a staple of This lineage, from the pioneering Casiotron to the cult-classic F-91W of the 1990s, leads directly to today’s A1000 models. They carry the same retro credibility and matte-metal minimalism, now elevated with polished stainless steel and a Milanese strap. It’s this blend of historic tech cool and modern refinement that makes wearing the watch both disarmingly ordinary and unexpectedly iconic. “It’s one of the few timepieces that slips into anyone’s life without demanding a costume change,” says stylist Ayesha Amin Nigam, who has been spotting them on shoots across Delhi and Mumbai. She tells me that, in the last year alone, she’s seen them on interns, models, production assistants, even accountants who wander on set in between takes. “It shapeshifts into whatever the outfit needs—grounding streetwear, sharpening suiting or sitting quietly against a The variants alone could fill a moodboard: the brushed-steel A1000MA, its gold-toned MG counterpart, the pastel-tinted MPR editions, the ultra-slim LA670s, and even the resin-cased F-series that collectors love for its purist ’80s silhouette. And unlike many vintage icons, most of these models are still in production and available directly at brand stores, while a handful of discontinued colourways and older A1000 batches quietly trade hands on resale platforms like My Almari and Luxepolis for those seeking a deeper There is another reality that also exists: Christie’s Geneva Luxury Week reported sales of 21,641,435 Swiss francs (approximately ₹242 crores) in rare watches, with a significant 34% of the bidders being millennials and Gen Z’ers. If younger consumers are willing to spend big at auction, why are modest, sub-₹20,000 digital Casios suddenly the cultural touchstone? Part of the answer lies in accessibility, nostalgia and the social currency of effortless style. “Casio democratised digital timekeeping long before it was fashionable,” explains Sarosh Mody, founder of Luxury Watch Works, an after-sales boutique based in Mumbai. “The G-Shock, for example, became—and remains—a cultural icon. Its popularity reflects the people’s choice, not marketing, not snob value. Casio understood utility decades before smartwatches were conceived. The calculator, TV, radio and camera watches were made by them way before the Swiss even thought about them. The brand has blurred the line between Today, reissues and collaborations like the Timex T80 x Maison Margiela and Omega x Swatch drops show that design credibility doesn’t need a luxury price tag. Together, these watches have become a global shorthand for personality, nostalgia and style that crosses generations and geographies. And style icons and collectors continue the trend: Casio watches were a mainstay of But why this watch and why now? I suspect that it’s because it is fundamentally reminiscent of a simpler time. The only complication in the watch is an alarm, just like the one you would wear in school, beeping at the end of an exam. It’s something you perhaps spotted on your father back in the day, and till today, it rings a bell. A personal connection in your wardrobe that tells a story: perhaps that’s the ultimate style flex.

article_title: Tara Sutaria’s floral skirt set is a comfortable alternative to heavy lehengas
sub_title: The actor went the minimal route to accessorise her Gauri & Nainika look
article_content: For her intimate Christmas celebrations at home, Tara Sutaria chose a look that straddled intimacy with high drama. Though technically a modern co-ord set, Sutaria’s look by Gauri & Nainika reads as something far more versatile. Inching towards a compelling alternative to an ornate lehenga, it appears equally suited to a destination wedding soirée where modernity is prized as much as tradition. At first glance, the ensemble feels like a modern-day lehenga reimagined through a contemporary lens. Comprising a high-waisted, billowing, floor-grazing skirt and a sculpted bralette, the set is lifted by painterly florals that bloom against a noir base. The ensemble is drawn from Gauri & Nainika’s Lakmē Fashion Week x FDCI Spring–Summer 2026 showcase, where the designer duo unveiled a collection rooted in wearable artistry. Inspired by painted canvases, dark roses and moody still lifes, the line translated romance into tactile form using organza, tulle and silk mikado, shaping silhouettes defined by volume, bows, ruffles and drama. On Sutaria, these themes distilled into a maximalist floral piece that felt opulent and of-the-moment. Black punctuated with bold florals has long held fashion’s imagination, from the late '30s’ bias-cut evening gowns to the lacquered rose prints of the ‘50s. This lineage is mirrored on her look. The high-waisted skirt elongates the frame, offering a sleek, cinched foundation, while the bralette’s open back introduces a sensual counterpoint. A sleek, centre-parted bun was adorned with red roses, complemented by a deep crimson lip, together conjuring a Frida Kahlo-esque romanticism. A pair of drop chandelier earrings added the final flourish, letting the noir florals take centre stage. With thoughtful styling, a skirt set, like hers, can seamlessly shift from a formal evening affair to a festive sangeet night. Swap the diamonds for polkis, dial up the drama with the makeup and you have a versatile statement that can be reworked and returned to, time and again.

sub_title: The entrepreneur wore statement polki pieces to style her look
article_content: What’s old is new again and Navya Nanda echoed that sentiment in a multi-hued lehenga by Mayyur Girotra that felt less like occasion wear and more like a cherished inheritance brought back to life. A pale gold tissue silk lehenga serves as the canvas of the look. As the New Delhi-based designer explains, “Navya Nanda wears Mayyur Girotra gold tissue silk signature lehenga. The skirt is paired with a vintage brocade blouse, which is intricately hand-embroidered in zardozi and tilla that is inspired by archival motifs. From the fabric to craft, it carries stories of the past into the present.” The time-honoured designs hark towards patterns that once adorned bridal trunks and temple textiles. The delicate craftsmanship techniques add depth and just the right dose of opulence. What animates the ensemble is the blouse. A multi-coloured counterpoint to the otherwise pared-back, neutral-coloured lehenga. Rendered in multiple hues and finished with vintage brocade, it brings a burst of colour and personality to the look. The plunging V neckline lends a contemporary edge, while the half sleeves, colour-blocked with heritage textiles and artisanal crafts, ground it in tradition. It is this interplay of textiles and techniques that makes the outfit feel polygonal, present and perennial. Nanda’s styling follows the same time-honoured philosophy. She went with soft, understated makeup in old rose tones along with open hair for glam. Jewellery, however, made a statement. She opted for a bold choker set and earrings from Shri Paramani Jewels, echoing the old-world mood of the lehenga. “This exquisite set features handcrafted chandbaali earrings adorned with luminous diamond polki, delicately shaped to reflect timeless artistry and regal charm. Paired with a premium diamond polki choker, the neckpiece showcases superior craftsmanship, rich detailing and a graceful silhouette that sits beautifully on the neckline,” reveals Vinay Gupta, founder, Shri Paramani Jewellers.

article_title: Bhumi Pednekkar aces Regencycore in a pastel Shehla Khan lehenga
sub_title: The actor’s lavender ensemble draws from period references and remains rooted in Indian occasion wear
article_content: For a friend’s destination wedding, Bhumi Pednekkar championed Regency era romance in a pastel lehenga. Part of Shehla Khan's latest couture collection, her ensemble felt like it had been pulled directly from the pages of a True to the collection's title, Romance Reimagined, Khan revisits the codes that first defined her eponymous label. “The idea behind each look of this collection was to go back to the original aesthetic of the brand. The textures, soft prints and intricate detailing come together to create unique and feminine styles that can be worn through years and seasons,” reveals Khan. A soft lavender print of large roses is emblazoned across a fluid lehenga skirt. “This lehenga skirt is paired with a bustier style blouse inspired by the romance of Victorian style with a lingerie-esque detail and embroidered buttons.” The blouse, with its scalloped lace neckline, structured printed cups, sensual open back and delicate buttons, brings corsetry codes into the Indian occasion conversation without feeling costume-driven. Puffed sleeves in sheer lace lend volume at the shoulder, further reinstating Regency silhouettes. “The dupatta, which is coordinated with the print of the lehenga and lace of the blouse, amplifies its lightness and adds the traditional touch,” adds Khan. Pednekkar’s stylist, Nidhi Jeswani, accessorised her look with a pair of chandbali earrings and a ring from Shri Paramani Jewels. Pednekkar braided her hair with lace trims, reinforcing the romantic mood. Regency era style romanticises femininity through flirty florals, fine trims and floaty silhouettes. In recent seasons, designers and celebrities have embraced these elements, translating historical cues into modern wardrobes. Pednekkar’s lehenga interpretation demonstrates how those references can be seamlessly adapted into Indian festive dressing.

article_title: Femininity, functionality, sensuality: Maria Grazia Chiuri on her return to Fendi
sub_title: Maria Grazia Chiuri was announced Chief Creative Officer of Fendi six months after her exit from Dior. It's where she began her career in 1989.
article_content: Staring down the barrel of Maria Grazia Chiuri’s kohl-framed gaze, I feel suddenly uneasy. “Designers who are men can do womenswear,” she says with heavy irony. “But designers who are women cannot do menswear.” I’ve just delivered a question about what will, in June, be her first menswear show as Warming up, she raises an eyebrow, smiles, and leans forward. “Because geniuses are only men! Creative people, only men!” She pauses, as if to consider: “ What about Wait. What about Chiuri’s own record of changemaking? In 2016 she became Christian Dior’s first-ever female Creative Director (of womenswear, haute couture, and accessories, but not menswear). Over the next nine years her feminocentric, feminist, collaborative approach to design and storytelling at the French house surely changed that discourse: because while yes, her collections sometimes divided the critics, they nearly always entranced the clients. And along the way, by the way, she close-to quadrupled revenues. “Yes, and everybody remembers me because I did the big number in Dior! When a male designer does a big number, [it is because] he has a sense of business. But if a woman designer does a big number, it is because she is In the face of friendly fire, it’s time to deflect. Let’s bring it back to Fendi, where Chiuri was announced Chief Creative Officer last October, six months after her departure from Dior. Fendi is where, aged 24, Chiuri takes control. “The Fendi sisters too. Everybody speaks only about Karl Lagerfeld, like they did nothing. I’m sorry, eh.” She laughs a full laugh, and the balloon is punctured. “I’m sorry eh! Boring possibly, but also tangibly true: just run a comparison of the number of female creative directors in top fashion houses as compared to male. And as Chiuri says, however, that she has not rejoined Fendi to prove any personal point. “I’m here to give back what they gave to me.” She adds: “I worked here for a long time, in another time, when fashion was completely different. This was a very small company, a family company. I learned so much at Fendi. I think for my generation it was incredible to work with the founders.” She is still full of admiration for the Fendi sisters, under whom she worked so long. “These were five women from Rome who called Karl Lagerfeld in Paris, before he was at Chanel, in 1965. I think that was not so normal, to maintain your tradition and background but at the same time to have a conversation with someone who is completely innovative and from a completely different camp. They were great visionaries.” Chiuri departed Fendi in 1999, shortly before it was acquired by LVMH. She left with Nearly 30 years after leaving it, the Fendi she has returned to, she says: “is different like all the brands today are different. The organization is different and the dimensions are different. And when I left, Fendi was a family company.” Which is not to say, of course, that the culture of Fendi’s present owner LVMH is unfamiliar to her: Dior is one of its subsidiaries, and leading that great French house for so long has given her another layer of experience and learning. Now the sum of all her experience is being applied to shaping a new phase for Fendi. Her arrival, she believes, coincides with the dawn of a broader period of evolution in the luxury fashion arena. “We are moving into another moment. I think the big impact in this system was about the new media. Everybody started to speak about fashion. Because fashion became more popular, there were not only the journalists and the people that know about fashion speaking about fashion. The impact of all these voices was very strong, but not all the time positive. I think part of it became an entertainment. But in the end, it [fashion] is not that.” She continues: “I think we have an idea that is more the narrative of this job, and less the reality of this job. Sometimes the narrative is that you [the designer] are there, like a light from the sky, and you just make a sketch… The reality is more complex. It is really teamwork. There are so many different technical skills.” But doesn’t she acknowledge that this complexity, even if true, is challenging to digest for those who prefer to enjoy the fantasy and image of fashion? “Yes. And we arrive at a point that could be more crucial to have a name for something, or a narrative, and you don’t see if someone Tomorrow’s fall 2026 show in Milan will be the first opportunity to transmit the energy of Chiuri’s new formula of desire at Fendi outside the closed circuit of her team. Asked to sell the essence of that formula, Chiuri again raises an eyebrow. “I am probably not a good seller! But I synthesize my vision for Fendi in this show. In the silhouette. In the accessories. In the shoes. For women and for men also—there will be some men in the show too, absolutely, because we did the collections together. I work in parallel with the two teams like they are the same team.” As previously established, however, Chiuri will also present a show during the menswear week in June. What about the accessories, traditionally alongside fur the core of the house’s offer? “Accessories are very important. We are working on every single category: sunglasses, jewelry, everything. I am trying to define all the iconic elements of the house and to put them all in order, these codes. This is very important. Sometimes—and not just for Fendi—the idea to communicate Chiuri says she is moving away from the recent orthodoxy to use branding as decoration through monograms, to return instead towards presenting a range of embroidered and other applied materials that can reflect the individual personalities of the clients. She says, “that was part of the story with the Baguette and the Peekaboo too.” She adds: “The logo is a signature. It is not decorative.” In order to clarify that signature, she recruited Leonardo Sonnoli to “renovate” the house Double-F logo and font. “I think we have to use it only with products that are right for the logo,” she adds: “not for all.” Instead of via the branding of its logo, Chiuri plans for Fendi to communicate itself through the substance of its silhouette. “Because I think we are now working in another time in the fashion industry, my point of view is very focused on the silhouette. It is important to define the silhouette of Fendi. And really that is the silhouette of the coat. The coat, the jacket. That is my job. And also what kind of women and men are the references.” Before Fendi became so famous for its accessories (an achievement of which Chiuri was a part) it was most renowned for the sophistication and richness of its furs. These were predominantly worn as coats and jackets. Each Fendi sister was responsible for a different element of their development and presentation, and Chiuri considered the core characteristics of the sisters while shaping this new silhouette. She says, “the reference is the sisters. They were very creative, but also pragmatic: they worked. So the way they were was very… functional. Then sensuality is very important also, because the element of fur is about something soft, light, and very close to sensuality. For Fendi, fur and feeling are the same.” To hear Chiuri mention fur unprompted is something of a surprise. While the house has never ceased producing its In 2021, during his four year period as Fendi’s Artistic Director of ready-to-wear, Kim Jones began showing couture beyond fourrure in Paris. Chiuri indicates she plans to continue it, without disclosing exactly when. She says, “It’s not possible to define everything at the beginning. You have to go step by step. I really want to do couture, but only when we are ready. Because it is very important to work on the global project, and the global vision. I’m happy because this first collection is the first step.” Another key step will be the simultaneous release of Chiuri’s first campaign for the house created with Jo Ann Callis, an artist whose lens of subversive honesty and self-possession seems finely aligned with that of the designer. These steps begin a journey Chiuri had neither any obligation nor need to embark upon. We are speaking in the Teatro della Cometa, the jewel-like 1950s theatre at the foot of Rome’s Capitoline hill that Chiuri bought and “For me Fendi is very important,” she says, and repeats: “so it’s very important to give back what they gave to me.” Then she leans forward again, gaze fixed. “Between us, I really have love for all the fashion brands. Not only Fendi. I really Before luxury’s recruitment consultants reach en masse for their phones, there is no doubt that for the foreseeable future Chiuri’s studies will remain solely focused upon the founders she knows most intimately: the Fendis. Chiuri demurs at the suggestion that her work ahead might also contain some autobiographical elements, drawn from her memories of arriving here for her first job, aged 24. “It’s difficult for me now to see myself then,” she says, shaking her head. And yet comparing her conversation today with her characterization of the sisters—as creatively imaginative yet pragmatically orderly, as hard-working yet passionate—suggests powerfully that Fendi’s new phase will also hew true to the soul of Maria Grazia Chiuri.

article_content: Returning to Chennai after more than a year away was a visceral shock to the system. I expected the familiar embrace of home; I didn’t expect the air to feel like a convection oven. We all know the "drink more water and We spoke to the experts to break down how to pivot your routine when the heat cranks up. It comes down to thermoregulation. When the air is hotter than your body, your skin relies almost entirely on evaporation to stay cool. "For every degree's rise in skin temperature, sebum production can increase by approximately 10%," explains Dr Kiran Sethi, skin and longevity doctor. This surge in oil, mixed with sweat and dead skin cells creates a ‘pore-clogging cocktail’ that leads to the dreaded trifecta: When your face feels like a slip-and-slide, the first instinct is to scrub. article_content: Fibre is, as we know, everywhere right now: in wellness advice, on supermarket shelves and in almost every conversation about digestion. But knowing how much fibre your body actually needs, regardless of all the noise around it, is paramount. Most people still do not know how much fibre they should actually be eating in a day or what getting enough of it even looks like in practice. That confusion can turn into a nightmare, especially when fibre is easy to underconsume and just as easy to overdo too quickly. Patel says the clearest signs of low fibre intake include low stool volume, feeling hungry again soon after eating, unsustainable energy, chronic constipation and over time, metabolic dysfunction. In other words, if your meals look healthy but never quite satisfy you, fibre may be the missing piece. The But fibre needs are not identical across the board. People who are taller, more active or simply Then comes the part most wellness advice skips: tolerance. Mayo Clinic and NHS guidance both stress increasing fibre gradually and pairing it with enough water, since fibre works best when it absorbs fluid. A more realistic way to assess your own needs is to ask three things: 1. Are you eating mostly refined carbs and protein, with very little fruit, vegetables, legumes or So the real guideline is this: use 25–30 grams as the general target, adjust upwards if you eat more, and let your gut set the pace. More fibre is not always better, at least not immediately. According to sports nutritionist and integrative health coach Nicole Linhares Kedia, people with IBS, chronic constipation, colorectal polyps or sensitive guts may need to personalise their intake rather than suddenly overload on bran, seeds or raw salads. Fibre also needs water to move properly through the gut. Without enough fluids, it can make constipation and bloating worse. The best sources are probably already in your household pantry: lentils, chickpeas, “All fibre is created equal” is one of the biggest myths around it, says Linhares Kedia. An oval face can be defined as one where your face length is bigger than the width of your cheekbones and your forehead is wider than your jawline, says Martin. article_title: How to wear the '90s bob hairstyle in 2026, according to pros
sub_title: A bob haircut has always been in style and the triumphant return of the '90s bob hairstyle proves just that
article_content: The '90s bob will always have a special place in the haircut hall of fame and it’s easy to see why it’s having a revival in 2026. Whether you’re rewatching “The bob is one of those timeless cuts that always comes back around. It just gets reinterpreted,” says Chris McMillan, the celebrity stylist behind Jennifer Aniston’s decade-defining haircut, the Rachel. “Right now people want hair that feels easy but still polished and the '90s bob does exactly that,” McMillan tells us. “It can be worn sleek and tucked, flipped, messy or even really textured and scrunched. It’s versatile, low effort and modern.” Tempted to try out the throwback cut for yourself? Ahead, expert stylists break down everything you need to know about the look. Also called the flipped bob or “flob,” the '90s bob combines the texture and volume of a bombshell blowout with the short length, movement and manageability of a bob. So while the look is (obviously) incredibly chic, it’s practical too. “The ’90s-supermodel bob has the line and length of the bob, but the top layers have much more texture, so it’s lighter on top and easier to flip around,” celebrity hairstylist Marc Mena says. This cut trends a little longer than other “I always tell people to focus on length first, because that’s really where the ’90s bob lives,” McMillan says. “It’s that in-between zone: not too short, not too long—what we now call the lob. Think super classic references like Christy Turlington.” For this cut, it’s all about the layers. “You want soft structure with movement, nothing too blunt or heavy,” McMillan says. “I also love adding in a side part or even a soft swoop bang to give it that effortless, undone feel.” Unlike a standard blunt bob, which demands consistency and precision when styling, the ’90s bob has versatility baked into its construction. “Flipping your hair can feel really heavy with a regular bob since it’s cut with no part, but the ‘flob’ is cut and parted all around: in the middle, on the left and then the right. So the ends are just texturised and it gives the To preserve fullness in the ends (a crucial component to the cut) Mena says barely there layers are key. “The layers are so light and blended you don’t actually see a layer,” he says. So be sure to request light layers at the salon. If the top is too heavy, it won’t flip, which is a key component of the look. A few washday considerations can ensure your ’90s-supermodel bob has all that va-va-volume from the get-go. Start by switching to a volumising shampoo and conditioner and apply conditioner only to the ends. “I don’t like to condition roots, especially with the flob,” Mena says. “Just a little bit on the ends goes a long way.” Next, Mena advises applying mousse to wet hair. Don’t skip the “A great blow-dry is everything for this look,” McMillan says. “You need a big round brush to get that subtle curl under at the ends and a really good prep product like a glassy blow-dry spray to smooth and polish the hair.” Since the haircut is designed to be flipped around, try blow-drying from different angles and parts to create Speaking of hair rollers, they can really take this look over the top when you have a little extra styling time. “Use a To lock in the style while keeping things soft, Mena suggests spraying texturising spray on your roots and some light, flexible hairspray all over to complete the look. “I always end with a lightweight oil to add shine and break up the finish a bit,” McMillan says. The good news? Without too much length dragging down your volume, the effort you pour into your blowout will actually last. “You can style your flippy bob one day and then the next day, when you wake up, just reset it at the top and it’s right back to where you started,” Mena says.

article_title: Someone needs to tell Gen Z men that foreplay is not optional
sub_title: A PSA for men who keep skipping the best part of the song
article_content: I first realised this was not just one rogue bad date or a stray complaint from an unlucky friend when my girl group chat had a string of unsatisfactory one-night stands, detailed over post-date debriefs. I brought it up with a few cousins, who then told me about their friends (all anonymously, of course) and a pattern quickly emerged: men who could talk about boundaries, vulnerability and emotional availability at length seemed to lose all nuance the second intimacy became physical. One 22-year-old stylist told me about a man who spent an entire week being achingly attentive over text, remembering details, flirting well, building anticipation—only to kiss her for all of 20 seconds before lunging ahead like he was late for a train. Another 24-year-old founder described being with someone who kept asking if she was ‘comfortable’ mechanically, but never paused long enough to notice that comfort and pleasure are not, in fact, the same thing. An alarming number of For women, desire does not arrive like a food delivery. It is a slower seduction of the senses. The kiss that lingers just long enough to alter the atmosphere. The hand at the waist that does not immediately start fumbling around like it is searching for lost keys. The Leeza Mangaldas, sexuality educator and co-founder of Leezu’s, puts it perfectly: “Dating apps have trained us to move fast and feel little.” That speed, she says, “leaks into sex,” creating a dynamic where people think, Heterosexual sex still suffers from an old branding problem. We keep calling the acts women most reliably enjoy ‘foreplay’, as though kissing, oral, hands, slow touch and clitoral stimulation are merely there to break the ice. Mangaldas is far blunter: “Foreplay is not a formality. It is essential.” In fact, the acts routinely relegated to prelude are, for many women, central to There is no universal minimum dose here, at least not in minutes. Rao says the more useful benchmark is readiness: “It's about recognising signs that the body has actually relaxed into the moment: shoulders dropping, the back unclenching, the mind becoming more present. The point is not to hit a certain timeline, but to notice whether someone seems genuinely settled enough to enjoy what is happening." To be fair, rushed foreplay is not always straightforward selfishness. Sometimes it is nerves or insecurities. Men worry about performance and speed up, conditioned by what they have seen in porn. But Rao is careful not to reduce this entirely to individual failure. She does not think Gen Z sexuality is defined by one neat set of mistakes so much as shaped by a culture that has given young people a huge amount of information with very little guidance. “Many have absorbed the language of sex positivity, consent and experimentation online, while receiving far less real-life support in how to actually inhabit those ideas in their own bodies. The result, she says, is that sex can start to feel like a checklist of what is ‘said’ to be right rather than something felt in real time," she adds. Perhaps both sides could use a better script. Rao suggests ways to slow down if you notice things are going too quickly: "Pause the touching, take a step back, really look at your partner, offer a genuine physical compliment, hold eye contact a little longer, whisper something flirty. If you keep working on your flirting game, there’s plenty of ways to make a moment sultry.” Women are often socialised to avoid ‘ruining the mood’ by giving direction, when in reality a well-timed “slower” or “I like it when you…” is not awkward but clarifying. Men, meanwhile, need to stop treating feedback like a performance review and start treating it like useful information. Read. Ask. Learn basic anatomy. Tacking on a cup of Yoghurt Regardless of the exact protein content, Peruvemba recommends pairing yoghurt with other foods, since protein and fats are really all it has to offer, tasty as it may be. Including fibre and complex Vegetables in general don’t serve up much in the way of protein, says Harbstreet. article_title: How to style thick hair, according to pro stylists
sub_title: Expert tips for thick hair to control volume, boost lasting hold and achieve smooth, frizz-free shine
article_content: Your super-dense hair may make you the envy of the salon but learning how to style thick hair isn’t always easy. Fullness and body may come naturally, but so can long drying times, tangles and frizz. Luckily, there are measures you can take to make Whether you’re blowing out your thick hair, curling, straightening or enhancing your natural texture, the right products are key. “I’d say a good styling cream or pomade, a smoothing serum for frizz and a heat protectant are essentials,” says Lia Hakim, a hairstylist and founder of Hott Salons. “A lightweight texturising spray is also great for adding movement without weighing the hair down.” Of course, no style looks its best without proper consideration for your hair health. “Thick hair’s support needs are taken into account, but often moisture is overlooked. Leave-in conditioners are great for this reason,” says Philip Downing, creative director and hairstylist at Bed Head. Ready to upgrade your thick No matter how you choose to style your thick hair, certain washday considerations will make your whole process smoother. “Use a hydrating shampoo and conditioner to keep it soft and manageable,” Hakim says. “Detangle while it’s wet with a wide-tooth comb or detangling brush, because the bristles move with hair and won’t cause as much breakage.” Since thick hair is naturally heavier, you may find it more difficult to make your styles hold all day. But the secret to maintaining shape isn’t just in your finishing products: “Starting on slightly damp hair, use a heat protectant and a styling cream, then blow-dry. This will hold the style well,” Hakim says. “I love this trick especially for a bouncy blowout.” Puffiness, frizz and tangles are also common concerns when styling thick hair. To keep things smooth, Hakim says that working in smaller sections when detangling and styling goes a long way. So the key to reducing frizz always comes back to hydration and moisture balance,” says Julissa Prado, CEO and founder of Rizos Curls. Make sure you’re using a sulphate-free shampoo and try adding a weekly hydrating hair mask or a leave-in that’s tailored to your texture. It can usually handle heavy-duty protection products without being weighed down. article_title: Haircare’s hot new collab: KATSEYE is all about hair that keeps up with them

article_content: Maybe you are someone with bouncy curls, luscious waves, love experimenting with hair colours and highlights, or just looking for frizz-free solutions—Matrix has products that work for everyone. These products have been a staple on salon as well as personal vanity shelves, and today, the brand brings on the global girl group KATSEYE as their new brand ambassadors—a perfect fit for the brand’s vibrant and youthful personality. Composed of six members coming from varying ethnicities and orientations, the band’s K-pop-inspired choreographies and high-octane performances have led to their rapid popularity, turning them into social media sensations and earning them a spot at the 2026 Grammys, too. The fit was natural. On one hand, there’s Matrix—a professional haircare and colour brand that has built its reputation on delivering high-performance results across all hair types. On the other, KATSEYE; a group that represents a different kind of performance—bringing together individuality, diversity and self-expression. Put them together and you have a rare cultural moment—one that not only embraces inclusivity but celebrates it. It is when you stand in front of the mirror—the clock ticking rapidly in the background—trying to coax your hair into something presentable, that you are reminded of days when your hair behaved exactly the way you wanted it to. Because so much rides on it. Your mood, the perfect Instagram story, the trajectory of your day, the first impression you make at your first big girl job. Stepping into adulthood is stressful as it is and worrying about your hair shouldn’t add to it. Matrix is determined to help with that. For KATSEYE, hair has always been an integral part of their energetic choreographies. Celebrating this exact idea is Matrix Moves, the global brand campaign starring the band. Helmed by director Cody Critcheloe, the campaign film coins the term ‘hairography’—a concept that is centered around hair being a catalyst of movement and self-expression. The visuals are fun and aesthetically pleasing; a mix of the band’s kinetic vibe and Matrix’s signature vibrant style. Each member of the pop band brings her own take on style, texture and personality, and that plays out beautifully across the campaign’s signature looks. Among them is Lara Raj, the group’s Indian-origin member, who showcases ‘The Sleek Swerve’—a look powered by one of Matrix’s most-loved ranges in India: Mega Smooth. If there’s one thing most of us can agree on, it’s this—the humidity in our country has a mind of its own. And more often than not, it affects our hair the most. That’s where the Mega Smooth range comes in. A fan favourite, it’s trusted for its ability to control frizz, smoothen hair and keep it glossy without weighing it down. At the end of the day, it’s about hair that looks good, feels good and stays that way no matter what the day throws at you—be it a packed Google calendar, a last-minute social plan or, in KATSEYE’s case, a full-blown performance.

sub_title: From restoring day-two hair to shampooing correctly, these easy hair hacks have totally transformed how I care for my hair
article_content: Growing up, I had honey Looking back, this transformation was the start of my hair obsession. You name a hair hack, I’ve tried it: I straightened my hair with a clothing iron when I didn’t have a flatiron; I dyed my hair red, chestnut brown and black and naturally, I once cut my own bangs. I’ve put my hair through a lot in chasing that good-hair-day feeling. Fortunately, throughout my career, I’ve met many hair experts who have helped bring my strands back to life. From restoring day-two hair to shampooing correctly, I’ve learned several easier-than-ever tricks that have totally transformed the way I care for my hair: enhancing my daily shine, texture, vibrancy and gloss. Below are the best hair hacks I’ve collected to make every day a good hair day. Straight out of the shower without any styling, my hair dries pretty lifeless and flat with no waves in sight. I’ve found that the perfect cocktail of products creates natural-looking waves, but unfortunately, by day two, it’s back to square one. While I would generally reach for a waver or curling iron for added volume, celebrity hairstylist and founder of Rōz hair care, Mara Roszak, gave me a hack to revive those textured waves: mix “My go-to ratio is about three to four pumps of leave-in to roughly 30ml of water,” explains Roszak. “You want it concentrated enough that your hair can drink up the weightless hydration, which helps bring life back to second-day hair.” To further zhuzh, Roszak says, reach for a root-texturising mist and apply it directly at the roots, then use creaseless clips to hold it in place. Not only does it extend the life of my hairstyle, but it also keeps my hair hydrated and I quit using dry shampoo for a long time because I felt it almost suffocated my hair (leaving it dry and straw-like), until I discovered dry-shampoo powder. Though this worked better at first, it didn’t solve my dryness issue. Soon after, I ended up on a Zoom call with celebrity hairstylist Sarah Hindsgaul—the pro behind the entire cast’s hair on the set of I’ve started applying it only on the spots that get particularly oily with a puff: behind my ears, at my hairline and along my part. The result? Perfectly tousled, fresh-feeling hair that doesn’t feel dry As a celebrity hairstylist and creative director at Virtue Labs, Adir Abergel has a knack for knowing what really works. With my fine, thin, colour-treated hair, there’s always a chance a product leaves my hair with an oily spot or heaviness that instantly makes me want to wash it out. But this simple tip from Abergel was a total game changer: “Smooth leave-in conditioner all over your hands, like a hand cream, then run it through your hair with your fingers,” he said. “That way, the product is distributed evenly and smoothly.” It sounds so simple, but since I started doing it this way, I haven’t had a concentrated greasy spot. This all but ensures I’m light-handed with my leave-in conditioner or The Meche Salon founder, Tracey Cunningham, gave me one of the best hair hacks that also works as a colour-preservation tip: protect your hair like you would your skin. “Your hair can’t do colour-changing tricks on its own,” Cunnigham told me. “So if it’s all of a sudden turning orange or green, it’s likely due to mineral buildup.” Some main mineral culprits: calcium can make hair appear darker; magnesium (combined with calcium) can create limescale that sticks to hair, messing with your texture; iron can cause unwanted brassiness and copper can oxidise and build up in the hair shaft, turning blonde hair shades of green. Her fix involved two parts. First, Cunningham suggests a shower head filter to help reduce the effects of minerals on your hair at home. This was actually a lifesaver for my hair, especially after moving to Austin (my hair had to adjust to the hard water). The second part applies to anytime you’re in a chlorinated pool, out in the sun or in the ocean. Because sunscreen for hair is not common, Cunningham tells clients to apply oil when it’s dry and put it up before swimming. Because hair is absorbent, like a sponge, it can absorb everything, including minerals that can change hair colour or texture. For example, the high salt concentration in seawater can strip hair of its natural oils, leading to dryness, breakage and colour fade. By applying an oil or mask first, your hair absorbs less of the harsh water. I never go to the beach without hair oil now; immediately, I noticed how much easier it was to brush out snarls or tangles after a pool or ocean swim. Over time, I realised it helped keep my highlights brighter and more vibrant longer, extending the time between colouring appointments. Celebrity hairstylist and founder of Iles Formula, Wendy Iles, tells me that the secret to bouncy hair is in the shampoo. She explained that to create a richer lather, improve shampoo distribution and avoid product buildup on my scalp, you need to add more water while using a sulphate-free shampoo, not more shampoo. Sulphate-free shampoos, she says, behave very differently from conventional formulas. “They are formulated with gentler surfactants that need both water and air to cleanse properly,” Iles says. “The air coming through the massage creates a soft, cushiony lather. If rushed or if the shampoo lather isn’t fully developed or rinsed away, even the most beautiful sulphate-free formulas can leave a slight heaviness.” In my experience, not only does this create a frothy lather that evenly coats and cleanses my entire scalp, but it also doesn’t strip my hair of its natural oils. The result is hair that feels clean but still silky and nourished. The underrated bonus is that I don’t go through shampoo as quickly now! article_title: How to treat rosacea on brown skin, according to dermatologists
sub_title: The signs to watch for, triggers that can worsen it and treatments that can help
article_content: For something so common, rosacea still has a remarkably good disguise. It is usually pictured in one particular way: visible redness, light skintone, flushed cheeks, a face announcing its distress. It's far more confusing on melanin-rich skin. The tenderness, stinging and bumps are there. What may not be there, at least not in the way we imagine it, is obvious redness. That misunderstanding changes the way people treat it. Skin gets labelled “reactive” or “sensitive” in the abstract, treated like acne or exfoliated into submission. We loaded up on products meant to fix texture or unclog pores, while the real issue keeps simmering underneath. Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory condition, shaped by a mix of genetics, immune response and environmental triggers, with symptoms that can include flushing, papules, pustules, visible vessels and eye irritation. “Your genetics predetermine whether you have rosacea–that’s the number one reason you get it,” dermatologist Dr Emma Craythorne That split between predisposition and provocation is part of what makes rosacea so maddening. The condition may be wired in, but it is often activated and aggravated by the habits of everyday life: heat, ultraviolet radiation, spicy food, alcohol, stress, vigorous exercise and irritating skincare. “Rosacea in deeper skin tones is less likely to be immediately identified because the colour cues are subtler,” says dermatologist and cosmetic formulator Dr Kavitha Arya. “Patients often describe burning, warmth, tenderness or breakouts that never quite look or behave like ‘typical’ acne. There is faint redness, but discoloration can also be more purple-toned." People spend months treating the wrong issue. If the skin is hot, reactive and bumpy, the instinct is often to reach for stronger acne products, exfoliating acids or foaming cleansers that promise to reset things. In practice, that can leave inflamed skin even more irritated. Rosacea can overlap with acne, seborrhoeic dermatitis, contact dermatitis and, in some cases, autoimmune conditions that need to be ruled out. Which is why the best treatment plan usually starts not with a miracle product but with some notes and a professional read of what the skin is actually doing. Dermatologists diagnose rosacea by examining the skin and eyes, asking questions about symptoms and triggers and, where needed, testing to exclude other conditions. Craythorne That immune reactivity is also why so many people with rosacea say their skin hates everything. Inflamed skin has a much lower tolerance for friction, fragrance, strong surfactants and strong exfoliants. Craythorne also name-checks demodex mites, which live in the skin’s sebaceous glands, as an inflammatory problem for those with rosacea. Once rosacea on brown skin is identified, treatment tends to be less flashy than the average skincare routine. Gentle cleanser, a plain moisturiser and daily sunscreen alongside medication tailored to the person's needs. “Topical prescriptions such as azelaic acid, metronidazole and ivermectin are among the standard options,” says Arya. “Treatment has to account not only for inflammation but for the pigment aftermath,” says Arya. “One-size-fits-all rosacea routines often fall short. You are treating the flare-up, but you are also trying not to create another problem while you do it.” Laser therapy can reduce rosacea-related colour changes, including the violet or brown-toned changes seen in darker skin, though energy-based treatment in skin of colour requires thoughtful device selection done by the right hands because of the risk of pigmentary change. For people with brown skin, the problem is not only rosacea itself but the lag between having it and having it recognised. When the condition is still largely imagined in one shade range, everyone else is left translating their symptoms alone.

article_title: How to choose between soluble and insoluble fibre for your body
sub_title: Both infamous fibre types support digestive health, just in different and contrasting ways for your gut
article_content: Most people are well aware that fibre is a nutrient we want to eat enough of. Fewer know that there are two distinct types: soluble fibre and insoluble fibre. Both play different but equally valuable roles in your body. Does In an effort to give fibre its full due, we broke it all down with the help of a few Fibre, sometimes called dietary fibre, is a type of carbohydrate found in plant foods. Its structure is formed by a bunch of sugar molecules, bound together in a way that makes it hard to readily break down and use as energy. The small intestine can’t digest fibre in the same way as other Lots of kinds of plants. Nearly all plant foods (which include vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, Where both types of fibre don’t always show up is in fibre supplements (like psyllium husk products) and fibre-fortified foods (like high-fibre Soluble fibre is fibre that is able to dissolve in water. While there are “typically fewer rich sources of soluble fibre in our food supply than insoluble fibre,” Desiree Nielsen, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, explains, you probably still have plenty of decent options sitting in your pantry. Soluble fibre is found in grains (like barley and oats), legumes (like beans, lentils and peas), seeds (like flaxseeds and chia seeds), nuts (like peanuts and macadamia nuts) and some When you eat these foods, the soluble fibre pulls in and swells up with water in the stomach, partially dissolving to form a thick gel-like substance that slows down Quite a bit. Because of its ability to decelerate digestion, soluble fibre has a knack for slowing or lessening the absorption of several substances that can have negative effects on our health if they build up too fast or rise too high. For instance, soluble fibre puts the brakes on the rate at which carbohydrates enter into the bloodstream, according to the FDA, which helps prevent spikes in blood glucose (blood sugar) after eating. “It’s going to ‘trap’ sugar molecules so that they’re absorbed more slowly, which is helpful for keeping blood sugar levels more regular,” Linsenmeyer explains. If you drink a glass of pure orange juice, for instance, that sugar gets metabolised pretty much immediately, causing your blood sugar to climb rapidly. But if you eat a whole orange, which contains soluble fibre, the sugar uptake is more gradual, Linsenmeyer says. This is helpful for anyone trying to maintain steady Soluble fibre also has a regulatory effect on the absorption of dietary fat and cholesterol. “It attaches to the cholesterol in food, so that it gets excreted from the body instead of absorbed by it,” Linsenmeyer says (remember, fibre doesn’t get digested the way other nutrients do). This can help lower the level of LDL cholesterol (the ‘bad’ kind) in your blood and in turn, potentially lessen the risk of heart disease. In fact, “consuming adequate soluble fibre is associated with healthy Soluble fibre can also boost your gut microbiome (the vast population of bacteria and other microorganisms that live in your digestive tract and mediate multiple aspects of your health) in a big way. More specifically, many soluble fibres (like inulin and fructo and galacto-oligosaccharides) can serve as prebiotics or food sources for Soluble fibre can also be helpful for If you’re guessing that ‘insoluble’ means this kind of fibre does Insoluble fibre doesn’t pull in water to form a digestion-slowing gel like soluble fibre. Rather, it has pretty much the opposite effect. Unlike its soluble sister, this kind of fibre passes right through us and exits virtually unchanged, speeding the movement of food through the digestive system and adding bulk to our stool. Yet another difference: It’s also not fermentable. In contrast to soluble fibre, which is inherently fermentable, insoluble fibre typically isn’t, so it won’t do much to act as a prebiotic or promote a Instead, “you can think of insoluble fibre as the broom that sweeps the gut clear,” Nielsen says. “It helps to increase motility and it helps to promote the turnover of gut cells.” Insoluble fibre can also be beneficial for various digestive conditions associated with sluggish or irregular bowel movements. For instance, the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) advises people with diverticulosis (a disease in which little sacs bulge out of the weak areas of your colon wall) to incorporate more fibre into their diets. Of course, if you have any other digestive condition, always speak with your doctor to find out what the best diet is for you before making any radical changes. In some cases, doubling down on fibre could cause digestive discomfort. Certain fibrous foods like The added volume in your stomach provided by insoluble fibre can also help enhance the sensation of fullness you get after eating, Linsenmeyer says. In fact, both soluble and insoluble fibre can help sustain post-meal fullness for longer. Insoluble fibre’s main claim to fame is its power to push waste along. Because of this, insoluble fibre beats out soluble fibre for While both kinds of fibre are needed for a balanced, well-functioning digestive system, insoluble fibre is especially critical for keeping you from getting backed up (or for getting things moving again). Not only does insoluble fibre encourage consistent bowel movements to help you stay regular, it also helps create softer stools that are easier to pass, Christine Lee, a gastroenterologist at the Cleveland Clinic, explains. In fact, constipation is a common sign there’s not enough Psyllium husk powder or Trick question! Fibre is generally awesome and in most cases, it’s not So while all of this fibre info is fascinating and useful, it’s not like you need to be tallying up how much insoluble versus soluble fibre you’re getting (that’d be pretty difficult to do, given that many nutrition labels don’t list them separately). And again, while it’s common for foods to have more of one kind than the other, most Now that you know getting enough total fibre is generally more crucial than getting a certain amount of either type, you might be wondering what ‘enough’ looks like. As with many nutrients, the optimal amount per day depends on your individual body: your And in case you were wondering, there aren’t any ‘good clear-cut guidelines’ for soluble versus insoluble One final thing to keep in mind here: while eating fibre is important, there’s no need to dial it up and overload on the nutrient. In fact, going too hard on fibre (especially by abruptly increasing your intake or relying too heavily on fibre supplements or fibre-fortified foods) can end up causing bloating, cramps and gas, according to the Mayo Clinic. In that case, your gut “isn't habituated to a higher-fibre diet,” Nielsen explains. Just as you wouldn’t head straight for the 25 kilogram Here are three suggestions for levelling up on fibre that can help prevent or minimise digestive side effects: Still, you can never eliminate the possibility entirely, so be prepared to give your body some grace and remember that a period of adjustment is totally normal, according to Nielsen. If you clock a bit more rumbliness than usual, she says, “just stay consistent and wait for that to pass.” Your gut (and your body as a whole) will thank you.

article_title: Could working out together be the secret to a happy marriage?
sub_title: The things we do for love
article_content: “I’m not training for a revenge body. I’m training for a marriage body,” reads every second In the early stages of love, effort is automatic. You Ishika Mehta Rohra and Aryaman Rohra admit they slipped into that pattern. “We got married, moved in and for a good two and a half years, weekends were about ordering in and binge-watching shows,” Ishika says. “We kept telling ourselves it was just a phase.” The shift came when they realised the lethargy was affecting their dynamic.“We made a rule: three Poor health rarely affects just one person. Fatigue, preventable illness, avoidable stress on the body are not individual experiences in a marriage. They ripple outward. It's no secret that long-term love requires work and that includes ensuring that your partner doesn’t have to carry the weight of consequences you could have minimised. It is easy to roll your eyes at any trend that tries to rebrand the gym. But this one touches upon something we need to hear: choosing upkeep after you have already been chosen is the highest form of love. Partners make concessions every day. They put up with long work hours and emotional unavailability during stressful months. They go to the restaurant they dislike because it’s your favourite. They watch the opera or the cricket match without complaint. They adapt. Then taking care of yourself becomes a matter of reciprocity, no? The least you can do is show up in your best possible form; not necessarily with a six-pack, but This trend also gives you the perfect opportunity for some quality time. Working out together, signing up for a new class, For Nikhil Jhangiani and Nriti Lulla, this was a conversation they had early on. “We decided in our first year of marriage that fitness would be non-negotiable for us,” Nikhil says. “Not for vanity, but because we didn’t want to burden each other with any potential health issues,” Nriti agrees. “Even when life is chaotic, we know we’re both putting in effort into our ‘marriage body’. That consistency keeps our respect for each other intact.” And yes, there is a line to watch. Any trend can slip into surveillance, especially when bodies are involved. The point is not to earn your partner by shrinking or sculpting yourself. The point is to remain capable of loving well, physically and emotionally. The language may sound theatrical, like something pulled straight from a wedding speech. But maybe those viral captions in all their dramatic glory are simply articulating something we should have been including in our real vows all along: I will keep choosing you. And I will keep choosing to be good enough to share this life with you.

article_title: Do you really need a face oil in your skincare routine?
sub_title: Everything you need to know before adding another bottle to your shelf
article_content: On one of those dreaded college mornings, when I was running late for a lecture and everything seemed to be conspiring against me, I spotted a friend walking toward our classroom, equally frazzled and equally sleep-deprived. And yet, her skin was gleaming away to glory. I had to ask what sorcery was at play. “A few drops of baby oil mixed into my usual moisturiser,” she said casually. As someone who was deeply oil-averse at the time, this revelation obviously did not sit well with me. I remember telling her that I could hear a dermatologist crying somewhere. But curiosity won. The next day, I mixed three drops of almond oil into my face cream, along with a silent prayer, and braced for a “Since most face oils are occlusive, when used on slightly damp skin or layered over a serum or moisturiser, they help to seal in hydration,” explains Dr Jaishree Sharad, cosmetic dermatologist. “Typically, 2-4 drops are enough. Excessive amounts can clog pores,” she cautions. This is where many of us misunderstand oils. They don’t hydrate on their own. They don’t add water to the skin. What they do is reduce transepidermal water loss, essentially acting like a sealant over existing hydration. Over time, I realised face oils come bearing both promises and perils. They play a supportive role, sealing in moisture, reducing water loss and supporting the For most people, a well-formulated moisturiser is enough. Face oil is not mandatory. But in the right context — dry skin, cold weather, barrier repair — a few carefully chosen drops can make a visible difference. As for me, I no longer hear imaginary dermatologists wailing when I reach for oil. But I also don’t treat it as a necessary step if I'm too tired or my skin is in a good place. article_title: I didn't expect a pair of jeans from my childhood to trigger an identity crisis
sub_title: Learning to dress for who you are is no easy feat
article_content: Between ages three and six, I practically lived in two pairs of When a childhood photograph resurfaced of me in my favourite pair, classic denim-blue with baby-pink flowers embroidered down the length, it did more than make me nostalgic. It made me realise how easily that conviction once lived in my body. I looked so sure of myself in those jeans. It occurred to me that that may have been the last time I was the truest version of myself; before taste became a language I learnt to speak in public and before I started dressing for contexts, expectations and cameras. Two decades later, I’m standing in front of a I needed to understand how it is that I can handle uncertainty at work, in relationships and life, yet still go completely blank in front of a closet or start questioning my life choices at the sight of a toddler's embroidered jeans. “A question that often shows up in the therapy room is ‘Who am I?’ or ‘How do I know this is me?’” says Juveriya Khan, counselling psychologist at Rocket Health. “It may show up when you start therapy or somewhere down the line, but it invariably always does as one sits with the grief of being and becoming and the loss of the self that accompanies it. And through this process, for many people, their wardrobe becomes [a form of] regulation, Deepti Chandy, COO and therapist at Anna Chandy & Associates, explains wardrobe paralysis in plain terms. “Paradoxically, an excess of choice can overwhelm rather than liberate,” she says. “When we’re faced with endless options—on what to wear, how to present ourselves, which version of ourselves to inhabit—the brain struggles to prioritise.” The result is “cognitive overload, decision fatigue and heightened anxiety.” Which is how you end up thinking: “I have so many clothes, yet nothing to wear.” So what does letting go require? A purge won't work, nor will picking an aesthetic. It requires rebuilding your stabiliser internally, so your wardrobe stops being the place where your uncertainty gets projected. “A self-reflective exercise that I recommend to my clients," says Khan, "is to ask yourself three questions: ‘Which part of me was most active today?’, ‘What was this part trying to do for me?’ and ‘Does this part stem from a younger version of me or the current one?’” That framework helped me come to the conclusion that I need a “current self” rack: a small, visible and frequently edited section of clothes I can wear on repeat without negotiation. When I feel the familiar freeze arrive, I don’t spiral and end up arriving 45 minutes late anymore. I go straight to the current-self rack, pick from a short list and let that be enough. The rest I sort through leisurely, retiring to the lofts what genuinely holds meaning and releasing what doesn't belong to me anymore.

article_title: Why you keep waking up with bruises your brain never logged
sub_title: Here's what's happening beneath the surface
article_content: We can explain the human body in very serious ways. As systems and structures. You can talk about strength and resilience and survival of the fittest. Or we can admit that we’re sacks of blood, tissue and muscles, with skin that can bruise if you look at it wrong. You wake up, Waking up with bruises feels almost mundane, which somehow makes it more confusing. You didn’t fall or have a night worth blaming. Most unexplained bruises aren’t the result of a single event so much as the accumulation of forces beneath the surface. From a medical standpoint, explains Dr Prashant Khanvalkar, MD, a bruise (ecchymosis) forms when small blood vessels beneath the skin rupture and leak blood into surrounding tissue. That blood gets trapped, then gradually broken down and reabsorbed. The familiar colour changes reflect the metabolism of haemoglobin into biliverdin and bilirubin, a process well documented in haematology and dermatology. What matters is not just that these vessels rupture, but how little force it can take to make that happen. This helps explain why bruises often appear after nights and days that felt entirely uneventful. Bruising is influenced not just by vessel damage, but by how efficiently the body repairs it. Vitamin C plays a central role in collagen synthesis and vascular integrity, and consistently low intake can weaken capillary walls. “These deficiencies don’t need to be severe to have visible effects. They often coexist with fatigue, cold sensitivity or heavy menstrual bleeding,” says nutritionist Aditya Malhotra, adding that routine blood tests should be done to check levels, especially if you have a sedentary lifestyle. While the degree varies from person to person, some medications and supplements can lower the threshold for bruising as well. “Common painkillers like ibuprofen interfere with platelet function. Antidepressants, blood thinners, steroids, From monthly menstruation to childbirth, women experience varying intensities of pain consistently throughout their lives. “I won't generalise by saying any gender has a higher pain threshold. Pain perception can depend on attention, stress levels and context," adds Khanvalkar. Minor knocks that don’t interrupt activity often fail to register as events worth remembering, even though they may still cause tissue damage. The absence of recall doesn’t mean nothing happened but that the brain didn’t flag it as important. Most unexplained bruises fade on their own in around two weeks. If you find the bruise growing in size, is ridged in texture or has accompanying symptoms like a high fever, it's time to seek a professional's guidance.

Mornings sound like the hiss of pressure cookers, cars groaning under your balcony and alarms reminding you to join one Zoom call after another. On the day I decided to commit to a silent My daily So I committed to 24 hours of silence. No talking and no doomscrolling—just a brisk walk at dawn, then diving into a pile of After years of constant digital connectedness and overstimulation, silence isn’t abstinence or escape. It has become essential maintenance for the modern nervous system. According to a 2023 paper on The authors note that this shift signals a move from activity-driven tourism to experiences that focus on emotional and physiological renewal. Avni Tripathi, director and CMO of Aahana, a forest But what was once inner work is now outer lifestyle, complete with plush robes and a buffet of In my search for a quieter frequency, I found there are still sanctuaries that honour silence in its original form. Dhamma Giri in Igatpuri, Maharashtra, has elaborate courses devoted to observing the mind without distraction and Guru Kubum Taklung Sang Choes Monastery in Sikkim holds daily spiritual silence and mindfulness sessions. At Bengaluru’s Art of Living centre, silence is a guided practice of breathwork, meditation and deliberate retreat into nature. At Kaizen Wellness’s Shunya retreat in Goa, quiet is woven into mindful art We may have outsourced silence to retreats and apps like Calm and Headspace, but to surrender to silence may, in fact, require not much more than willpower. Prerna Khetrapal, holistic wellness expert and founder of Kaizen Wellness, explains some ways one can create zen at home. “Start with phone-free mornings, silent meals, a mindful walk without headphones or a few minutes of conscious breathing before bed. These micro-pockets of quiet can mimic the restorative effects of longer retreats.” During my own brief silent detox, I realised that our relationship with quiet has always been sensorial. Everything ordinary turned vivid: the smell of wet earth after the first rain, the pulse at my wrist, the clarity of a thought that had been waiting its turn. Without the weight of words, attention migrates elsewhere, to texture, to breath, to sensation. You taste your food more slowly, sleep deeper, notice your posture and stop reaching for your It wasn’t grandly transformative, but the results were noticeable. I woke up the next morning without the claws of habitual anxiety gripping my ribs. I began repeating the practice every alternate weekend. The more I embraced it, the less I felt the need to fill silence with sound. I was able to make clearer and quicker decisions, experience calmer The silence has, in a way, fine-tuned my nervous system. It has allowed me to discover that the quiet isn’t empty, it has its own language. All we have to do is listen.

article_content: Rarely a day goes by that protein isn’t dominating headlines, mostly for its benefits and the best ways to eat it ( Many of us get our protein in one of the classic American ways: all at once at dinner or downed quickly in a shake. But in reality, timing is key. There’s only so much protein our bodies can absorb at a time and eating more than that amount in one sitting won’t increase benefits. So when Protein gets the most hype for its Exactly how much you need is determined by a handful of factors like your size, height and age, but one to two grams per kilogram of bodyweight is generally recommended, Edwina Clark, MS, RD, tells us. The per meal stat is what’s most important here because that’s roughly the max amount of Dinner is when we’re most likely to overemphasise protein, though it’s not totally clear why, Wendy Lopez, MS, RD, CDCES, cofounder of Diabetes Digital, tells us. It could have something to do with the fact that chicken and beef are the most widely used Whatever the reason, there’s nothing wrong with eating protein at dinner. In fact, one study found that doing so led to fewer wake episodes during Eating more protein to make up for what you might have missed earlier in the day may seem logical, but doing so is more likely to defeat your good intentions than provide the benefits you’re seeking. For instance, Lopez says that protein has a satiating effect because it takes a long time for the body to digest. That’s helpful during the day when you need to feel full to power through work and other activities, but could make for a gassy and What’s more, extra protein is either used by the body as an energy source (like carbs) or absorbed and stored as fat. That said, eating too much on a regular basis may be a blocker for anyone trying to lose The dietitians we spoke with all agreed that you’ll get the most out of protein by eating it consistently and proportionally in all of your meals. That being said, there are a couple of times when it does deserve to be prioritised like first thing in the morning. “ Including more protein in your snacks is another way to ensure that you get the most bang for your buck. “Protein-rich snacks are a strategic way to help sustain energy between meals, prevent extreme hunger and reduce the likelihood of overeating later,” Cording says. “They also support muscle maintenance and blood sugar stability, which is really important for active people or those who are going long stretches between So while there isn’t one perfect time to get your fix, it’s almost always a perfect time for (at least some) protein.

article_title: My wellness journey ended with disordered eating
sub_title: A Malai obsession revealed that I had fallen off the body positivity wagon, again
article_content: The past year was marked by newness. Pilates, swimming, running. Experiments with a no-dairy month, a no These months were also shaped by another fixation. A tiramisu obsession that lasted two months, replaced by bun maska, followed by a seductive malai phase that had me standing in front of the fridge late into the evening. I was hooked on the idea of wellness. I was doing everything the influencers and wellness gurus said to maximise wellness or what they never said out loud, to lose weight. A strange thing began happening. People started complimenting the thinness of my face. They would look at me, excitement rising in their voice, tell me how incredible it was that I’d lost weight, then pause, glance at the rest of my body and correct themselves. “Your face has really lost weight.” Friends. Their sisters. Uncles and aunts. Relatives and neighbours. The implication was clear. My face had changed. My body had not. Over time, I became obsessed with my face, watching every shift, running an extra kilometre at the hint of a puffy chin, enjoying the hollowed look. I wasn’t chasing thinness for myself. I had never needed it. But the half-formed validations convinced me I was close, that if I kept going, I would be thin enough to be told, wow, you did it. Was it just a trend? Did I buy into body positivity because it was ‘in’? Or because at sixteen, I was tired of hating my body and wanted to love it instead? The tide pulled hard in a different direction and suddenly I, an ardent body positivity activist who had sailed the movement with ferocity, was stuck on a boat barely holding its sails. I was drowning. As shared in a Did the world ever separate wellness from toxic body standards and disordered eating or was the failure just on my part? “Body dysmorphic disorder is a mental health condition in which people experience a perceived flaw or defect in their appearance, and an extreme, obsessive form of body image distortion. An intense focus on these flaws drives repetitive behaviours such as checking or grooming, all of which interfere with daily functioning,” shares Ashwini Nadkarni, MD, Assistant Professor of Psychiatry at Harvard Medical School. Much of wellness culture asks us to buy into ideas of betterment–mentally and monetarily. Accessing these tools isn’t inherently wrong. But algorithms flood our screens with idealised bodies, reinforcing a steady anxiety about how we look and live. The influencer telling you which hip mobility exercise will help you walk in your eighties is also a seller, hoping you’ll subscribe, even if it’s just through attention and shares. “The challenge with wellness trends is that while they aim to optimise health, their impact can be the reinforcement of obsessive behaviours or unattainable physical standards. Practices meant to promote A newer wellness phrase that haunts me is “taking care of myself”. Lip filler. The wake-up calls came the way they usually do. A month-long illness forced me to eat properly. With real carbs back in my body, I saw how I had swapped wellness for weight loss, strength for thinness–an ache of my sixteen-year-old self carried forward. I decided to step back from disordered eating and I'm still going to be a wellness girl, but this time, with an actual focus on what wellness looks like for I undid some damage. Instagram is off my phone, the calorie counter is gone and the weighing scale is hidden. Meals make me full and I eat whenever I’m hungry. Road to recovery? Way ahead of it. That’s the thing about falling often. You learn how to get up faster.
