article_title: Why I’m a retired party girl at 23
sub_title: In a strange turn of events over the last year, my Friday-night personality resigned. Turns out I'm not the only one
article_content: My body has started treating certain plans like threats. It’s a foreign feeling, almost embarrassing, to want to cry when someone proposes going to the club. Especially because I was the friend who’d say yes, convince everyone else and still be standing at the end of the night like I had a second battery pack installed. I knew the whole circuit: who was DJing where, what time you should actually arrive, which friend to drag out of the bathroom before she got philosophical. It was fun in the way chaos is fun when you can bounce back without consequences. Until I realised the bounce-back was weakening. It hit me one morning after a long night out. I woke up bloated and with a head way too heavy and foggy; a feeling I was accustomed to. My mind had that anxious, scratchy energy where everything feels too loud and too much. I snapped at my mother. I snapped at my friends. And I remember thinking very clearly: the night out is four hours. The aftermath is twenty-four. The ratio stopped making sense to me. What replaced those nights is almost comically wholesome. My closest friends and I have now started making plans that sound like we’re auditioning to be someone’s life coach instead: a Here's what people don’t get about the “retired party girl” in her early twenties: it’s not that we’ve become boring; we’re tired in a very specific way. We don’t want harsh stimulation after already running on cortisol and When Mumbai's Coastal Road promenade and the Malabar Hill Elevated Nature Trail opened up to the public, the city was handed a social life that isn’t built on drinks, loud music and shouting: walking, sitting, talking, watching the sea do its thing. And it’s not just Mumbai. The “going out” culture is getting a makeover across cities by people our age who still love a good time, just not the aftertaste. Fitness studios feel like social clubs, cute cafés with In the era of searchable consequences, we’ve seen older generations normalise “work hard, party harder” and then pay for it. Meanwhile, our feeds serve us bite-sized health information with terrifying clarity. So when we skip a third drink, it’s not always a moral stance. Sometimes, it’s just math: tomorrow Gen Z hasn't taken this turn because we’re virtuous. We’re just over-informed and data-obsessed. Every habit is Googled. Alcohol has been studied. Symptoms are logged into ChatGPT. Once you’ve seen the data, it’s hard to unsee it. Of course, we still party. We're just more likely to do a house party where the music is good and the bathroom doesn’t require physical resilience. We’ll go out, dress up and drink occasionally. But the default social plan has shifted from “let’s get sloshed” to “let’s do something that makes us feel better tomorrow, too.” “Retired party girl at 23” sounds dramatic. But it's an evolution of a certain kind. I still love my friends. I still love music. I still love a plan. I just don’t need my weekend to feel like a second job; one that pays in hangovers.

article_title: Are you ready for couture-inspired makeup?
sub_title: Kay Beauty x Falguni Shane Peacock’s Kay Kouture is proof that your lipstick can be a keepsake
article_content: If there's one childhood memory we all collectively share, it's our mother's makeup bag feeling less like a pouch and more like contraband. It lived on the top shelf, brought out mostly for weddings, festivals or “important” dinners. Lipsticks clicked shut and compacts opened to tiny mirrors that made you feel grown-up for exactly five seconds. Long before I understood shade names or finishes, I understood this: makeup was more than just product. It was permission, transformation and something powerful. I'm happy to report that that relationship has not disappeared for most of us. It has simply evolved. What began as a private, girlish fascination the thrill of holding something beautiful that wasn’t meant for you has grown into becoming a keepsake; a collectable object you want to leave out on your dresser instead of tucking away. In 2026, Indian For Katrina Kaif, the starting point was never glam for its own sake. “Falguni and Shane were very clear that this had to feel globally glamorous, but deeply Indian at its core,” she says. The visual bridge came from the Gatsby era. “The 1920s allowed us to play with structure, geometry and metallic detailing,” she explains. “But the Indian textiles gave the collection its soul. That’s where the emotion lives.” Banarasi silks translate into depth and richness. Mulberry and brocade inform undertones that feel layered rather than flat. These shades are not literal references to saris or lehengas. They are interpretations of how Indian textiles move, catch light and make you feel when you wear them. Couture-inspired beauty often risks becoming special-occasion-only. Kaif was clear she wanted to avoid that. “Makeup has to be enjoyed,” she says. “The packaging can feel elevated, but the formula must stay comfortable, wearable and something you reach for without thinking.” This balance is what gives the collaboration its weight. The For Kay Beauty’s early years were focused on building trust, consistency and a clear point of view. Only after that foundation was laid did couture makeup feel like a natural progression. “Indian beauty is ready now for that intersection of luxury and authenticity,” Kaif says. Adwaita Nayar, co-founder of Nykaa, sees the same shift. “The Indian beauty consumer today is seeking more than performance,” she explains. “There is a growing desire for products that feel expressive and resonant in everyday life. Design and storytelling matter just as much as formulation.” Makeup is increasingly being treated like an It's not the gold packaging alone but the mindset behind it. Makeup is now permitted and even expected to be decorative, symbolic and a little indulgent, much like that first lipstick you were never meant to touch, but never forgot.

article_title: Ozempic has entered the desi family WhatsApp group chat
sub_title: Meals may be shared, but so is scrutiny. With GLP-1s on the table, thinness remains the prized serving in many homes
article_content: In desi families, there are few greater achievements than thinness. Degrees gather dust but compliments for weight loss never expire. Every gathering doubles as a body audit. The number on your scale is discussed over tea, measured against cousins. A single remark—“She’s put on”—is passed around the room like a side dish. What looks like small talk often becomes a pageant without prizes. The obsession is older than us. Decades of research have spelt it out: The constant comparisons don’t always fade, they can often calcify into anxiety, eating disorders and lifelong unease with food. Goyal sees these scars in her own And now, into a culture already steeped in comparison, a new variable has entered the field. The GLP-1 drugs we know as She adds that the injections are approved for medical obesity, not slimming down, and warns that those who use them cosmetically face health risks, high expenses and the likelihood of weight regain once they stop. Beyond the medical complications, Goyal warns that their arrival intensifies social pressure. “They validate the belief that you should lose weight quickly. It is no longer a private fear; the whole ecosystem reinforces it.” With GLP-1s being discussed as freely as intermittent fasting and juice cleanses, the idea of weight loss has shifted from a private journey to public discourse. For those already uneasy in their Psychotherapist Naina Garewal has seen how quickly family pressure can override caution. One client with PCOS feared the nausea and dizziness her doctor had warned of, but her family waved those concerns away. Now that the injections were here, why wasn’t she on them already? Another client told a different story. After developing pregnancy-related diabetes (known as gestational diabetes mellitus), Both can be considered ‘medical needs’ for using GLP-1s and Garewal says the policing of who should and shouldn’t use it exists in shades of grey. “I would encourage people to speak to a mental-health expert alongside the prescribing specialists before starting GLP-1 treatment. They can guide you to question the intention behind its use—will it help or harm you further?” The two stories reveal how the same vial can hold opposite meanings. In one household, GLP-1s were pressed on a young woman whose parents brushed aside her fears of side effects, weary of the remarks they themselves fielded about their daughter’s weight. In another, the GLP-1s were meant to give their users control. Yet control slips easily into other hands. Sometimes it belongs to the chorus of relatives, the silences at the dinner table, the comments waiting at the next wedding. Sometimes the quickest way to quiet the room is to give in. Which leaves the harder question lingering: If the choice is made to hush everyone else, was it ever really yours? When control drifts outward, resistance is never simple. Some people still try to step away from the race to thinness; silence can be a kind of defiance. Goyal calls these ‘small refusals’: changing the subject, finding safe company, holding on to what the body can do rather than how it looks. “The least we can do is be kind to ourselves.” But kindness only softens the edges. Elsewhere, GLP-1s have been folded into memes, shorthand for the revival of Y2K thinness. Body In India, the drug doesn’t need meme culture to travel. It moves easily into the rituals already in place—the lehenga fitting, the auntie’s glance across the buffet, the cousin weighed against another cousin. A vial meant to steady blood sugar steadies little else. It only confirms what the room has already decided: There’s value in thinness and the body must keep proving it.

article_title: Has Botox officially left the building? Experts break down its alternatives

article_content: There was a time when everyone was getting Botox, but few admitted to it. Then came the wave of Strictly speaking, Botox is a brand name for botulinum toxin type A, a wrinkle-relaxing injectable that works by temporarily quietening specific facial muscles, which in turn softens existing lines (like forehead creases and crow’s feet), prevents new ones from etching in as deeply and gives the face a smoother, more “rested” look for a few months at a time. As for those who refuse to go down either the surgical or injectable route, there's always the "Botox in a bottle" option (products that claim to work as well as the injections). The real question, then, is: does the “#NoTox” counterculture signal the end of the Botox era or is it only the Botox works at the neuromuscular junction to stop the But the 'why' behind this shift is more layered. "When injectors use the same technique on every face, you lose individuality. Poor training also played a role. Good injectables should disappear into the face, not announce themselves," explains Dr Sagar Gujjar, dermatologist and founder of Skinwood Luxury Aesthetics Centre. In response to the decrease in demand for injectables, brands have launched potent potions comprising everything from serums to But can they match up to the original? The answer is a hard no, according to Dr Aneesh Sheth, cosmetic chemist and director of Dr Sheth's Skin and Hair Clinics. "I don't think that there is something that can replicate the effects of Botox. A lot of people claim to have Dr Mikki Singh, dermatologist and cosmetologist, founder and medical director at Bodycraft Clinics, puts this in perspective, "Products that claim 'Botox-like' results typically use As for collagen supplements, "Good collagen banking can delay injectables, but not replace them," cautions Feriyal Gilani, lead trichologist and cosmetologist at JCBounce Group. "It works on balancing both sides of the face through muscle activation and re-training, thus offering a cleaner, more holistic, toxin-free path that gives long-term structural benefits rather than short-term volumising fixes," she says. The secret here, though, is consistency and a solid skincare routine that includes daily sunscreen, a good Finally, does this all boil down to the fact that the “#NoTox” age is here to stay? Not quite, says Mittal Gupta. "Injectables aren't going anywhere, but expectations are evolving. People want transparency, long-term safety and results that still look like them. The industry isn't rejecting injectables, just redefining how to use them well," she concludes.
